To clarify that when all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted, the mind attains mastery, and when the mind attains mastery, all fetters are exhausted—there being no temporal sequence between them, yet in meaning there is a beginning and an end—one can only say that because the fetters are exhausted, the mind is mastered; one cannot say that because the mind is mastered, the fetters are exhausted.
"His names are as follows": the following section constitutes the fifth item, the listing of names.
Although there are twelve thousand arhats, twenty-two are listed here in brief.
Furthermore, regarding "Ajñātakauṇḍinya": *A* means "non-" and *jñāta* means "knowledge," thus he is designated as "one without knowledge.
*Kauṇḍinya* is a foreign surname; it has no equivalent translation in this region [of China].

The reason for this is that before the Buddha appeared in the world, this person was a non-Buddhist who clung solely to the sickness of conditioned existence; when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he perceived that the man’s faculties were mature and taught him the principle of unborn emptiness, whereupon he later attained arhatship.
This clarifies that this person gave rise to wisdom from the principle of emptiness of non-arising;
therefore, he is called Ajñātakauṇḍinya. As for "Mahākāśyapa," *mahā* means "great" and *Kāśyapa* is his clan name, which is translated here as "tortoise."
The reason he is called "Great" (Mahā) is that he is distinguished from the three minor Kāśyapas; therefore, this person is called Great.
Regarding "Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa," the following three individuals were all brothers who each led five hundred followers and resided in separate locations; "Kāśyapa" is their family name.
"Uruvilvā" is a foreign term; here it is translated as "Forest of Wooden Gourds.
This indicates that in the past, this person led his disciples while residing in a forest of wooden gourds, and thus he was named after his original dwelling place.

Regarding "Gayākāśyapa": In former times he was also a non-Buddhist practitioner who worshipped fire; leading five hundred followers, he resided in the city of Gayā. When the Tathāgata went there to convert him, he immediately abandoned his heterodox ways and correctly attained the path of an Arhat. He was named after the city where he originally resided.
"Nadī-Kāśyapa": Kāśyapa is his clan name, while Nadī is the name of a river.

Formerly he was a non-Buddhist who worshipped external deities; leading five hundred followers, he resided on the banks of the Nadī River. Having encountered the Buddha and received the Way, he attained the state of an Arhat, yet he retained the name of that former river.
"Śāriputra" is also a foreign term; "Śāri" means body, and "putra" means son. Because his mother's name was Śārī, he is called Śāriputra (Son of Śārī).
Later, he attained arhatship; among his peers, he was foremost in intelligence.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana" is also a foreign surname that has no equivalent translation in this land [China]; his personal name is Kaulita, which is the name of a tree deity.
His mother had no children and constantly made offerings to a tree spirit, praying for a son.
When she later obtained a son, being ignorant of the workings of karma, she claimed he was bestowed by the tree spirit; consequently, she gave him the name Kṛtaka.
Having encountered the Tathāgata and attained the fruit of Arhatship, that person was foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, he and Śāriputra associated with one another with sincere hearts, vowing that whichever of them should first attain the Way would inform the other.
Regarding "Mahākātyāyana": *mahā* means "great," and *Kātyāyana* is his clan name. Having attained arhatship, he was foremost among those who discourse on the meaning of the Dharma.
"Anuruddha" is also a foreign sound; in this land, it is translated as "An-ā-pau-lo-to," where "an" means "non-" and "pau-lo-to" means "poverty," thus referring to the "Bhikṣu Without Poverty."
This arhat did not accumulate vast treasures; rather, wherever he went, his clothing, food, and drink, as well as everything he encountered, surpassed those of others.
In five hundred past lifetimes, this person extensively practiced giving to relieve the poor; now, as the remaining karmic fruit has not yet been exhausted, he is called "Without Poverty."
"Kapphiṇa" is also a foreign term; in this land, it is translated as "lodging in a monastery" (*fangsu*).

To speak precisely, this person was lodging within a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*). The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were mature, transformed himself into an elderly bhikṣu and stayed with him overnight. That very night, he caused him to attain the Way; therefore, he is called "Lodging in a Monastery."
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
"This person is from the country of Kapilavastu, and was named after that country.
The former interpretation is certain, whereas the latter is not necessarily so.
"Gavāmpati" is a foreign name; in this land it is called the "Cow-Chewer Bhikṣu.
Although this person had attained arhatship, he still possessed two traits resembling an ox:

first, his mouth would pant with empty breath, and second, his footprints resembled ox hooves. He was frequently ridiculed by the other bhikṣus, so the Tathāgata used his supernatural power to transport him to the Brahma Palace. However, the devas did not mock him; thus, having placed him in the celestial palace, the Buddha recounted his past causes and conditions, explaining that for five hundred previous lifetimes this man had always been an ox king. Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* refers to him as the "Venerable Ox King," which is precisely who he is.

"Lipota" refers here to the bhikṣu Nakṣatra. His mother had no son and constantly prayed to the star deities; subsequently, she obtained a child. As he did not understand the workings of karma, she claimed the child was a gift from the stars, and thus he was called Nakṣatra. He is also said to have been a "conjoined body."
“Pilingāvatso” is also a foreign term; in this language, it refers to a bhikṣu with residual habits who reviled the deity of the Ganges River.

The bhikṣus questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha explained the causal conditions, saying: "In five hundred past lives, he was constantly a jailer; even though he has now attained arhatship, he still possesses residual habits."
"Bakkula" is translated here as the Bhikṣu "Excellent Appearance," for his deportment and gestures were worthy of contemplation;
furthermore, by observing the single precept of non-killing, he obtained the retribution of five times not dying.

Regarding "Mahākoṣṭhila," in this context *mahā* is translated as "great" (*mahat*), and *koṣṭhila* means "knee"; thus it refers to the Bhikṣu Mahākoṣṭhila, who was the same as the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha. This man was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra.

"Nanda" translates as "Joy. This clarifies that because this person constantly practiced patience throughout past lives, all who see him in his present body give rise to joy; furthermore, he is the younger brother of the Buddha.

"Sundarananda" was the Buddha’s younger brother; while he was still a layman, he had a wife named Sundarī. He is identified here by mentioning his wife so that it may be known that he is the younger brother.

Although that person had attained arhatship, his residual habits were not yet exhausted; he constantly harbored a sense of inequality while in the Jeta Grove. In the present life, he served as a *karmadāna* (ceremonial master), and in past lives, he had engaged in activities such as dividing fish.
"Pūrṇa" is his name; "Maitrāyaṇīputra" means "Son of Maitrāyaṇī," which translates as "Son of Full-Vow.
Therefore, when the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* refers to the "Venerable Son of Full-Vow," it is this very person.
“Subhūti” is translated as “Śubhāṅga” (Good Fortune). This clarifies that this person possesses virtue and constantly brings benefit to others through auspicious deeds.

The reason for this is that in the past, this person gave rise to feelings of resentment and jealousy toward those who were fields of merit; consequently, he transmigrated through the hells and suffered endless pain. Now, however, he has made a vow never to disturb others. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

“If there are sentient beings who resent my sitting, I shall remain standing for the rest of my life without moving from my place; the same applies to walking or lying down. Thus, his vows ensure that whatever he does serves as a source of auspiciousness for all beings.

"Ānanda" is translated as "Untainted. His physical appearance was lovely, and he constantly followed the Tathāgata among humans and devas. Although he beheld the forms of the five sensory objects and encountered pleasing environments, he always sought to benefit sentient beings and possessed no heart of attachment or defilement. Furthermore, having attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, he was foremost in dhāraṇī-retention.

"Rāhula" is translated as "obstruction. Due to the circumstance of blocking a rat's burrow, he remained in the womb for six years; for this reason, he was called the Bhikṣu Covered by Obstruction, and he also attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
"Thus known by the multitude"—this marks the sixth section below, which resolves doubts and provides a conclusion.
At that time, the assembly raised a doubt, saying:

"Among these twelve thousand people, there are only eleven thousand nine hundred and ninety-eight who are Arhats; Ānanda and Rāhula, these two individuals, are themselves among the class of Śrotāpanna learners. Why now are they treated as the same as those who have attained the state beyond learning (aśaikṣa)?"
The commentary states:
"Although these two individuals are still learners (śaikṣa), they are well-known to the great assembly; therefore, they are categorized among those of renown and are equal to the great arhats."
The questioner spoke again:
"Is it that there are 'lesser arhats,' such that you now speak of 'great arhats'? He explained:
"The stage of Arhatship is uniform; in reality, there is no distinction of great or small. It is now because of the seven types of trainees that the term 'great' is applied.
The questioner spoke again:
"The seven types of trainees are not called Arhats; what do they resemble?"

He explained: "When sages establish names, there are both general and specific applications. In the specific sense, it is not so; in the general sense, it is always thus. How is this different from the fact that a *srotāpanna* is also called 'one in training' (*śaikṣa*)?"

"Furthermore, there were two thousand [monks], both learners and those beyond learning. Among the assembly, there were originally two categories; this section below is the second, referred to as the "group of those with limited renown," who did not necessarily always follow the Tathāgata.

Within this assembly, according to the previous principle, there should likewise be six meanings; however, since the six sections have already been fully explained for the preceding assembly, there are now only two sections in this assembly:

first, "those in training and those beyond training," which refers to their stages of attainment. Only two types are mentioned here: first, "those in training" (śaikṣa), which refers to the seven kinds of persons in training; second, "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa), which refers to the Arhats who are beyond training.
Second, the mention of "two thousand" refers to their number.

Regarding "Mahāprajāpatī," there are two [categories] among the ordained śrāvaka assembly; this section below is the second listing of the bhikṣuṇīs, which likewise serves as testimony that they were present and heard [the teaching].
Furthermore, it is said that the community of nuns is also twofold:
first, those who are renowned; second, those who possess minor renown.
The first refers to "the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī," who is designated as the group of the renowned.
How is this known? Because she fulfills two meanings.
First, regarding her status as a layperson: she was the Buddha’s maternal aunt and was held in high esteem by the Tathāgata.
Second, regarding the meaning of the dharma: she was the very first among women to leave the household life and served as a renowned figure for the great assembly; therefore, she is listed first.
The second mentioned is "the Bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā," who is designated here by her well-known title.
How is this known? There are two reasons:

first, while he was still a layman, he was not held in high esteem by the Tathāgata; second, he entered the Dharma late, and his fame had not yet spread far and wide among those who knew him. Thus, before the assembly of nuns, he was addressed by the informal name "Little Renown" (Xiaomaming).
Each [name] has three meanings. Now, regarding the fact that there are three meanings within the group known by name: first, "Mahāprajāpatī" is the statement of her actual name.
"Mahā" means "great. "Prajāpatī" means "Lover of Beings," thus referring to Mahāprajāpatī.
Second, the term "bhikṣuṇī" refers to her species; it clarifies that she belongs to the class of women who have left the household life.
“Together with six thousand followers” is the third [point], describing the number of his retinue.
“The mother of Rāhula” refers to the following section, which concerns the second group: the nuns of little renown.
There are also three meanings: first, the mention of "Yaśodharā" indicates her name;
second, the mention of "bhikṣuṇī" identifies her as a human being.
The third statement, "together with his retinue," clarifies the number of those in the retinue.
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattva"—the following section constitutes the second [part], the listing of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The reason for this middle section is that its intent is also as previously explained.
Now, within this assembly, there are six parts:

first, a discussion of their human category; second, an enumeration of their number; third, an elucidation of their stages and positions; fourth, a praise of their virtues; fifth, a listing of their names; and sixth, a summary by citing their categories and numbers.
Regarding the current term "bodhisattva-mahāsattva," it first describes the class of person, who belongs to the Mahāyāna class of beings.
If one were to preserve the foreign name in its entirety, it should be called *mahā-bodhisattva*.
The term *mahā* is translated as "great," *bodhi* is termed "the Way," and *sattva* means "mind"; thus, it refers to one who possesses the mind of the Great Way.
Now, in calling someone a person of the mind of the Great Way, there must be two meanings:
first, length; second, breadth.
To seek the fruit of Buddhahood from afar without attaining realization midway—this mind is called "long.
To resolve to bring universal salvation—this mind is termed "vast.
However, because the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot reach this level, their minds are disparaged as narrow and short, falling short of those of the Bodhisattvas.
“Eighty thousand people”—this is the second [point], describing their number.
“All of them are non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*”—this is the third [point], discussing their stage of attainment.
However, what is discussed here is based on the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward, clarifying that these bodhisattvas abide within the stage of non-retrogression.
Now, there are three kinds of retrogression:
first, retrogression from rank; second, retrogression from practice; and third, retrogression from mindfulness.

From the sixth mind and below, one remains at the stage of light down; as the five faculties, headed by faith, have not yet been perfected, one may encounter evil friends and thereby sever the roots of goodness to regress into the current of evil. Therefore, this stage is called "regression."

Second, from the seventh mind upward until the sixth stage downward, this is designated as "retrogression in practice," which clearly explains that there is retrogression and loss within the practice of entering into patience (*kṣānti*).

Third, the seventh stage (bhūmi) and the first stage are referred to as "retrogression of mindfulness" (*smṛti-vyavakṣepa*). This explicitly clarifies that the mindfulness regarding the two truths is not constant; hence, it is called "retrogression of mindfulness.
Nevertheless, even within this retrogression, there is the sense of non-retrogression.
How is this known?

For when a single good deed taints the spirit, it remains undecayed throughout kalpas; thus, the principle of the causal habit does not perish, and the principle of summoning happiness is not lost, so there can be no regression from that state.
However, from the sixth mental state downward, there is only the case where a single good deed taints the spirit such that one does not regress.

Furthermore, there are three types of regression: regression of status (*avasthā-vihāni*), regression of practice (*caryā-vihāni*), and regression of mindfulness (*smṛti-vihāni*); for this reason, one cannot yet receive the name of "non-regression.

Moreover, from the seventh mind upward through the sixth ground downward, there is also the sense of non-regression; having ascended to the head of faith, the five faculties no longer undergo transmigration. Even from the first ground upward through the sixth ground downward, the mind accords with the realm of signlessness (*animitta*) and the intellect enters into the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Receiving non-regression, one is eternally tranquil."
The reason why they do not receive the name "non-retrogressive" is that, although their stage is indeed non-retrogressive, there still remains the sense of two types of retrogression:

first, it clarifies that while practicing the conduct of patience (*kṣānti*), there is a semblance of outflow-free attainment wherein one loses what has not yet been acquired; second, it clarifies that the mindfulness of the Two Truths does not constantly manifest before them. For these reasons, they receive the designation of "retrogression in practice."

When a Bodhisattva at the seventh stage attains the first level of patience (*kṣānti*), there is truly no retrogression. Upon entering patience, all practices are attained as soon as the mind is aroused. However, because defilements associated with residual conceptual marks (*nimitta*) have not yet been exhausted, there still remains a distinction between entering and emerging from meditative absorption. Consequently, the clear understanding of the two truths does not constantly manifest before one; for this reason, they receive the designation of "retrogression in mindfulness."

Now it is clarified that Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward have forever severed the three types of regression associated with the lower stages; having ascended to the stream of Dharma, they do not emerge from contemplation for long, and every thought-moment is luminous—how could there be any regression of thought?

The reason for this is twofold: first, it clarifies that upon ascending to this stage, one no longer advances or retreats in terms of training; second, it clarifies that while secondary evils are not yet exhausted, only their roots have been severed.

Regarding the statement that they do not regress from the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-sambodhi*): "three types of enlightenment" refers to the knowledge of the correct and universal way (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*). Since "way" (*mārga*) is the cause, this clearly explains that these bodhisattvas no longer regress within the cause of unsurpassed, correct, and universal knowledge.
"All have attained dhāraṇīs": the following section is the fourth, which extols their virtues.
It consists of twelve phrases, arranged into four groups, which are further combined into two pairs.
What are they? First, there are three phrases praising his virtues;
second, from "making offerings to the immeasurable" downwards, there are three phrases designated as praising his practice.
The third section, from "cultivating the body with loving-kindness" downward, consists of four phrases and is termed the praise of the essence;
the fourth section, from "his fame is heard everywhere" downward, consists of two phrases and is designated as the praise of the name.
Regarding why there are two pairs: the former two refer to virtuous conduct (*guṇa*), while the latter two refer to the substance and name (*nāman*).

As for why one first praises virtuous conduct and subsequently praises the substance and name: when speaking of "substance and name," both good and evil possess them, and this applies equally to ordinary beings and sages. A Tathāgata possesses a substance, yet an icchantika is not without one either. If one were to say that because a Buddha is the most virtuous person he alone possesses a substance, then the icchantika, being the ultimate evil, should have no substance; yet now we see that both the Buddha and the icchantika possess a substance. Therefore, we know that goodness and evil do not reside in the substance itself.

The name is likewise so: the sublime resonance of the Tathāgata flows forth and is heard by all, while the evil reputation of an icchantika is known throughout the world; thus, the substance of the name pervades universally, existing among both ordinary beings and sages alike.

If one wishes to verify what is true and what is false, there is nothing better than examining virtue and conduct; therefore, he first praises their virtue and conduct before mentioning their physical forms and names.
The questioner asks:
"Since both are praised at the outset, why does he praise their virtue first and their conduct afterwards?"
The commentary states:
"This has two meanings:
first, 'virtue' refers to the fruit, while 'practice' refers to the cause."
Second, "virtue" (guṇa) refers to its function in the present, while "practice" (caryā) refers to its cultivation in the past.
Since the fruit accords with these two aspects of the present, and the cause accords with these two aspects of the past, one first praises his virtue and subsequently praises his practice.
The questioner asked:
"What is the name of its essence?
The respondent replied:
"There are both internal and external [qualities]. How is this known?
One must first possess a virtuous substance before there can be a superior reputation heard abroad; therefore, one first praises their substance and subsequently praises their reputation."
Furthermore, within these four sections of praise, each is further divided into two.
Regarding the praise of their virtues, there are two parts:

first, the statement "they have all attained *dhāraṇī* and the eloquence of joyful speech" (*pratibhāna*); these two phrases constitute the praise of internal virtue, while the subsequent phrase is termed the praise of external transformation.
"Dhāraṇī" is a foreign term; here it is translated as "total retention" (saṃgraha), meaning that one is able to retain all the sublime teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Regarding "eloquence of joyful exposition" (*pratibhāna*), some explain it as a virtue of external transformation, correctly stating that it refers to delighting in speaking for others.
However, according to the tradition of our own school, it is still considered an internal virtue.
How is this known to be so? It is because there are two reasons: first, principle (*li*); second, teaching (*jiao*). As for principle:

it is fundamentally stated that the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) are gates of wisdom and not meritorious qualities. Within the gates of wisdom, there is fundamentally no external transformation (*parāvṛtti*). Now, when one speaks of the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), this is simply one of the four analytical knowledges; how, then, could it be a transformation?

As for the "teachings," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: the wisdom that understands phenomena is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); the wisdom that understands meanings is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*); the wisdom that understands expressions is called the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*); and the wisdom that takes delight in eloquent exposition is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). That which takes delight in eloquent exposition refers simply to the spiritual capacity of the person before one.

Just as those with the capacity of śrāvakas delight in hearing the Four Noble Truths, and those who are pratyekabuddhas delight in hearing dependent origination, they know only the dharmas that others find delightful; since the dharma is the external object, here the term for the object is used to designate the wisdom [that perceives it], and thus it is called "eloquence in joyful exposition."

Regarding "turning the wheel of non-retrogression," this third phrase is the second point within the praise of virtues; it is termed "external transformation" (*bāhya-vikurvaṇa*) and correctly clarifies the sphere of knowledge and wisdom from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
"Cakra" (wheel) is a name derived from a metaphor.

"Worldly" clarifies that the wheel possesses the sense of crushing and subduing; here, we clarify the essence of the wheel: taking the state from the eighth stage upward as its object, where cognition is free from the three types of regression, it is called the "Wheel of Dharma of Non-regression."
Furthermore, it fulfills the nature of all sentient beings, analogous to the circularity of the wheel's substance;
it enables ordinary beings to attain sainthood, like the meaning of the wheel’s rotation;
and it can subdue the afflictions of sentient beings, like the wheel’s capacity for crushing and overcoming.
It is said that because these realms and wisdoms of the eighth stage and above are explained to others, it is called "turning the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma.
Regarding the praise of the practice, there are two parts: the first two lines constitute the actual praise of the practice, while the final line serves as its corroboration.
"Making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas": this phrase first praises the beginning of the Bodhisattva’s planting of roots of merit.
"Planting the seeds of the roots of virtue in the presence of all Buddhas": this phrase praises the culmination of the practice.

These two phrases correctly praise the practice; however, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, these are the manifold virtues, while up to the seventh stage, they are the foundation of those manifold virtues.

"Constantly praised by all Buddhas"—this single phrase is the second proof establishing the praise of the practice. This differs from the practices of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), which may either praise or disparage: at first, it was said that one who accords with my Dharma brings me joy, yet later it was disparaged as being like parched grain seeds.
Regarding the praise that there are two aspects within the essence: one phrase praises the body and three phrases praise the mind.
The initial statement, "cultivating the body through loving-kindness," is the phrase praising the body.
The questioner asked:
"From the eighth stage upward, there is only wisdom; how can there be a body?
The respondent replied:
"This discussion concerns the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); how could there be a *vipākaphala* (retribution body)?

The reason it is so is that through the practice of compassion over vast eons—since the root of compassion is to benefit sentient beings—the *nirmāṇakāya* comes to exist. It is by the power of compassion that it bestows happiness and extracts suffering; this does not depend on other virtues."
"Skillfully entering the Buddha's wisdom": the following three phrases constitute the second section, which is designated as the praise of the mind.
Furthermore, these three phrases also function as the three types of wisdom (prajñā).

First, regarding "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom": this phrase clarifies the wisdom that illuminates emptiness. While those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage also enter the Buddha’s wisdom, they cannot yet be said to have entered it "skillfully. Only at the eighth stage does one enter the stream of the Dharma and constantly illuminate non-arising; therefore, it is called "skillful."
The second statement, "penetrating great wisdom," clarifies the wisdom that illuminates existence (*bhāva*).

The third, "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*), summarizes both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence; for it is precisely because one has reached the other shore that one enters well and attains penetration.
Principles have degrees of depth, and wisdom attains varying magnitudes. From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downward, one has not yet entered the stream of the Dharma; this is called "this shore.
From the eighth stage upward, one constantly illumines the two truths and never departs from contemplation; this is called "the other shore."
"His fame is heard everywhere": the following two lines constitute the fourth praise of his name.
This also has two parts:
the first line directly praises his name, clarifying that the reputation of these Great Beings for their lofty and far-reaching virtues is known by all sentient beings who possess consciousness.

The second statement, "capable of delivering countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings," explains and establishes this name; because this Bodhisattva saves beings through his manifested bodies, it is thus universally known throughout the world, and therefore it is understood as an explanatory establishment.
"Those named as follows": the following section is the fifth [part], a brief enumeration of the names of the eighteen bodhisattvas.
"Such bodhisattvas as these," up to "eighty thousand people," is the sixth [part], a summary that cites their types and enumerates their number.

"At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra" introduces those who heard the teaching together; this section consists of three parts. From here until "retreated to sit to one side" constitutes the third listing, which comprises the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The reason for placing this last is as previously stated.
Now, within this section, there are six kinds of assemblies, which form six parts:

first, the listing of the celestial assemblies; second, the listing of the nāga assemblies; third, the ghost and spirit assemblies; fourth, the asura assemblies; fifth, the listing of the garuḍa assemblies; and sixth, the human assemblies.

Now, there are two ways of analyzing this: first, to clarify the meaning of the non-sequential order; second, to clarify the meaning of the absence of the six destinies and the absence of the formless realm.

As for why the ranks of honor are distinguished in a non-sequential manner: it is simply because the Tathāgata preached the Dharma among human beings, and King Ajātaśatru was the lord of Rājagṛha. Following the principle that the host should yield precedence to the guest, the five classes of noble disciples were listed first, followed by the assembly of humans.

Furthermore, regarding those who do not follow the sequential order among the guest assemblies, it is simply because among the five types of guest assemblies, the celestial beings possess the most excellent retribution; therefore, the celestial host is listed first, followed by the other realms.
If the guest deities are arranged in order of precedence, the asuras follow the devas; however, the nāgas alone are superior for two reasons:
first, they are the retinue of the devas, and second, they have rendered kindness to human beings.
The dragon is able to ascend into the clouds and bring down rain, which accords with the meaning of "heaven"; therefore, people of the world commonly speak of "rain from heaven.
Because it possesses these two virtues, it is listed first.

As for why the host of ghosts and spirits is listed next, it is because this assembly consists entirely of the musical deities of the various heavens who follow behind the heavenly beings; therefore, they are listed thereafter.
Furthermore, within these six sections there are no six realms of existence.
Why is this? Because the sentient beings of the hells possess deeply heavy karmic obstructions and retributions such that they are unable to come; thus, there are only five realms.
The reason there are six sections is that although the nāgas and the garuḍas are both animals, they are now divided into two groups; therefore, there are six sections.

Furthermore, among the enumerations of the celestial hosts, there are some that are not exhaustive; specifically, only the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are listed, while those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are omitted. There are two reasons for this:
first, it is because they rely on the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, which hold that in those [formless] places there is no form; since there is no form, there is neither going nor coming.

Second, it clarifies that among the retributions of the three realms, this place is the most superior; yet because of deep attachment, it obstructs the reception of the Right Path, which constitutes the "difficulty of the Long-lived Heavens.
Now, within the enumeration of the heavens themselves, there are two sections:
first, the preliminary enumeration of the various heavens of the Desire Realm; second, the enumeration of the various heavens of the Form Realm.

Even when listing the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are not exhaustive; only the first two and the last two heavens are listed, totaling four heavens, as the two intermediate heavens are omitted for brevity.
Furthermore, it is not in sequential order.
As for "Śakra Devānām Indra," he is the second heaven of the desire realm and is the Buddha’s donor among the devas; therefore, he is listed at the beginning.
The foreign name for him is Śakra Devānām Indra, which translates as "Capable of Being Lord of the Gods.
Those listed below—such as Moon, Universal Fragrance, and Jewel Light—are all ministers who assist Śakra; therefore, they are enumerated in succession below him.

The "Heaven of the Four Great Kings" (Cāturmahārājakāyika) is listed here in reverse order as the first heaven of the Desire Realm; these are the leaders at the four corners of Mount Sumeru, each of whom likewise has their own retinue.

The "Sovereign Son of Heaven" (Īśvara-devaputra) refers to the fifth heaven of the desire realm, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), where one is able to emanate whatever is required by oneself.

The "Great Sovereign Son of Heaven" (Maheśvara-devaputra) refers to the sixth heaven of the desire realm, the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), which clarifies that all requirements are emanated by others.

The third, the Yama Heaven, and the fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven, are omitted from the list; however, since the first and last of these four heavens are enumerated, the two intermediate heavens can be understood by implication.
Regarding the phrase "Brahmā, Lord of the Sahā World," the following section enumerates the second category among the heavens, listing the various deities of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The present mention of "Brahmā, Lord of the Gods" refers specifically to the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna.
"Śikhin Mahābrahmā" refers to the Brahma King of the Second Dhyāna.
"Prabhāsa Mahābrahmā" refers to the Brahma King of the Third Dhyāna.
The term "etc. refers to the heavens of the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "there are eight dragon kings," the following constitutes the second assembly of dragon hosts.
From this point onward, the four assemblies, including the dragon deities and others, each follow the same pattern of having three parts:
First is the general enumeration of the number; second is the listing of the names;
third is the summary conclusion. "Nanda" is translated as "Joy"; "Upananda" is translated as "Excellent Joy."
Transforming into human form, he listened to the Dharma by the Buddha’s side; having received the grace of the Buddha’s moistening influence upon him as a human, he felt joy whenever he saw people.
A dragon may not transform its body during five periods:
first, when sleeping; second, when dozing; third, when angry; fourth, when lustful; and fifth, at the time of death.
"Sāgara" is named after its country.
"Vāsuki" is translated as "Many-Headed," referring to the Nine-Headed Dragon King.
"Takṣaka" is translated as "Many-Tongued. "Anavatapta" is translated as "Heatless";

for while among the scales of other nāgas there are small insects that bite and feed them, they must thus expose themselves to hot sand and suffer from the pain of that heat, this nāga alone has no such insects and therefore suffers no pain from hot sand.
“Maṇasa” is translated as “Great Body,” referring to the one who encircles Mount Sumeru seven times.
“Utpala” is the name of a pond; this dragon dwells within a pond of utpala flowers, and thus it is named after the pond.
"Regarding the 'four kinnara kings'": the following section constitutes the third assembly of spirits and deities; they are all the musical deities of Śakra.
Of these, the first four deities are named Dharma-music (dharmasaṃgīti), and the latter four deities are named Worldly-music (lokasaṃgīti).
"Kiṃnara" is translated as "doubting deity.
Regarding the initial mention of the "Dharma Kiṃnara," this deity manifests the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths amidst the strings and pipes [of music].
"The Kinnara of the Sublime Dharma" refers to this deity who, within the strings and flutes, performs the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
"The Kinnara of the Great Dharma" refers to this deity who, within the strings and flutes, manifests the Dharma of the Six Perfections.

Regarding "Dharmadhara Kinnara," one should say "Upholder of the Dharma"; the scriptural text is abbreviated here. Among the strings and flutes of this deity, the wheel of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles is also proclaimed.
"There are four gandharva kings. The four deities mentioned below are the deities of secular music belonging to Śakra.
Regarding the first, "the gandharva king Rati," this refers to a deity of pleasure who is devoid of vocal sound.
"Musician" refers to one who possesses vocal sound.
"Beautiful Gandharva" refers to one who is supreme among those without vocal sound.
"Beautiful-voiced" refers to one who is supreme among those with vocal sound.
"There are four asuras. This section below constitutes the fourth listing of the asura hosts.

"Asu" means "non-" and "ura" means "wine," thus they are designated as "wineless gods. Because they are attained through inferior merit, they are not actually ghosts; however, due to their excessive flattery and crookedness, they are disparaged as "gods. While the retributive fruits of such "gods" generally involve a fondness for wine, these various asuras do not drink wine at all due to the causal conditions of their supernatural powers.
"Bali" is translated as "the bound.
Vemacitrin had a daughter named Śacī, whose lovely appearance was highly esteemed by Śakra; he took her back to the heavens to serve as his queen.
After becoming the husband, he no longer maintained relations with his father-in-law; King Vimalacitra immediately dispatched Pāñcika to lead an army to wage war against Śakra.
Since Śakra had served the Tathāgata and constantly recited the Prajñā divine mantra, by the causal power of that mantra, he caused Pāñcika to be bound.
*Kharaskandha* is translated as "Broad Shoulders. *Vemacitra* is the father-in-law of Śakra;
it is traditionally said that there is no [equivalent] Chinese translation for this name.
"Rāhu Asura" is translated as "The Obstructor.
This being has extremely long arms and legs; at times he uses his hands to shield and obscure the sun and moon, hence he is called "The Obstructor."
"There are four garuḍas": this below is the fifth section, listing the assembly of golden-winged birds (garuḍas).
Because they possess great majestic power, they are called "of great majestic power."
Because its physical dimensions are truly vast, it is called "Great Body" (Mahākāya).
Because it always attains full satisfaction in its desire to consume various nāgas, it is called "Great Fulfillment" (Mahāpūrṇa).
Because it acts with sovereign freedom in its desire to consume various nāgas according to its will, it is called "As One Wishes" (Yathākāmam).
"Videhīputra": the following section constitutes the sixth list of the assembly.
This section itself has three parts.
First is the naming of "King Ajātaśatru. His mother was Videhī; here, he is referred to by his mother's name, hence he is called "Videhīputra."
In foreign lands [the name] is called Ajātaśatru; here it is translated as "One Without Enmity.
Second, regarding the phrase "with his retinue of about one thousand," this is a general enumeration of the various classes of followers.
Third is the act of salutation.

Following the precedent of the aforementioned five groups, each should likewise prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdraw to sit to one side; however, as the sutra text is abbreviated, this is not mentioned.
The explanation of the general introduction is concluded.

From the passage beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly" until the end of the chapter constitutes the second section, designated as the specific introduction.
This clearly elucidates the meaning that each of the various sutras differs and that each section is distinct, as detailed previously.

Furthermore, there are five types of introductory sections (*nidāna*), also explained as before: first, the assembly; second, the auspicious signs; third, the arising of doubt; fourth, the posing of questions; and fifth, the answering of questions.
Now, within the five distinct introductory sections, each is further divided into two parts.

Regarding the two parts of the "Introduction on the Assembly Gathering": the first correctly clarifies the gathering of the assembly; the second, from "Making offerings and paying respect" onwards, describes the appropriate conduct of the assembled multitude.
Now, regarding the statement "surrounded by the fourfold assembly," this is the first point that clearly explains the gathering of the assembly.
Although there are the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, none surpass these four categories; namely, the fourfold assembly of those who have left the household life.

Regarding "making offerings and showing reverence": the following section constitutes the second part, which describes the essential nature of the assembled multitude; herein, there are both general and specific aspects.

The initial term "making offerings" (pūjā) serves as the general heading, while the subsequent passage specifically enumerates the three types of karmic offerings: "reverence" (gaurava) refers to the karma of body; "respect" (satkāra) refers to the karma of mind; and "praise" (praśaṃsā) refers to the karma of speech. When expressed through speech, one extols the holy virtues; when in the mental ground, one respects the Tathāgata; and when involving the body, one shows reverence toward the Buddha. However, all these phrases are the words of the compiler of the sutra.

"Expounding Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of all bodhisattvas"—from here until "erecting stūpas of the seven treasures with the Buddha’s relics"—constitutes the second section of the introductory sequence of auspicious signs, which also consists of two parts.

First, the manifestation of signs within this land is clarified; second, from "In this world, they see that land in its entirety" onwards, the manifestation of auspicious signs in other lands is clarified.

Within these two sections, there are six subsections each. Now, regarding the six kinds of auspicious omens in the first section: first, the preaching of the *Anantārthasūtra*; second, entering the concentration of infinite meaning; third, the rain of four flowers from the heavens; fourth, the earth shaking in six ways; fifth, the great assembly rejoicing; and sixth, the Buddha emitting supreme radiance.

Furthermore, these six kinds of auspicious signs form three pairs. Regarding the first pair: when moving, he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; when still, he enters meditative concentration to contemplate the principle. This constitutes the correspondence between movement and stillness.
Regarding the second pair: the former clarifies that the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers, while the latter clarifies that the earth shook in six ways;

these two correspond to the upper and lower realms. Regarding the third pair: at that time, the assembly rejoiced within their hearts, while the Tathāgata radiated light outwardly; these two correspond to the internal and external.

Regarding what is called a "portentous sign" (śakuna), the "sign" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the external, while the "portent" (śakuna) refers to the internal; yet the sign is itself the portent, and the portent is itself the sign. It is only that they are termed "portents" when they provide secret intimations, and "signs" when they manifest distinct characteristics.
How is this known to be so?

It is because he intends to clearly expound the principle of a single cause and a single fruit, clarifying that practitioners of the three vehicles all return to the attainment of Buddhahood. These six kinds of signs are called "omens" by sentient beings; these six specifically indicate that he will certainly preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and thus they are termed "signs."
Regarding why the *Anantārthika Sūtra* serves as a prologue to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there are generally two schools of interpretation.
One school explains:
"This sūtra clarifies the principle that immeasurable myriad virtues all converge, ultimately leading to the attainment of the Buddha-way; therefore, it is named the *Anantārthika Sūtra*."

However, what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* elucidates is precisely that there are neither two nor three [vehicles], but rather that the three are unified into the one; yet the *Anantamukha-sūtra* directly explains that all myriad virtues lead to Buddhahood, without mentioning "neither two nor three" or the sublation of the three to unify them into one. Because it differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the latter was able to serve as its prolegomenon (*yuxu*).
The second school says:

"The *Anantārthasūtra* clarifies that the principle of emptiness of non-arising (*anutpāda-śūnyatā*) cannot be measured or sought after by limits; therefore, it is called 'immeasurable' (*ananta*). This very emptiness is the meaning of the myriad phenomena."
Since both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also clarify the meaning of signless emptiness (*animitta-śūnyatā*), why did [Dao’an] not compose prefaces for them?
Such is the evident nature of Master Yi’s comprehensive statements: first clarifying the Three Vehicles and subsequently clarifying the One Vehicle—this is the true preface; what more could one seek?
The commentator says: "While it is not that this principle does not apply to the sequence of the five periods, those who adhere to fixed doctrines are overly fond of arranging them in such a manner.

Now, to clarify that this serves as the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it correctly demonstrates that for each single period, single session, and single sūtra teaching, there is its own respective introduction, main body, and dissemination. How is this different from the fact that the teachings of the five periods all possess an introduction, main body, and dissemination?"

Now it is clarified that the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī Sūtra* (or *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*) is still a teaching suitable for those who are worthy to hear the *Lotus Sūtra*. Although these disciples have heard this sūtra, it was still preached as the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* prior to the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* clarify the meaning of signless emptiness (*animitta-śūnyatā*), they still state that the causal practices of the three families serve as the measure [of attainment], and thus the fruits realized by the three vehicles differ.
However, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* states:
"Those who practice goodness shall all attain the fruit of Buddhahood. For this reason, it differs from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, [the Nirvāṇa Sūtra] speaks directly of the myriad virtues achieving Buddhahood without clearly explaining the convergence of the three vehicles into one;
for this reason, it differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Since it stands between these two positions, it is therefore able to serve as a preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This sutra is a teaching of the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is said to be "a Mahāyāna sutra spoken for the sake of all bodhisattvas. Because it is what the Buddha holds in high esteem, it is said to be "that which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind."
The very use of this sutra signifies that he will certainly preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; this is the meaning of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it possesses the capacity to provide a secret report; this is the meaning of "omen" (*nimitta*).

"From the words 'After the Buddha had spoken this sutra' onwards, this is the second auspicious sign. It signifies the purpose of entering meditative concentration immediately after finishing the preaching of the *Anantārtha-sūtra*: it is intended to serve as a pretext for Maitreya to pose his questions to Mañjuśrī. Had he not entered concentration, Maitreya would have had to question the Buddha directly; therefore, there is a specific reason for him to enter concentration before raising his inquiry."
The questioner asks:
"One should enter only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*; for what reason does he enter immeasurable concentrations?
The commentator explains:
"If one has entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, how could there be a 'preface' for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* composed through conditioned effort?

As for the 'Place of Immeasurable Meanings,' the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra* clarifies that all myriad virtues lead to Buddhahood; the fruit of Buddhahood is the destination to which these immeasurable meanings return."

Furthermore, it is clarified that because the Tathāgata was about to expound the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he first entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings; this signifies that he would certainly preach the *Lotus Sūtra*, which is the meaning of the "sign," and it secretly informs the assembly, which is the "omen."
"At that time, it rained from heaven. The following section clarifies the third point: that it rained four kinds of flowers as an auspicious sign.
"Mandārava flowers" are translated as "small white round flowers."
“Mahāmandārava flower” is translated as “great white cluster flower.
“Mañjūṣaka flower” is translated as “small red cluster flower.”
"Mahāmañjūṣaka flowers" translates as "great red spherical flowers.

Although there are four flowers, they are now grouped into two pairs: the first two white spherical flowers represent the two assemblies of the laity, and the latter two red spherical flowers represent the two assemblies of the ordained.
Although these two pairs share a single underlying intent,
why is this? It is because one wishes to clarify that all the practices undertaken by the fourfold assembly in the past were merely flowers and not yet fruits.

Furthermore, regarding the scattering [of flowers] upon the Buddha and the great assembly: this clarifies that the flowers of the myriad virtues of sentient beings will certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, the flowers are scattered upon the Buddha and the great assembly.
That it signifies the inevitable preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes its "mark" (*nimitta*);
that it possesses the merit of a secret report constitutes its "omen" (*praśasta*).
“The entire Buddha-world shakes in six ways” is the fourth auspicious sign.

“Entirely” means that from the time sentient beings with karmic affinity have perceived the Buddha-world, it has all been vibrating. The great earth is normally stable, yet now it suddenly moves; this is a marvelous event that clarifies the meaning. It is simply that practitioners of the Three Vehicles each possess six kinds of attachments; they cling to the three causes and three fruits, asserting them as fixed and definitive in various ways. This [earthquake] serves to startle and shake their stubborn attachments.
Another interpretation is that "the six kinds" at that time refers to the movement of the multitudes, meaning that sentient beings of the six realms will all attain Buddhahood.
"At that time, within the assembly"—from this point downward is the fifth auspicious sign.

The great assembly rejoiced; it was appropriate that auspicious signs should appear beforehand to communicate spiritual portents, manifesting that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* would surely be preached—this is the "sign.
That these possess the capacity for secret notification is the "portent."
"At that time, the Buddha emitted... From here below is the sixth auspicious sign of the emission of light.

Light fundamentally dispels darkness and can manifest colors so they appear; this light is intended to clarify the understanding of the single cause and single fruit, which is like the manifestation of color.
Furthermore, it can eliminate the delusion of clinging to the three [vehicles], just as it dispels darkness.
The former clarifies that which illuminates, while the latter clarifies that which is illuminated.

Regarding its placement at the top: it is like the human body, where the head is supreme; this secretly symbolizes that the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle transcend and sit above those of the Three Vehicles.
That which is between the eyebrows also secretly symbolizes the principle of the Middle Way as the cause and effect of the One Vehicle.
From the passage "shining toward the east" onwards, it clarifies that which is illuminated.
Although light should illuminate the ten directions, the fact that it now clearly shines toward the east is intended to use this single direction to symbolize a single cause and a single fruit.
Furthermore, the east is the foremost among all directions.

Regarding the "eighteen thousand worlds": ten thousand is the ultimate number, which secretly indicates that the assembly at this time will necessarily fulfill the causes and attain the fruits [of enlightenment].
Eight thousand is a deficient number, clarifying that what the practitioners of the three vehicles have practiced from the past is the cause, yet it remains insufficient.
"Nothing is not pervaded" refers to the horizontal dimension, meaning that the light fully illuminates eighteen thousand lands to the east, and likewise throughout the eight directions.

"Shining downward to the Avīci Hell and upward to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven" refers to the vertical dimension, meaning the light reaches both the upper and lower limits; this is intended to signify that all the myriad virtues of the world converge upon the ultimate fruit.
Now, taking "teaching" as the intended meaning, it has not yet been clarified whether form exists in the formless realm; therefore, it is omitted here.
There is one interpretation:
from the passage "downward to the Avīci Hell" and below, this constitutes the second manifestation of auspicious signs in other lands.
If one follows this interpretation, it is extremely convenient for the following verse.
For now, however, we shall follow the previous judgment.
From the passage "seeing all those lands within this world," what follows below is the second section, clarifying the manifestation of auspicious signs in other lands.
Within this, there are also six kinds of auspicious signs:
first, seeing sentient beings of the six realms due to the light;
second, "furthermore seeing the Buddhas currently residing in those lands," which clarifies that one sees the Buddhas of the eastern direction due to the light.
The third section, "and hearing the sūtras and dharmas preached by the Buddhas," clarifies that one hears the Buddhas of other lands preaching the Dharma because of the light;
the fourth section, beginning with "and seeing those bhikṣus," clarifies that one sees persons of the two vehicles practicing because of the light;
and the fifth section, beginning with "furthermore seeing the bodhisattvas," clarifies that one sees persons of the Mahāyāna practicing because of the light.

The sixth section, beginning with "Furthermore, he sees the parinirvāṇa of various Buddhas," clarifies how, by means of the light, he sees the parinirvāṇa of Buddhas in other directions, up to the point of erecting stupas and making offerings to them.
The old interpretation states:
"In meditative concentration, there are six views and one hearing of an object.
This does not perceive the true meaning; it is not so according to the tradition practiced by our own school.
Furthermore, these six kinds also constitute three pairs:

the first pair begins with seeing sentient beings in the six realms and ends with seeing the Buddhas; this is the contrast between the ordinary and the sage—beginning by departing from [the mundane] one becomes an ordinary person, and ending by attaining union one becomes a sage.

Regarding the second pair: first, one hears the Buddha preach the Dharma; next, one sees those of the Two Vehicles practicing it. This constitutes the correspondence between preaching the Dharma and receiving and practicing it: at the beginning, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma; subsequently, the disciples receive and practice it.

The third pair consists of seeing the Bodhisattva’s practice and seeing the Buddha’s nirvana; this represents the correspondence between cause and effect, wherein one begins by practicing the cause of the Mahāyāna and ultimately attains the fruit of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "various causes and conditions" mentioned in the fifth auspicious sign, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva fully practices the four immeasurables and the six perfections as the various causes and conditions for purifying the Buddha-lands.
"Various inclinations" refers to faith, understanding, practice, and progress, up to the purification of Buddha-fields.

"Various characteristics" refers to the characteristic of relinquishing material things, the characteristic of observing the precepts, and the characteristic of practicing patience; therefore, they are called various characteristics.
These are precisely the six kinds of auspicious signs in that other land, signifying that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* will certainly be preached; they are the "signs" (*nimitta*).
They all possess the capacity for secret notification; this is what constitutes being "auspicious" (*praśasta*).
"At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought": from here below is the third section, titled the "Introductory Chapter on Doubtful Reflection.
It also consists of two parts:
first, it clarifies that Maitreya initially harbored a doubtful reflection;
Second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus" down to "Now, whom shall we question? describes how the great assembly harbors doubts.
Within Maitreya’s own reflections, there are three stages of thought: initially, he possesses two doubts; finally, through deliberation, these resolve into one.
The great assembly has two thoughts, which constitute two doubts. Regarding Maitreya’s three thoughts:

from "At that time, Maitreya had this thought" down to "By what causes and conditions does this auspicious omen appear?"—this is the first thought, which is the first doubt. This specifically questions why these two sets of six kinds of auspicious signs have manifested.

There are two phrases here: first, from "At that time, Maitreya had this thought" onwards, it clarifies the thoughts prior to the doubt; second, "By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign appeared? correctly clarifies the doubt itself.

However, the names of these auspicious signs may all be interchanged; one might also say that the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, has manifested these supernatural and auspicious signs. By what causes and conditions do these auspicious signs exist?
One may also state both together, saying: "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifests these signs of supernatural transformations; by what causes and conditions do these signs exist?
'Spirit' (shen) refers to internal power, while 'transformation' (bian) relies on external application."

Why is this? If we speak of the Tathāgata’s *sarvajñajñāna* (all-knowing wisdom) from an internal perspective, no being can fathom it; this is precisely what is meant by turning the waters of the ocean into ghee and curd, altering the dimensions of length and shortness, and allowing the small and the large to contain one another.

The second [thought] extends from "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered samādhi" up to "To whom should I ask? Who is able to answer? This is the second thought; since such auspicious signs have appeared, one wonders whom to question—this is the second doubt.
There are also two parts:
first, from "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered samādhi" onwards, it clarifies the thoughts prior to the doubt;
from "Whom should I ask? onwards, it explicitly clarifies the doubt itself.
"If the Buddha had not entered meditative absorption, I would have questioned him; now that the Buddha has entered absorption, whom shall I question?

From "Again he thought" up to "I shall now question him," this constitutes the third reflection. In it, he recognizes that Mañjuśrī is the one to be questioned; this is the third reflection, which resolves the second doubt mentioned above.

Regarding the second doubt mentioned above, [the Buddha] did not know whom to ask; now that he knows Mañjuśrī is the one from whom he may inquire, it should be understood that this very knowledge resolves the second doubt, leaving only the first primary doubt concerning the auspicious signs.
Therefore, Maitreya, there are generally three stages of reflection: initially possessing two doubts, which finally result in three reflections and one doubt.

From the passage "At that time, among those in the assembly were bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs" down to "Now, whom should we ask? is the second section, describing how the great assembly harbors doubts and reflections.
Now, within the great assembly there are two thoughts, which constitute two doubts.
The first thought is to correctly reflect upon the aforementioned twelve kinds of auspicious signs; this is the first doubt, which asks: "What is the purpose of these auspicious signs?"
Radiance is the most prominent among the six [elements]; therefore, that which is most prominent is cited as the first.
Regarding the second thought, it says, "Whom should I now question? This constitutes the second doubt, a doubt consisting of not knowing whom to question.
Within the first doubt of Maitreya above, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the thought prior to the doubt; second, correctly clarifying the doubt itself.
Now, within the first doubt of the great assembly, there is only the thought prior to the doubt; the second part, which correctly clarifies the doubt, is omitted.

In the second section of Maitreya’s initial doubts, there are likewise two parts. Now, among the great assembly, there is only the second part, which clearly indicates the doubt regarding not knowing whom to ask; it omits the reflection that precedes the doubt, as the meaning is already clarified through the mutual exchange of the textual passages.

However, Maitreya had three thoughts and the great assembly had two; at that time, none of them spoke aloud, but these were merely recorded by the compiler of the sutra to convey their underlying intentions.

The reason the great assembly lacks a third thought is that, while in reality there is no one who surpasses Maitreya, one might expect a third thought regarding Maitreya. Since the assembly knows there is someone capable of answering yet lacks such a person, this is intended to highly extol Maitreya as the Great Being in his final birth (*caramabhavika*), who alone can know of one capable of answering;
for the assembly, not being in the rank of a candidate for Buddhahood, is unable to discern the presence of a third thought.

Furthermore, as for what is appropriate from this day forward, it is simply that Maitreya raises the doubts of the great assembly to question Mañjuśrī; it is not said that the various great Bodhisattvas are unable to raise their doubts, but rather that [Maitreya] highly defers to the one who is to succeed him (the Future Buddha), and for this reason there is no third thought.
The questioner said:
"If the Buddha is currently in meditative absorption, how can one question him?

Furthermore, let us wait for the Buddha to emerge from absorption before questioning him; when the Buddha causes this sutra to be spoken immediately upon his emergence, that would be the 'proper discourse' (bhāṣita). Why, then, is it called the 'introduction' (nidāna)?"

One should simply ask Mañjuśrī to cite the past as proof for the present; knowing that he would certainly preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* upon emerging from samādhi, the narration of Śāriputra serves as the introduction.
An objector further says:
"Does Śāriputra’s question concern whether Maitreya himself possesses the three thoughts, or whether he possesses them for the sake of sentient beings?"
The commentator says: "If one abides as the fundamental substance of things, how can one allow for self-interrogation and response?
Furthermore, if one acts as the substance of things, why would one permit others [to exist]?"
The commentator says:
"This is intended solely for bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice and for ordinary worldlings.
The questioner speaks again:

At that time, there was among the assembly one who possessed the knowledge of others' minds; he saw that Maitreya had such a doubt and such an interpretation of the meaning, thinking: "How could this possibly constitute a real entity?"

The commentator further states: "Precisely this wisdom constitutes a 'thing' (vastu). Now, when one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds perceives that Maitreya himself harbors the doubt within his own mind that [the teaching] is a 'thing,' he should inquire of Mañjuśrī.

Mañjuśrī’s response is not merely the knowledge of others' minds; rather, because such a person possesses this wisdom which secretly aids their progress, they can infer that the Tathāgata will preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. To understand it in this way is beneficial for all things; therefore, whatever is undertaken shall not be in vain—this is what is meant."
*Fahua Yiji*, Scroll One. *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Yiji*, Scroll Two,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Fayun of Guangzhai.
2. "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva desired to resolve his own doubts. From here until the end of the verses is the fourth introduction to the inquiry.
This also consists of two sections:
First, the sūtra author describes Maitreya’s own intention to inquire;
second, from "He then asked Mañjuśrī" up to the end of the verse, is the actual inquiry.

Furthermore, within these two sections, each is further divided into two parts. Regarding the sūtra’s account that there are two intentions for Maitreya’s inquiry: first, it states, "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva desired to resolve his own doubts," which records Maitreya’s own intention to inquire.

Second, from "further observing the fourfold assembly" up to "the minds of the gathered multitude," this clarifies that the sūtra author describes Maitreya as having the intention to include others; the intention to include others is to voice the doubts of the great assembly in order to question Mañjuśrī.
"Then he questioned Mañjuśrī," from this point down to the end of the verses, constitutes the second section: the formal inquiry.
This section also contains two parts:
first, from "then he questioned" down to the fifty-fourth verse, is designated as the formal inquiry.
Second, from "The Buddha emits a single ray of light" onwards, there are eight lines of verse which are designated as the Request for an Answer.
Furthermore, these two sections are each divided into two parts.
Regarding the two types of correct questioning:
the first is the prose section, which constitutes a brief inquiry;
the second consists of fifty-four stanzas of verse, which constitute an extensive inquiry.
The second part, consisting of eight lines, requests a response in two sections:
first, the three lines of verse beginning with "The Buddha emits a single ray of light" present the phenomena observed and formally request a response.
Second, from the passage "the fourfold assembly looks up with joy," there are five lines of verse; these explain the resolution of objections and the conclusion of the request.

As for why the prose refers to a "brief explanation" while the verses speak of "extensive inquiry," if one were to judge according to the underlying principle, then the prose would be extensive and the verses would be brief.
How is this known to be so?

Because within the long prose sections, each [chapter] exhaustively poses general questions regarding all twelve types of auspicious signs for both [the Buddha and the disciples]; yet, when it comes to the verses, each [chapter] provides individual stanzas that do not exhaustively cover them.
Now, interpreting the meaning according to the text, the verses herein are the detailed exposition and the long prose is the summary. Why is this so?
Because there is more text in the verses and less in the long prose.
Now, within these two explanations—the concise and the extensive—each is further divided into two parts.
Regarding the two sections of the prose (*gadya*):
the first, from "and asked" down to "the marks of supernormal power," constitutes a general inquiry concerning the six kinds of auspicious omens appearing here.

From the second section, "Emitting Great Radiance," down to the end of "Adornment of the Realm," there is a general inquiry as to why he causes me to see these six kinds of auspicious signs in other lands.
Regarding the inquiry into the auspicious signs of that land, there are two parts:
first, from "emitting great light" onwards, which clarifies the origin of the auspicious signs;
second, from "all seeing that buddha-land" onwards, which constitutes the actual inquiry.
Although there are fifty-four lines of verse within this extensive inquiry, they are further divided into two parts:
the first consists of four lines of verse, which extensively praise the aforementioned inquiry regarding the witnessing of auspicious signs in this world;

the second, beginning from "The Radiance Between the Eyebrows," comprises fifty lines of verse, which extensively praise the aforementioned inquiry regarding the witnessing of auspicious signs in other lands.
Now, these four verses only praise four kinds of auspicious omens; they do not praise the first and second omens. The first verse praises the sixth [omen], the emission of light;

the next one and a half verses praise the third [omen], the rain of the four flowers from heaven; the next half-verse praises the fourth, the earthquake; and the final verse praises the fifth, the joy of the fourfold assembly.
The first verse now asks about the emission of light, designating the Buddha as the "Teacher.
However, the initial phrase "For what reason" serves as a general heading for all the auspicious signs.

Regarding the line and a half beginning with “Vṛṣṭimanta,” this now versifies the aforementioned rain of flowers. Above, there were four types of flowers; here, only two types are versified—namely, the small white flowers and the small red flowers—and these are expressed in only half a verse-line.
The line "sandalwood-scented winds" expresses the meaning of the [preceding] prose section, and thus is subsumed under the raining of flowers.
The half-verse "and this world" praises the aforementioned shaking of the earth.
The single verse beginning with “At that time, the fourfold assembly” now versifies the joy of the aforementioned four assemblies.
While the preceding general inquiry contained six aspects, this verse now versifies four of them.
However, the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī Sūtra* was not recited in verse, nor was the entry into meditative concentration;
there were two reasons for this omission:
first, the text was concise, and second, it would have been inconvenient within the context of the event.
How do we know this is so?
Since the Tathāgata was in the world, there has never been a time when he did not preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; why then does he suddenly ask today:
"For what reason have you preached the *Anantārthasūtra*?"

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are constantly in samādhi and perceive all Buddha-lands without dualistic characteristics; why then do they suddenly ask again, "For what reason have you entered meditative concentration?"
This would be inconvenient within the context of the matter; therefore, it is omitted and not versified here.

Regarding "the radiance from between the eyebrows," there follow fifty stanzas which constitute the second extensive verse section, elaborating upon the brief inquiry in the preceding prose concerning the vision of the auspicious signs in other lands.
There are generally two ways to analyze these fifty verses; for now, we shall follow the initial analysis provided in the prose commentary and divide them into two sections.

First, the one and a half verses beginning with "The Radiance Between the Eyebrows" commemorate the first section of the original text concerning the reasons for perceiving the auspicious signs. This radiance itself is not an auspicious sign from another land, but rather it is by means of this radiance that one perceives the auspicious signs of other lands.
The second section, consisting of the remaining forty-eight and a half lines, versifies the second part: the formal inquiry regarding the auspicious signs observed in other lands.
It versifies only five types of auspicious signs, omitting the fourth sign in brief.
Now, within these forty-eight lines and a half, the text is divided into three major sections:
first, from "In all worlds" downward for eight lines and a half, there is a brief verse summarizing the three types of auspicious signs perceived in other directions.

The third section, beginning with "I see bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that land," consists of thirty-eight and a half lines of verse that extensively praise the inquiry into two auspicious signs: namely, the practice of great beings from other lands and the parinirvāṇa of Buddhas from other lands, up to the construction of stupas and their veneration.

The second section on "Retreating from the Path" consists of one and a half verses beginning with "Mañjuśrī, I abide here," which are designated as a summary of what preceded and an opening for what follows in detail.
Regarding the first eight lines and a half that briefly summarize the three auspicious signs: the first line and a half summarizes the first [sign], seeing the sentient beings of the six realms;
the second half-line summarizes the second, seeing the Buddhas of the eastern direction;
and the third, consisting of six lines and a half, summarizes the third, hearing the Dharma being preached by the Buddhas of other regions.
Furthermore, within the first one and a half lines, there are two stages:
the first line and its single phrase correctly versify what is seen;
the second phrase, "seeing all therein," clarifies the capacity for seeing.
Within what is seen, there are generally four points:
first, the second half of the verse beginning with "In all worlds" correctly clarifies the six realms;
the single phrase "the destination of birth and death" clarifies that this refers to saṃsāra.
The phrase "the conditions of good and evil karma" clarifies the cause;
the phrase "receiving retributions, whether favorable or unfavorable" clarifies the fruit of retribution.
As for "the conditions of good and evil karma," this is precisely the cause of the six realms of existence.
The two characters "good" and "evil" serve to distinguish: "good" refers to the causes for the three happy realms, while "evil" refers to the causes for the three miserable realms.
The two characters "karma" and "conditions," however, apply to both good and evil.

Regarding the phrase "the excellence or inferiority of the retribution received": the two characters "retribution received" (shoubao) collectively refer to the fruits of the six realms of existence; the three good realms are also "retribution received," and the three evil realms are likewise "retribution received."
The two characters for "good" and "ugly" are distinct names for the retributive fruits of the six realms of existence. How is this known?
"Good" refers to the retributive fruits of the three wholesome paths, while "ugly" refers to the retributive fruits of the three unwholesome paths.
"Furthermore, beholding the Buddhas, the Holy Lords and Lions"—this half-line constitutes the second [section], which is a verse praising the vision of the Buddhas of the eastern direction.
"Expounding the sutras"—the six and a half verses following this constitute the third [section], which is a verse praising the hearing of the Dharma being preached by the Buddhas of other directions.
Within these six lines and a half, there are naturally five stages:
First, it says, "He expounds the sutras, which are subtle and foremost," comprising half a verse. It then asks:
"For what reason does he cause me to hear the Buddha’s teaching as surpassing that of devas, māras, and non-Buddhists?"
The second verse, "Its voice is pure," asks:
"For what reason do you cause me to hear the Buddha’s teaching as something that transcends all other holy sages?"
The third verse, "The Brahma-voice is profound and wondrous," asks:
"For what reason does it cause me to hear the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, which delights the hearts of the assembly?"
The fourth section, "Various Causes and Conditions," consists of one verse that asks:
"For what reason is it that when I hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, I am able to propagate the Buddha-way above and rescue sentient beings below?"
The first three lines clarify the upward propagation of the Buddha-way;
the single line, "Awakening sentient beings," clarifies the downward salvation of the masses.
The final three lines, beginning with "If a person encounters suffering," pose a question:
"Why is it that I have been made to hear the Buddha’s teaching, which accords with the capacities of those of the three vehicles?

These three verses constitute the path of the three vehicles: the first verse is for the śrāvakas; the verse "If a person has merit" is for the pratyekabuddhas; and the verse "If there is a son of the Buddha" is for the bodhisattvas.
