Regarding the two verses beginning with "By this one knows the present Buddha," the second half-line of each verse praises the conclusion of the second point—that the matters to be seen hereafter should be identical.

In the preceding prose, it was stated: "Therefore, I reflect that today the Tathāgata shall preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Within these two half-lines, there are likewise two meanings. First: "By this one knows that the present Buddha intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*"; this refers to the identity of the names according to principle.
It should be the same as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* of old: after the Tathāgata emerged from meditative absorption, he preached the fruit of the sutra and named it the *Dharma-puṇḍarīka*.
The second statement, "Now the Buddha emits light to assist in the manifestation of the meaning of the true mark," should likewise correspond to the name [of the sutra] in principle.

The reason for saying "it assists in bringing forth the meaning of the true reality" is that the Tathāgata manifests these signs precisely because he wishes to assist sentient beings in awakening the potential for the Mahāyāna.

Once the Mahāyāna potential has been awakened in sentient beings, the Tathāgata emerges from meditative concentration and declares that this sutra opens the gate of expedient means to reveal the true reality; "true reality" refers here to the ultimate principle (*tattva*).
"May all people now know"—the two lines of verse below this constitute the answer.
Within the introductory inquiry there were originally two parts; what follows here is the second, which serves as an exhortation to open the minds of sentient beings and concludes the response.
Within this, there are also two parts: the first verse clarifies that auspicious matters are yet to come, which is to manifest the "one" and the "distant.
The latter verse represents the second intention, clarifying that inauspicious matters are about to depart.
Doubt and regret shall be explained at the beginning of the second fascicle.
Section Two: The Main Body of the Teaching; Chapter One: The Chapter on Expedient Means. From here onwards constitutes the main body of the sutra.
The preceding introduction having been concluded, we now proceed to explain the main body of the text.

The establishment of these chapter headings reflects the intention of the one who produced this scripture; it may also be seen as a transmission of the Buddha’s sacred intent, following the principle of "narrating without composing."

If names were established according to their ultimate principle, it should have been called the "Chapter on the True Aspect" (Shixiang pin) rather than the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Fangbian pin); for it is only today that this sutra clearly reveals that the teachings of the three vehicles from the past were merely expedient means.

The teachings of the three vehicles are merely provisional expedients; at the time of the past, these were originally considered the true teaching and were not termed "expedient. Now that the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle has been expounded today, this clearly reveals that the former three vehicles were indeed expedients.
Therefore, the text of the subsequent scripture states: "This sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the true aspect.
This explains that the aspect of cause and effect today is the true one, thereby manifesting that the cause and effect of the past were not true.

Now, this chapter is named "Expedient Means" (upāya) according to that which it reveals. The meaning of "expedient means" refers to the capacity for skillful mastery; these teachings spoken by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of expedient means are designated as "gateways" (mukha).

The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the principle taught by the Tathāgata’s true wisdom; because it is based on this principle, it is called the "true aspect. Since the true principle of today had not yet been taught, there was the sense that the gate of expedient means (*upāyamukha*) was closed; now that the true aspect of today has been taught, there is the sense that the gate of expedient means from the past is opened. This chapter contains two meanings: first, to clarify the reality of the present; second, to reveal that the past was merely an expedient.
The questioner said:
"Today should be the time to close the gate of skillful means.
How do you know this?"
"Today, the three [vehicles] have converged into one, all of which are the ultimate truth; how can you say there is a 'gate of expedient means' that may be closed?
The commentator replied: "This is not so.

The reason it is not so is that the meaning is revealed through an external analogy. For instance, suppose there were this wooden gate, and at that time the gate was closed and not opened; people only knew that there was this wooden gate, yet they remained entirely unaware that within this gate there was a fine golden image."

If this person were to open this door with their hand, then at the moment the door is opened, everyone would see the image of pure gold; thus, the hand that opens the door possesses two capacities: first, the capacity to open the door, and second, the capacity to reveal the true image to people.
Now, the teaching of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* possesses two capacities, like a hand:

first, it explains that the former teachings of the three vehicles were expedient means; thus the text below states, "The Buddha, by the power of expedient means, manifested the teachings of the three vehicles," which is like a hand being able to open a door.

Second, it explains the principle of the long-term duration of the present [teaching]; thus the text below states, "After a long time, O World-Honored One, you must surely speak the truth," clarifying the principle of the ultimate convergence and the longevity of the life-span, which is like a hand pointing toward a golden image.

A "gate" (mukha) is that which has the capacity to allow people to enter and exit. In the past, the teachings of the Three Vehicles served as a remote gateway for practitioners; to now attain the realization of the One Vehicle is the meaning of "entering through the gate. It is precisely because there were the teachings of the past as skillful means (upāya) that the present reality could be revealed; this is the meaning of "exiting through the gate. Therefore, one should know that this chapter derives its name from what it reveals, and is thus called the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) Chapter.

However, at the beginning of this chapter, the two wisdoms were praised as the primary cause for the approximate opening of the school’s tenets; therefore, we shall now briefly describe these two wisdoms. There are five layers of explanation regarding their names and meanings:
first, a further clarification of their essential nature and characteristics;
second, an explanation that the names have both general and specific applications.
Third, it clarifies that their application has periods of flourishing and decline;
fourth, it explains and reconciles the sūtras of the five periods, thereby distinguishing the differences between the two types of wisdom;
fifth, it explains the etymological meanings of the names.
Regarding the names and meanings of the first two types of wisdom: they are the wisdom of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*).
Now, the wisdom of reality has two names:
first, it is called the wisdom of reality; second, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
The wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) also has two names:
first, the wisdom of verbal skillful means; second, the wisdom of expedient power (*prajñā-upāya*).
Regarding "skillful means," some explain it as follows:
"Method" (*fang*) refers to a specific place or location; "expediency" (*bian*) refers to skillfulness and timeliness.

If one's practice is not otherwise [understood], it should be correctly stated that these two characters constitute a single phrase: "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the capacity for skillful artistry.
This clarifies that the wisdom of the sages possesses the skillful application of means; therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"The term 'fang' (方) signifies correctness, while 'bian' (便) signifies skill."
"Expedient means (*upāya*) refers to that which is provisional and temporary; it does not signify permanence.

However, while these two—the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyajñāna*) and expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*)—differ in their nomenclature, what is here termed "wisdom of skillful means" receives its name according to its essential nature (*tattvārtha*), thereby clarifying that the wisdom of the Sage possesses the capacity for skillful artistry.
"Expedient wisdom" (prajñā-upāya) derives its name from its object. How is this known?

It is because it clarifies that the preceding objects are expedient; by borrowing the objects of the former three vehicles and so forth, they are momentarily transformed into the One Vehicle. Therefore, these expedients are provisional and not ultimate. However, wisdom illuminates these provisional and expedient objects; here, the name of the object is used to designate the wisdom, and thus it is called "expedient."

Furthermore, within the scope of these meanings, this wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) and provisional wisdom mutually support one another: if one raises the realm of the provisional, it reveals that the Sage possesses the capacity for skillful artifice; if one raises the wisdom of skillful artifice, it reveals the establishment of the provisional and conventional realm.
However, it is but a single wisdom; it is simply that because it appears in various sūtras and śāstras, it has two names.
"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is a designation for the mind’s function of discerning and illuminating, while "true wisdom" (*jñāna*) is a name for that which is devoid of falsehood.
Furthermore, although "wisdom" (prajñā) and "real wisdom" (bhūtaprajñā) are both designated by different names, "wisdom" receives its name based on its own essential nature,
whereas "real wisdom" derives its name from its object.

Regarding the statement that "wisdom" is named after its essential substance: it originates from the fact that the fundamental nature of this mind's functioning is one of discerning illumination, and furthermore, this exists throughout both cause and effect.
How is this known?

Therefore, when it is the mind like a vajra, this wisdom has already fully illumined its objects. If this vajra-like state is transformed into the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, even that transformative wisdom carries the meaning of "discerning illumination. Thus, we know that the name "wisdom" (prajñā) is derived from its fundamental essence itself.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) derives its name from its object," the preceding object is the reality. How is this known?

The principle of cause and effect of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is the definitive, true realm of the world. Although those at the stage of the six minds may regress to the Two Vehicles, they do not regress permanently; because the three vehicles ultimately converge into the One Vehicle, it is called "real."

The Tathāgata’s wisdom illuminates this actual reality; now, by citing the object to designate the wisdom, it is still called "real wisdom. Thus, one knows that real wisdom derives its name from the object.
Furthermore, these two names—“wisdom” (prajñā) and “real wisdom” (bhūta-prajñā)—are mutually constitutive. How is this known?
If one mentions real wisdom, it simultaneously reveals the name "wisdom"; precisely because the object is real, it reveals that wisdom is the name for discerning illumination.

If one raises the name of "wisdom" (prajñā), it further reveals the name of "real wisdom" (bhūtaprajñā); it is precisely because I am able to reflect and illuminate that the realm of reality is revealed. Thus, we know that these two names mutually support and complete one another.
Furthermore, these four names all relate to one another in terms of preceding and succeeding. Why is this?
The previous mention of "skillful means wisdom" (upāya-jñāna) was named according to its essential nature; now, "wisdom" (jñāna) is likewise named according to its essential nature.
The preceding [section] explains that provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) receives its name from its object; now, this true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) likewise receives its name from its object.
Just as the two meanings of the preceding expedient wisdom and provisional wisdom mutually complement one another, so too do these two names—wisdom and true wisdom—mutually complement one another.
Although these four names are presented in pairs, they collectively manifest the two wisdoms.

This is the second section, which further clarifies the essence and characteristics of the two wisdoms. Regarding the essence of the two wisdoms: their essence consists of the functional capacity to illuminate objects that exists within the divine discernment of the karmic fruition. If one wishes to know their essence and characteristics, one need only examine and apprehend the essence of the two wisdoms through their engagement with objects.
The objects illuminated by the wisdom of skillful means consist of three sets of three:
first, the three teachings; second, the three capacities; and third, the three types of persons.

Illuminating this realm of three times three, one should know that this wisdom is the essence of provisional wisdom. In the past, there were three types of people; for each person, there were three aspects, and each person possessed three capacities. These three capacities responded to three [teachings]; therefore, as the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom illuminated this realm of three times three, he immediately expounded the three teachings.
One should transform three types of capacities into three kinds of persons; for this reason, one examines these ninefold realms to grasp this wisdom.
One should know that the illumination of these ninefold realms is the essence of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the essence of true wisdom is also verified by its preceding objects.
There are four kinds of objects illuminated by true wisdom:
first, the unity of the teaching; second, the unity of principle; third, the unity of the capacity [of the listener]; and fourth, the unity of the person.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata clearly illuminates these four "onenesses"; this is precisely what constitutes true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding what is called the oneness of teaching and the oneness of principle: today we proclaim that because there is no difference in the cause, there is no distinction in the resulting fruit; yet, as for the meaning of ultimate reality, its principle is non-dual.
Since the principle that is expounded is one, how could the teaching that expounds it possibly be two?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the capacity is one": this refers to the single capacity for attaining the one fruit among the assembly at the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* discourse.

Regarding "the person is one," this clarifies that the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others of former days have all today transformed their minds to become bodhisattvas; as the text of the subsequent scripture states: "He transforms only bodhisattvas, with no śrāvaka disciples."

It is also said that each person possesses a single capacity for resonance, a single teaching, and a single principle; thus, the Tathāgata employs a single teaching to expound a single principle, responding to one capacity to transform one person.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s wisdom illuminates this realm of the fourfold unity; this is precisely the essence of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
The questioner says:
"If the realm illuminated by true wisdom consists of the fourfold unity, then there is a further principle of 'unity-in-reason' (*li-yi*)."
"If it is said that the objects illuminated by expedient wisdom should number four or three, why is it that there are now no three principles, but only 'three threes'?
The commentator replied:
"If there had been three principles in the past, they would have to exist as actual realities; how then could it be said that the One Buddha Vehicle is taught as three through expedient means?"
Therefore, we know that within the teachings of the past, there were not three distinct principles.

As the text of the *Sutra* states: "It is merely by means of provisional names that sentient beings are guided. If one were to say that there truly exist three principles within the three teachings, then one ought to say that sentient beings are guided by real names; why then would it be said that they are guided "merely by means of provisional names"?
The questioner spoke again:
"The three teachings fundamentally expound principle; if there were no three principles beneath these three teachings, what would these teachings ultimately expound?"
"If there were no three principles to be expressed, there would likewise be no three teachings capable of expressing them.

The commentary explains: "It must be that sentient beings truly possess three capacities; therefore, in the past, there were truly three teachings, yet truly no three principles. Rather, the three teachings of the past were intended to express a single principle. Since the single reality-principle could not yet be spoken of in the past, the provisional verbal teachings of the three vehicles were used to indirectly express the single reality-principle of today. Thus, although one cause was previously described as three causes, its actual nature is that of a single cause."
The text of the subsequent scripture states, "That which you practice is the bodhisattva path. Thus, we know that there are not three distinct principles, but rather three types of verbal teachings.
The former clarifies provisional wisdom, which is the opening of the gate of skillful means; the latter clarifies ultimate wisdom, which is the manifestation of the true reality.
Next, the names and meanings of the two types of wisdom are explained, which include both general and specific senses.

The third, the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), possesses the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*); this wisdom of skillful means possesses the meaning of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), and true wisdom possesses the meaning of the wisdom of skillful means.
How is this known?

Wisdom fundamentally takes "illumination" as its essential meaning; yet, if the wisdom of skillful means does not penetrate and discern the capacities and natures of those of the three vehicles, how could one preach the Dharma to transform sentient beings?
Thus we know that the entire substance of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) is that of discerning illumination; this is precisely the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

As for why this wisdom of skillful means is also the meaning of "real wisdom" (*tattva-jñāna*): real wisdom fundamentally possesses the meaning of being non-false, authentic, and definitive. Since this wisdom of skillful means of mine is likewise truly existent, and because it is truly existent, the wisdom of skillful means is itself the meaning of reality.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is itself skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*)," skillful means has "expediency" as its meaning; this true wisdom explains the principle of a single cause and a single fruit, describing it as a profound, subtle, and mysterious principle that is difficult to comprehend.

The subsequent scriptural passage praises true wisdom, stating: "The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable. This single cause and single fruit constitute the objects illuminated by true wisdom; as for these objects, when considered vertically, they are bottomless, which constitutes their profound depth;
when considered horizontally, they are boundless, which constitutes their immeasurability.
However, while the principle is profound and vast and difficult to know, it is in fact illuminated by wisdom; this is precisely the meaning of skillfulness (*kauśalya*), which is *upāya*.
Question:
"If that is so, although there are two types of wisdom, are they now made to be entirely indistinguishable?"
The commentator says:

"Now, in order to establish a distinct name by force and differentiate it from the general, and furthermore to clarify the distinction between skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), we consider that correct principles are easy to understand while subtle meanings are difficult to illuminate. Thus, it is like a master craftsman wielding his axe upon a single piece of wood: if this wood were round and straight and easy to work with, the craftsman could complete a vessel using his axe and marking line;

yet one would not perceive the man’s skill at that time. However, if the wood were twisted and curved and difficult to work with, and the man nonetheless succeeds in producing a marvelous vessel, only then does one realize the man’s mastery of craft."

Now, the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) is likewise: the preceding realm is provisional and circuitous, not the true and ultimate principle of the world; yet this wisdom of skillful means can circuitously illuminate the capacities of sentient beings and skillfully expound the three teachings to accord with their circuitous dispositions. Only then does one perceive the skillful capacity of this wisdom; herein, the meaning of "skillfulness" is manifest, while the meaning of "wisdom" remains implicit.

Furthermore, regarding the sense that ultimate wisdom (實智) is predominant while expedient wisdom (權智) is subordinate: now, within this single teaching, single principle, single capacity, and single person—these four "ones" constitute the realm of ultimate reality. Since the Tathāgata’s wisdom accords with this ultimate reality to illuminate it, there is no sense of compromise or conformity; thus, the meaning of ultimate wisdom is manifest, while the meaning of skillful means is latent.

Furthermore, that which is illuminated by true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) consists of both the reality of the principle and the reality of the teaching; however, that which is illuminated by provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna) contains only the teachings of the Three Vehicles and lacks the principles of the Three Vehicles. Thus, if that which is illuminated by provisional wisdom possesses only a single reality, then the meaning of true wisdom would not be fully manifested.
However, that which is illuminated by true wisdom possesses both scriptural reality (*yathāruta*) and logical reality (*yuktatattva*); thus, the meaning of true wisdom is made manifest.
All of these [approaches] involve each submerging one's own shortcomings while bringing forth another's strengths.

Next, it clarifies that the functions of the two wisdoms have their periods of arising and ceasing: the fourth, the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), arose in the past but has now ceased; the true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) has now arisen but ceased in the past.
How is this known?

In the past, at the Deer Park, you preached the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles; at that time, only provisional wisdom was active while true wisdom was set aside. Today, at the Royal City, you preach the principle of the true mark—the single cause and single fruit; thus, today true wisdom flourishes while provisional wisdom is set aside.
Thus, there is mutual alternation between decline and flourishing; this is because the engagement with and transformation of sentient beings involves such rise and fall.
The questioner says:

"The Tathāgata’s seed-awakening (gotrabhū-jñāna) and myriad virtues are eternally tranquil. Now, to say that the two wisdoms have rise and fall not only implies that the seed-awakening is not luminous, but also lacks the illumination of eternal tranquility."
The commentator says:

"The myriad virtues are eternally profound and still, as the Tathāgata has taught; yet that we now speak of arising and ceasing is discussed from the perspective of engaging with and transforming sentient beings."

In the past, sentient beings possessed small minds and inferior capacities, unable to hear the proclamation of the true reality (*dharmatā*). At that time, provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) expounded those three teachings to suit those three types of capacity; at that moment, actual wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) had no function of manifesting transformation, and thus it is termed "abolished" in this sense.

Today, the assembly is capable of hearing the principle of true reality; actual wisdom expounds this single principle to suit this single capacity, yet provisional wisdom has no function of manifesting transformation today, and thus it is termed "abolished" in this sense.

If we consider it from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s threefold supernormal knowledge: the celestial eye perceives that there are those with the potential for the Mahāyāna in the future; this is the function of true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of past lives perceives that there are those with the potential for the three vehicles (*triyāna*) in the past; this is the function of expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*).
If that is so, what rise or decline could there be?

Furthermore, just as the Tathāgata manifests emanations throughout the ten directions to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, if the wisdom of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-jñāna*) in the royal city preaches the Dharma to transform beings, it is likewise possible for the wisdom of expedient means (*upāya-jñāna*) in the ten directions to deliver beings, or for the wisdom of expedient means here to deliver beings, or for the wisdom of ultimate reality in the ten directions to preach the Dharma. Whether discussing the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) from a vertical perspective or speaking of the ten directions from a horizontal perspective, these two wisdoms—expedient and ultimate—are without rise or decline.
Now, based on the principle that all things have a beginning and an end, there is arising and ceasing.
Next, we clarify the differences between the two types of wisdom as explained in various sutras. Fifth, regarding the differences among the various sutras, there are five kinds in total:

First, concerning the two types of wisdom explained in the teachings with signs (*sanimitta*) from before the twelve years [of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*]: if it illuminates the realm of segmented impermanence, such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is called provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); if it illuminates momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇika-anityatā*), it is called true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

Second, regarding the two kinds of wisdom elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: if one illuminates that which exists provisionally through causes and conditions, this is expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); if one illuminates that this provisional existence is itself emptiness, this is true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

The third is the two kinds of wisdom elucidated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: if one knows the illness and recognizes the medicine, serenely illuminating the capacities of sentient beings, this is true wisdom (*jñāna*);
if one can respond to the illness by administering the medicine so that it may be taken and practiced, this is skillful means wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Fourth, regarding the two kinds of wisdom elucidated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: if one illuminates the dharmas of birth-and-death—impermanence, suffering, and emptiness—up to and including the diamond-like [samādhi], this is the wisdom of skillful means;
if one illuminates the true dharmas of nirvāṇa—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is precisely the wisdom of reality.

Fifth, regarding the two types of wisdom elucidated in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: if it illuminates the realm of "three threes," it is expedient wisdom; if it illuminates the realm of "four ones," it is true wisdom.
Thus, the two kinds of wisdom with characteristics mentioned twelve years prior were discussed in terms of their relative proximity;
the two kinds of wisdom elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* constitute two wisdoms by means of a horizontal illumination of the two truths;
and the two kinds of wisdom in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are discussed in terms of a vertical progression.

The two wisdoms elucidated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* are based on the distinction between the fundamental and the derivative: knowing the illness and identifying the medicine is the fundamental, while applying the medicine in accordance with the illness is the derivative.

The two wisdoms elucidated in the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, however, are defined according to the sequence of beginning and end: at the beginning, there is the provisional wisdom that teaches the three vehicles; at the end, there is the ultimate wisdom that teaches the one vehicle.
The sutra consists of three sections. The first, which clarifies both the general and specific prefaces, is now concluded.

From here until the end of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," including the fourteen and a half chapters from where Maitreya speaks the verses in response to the Buddha’s prose, constitutes the second section: the Main Exposition. Within this Main Exposition, there are originally two parts: the first clarifies the cause, and the second distinguishes the fruit.

From here down to the end of the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anle-xing pin*), there are twelve chapters of the sutra; this first section is titled "Opening the Three to Reveal the One" (*Kai-san xian-yi*) and primarily elucidates the meaning of the cause. Second, from the "Chapter on the Emergence" (*Yongchu pin*) until Maitreya’s recitation of verses following the Buddha’s prose, there are two and a half chapters of the sutra, titled "Opening the Near to Reveal the Far" (*Kai-jin xian-yuan*), which elucidates the meaning of the fruit.

Previously, it was explained that both the cause and the effect each consist of four aspects; setting aside for now the four aspects within the effect, we shall now further clarify the four aspects within the cause. First, from the beginning of this chapter down to the prose and verse sections, is designated as the "Brief Exposition Opening the Three to Reveal the One," which stirs attachments and gives rise to doubt.

Second, from the passage "At that time, among the great assembly were various śrāvakas, arhats whose outflows were exhausted" onwards, is designated as the "Great Assembly’s Doubt and Request. Thus, since the doubt has arisen and the desire to inquire has reached its peak, the third section—from "The Tathāgata, having received your earnest triple request" down through the seven-and-a-half chapters ending with the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Learners and Non-learners"—is the formal and extensive exposition of "Opening the Three to Reveal the One," which severs doubt and engenders faith.

Thus, since the doubts of the great assembly have been dispelled and awakening to the "three in one" has already arisen, the meaning of this One Vehicle (Ekayāna) should now be propagated where it was previously unheard; for this reason, the fourth section—from the "Dharma Master Chapter," the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa," the "Chapter on Upholding," and the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct"—clarifies the specific meaning of the propagation of the teaching.

Now, within these four sections, the first and second each contain two layers, while the third and fourth each have three distinct parts. Regarding the first section, which addresses the arising of doubt from the movement of attachment, there are two parts:

first, the conclusion of the sutra’s narrative describing the manifestation of entering samādhi and preaching the Dharma; second, the formal praise of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, which opens up the three to reveal the one. The latter three sections will be explained when the time comes.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are constantly in samādhi and perceive all Buddha-lands without dualistic characteristics. The reason it is now said that they "arise serenely from samādhi" is to provide a model for sentient beings; for when ordinary people, lacking wisdom, utter a single word or make a single sound, they do so impulsively with a frivolous mind and in distraction. Now, the Tathāgata, being about to preach the Dharma, first demonstrates entering meditative absorption to contemplate the principle, so as to cause ordinary people to first still their minds and thoughts before giving rise to their intentions and engaging in detailed exposition. It is for this purpose that he says he arises from concentration.

Within the second section, which is the formal praise of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—there are two parts. First, from the verse "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable" down to the seventeenth and a half verses, this is designated as the introductory praise of the two wisdoms, which serves as a preliminary opening of the central theme.

The second section, beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ," consists of three and a half verses, which are designated as a detailed explanation of the meaning of "opening the three and revealing the one."

The reason it is said that by praising the two wisdoms, the fundamental tenets are provisionally revealed, is that today’s teaching reverses the conventional doctrine. Formerly, it was said that the three vehicles have distinct practices, each with its own destination; it was said that the Śrāvaka vehicle is different, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is different, and the Bodhisattva vehicle is different, such that the three families could not interpenetrate one another.
Now, however, it is clarified that the practices of the three vehicles share the same single cause and are equally Bodhisattvas, all of whom alike attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

If one were to suddenly clarify the teaching that there are no three vehicles and the principle of the single reality, those who cling to the three would likely give rise to slander; therefore, it cannot be clarified all at once. It must be explained gradually and incrementally to provide a starting point for moving away from fixed attachments; thus, there is the "approximate opening of the school."

To speak directly, the Tathāgata has both the teaching of the difficult-to-understand *upāya-jñāna* (expedient wisdom) and the teaching of the profound *bhūta-jñāna* (true wisdom). When the assembly heard that there was both a profound true wisdom and a difficult-to-understand expedient wisdom, they all became doubtful, saying: "In the past, the Buddha taught the doctrines of the Three Vehicles as being entirely true; yet now he says there is both the real and the expedient."

At that time, the assembly’s minds gradually began to waver; therefore, the second three and a half verses were spoken clearly and concisely, stating: "The Dharma of the World-Honored One must, after a long time, speak the truth."

It further states that the Buddha, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), manifested the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) to lead sentient beings—who were attached in various places—to liberation.

Having thus clearly and briefly explained the meaning of the unity of the three vehicles, the assembly at that time gave rise to doubts regarding the ultimate truth and their attachment to the three vehicles was stirred. For this reason, it is said that the fundamental principle was "vaguely" opened.
Furthermore, within each of these two sections, there are two further divisions; the "two" mentioned in the opening of the main doctrine refer to the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*).

The final three and a half verses clearly and briefly explain that there are two aspects: first, one verse and a half uses the various Buddhas to manifest the "one," and second, two verses address Śākyamuni to reveal the "three."

Setting aside the verses for a moment, within the prose itself there are two distinct sections. The first, from the beginning of the chapter down to "accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas," is designated as praising the two wisdoms by means of words. The second, from "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and expound all dharmas" onwards to the end of the prose, is designated as praising the two wisdoms by means of transcending words. This does not mean transcending the four propositions; rather, it is called "transcending words" because [the Tathāgata’s teaching] is beyond verbal expression.
Because the lower does not reach the higher, it is called "transcending words" (*jueyan*).
It is also called "stopping words to praise.

Furthermore, within these two sections, each contains two parts. Regarding the two praises expressed through words concerning the two wisdoms: first, wishing to praise and explain the two wisdoms of Śākyamuni, one first expresses praise for the two wisdoms of all Buddhas by means of words.
The second section correctly employs words to praise and explain the two types of wisdom of Śākyamuni.
The reason for doing so is to provide a point of comparison.

Since all Buddhas likewise possess both true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and skillful means wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), with the former three [vehicles] preceding the latter one, how much more so does Śākyamuni possess both true wisdom and skillful means wisdom, with the former three preceding the latter one? To speak of skillful means wisdom is to explain the teaching of the Three Vehicles; to speak of true wisdom is to explain the teaching of the One Vehicle.
Within each of these two sections there are three parts. Now, regarding the praise of the two wisdoms of the Buddhas, there are three stages:
first, the direct praise of the two wisdoms; second, the general explanation of the two wisdoms; and third, the dual conclusion.

Thus, within the clarification of the cause, he addresses the śrāvakas; within the discussion of the fruit, he addresses the Great Beings (mahāsattvas), yet he does not address the śrāvakas [in the latter].

The reason for specifically addressing these two individuals is that all treatises are composed according to conditions: among the śrāvakas, Śāriputra is foremost in intelligence, and among the bodhisattvas, Maitreya is the Great Being who is next to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, by specifically addressing these two, he reveals the inferiority of all others.
Regarding the formal praise of the two types of wisdom, the praise of the wisdom of reality (*jñāna*) comes first, followed by the praise of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*).
Within the praise of the wisdom of reality itself, there are two phrases; since one intends to praise "the wisdom of all Buddhas" with the first phrase, the wisdom of reality is presented first.
The single phrase "profoundly immeasurable" is the second correct praise of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
It is called "profoundly immeasurable" because it is described as "profound" in its vertical dimension and "immeasurable" in its horizontal dimension.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time possess this true wisdom; therefore, it is called "profound.
When considered horizontally across the Buddhas of the ten directions, their true wisdom is called "immeasurable.
Because it is remote and unfathomable when looked toward, it is called "profound."
Because its limit is unknowable, it is called "immeasurable.
This is a true praise of actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the gate of his wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter," this praises the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Within this, there are three parts: the first phrase, "the gate of his wisdom," raises the essence of provisional wisdom (*prajñā*); the second phrase, "difficult to understand and difficult to enter," is the formal praise itself.
"From 'All śrāvakas' onwards, the third [section] concerns those who do not know the person.

Expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is the gateway to true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*); because the teachings of the three vehicles are expounded through expedient wisdom, true wisdom attains universal penetration."
How is this known?

Because one first expounds the three teachings and only then does the single teaching become appropriate; it is like immediately establishing a gate through which the Buddha enters and exits, yet still calling it the "Buddha-gate" without distinction. Because of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) attains passage; therefore, expedient wisdom is designated as the gateway to true wisdom.
Now, when it says "that," it refers to its actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), which is to say its "household"; who is this?

It says that it is precisely the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "difficult to understand and difficult to enter," this is the second [point] which correctly praises the wisdom of skillful means; it says it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter because the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) cannot fathom this wisdom of skillful means, and therefore it is called difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

The reason it is not designated as "unintelligible" or "inaccessible" is that if one were to say it is unintelligible and inaccessible, then since the Buddha is precisely the one who can understand and enter [it], it would not be unintelligible.

However, because this principle is profound and subtle, it is difficult to understand; only the Buddha can understand and enter it. As for whom it is not unintelligible or inaccessible—it is everyone else. Thus, the third point identifies those individuals: all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—that is, these people of the two vehicles—are precisely those who cannot understand or enter it.

"Why is this so?"—the following section constitutes the second general explanation of the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas. This passage cites the past practices of all Buddhas to explain the reason for these two kinds of wisdom: why is it that the true wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable?
Furthermore, why is it said that this gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter?

It is because the Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and fully practiced the conduct of all those former Buddhas; thus, he has attained these two kinds of wisdom, which are profound and subtle.
Within this very commentary, there are three parts:

first, from "The Buddha formerly drew near" onwards, which clarifies the basis of practice; second, from "He fully practiced all Buddhas' [teachings]" onwards, which properly clarifies the performance of practice; and third, the single phrase "His fame was heard everywhere," which serves as a concluding manifestation.
In the third pair, which concludes the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas, there are two parts.
First, "accomplishing the profound and unprecedented dharma" concludes the aforementioned wisdom of reality (*tattvajñāna*), stating that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profound and immeasurable.

The second section, "The Intentionality of What is Taught According to Circumstances is Difficult to Understand," concludes the aforementioned wisdom of skillful means, stating that the gateway of this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

The reason it is said to be "according to what is appropriate" is that this skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) can adapt to what is suitable for beings: it teaches suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to what is appropriate for *śrāvakas*; it teaches the twelve links of dependent origination according to what is appropriate for *pratyekabuddhas*; and it teaches the six *pāramitās* according to what is appropriate for *bodhisattvas*. Therefore, it is called "according to what is appropriate."

"Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood... From this point downward is the second section of the "Praise of the Two Wisdoms through Metaphorical Language. This is titled "Praise of Śākyamuni’s Provisional and Real Wisdoms through Metaphorical Language," and within it there are three layers:
first, a singular praise of Śākyamuni’s wisdom of skillful means; second, a singular praise of his real wisdom; and third, a singular conclusion regarding his real wisdom.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, the actual praise of the wisdom of skillful means; second, from "Why is this so? onwards, the explanation.
Within the actual praise, there are three parts:
First, "Śāriputra, since my attaining Buddhahood... clarifies the timing of the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);
second, from "various causes and conditions" (*nānā-pratyaya*) onwards, it formally praises the provisional wisdom;
third, from "guiding sentient beings" onwards, it concludes by manifesting its significance.
Now, the second part, which correctly praises expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), refers to that which is accomplished by expedient wisdom.
"Various causes and conditions" is a name for the Dharma taught by the expedient wisdom of Śākyamuni.

Śrāvakas take the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths as their causal condition; Pratyekabuddhas take the contemplation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as their causal condition; and Bodhisattvas take the contemplation of the Six Perfections as their causal condition; therefore, it is said that there are various kinds of causal conditions.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "various parables," it means that when the causes for the practice of the three vehicles are illustrated: the śrāvaka is like a hare, the pratyekabuddha is like a horse, and the bodhisattva is like an elephant.

When the fruits of the three vehicles are attained, the śrāvaka is compared to a sheep-cart, the pratyekabuddha to a deer-cart, and the bodhisattva to an ox-cart; thus, they are called "various parables."

Regarding the phrase "extensively expounding verbal teachings through countless skillful means": it does not refer merely to preaching the Dharma; rather, because the circumstances and timing vary in manifold ways, it is said that he extensively expounds verbal teachings through countless skillful means.
"From 'Why is this so? onwards is the second section, which is a singular praise of Śākyamuni’s skillful means wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
As for the statement 'Why is it that Śākyamuni possesses this skillful means wisdom, enabling him to preach the Dharma through such various causes, conditions, and parables?'—what does this mean?"
This is precisely because the Tathāgata has fully perfected the pāramitās of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.
In foreign lands [Sanskrit], they are called *pāramitā*; here [in Chinese], it means "reaching the other shore."
The Tathāgata’s wisdom penetrates and discerns the capacities of beings, reaching the other shore; thus, he possesses this skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of wisdom.
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound"—this is the second section, a singular praise of Śākyamuni’s actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), which itself has two parts:
first, "vast and profound," which establishes two topical headings: (1) vastness and (2) profundity.

That which encompasses all without exception is termed "vast"; that which transcends the lesser sages is termed "great"; that whose bottom cannot be reached is termed "deep"; and that which has been attained through long-standing causal practice is termed "distant."

The second statement, "immeasurable and unimpeded," explains the two preceding chapter-headings from below. First, there are six phrases explaining the chapter-heading of "vastness," followed by one phrase explaining the chapter-heading of "profound depth."

Now, for the first time, there are immeasurable and unimpeded [knowledges]; whereas formerly it was said that the Tathāgata possessed only the four unimpeded knowledges, now he possesses immeasurable unimpeded knowledges.
Formerly it was said that the Tathāgata possessed only the ten powers, now he possesses immeasurable powers.
Formerly it was said that the Tathāgata possessed only the four fearlessnesses, now he possesses immeasurable fearlessnesses.
Formerly it was said that the Tathāgata possesses only eight dhyānas, whereas now it is said he possesses immeasurable dhyānas;
formerly it was said that the Tathāgata possesses only eight liberations, whereas now it is said that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable liberations;
formerly it was said that the Tathāgata possesses only three samādhis, whereas now it is said that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable samādhis.
The preceding "immeasurable eye" (ananta-cakṣus) generally encompasses these six kinds of dharmas; if one follows the previous [section], they should also be present there. Why is this?

When it is said that the Tathāgata possesses real wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) that is vast, great, and profound, what else could it be but the immeasurable, unimpeded [knowledges] up to the three samādhis and so forth? It is simply that these six kinds of dharmas explain the term "vast" within the aforementioned real wisdom.
The phrase "profoundly penetrating the boundless" explains the term "profound and far-reaching" within the aforementioned section on true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

"Accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas" is the third individual conclusion regarding Śākyamuni’s true wisdom; it specifically concludes the preceding statement that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast, great, profound, and far-reaching.
When examining the interaction between the two types of wisdom of all Buddhas and Śākyamuni, there are four distinct differences. What are they?

First, among the aforementioned Buddhas, both types of wisdom are praised together, whereas among those [instances] concerning Śākyamuni, only one type of wisdom is praised; this is the first difference.

First, the previous Buddhas first praised true wisdom (*jñāna*) and subsequently praised skillful means (*upāya*), whereas Śākyamuni first praised skillful means and subsequently praised true wisdom; this is the first difference.

Second, the previous Buddhas cited past causes to explain the two wisdoms, while Śākyamuni cited the various merits of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) to explain the two wisdoms; this is the second difference.
Third, the previous Buddhas concluded by summarizing both wisdoms together, whereas Śākyamuni concluded by summarizing only true wisdom; this is the fourth difference.
The commentator says:
"It is not that there is no reason for this.
The reason why all Buddhas praise the two wisdoms in tandem, whereas Śākyamuni does not praise them in tandem, is because he wishes to manifest that their essence is one."
The double praise of the two wisdoms of all Buddhas is intended to clarify that although their essence is one, their functions differ;
the single praise of the two wisdoms of Śākyamuni is an instance of citing one side by way of contrast.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that all Buddhas first praise true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) and subsequently praise skillful means (*upāyajñāna*, while Śākyamuni first praises skillful means and subsequently praises true wisdom): the fact that all Buddhas first praise true wisdom and subsequently praise skillful means clarifies the sequence of the fundamental and the derivative.
Why is this? It is simply because there is a root that there is a branch.
That Śākyamuni first praises skillful means and subsequently praises true wisdom clarifies the sequence of his teaching and transformation.

The reason why there is a mutual relationship between the root and the branches, and a sequence of before and after, is that each instance cites one side to clarify a single principle from two perspectives.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Buddhas cite past causes to explain the two wisdoms, while Śākyamuni cites the various merits at the stage of fruition": when it says "the Buddhas cite past causes to explain the two wisdoms," this clarifies that a supreme cause must necessarily result in a perfect fruit.

Regarding the explanation that Śākyamuni enumerates the various merits of the fruit to clarify the two types of wisdom: this demonstrates that the perfect fruit necessarily recompenses the superior cause; this, too, is an enumeration of one side of their mutual relationship.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the Buddhas of the ten directions "doubly conclude" with the two wisdoms while Śākyamuni "singly concludes" with the wisdom of reality (*dharmatājñāna*): this is intended to clarify the meaning of arising and ceasing. When discussing the time when the two wisdoms of the Buddhas arise, they "doubly conclude" with the two wisdoms.

Today is the time when Śākyamuni abolishes the provisional and reveals the real; because it is for the purpose of abolishing the provisional, he does not combine the provisional wisdom, and because it is for the purpose of revealing the real, he combines only the real wisdom.
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
"The preceding Buddhas paired the two wisdoms (jñāna) together in order to clarify that these two wisdoms are but a single essence illuminating the threefold-threefold realm.

Now, when it is said that Śākyamuni singles out only the wisdom of reality (bhūta-jñāna), this is done to follow the distinctions of function regarding superiority and inferiority; yet it is intended merely to clarify that within the Sage’s embrace, what ultimate superiority or inferiority can there be between the two wisdoms?"
"However, it is simply because he follows after phenomena.
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to differentiate in various ways"—from here below is the second section, which praises the two types of wisdom by means of the ineffable.
The question asks:

"Although words have been employed to praise these two wisdoms, it is clarified that these two wisdoms cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments nor reached by clumsy speech; thus, let this discourse cease for now. Therefore, the subsequent text states, 'Only the Buddhas can know them,' as they are beyond the reach of lesser sages."

Even within these words that transcend speech, there arose among the great assembly the seeds of doubt and the stirring of their attachments; at that time, the assembly asked: "For what reason does the Tathāgata emerge from samādhi and personally extol the profound depth of the two kinds of wisdom?"
If they are nonetheless abandoned, for what reason?

Therefore it is said: "To praise the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) is the starting point for the movement of attachments; to praise the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) is the starting point for the arising of doubts.
The questioner asked:
"If you say that words have been transcended, for what reason do you praise it by means of the Path? The commentator says:
"If one were to remain silent without speaking when words should be transcended, how would the assembly know at that time that these two types of knowledge should transcend speech?"
Regarding this "utterance of words" within the praise, there are three aspects:
first, the prior presentation of the dharmas that transcend speech, which are the two types of wisdom;
second, the explicit clarification of the utterance of words as praise.
The third section, beginning with "For what reason," explains the meaning of why words are cut off.

Here, first the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is presented, followed by the ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*). From the four lines beginning with "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to distinguish in various ways," the provisional wisdom is specifically elucidated within the context of the three sets of three objects. This clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to explain the causes and conditions for the teaching for śrāvakas, the causes and conditions for the teaching for pratyekabuddhas, and the causes and conditions for the teaching for bodhisattvas; hence, it is said that he "distinguishes in various ways."

Regarding the phrase "skillfully explaining all dharmas," this clarifies that the Tathāgata, through the skillful means of his wisdom, explains the single vehicle (ekayāna) dharma and manifests it as the various dharmas of the three vehicles. Therefore, the subsequent scripture states, "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three. For this reason, it is called "skillful explanation."
It is said that these three vehicles of teaching were tailored to the capacities of sentient beings in the past; therefore, their phrasing was gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude.

From the passage "Śāriputra, to speak briefly" down to "the Buddha has fully accomplished," this section focuses specifically on the single realm of principle (*li-yi-jing*) within the fourfold single realm, thereby revealing true wisdom (*shizhi*).
If we discuss this by taking the essential point, true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is what is required today. How do we know this?
Today is the time for manifesting the truth and setting aside the provisional.
"Cease, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further. This single phrase is the second [section], which correctly clarifies the praise of the ineffable. Why is this so?

From here until the end of the prose section is the third [section], which explains the reason for the ineffability: it is precisely because the two wisdoms involve a sublime person and a profound realm that they are beyond words.
Therefore, this third explanation of the ineffable itself contains two parts:
first, the exaltation of the person, which refers to one who has attained wisdom; second, the profundity of the object of focus.
Now, from the words "For what reason? up to "is able to exhaustively fathom," this is designated as the exalted explanation that transcends speech regarding the person who has been cited.
Why does [the Buddha] stop Śāriputra and not require him to further explain the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real?
Only the Buddhas can know the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real; how, then, could they not cease [their teaching]?

Regarding the exaltation of the person, there are two aspects: first, the "most rare and difficult-to-understand Dharma" refers to the two wisdoms attained by the Buddha; second, from "only Buddhas with Buddhas... onwards, it correctly clarifies the exaltation of the person.

Regarding the phrase "the true reality of all phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*): the following section explains the second reason why speech is transcended within the context of "transcending words. It is not merely because the person [who realizes it] is sublime that the two wisdoms are subtle and ineffable; rather, speech is transcended because the objects illuminated by these two wisdoms are profound.
Furthermore, regarding the objects illuminated by these two types of wisdom, there are three parts:
first, the dual opening of the two chapter-gates; second, the dual explanation of the two chapter-gates; and third, the dual conclusion of the two chapter-gates.
Regarding the opening of two chapter-gates: the two characters "all dharmas" (zhūfǎ) constitute the chapter-gate of the objects illuminated by the wisdom of skillful means;
the two characters "true reality" (shíxiàng) constitute the chapter-gate of that which is illuminated by real wisdom.
However, regarding the objects illuminated by expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), there are three sets of three objects; here, we take only those that illuminate the Three Teachings.
Regarding the objects illuminated by ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), there are four sets of one object; here, we take only that which illuminates the One Principle.
The commentator says:

"Among the nine realms illuminated by expedient wisdom, the essential are the three teachings. Those who advance toward practice must rely upon verbal instruction to enter the Way; therefore, it is said that all dharmas [are taught]."
Because the teachings of the Three Vehicles are not uniform, they are called "all dharmas.

As for the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is the "unity of principle" among the four kinds of unity; since this unity of principle within the four unities is the most essential, it is what is directly illuminated.
To directly illuminate the three teachings is the meaning of opening the gate of expedient means; to directly illuminate the oneness of principle is the meaning of revealing the true aspect.
How is this known?
In the following explanation, the cause and effect are cited to elucidate this; one should know that cause and effect are in essence but a single principle.

Regarding the phrase "so-called all dharmas," the following constitutes the second pair of explanations for the two preceding topical gates. There are nine sentences in total: the first five sentences explain the topical gate of "all dharmas," while the subsequent four sentences—beginning with "such causes and such conditions"—explain the topical gate of "true reality" (*dharmatā*).

The phrase "such characteristics" (evam-lakṣaṇa) signifies the sense of distinction; for when one surveys the teachings of the three vehicles, all possess distinct characteristics—the teaching of the Śrāvaka vehicle is distinct, the teaching of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is distinct, and the teaching of the Bodhisattva vehicle is distinct—and thus it is called "such characteristics."
"Suchness of nature" (*tathatā-dharmatā*): "nature" (*dharmatā*) has the meaning of being unalterable.

It is simply that the teaching for *śrāvakas* of former times cannot be altered into the teaching for *pratyekabuddhas*, and the teaching for *pratyekabuddhas* cannot be altered into the teaching for *bodhisattvas*; therefore, it is called "suchness of nature."

Regarding the phrase "such a substance" (*tathā-bhāva*): "substance" (*bhāva*) here signifies distinct entities. For the Śrāvaka, their practice takes the teaching of the Four Noble Truths as its substance; this means encountering suffering and generating weariness toward birth, old age, sickness, and death. For the Pratyekabuddha, it takes the teaching of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as its substance. For the Bodhisattva, it takes the scriptural teachings on the Six Perfections as its substance. Therefore, it is called "such a substance."

"Such power" refers to the power of the Śrāvaka teaching to sever the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) by means of conditions; the power of the Pratyekabuddha teaching to invade and sever the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) by means of conditions; and the power of the Bodhisattva teaching to sever the residual impressions completely and achieve Buddhahood by means of conditions; therefore, it is called "such power."

Regarding the phrase "acting in this way," the Master of the Treatise states that "arising" refers to the aspect of activity; thus, one knows that "acting" (*karman*) simply carries the meaning of "activity" (*saṃskāra*).

This clarifies that within the teachings of these three vehicles there is the sense of activity: the practice of the śrāvaka involves purposeful action, and even the practice of the bodhisattva involves purposeful action. These five phrases all explain the preceding categories of dharmas and are designated as the realm of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Regarding "such causes," the following four lines explain the preceding chapter on the true nature (dharmatā), designating it as the object illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
The reason for knowing that this is the object illuminated by true wisdom is stated in the subsequent verse: "Because such is the great fruit of retribution."
"Such causes" (evam-hetu) means that which brings about the fruition. "Such conditions" (evam-pratyaya):

"condition" (pratyaya) signifies "by means of. That the myriad virtues can bring about the fruition is the meaning of "cause"; that this fruition is obtained by means of the myriad virtues is the meaning of "condition."

Regarding the phrase "such a fruit": "fruit" (phala) takes the sense of being in opposition to a cause; "retribution" (vipāka) takes the sense of a response or repayment. Since they refer to one and the same result that corresponds to a cause, it is designated as "fruit."

This fruit possesses the sense of repaying the power of the cause, which constitutes the meaning of retribution (*vipāka*). These four phrases precisely explain the preceding chapter on the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the phrase "Thus, from beginning to end," the following is the third section, which concludes both chapters. Now, by saying "Thus, from beginning to end," this concludes the chapter on the realm of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*): "beginning" refers to the initial "thus-ness" (*tathatā*), while "end" refers to the final "thus-doing."
"Ultimate equality" refers to the single cause and the single fruit; "ultimate equality" here concludes the topical section on the realm of realized wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, to explain the meaning of "cause and condition": some explain that "the cause is proximate while the condition is remote."
The reason for saying that [the cause] is "proximate" (pratyaya) is this: this effect was originally non-existent and now exists; this is the meaning of "proximity.
Why is this so? Because it is capable of causing that which was originally non-existent to come into existence.

Furthermore, regarding those designated as "distant," they are identical to this very result; it is impossible for things such as two heads or three hands to arise, yet within the principle (*yukti*), there exists the sense that they can arise.

If you say that while they cannot arise within the principle, the power of causes (*hetu-bala*) can nevertheless cause them to arise, then why does the power of causes not cause the arising of two heads or three hands, which are likewise impossible?
If that which is incapable of arising by the power of causes could nevertheless arise, then one might designate the cause as "proximate" (*pratyaya*).

Since the fruit possesses the sense of being capable of arising, the cause stands in a "remote" (*hetu*) relationship to the fruit; yet because this fruit was originally non-existent and now exists, this cause stands in a "proximate" relationship to the fruit.
Furthermore, since the fruit possesses the principle of being capable of arising, this cause stands in the sense of being a "condition" (*pratyaya*) for the fruit.

Now, Dharma Master Guangzhai explains that there is no distinction between "proximate" and "distant" in meaning; he states directly that "cause" (yin) means that which corresponds to the fruit, while "condition" (yuan) simply means that which serves as a basis or support.
If one considers the myriad practices in relation to the fruit, they possess the meaning of being "confronted with" the fruit and are thus designated as causes;

if one considers the fruit in relation to the myriad practices, this fruit is obtained through those myriad practices, and in relation to the fruit, they possess the meaning of conditions (*pratyaya*).

"At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse. Regarding the praise of the two wisdoms, there are two parts within the general opening of the treatise:

the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*). What follows below is the second part, which correctly elucidates the verses; however, within the prose section itself, there are originally two sub-sections: first, praising the two wisdoms by means of words; second, clarifying the praise of the two wisdoms by means of transcending words.
Now, these seventeen and a half verses are also divided into two parts:

first, four verses that directly eulogize the two wisdoms by means of indirect expression; second, thirteen and a half verses beginning from "Such a great fruit of retribution," which eulogize the two wisdoms by means of words that transcend expression.

However, in the preceding prose section, the praise of the two kinds of wisdom is presented in two parts: first, because one wishes to praise the two kinds of wisdom of Śākyamuni, one first praises the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas;
second, there is the direct praise of the two kinds of wisdom of Śākyamuni.
Within each of these two pairs, there are three sections:
first, the direct praise of the two wisdoms; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
Now, the four-line verses that serve as the body [of this section] are likewise divided into two parts:

The first two lines of verse together praise the two wisdoms of all Buddhas and Śākyamuni; the latter two lines likewise praise the explanation of the two wisdoms by all Buddhas and Śākyamuni, thereby concluding the two layers of the two wisdoms.

Furthermore, regarding the two verses that collectively praise the two types of wisdom of all Buddhas and Śākyamuni, the former verse praises the two wisdoms of all Buddhas, while the latter verse praises the two wisdoms of Śākyamuni.

In praising the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas above, the real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) was praised first and the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) was praised later. Within the praise of the real wisdom that came first, there are two phrases:
the first raises the essence of wisdom by saying "the wisdom of all Buddhas," and the second phrase praises it directly by saying "profoundly deep and immeasurable."
The subsequent praise of expedient wisdom has three parts:

first, it presents the essence of wisdom by describing its gateway; second, it offers formal praise by stating that it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; third, it identifies those who do not know it, stating that it is something which all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know.

Now, the single phrase "The Hero of the World is immeasurable" simultaneously encompasses two lines each for both the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*) and the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), namely: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable," and "The gateway to that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter."

That all Buddhas are identical to those of the ten directions is the meaning of "worldly" (loka); that they subdue the four māras and overcome non-Buddhists is the meaning of "heroic" (vīra); and because the two wisdoms of skillful means and reality cannot be fathomed by inferior persons, it is said they are "immeasurable" (aprameya).

"Neither the devas nor the people of the world, nor any class of sentient beings, can know the Buddha"—the final three lines of this verse praise the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) mentioned above; the third line from the bottom identifies the group that does not know, while the preceding line states that it cannot be known by any *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.
Furthermore, there are four points of difference between this present verse and the preceding prose section.

First, in the preceding prose, the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*) and the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) were praised separately, whereas in this verse, the two wisdoms of provisional means and reality are praised together; this is the first difference.

Second, in the preceding section, the two wisdoms of provisional means and reality were praised by way of their essential nature, whereas in this verse, the two wisdoms are praised by citing the person [who possesses them]; this is the second difference.

First, in the preceding section it was clarified that ignorance regarding others is tied solely to the wisdom of means (*upāya-jñāna*); whereas in this present verse, it is shown that ignorance regarding others is doubly tied to both types of wisdom—this is the first difference. Second, in the preceding prose (*gadya*) exposition, ignorance regarding others was identified as pertaining only to the two classes of *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*; whereas in this present verse, it is extensively expanded to include humans, devas, *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and even reaching up to *bodhisattvas*, thereby including all those of the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*) who are ignorant of the masses—this is the second difference. Why is there such a difference?
The commentator says:
"This meaning is also subtle; there is a reason why it exists."

Regarding why the two types of wisdom (jñāna) are praised separately in the preceding prose section: it is to clarify that their meanings and functions differ. These two wisdoms are simply the Sage’s spiritual understanding applied to practical use; they are explained in accordance with the capacities of beings, yet this is not as [profound] as expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna). Since this expedient wisdom must have its source, the text first praises real wisdom (tattva-jñāna) as the foundation of expedient wisdom, and subsequently praises expedient wisdom as the function of that foundation. Thus, by praising the real and the expedient alternately, it is shown that there is a distinction in the superiority and inferiority of their applications.

Regarding the combined verses within the gāthās: this clarifies that although these two wisdoms possess the two designations of "expedient" and "real," when clearly illuminated, their essence is one and not otherwise.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"While there may be various numbers of worlds in the ten directions, there is no variation in unimpeded wisdom."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "one should directly praise the two wisdoms," this clarifies the fundamental intent of this sutra; therefore, within the verses that directly praise [the Buddha], it is explained that the person is constituted by the two wisdoms, and thus the person is cited as a whole to praise the two wisdoms.

Furthermore, it was stated above that "those who do not know" were linked only to the provisional wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*). Now, in this verse, they are linked to both types of wisdom. Regarding those linked to the provisional wisdom above: it is appropriate to disparage the two types of people there as having narrow and inferior wisdom; although they received the teachings of the provisional wisdom from the past, they were unable to thoroughly comprehend them. For this reason, those who do not know were mentioned above and linked exclusively to the provisional wisdom.

Now, regarding the phrase "doubly bound below the two wisdoms" in this verse: it clarifies that these followers of the Two Vehicles not only fail to understand the function of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), but their realization of ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) is likewise obscure and unfathomable; for this reason, they are said to be "doubly bound below the two wisdoms."

Furthermore, it is said that while the preceding prose section mentions only those of the Two Vehicles, the verse states that "among all classes of sentient beings, none are able to know the Buddha," thereby extensively including those of the Five Vehicles. This is intended to resolve the doubts of the audience; however, the primary purpose of today’s teaching is to refute the dogmatic attachments of the Two Vehicles. For this reason, the prose specifically addresses the Two Vehicles, yet at various points it is stated that the two types of wisdom are merely understood by the Two Vehicles and not otherwise, implying that beyond the Two Vehicles there must surely be those who do understand them.

Therefore, the verse states that it is not only the followers of the Two Vehicles who do not understand this principle of the provisional and the real; humans, devas, and bodhisattvas likewise do not understand it.
This can be understood by citing similar verses of this kind.
"Buddha-power and fearlessness"—this single verse correctly praises and extols the two types of wisdom of Śākyamuni.

In the preceding section that praised the two wisdoms of Śākyamuni, the provisional wisdom was praised first and the ultimate wisdom was praised later; now, in the first half of this line of verse, the ultimate wisdom of Śākyamuni is praised first, and in the second half of the line, the provisional wisdom is praised in succession.

However, within the preceding praise of Śākyamuni’s true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), there was first a formal praise of that true wisdom, followed by the citation of his powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Now, this half-verse serves as a concise summary of those aforementioned phrases concerning his various merits; it does not summarize the phrases of the formal praise itself.
"And none among the Buddha’s other dharmas can measure it" is a half-line of inverted verse that praises the preceding phrase concerning Śākyamuni’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Within the praise of Śākyamuni’s provisional wisdom above, there are three layers of praise: first, "Since my attainment of Buddhahood" clarifies the temporal duration of his provisional wisdom; second, "By means of various causes and conditions" and below constitutes the actual praise; and third, "Guiding sentient beings" and below reveals its manifestation.
This present half-verse only praises the second phrase, which is the formal eulogy; it does not praise the first and second phrases.
The reason for saying "and all other dharmas of the Buddha" here is that expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) follows [wisdom], and is therefore referred to as "other."
This provisional wisdom is taught in various ways for people of three different capacities; therefore, it is called "various" (*zhū*).
Furthermore, this single verse is used to restate the prose section in three different ways.

Why is this? In the prose section, the provisional wisdom of Śākyamuni is praised first and his ultimate wisdom is praised later; however, in these verses, the ultimate wisdom is praised first and the provisional wisdom is praised later—this is the first point of difference.

In the preceding prose section, the statement "The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound" specifically praises true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*); the subsequent enumeration of various merits serves as an interpretive praise for that same point. Now, in these verses, only the portion enumerating the various merits to interpret the praise of true wisdom is recited; the portion specifically praising true wisdom itself is omitted. Thus, there are two differences [between the prose and the verse].

In the preceding prose section, the praise of Śākyamuni’s two types of wisdom did not mention that they do not know the multitude; now, in this verse, it says "none can measure them. Thus, there are three differences [between the two].
The commentator says:

"As for why the preceding prose first praises provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) and subsequently praises ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), this clarifies that the intent of Śākyamuni’s appearance in the world is to present the provisional first and the ultimate later. As for why the verses first eulogize ultimate wisdom and subsequently eulogize provisional wisdom, this clarifies that it is now the time for practical application.
