These instances all involve alternating mentions of the preceding and following; by mutually illuminating one another, their meanings are naturally made manifest."

Furthermore, it is said that while the prose contains both the actual praise of true wisdom and its explanation, the verse only recites the explanatory phrases; this clarifies the principle that while the substance is one, the functions differ.
The preceding prose explains the meaning of its distinct function.
How is this known? Its function is that of wisdom’s discerning illumination.

To clarify that the realm illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) possesses the meaning of "fourfold oneness," there are four aspects: oneness of teaching, oneness of principle, oneness of capacity, and oneness of person. Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom illuminates these four realms, it is called true wisdom.

Since the various merits such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) do not themselves denote the act of discerning and illuminating, we know that the prose section refers to their functional application.

As for the fact that the verse only praises these various merits, this clarifies that merit and wisdom are of one and the same substance: apart from these powers, fearlessnesses, liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis, there is no separate wisdom; likewise, apart from this wisdom, there is no separate merit.
Therefore, we know that while their essence is one, when based on their functions, there is a distinction between merit and wisdom;
yet if one sets aside function to discuss essence, wisdom and merit are but a single entity.
In all these cases, the preceding and succeeding sections are mutually cited to clarify both meanings simultaneously.

Furthermore, it was stated in the prose that the praise of Śākyamuni’s two wisdoms did not go beyond "not knowing persons"; now, in this verse, the phrase "none can fathom him" specifically expresses "not knowing persons," thus again citing the preceding and succeeding sections in mutual relation.
If the verse mentions someone who is unknown, the prose commentary should also mention them; since the prose commentary does not mention them, they should likewise be absent from the verse.
That one exists while the other does not is a case where the two mutually clarify each other's meaning.

"From the beginning, they have followed countless Buddhas and fully practiced all paths. From this point downward, the two lines of verse repeat and praise the two layers of both the Buddhas' and Śākyamuni's expositions and conclusions; the first verse praises the two types of wisdom in the Buddhas' exposition and conclusion, while the latter verse praises the two types of wisdom in Śākyamuni’s exposition and conclusion.
Within the first verse, the half-verse "From the beginning, following countless Buddhas, they have fully practiced all paths" praises the second explanation of the two wisdoms of the Buddhas.
Why is this so? Because the Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas and has fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma of all those Buddhas.

Regarding the half-verse, "The profound and subtle Dharma is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend," this summarizes the third point from the preceding prose section: the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas.
This half-verse constitutes two meanings:
"The profound and subtle Dharma" is this first line, which concludes the discussion on ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), stating that one has accomplished a profound and unprecedented dharma;

"Difficult to see and difficult to comprehend" is this second line, which concludes the discussion on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), stating that the underlying intent of what is taught according to suitability is difficult to understand.

Regarding the line "Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas," this single verse serves as a double-layered commentary on the preceding prose (*śloka*) and its conclusion. This single line thus fulfills two purposes:

"Having practiced these various paths throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas" constitutes one meaning; the other half-line comments upon the two types of wisdom mentioned in the prose. Although the prose is brief and does not explicitly state the past causes, since they are present within the verse, they reflect back upon the preceding text to fulfill the function of a commentary.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the fruit at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa), this second half-verse precisely praises the aforementioned Śākyamuni’s singular realization of the wisdom of fruition (*phala-jñāna*). While the previous summary stated that he "accomplishes all unprecedented dharmas," that section merely spoke of the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*);

here, we present the assembly where the wisdom of fruition is attained. This refers specifically to when the Tathāgata sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained Buddhahood—when the World-Honored One’s great awakening was radiant and clear—he attained this wisdom of fruition. Therefore, it says: "I have fully known and seen the attainment of the fruit at the site of enlightenment."
The second section, "Such is the Great Fruit," consists of the following thirteen and a half verses, which eulogize the two types of wisdom by means of words that transcend speech.
Within this eulogy of what transcends speech, there are three parts:
first, presenting the reason why the dharma transcends speech; second, the actual clarification of the eulogy that transcends speech; and third, the explanation of the meaning of transcending speech.
These thirteen lines and a half also contain three intended meanings, which are recited in reverse order from the bottom up:
first, the single verse beginning with "Such is this great fruit of retribution" reversely recites the third section of the preceding prose, which explains the meaning of being beyond words;
second, the twelve lines that follow recite the second section of the preceding prose, the formal praise of being beyond words.
The third section contains one and a half lines of verse that invert the first [section] above to explain the method of transcending words.
However, within the third section’s explanation of "transcending words," there are two parts:
first, a preliminary praise of the person who possesses the two wisdoms, whose loftiness is ineffable; and second, the actual explanation of the ineffability.
Second, because the realm of the two wisdoms—expedient and ultimate—is profound, it cannot be expressed in words.
Now, this verse is also inverted; the half-line verse, "Such is the great fruition," first praises the profundity of the realm.
"I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know this matter"—this half-line of verse follows to praise the loftiness of the person.
However, within the profound upper realm, there are originally three parts:
first, the simultaneous opening of two chapter-gates; second, the simultaneous explanation; and third, the simultaneous conclusion.
Now, I do not recite the first and third [sections], but only recite the middle second section to provide a dual explanation of the two chapter-gates.

In the aforementioned dual explanation, there were five lines at the beginning explaining the chapter-gate of the realm of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and four lines at the end explaining the chapter-gate of the realm of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*); now, I likewise recite them in reverse order.

The phrase "such great fruit and retribution" first provides a verse-commentary on the sphere of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). It only praises the fruit and the retribution, omitting the cause and conditions for brevity. Now, by citing the fruit to verify the existence of causes and conditions, it is called "great. This also resolves the doubts of sentient beings: since the causes of the Three Vehicles are likewise causes and the fruits of the Three Vehicles are likewise fruits, for this reason the word "great" is used to mark its distinction, clarifying that these are the causes and fruits of the Mahāyāna, not those of the Hīnayāna.

The phrase "the meaning of various natures and characteristics" (zhǒngzhǒng xìngxiàng yì) is a retrospective verse summarizing the sphere of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Within the sphere of provisional wisdom there were originally five phrases; here, only the [first] two—nature and characteristics—are versified, while the remaining three are omitted. Furthermore, this particular phrase is also presented in reverse order.
Previously, it was stated that there are such characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and such nature (*svabhāva*); now, however, the verse first praises the nature and subsequently praises the characteristics.

As for the use of the term "various" (*nānāvidha*), it further resolves the doubts of sentient beings: in the Mahāyāna, there is both nature and characteristic. For this reason, the name "various" is employed as a designation; it is not that the nature and characteristics of the Mahāyāna alone are various, but rather because the natures and characteristics of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are not uniform, they are said to be "various."

The half-line verse, "Only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter," is a retrospective commentary on the first point within the discourse on the ineffable: it clarifies that the person is supreme, echoing the previous statement, "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom [this]."
"This Dharma cannot be shown. Below this are eleven lines that recapitulate the second section above, which definitively cuts off verbal expression.

Previously it was said, "Cease, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further. Now, within these eleven lines, only half a line directly recapitulates the aforementioned definitive cessation of speech and its praise; the remaining ten and a half lines clarify the underlying reason for such a cessation, precisely demonstrating that neither the Śrāvakas nor the Bodhisattvas understand it.
This half-verse now has two meanings:
"This Dharma cannot be shown" correctly versifies the preceding "Cease, Śāriputra";
"The characteristics of words are quiescent" versifies the preceding line "There is no need for further explanation."
"None of the other classes of sentient beings are able to understand it"—the following ten and a half lines constitute the second meaning. Within these ten and a half lines, there are three sections:
first, this current half-line generally clarifies that the assembly does not know;
second, the subsequent half-line excludes those who do possess knowledge.
The third section, spanning nine lines and a half, separately excludes those who do not know the assembly.

The second section excludes those who possess knowledge; this specifically means excluding from among the bodhisattva assembly those whose power of faith is firm and who can know for themselves. However, even their knowing is not through direct perception but rather through faith; this is intended to draw in śrāvakas and others toward the Mahāyāna, causing them to abandon their narrow and inferior minds and establish the great resolve of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the phrase "the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples," the following nine and a half lines constitute the third section, which specifically identifies those who do not know [these two wisdoms].
There are three types of people who do not know these two wisdoms;
first, there are four lines that clarify how the śrāvakas do not know them.
The second section consists of two verses clarifying that *pratyekabuddhas* do not know [this], beginning with "The sharp-witted *pratyekabuddhas*.
The third section consists of three and a half lines clarifying that bodhisattvas do not know [this], beginning with "Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds."
Regarding the first section, which clarifies that the śrāvakas do not know, there are three parts:

first, one and a half lines that directly clarify what the śrāvakas do not know; second, one line that uses a hypothetical assumption to clarify their ignorance; and third, one and a half lines that resolve doubts.
The word "even" (縱) implies that even if one were as possessed of spiritual insight as Śāriputra, it would be of no benefit for the matter at hand;
the word "suppose" (假) implies that even if other disciples each had their own understanding, they likewise could not know it.
Regarding the third point, clarifying that Bodhisattvas do not know [the intermediate state], there are two parts:
first, two and a half lines clarify that ordinary beings and Bodhisattvas do not know it;
second, one line clarifies that Bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the sixth stage do not know it, as this is for the purpose of discussion within the teachings.

"Furthermore, it says to Śāriputra, 'The untainted and inconceivable. Within this, there is one line and a half that is a subsequent verse (anuvṛtta) explaining the reason why speech was cut off—the dharma by which speech is cut off, as the first point among those where speech is suspended.
The previous statement that the Tathāgata is able to perform various kinds of discernment first brought forth his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);
here, for the sake of brevity, it is not versified.

Only the passage concerning the emergence of his ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*)—namely, "To state the essentials: the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas"—is versified above.
However, within these one and a half lines, the first line is the actual verse, while the latter half of the line cites the testimony of all Buddhas to establish the proof.
This is the interpretation according to the Śīlabhadra Monastery.

"Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas are not different"—the following three and a half verses constitute the second section, which provides a clear and concise explanation of the opening of the three and the revelation of the one, intended to resolve the attachments of sentient beings and address their state of doubt.
Within these three and a half lines, there are also two sections:
first, one and a half verses which manifest the "one" by means of all Buddhas; second, the remaining two verses which establish the "three" based on Śākyamuni.
Each of these two stages consists of three sections. Regarding the manifestation of the Buddhas, there are three sections within the first:
the first states, "Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas are not different. This half-verse first establishes that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.
"One should give rise to great power of faith regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha"—this half-verse is the second exhortation and injunction to believe.

"The Dharma of the World-Honored One will, after a long time, necessarily reveal the truth"—this half-verse is the third, which correctly demonstrates the oneness of all Buddhas; this single principle is the truth.
Regarding the three layers within Śākyamuni’s exposition of the Three Vehicles:

first, the line "Addressing the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas" constitutes one verse. This serves as the purpose for Śākyamuni’s exposition of the Three Vehicles for the sake of those of the two vehicles; specifically, it is directed first toward those among the followers of the two vehicles whose attachment to views is heavy.
The second section, "The Buddha, through the power of skillful means, reveals the teachings of the Three Vehicles," this half-line specifically addresses Śākyamuni’s opening of the three paths.

The third section, "Sentient beings are attached everywhere; he leads them so they may emerge [from suffering]," this half-verse explains the intent behind Śākyamuni’s bestowal of the three: it is solely because sentient beings encounter objects and become fixated on them, giving rise to defilement everywhere, that the Tathāgata establishes provisional expedients to guide and transform them.
This concludes the brief explanation of opening up the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, which ends with the arising of doubt due to the movement of attachment.

From the passage, "At that time, among the great assembly there were various śrāvakas," down to the end of the section where he earnestly requests three times, there are four parts explaining the causes; this current section is the second, wherein the sentiments of the assembly harbor doubts and thus bring forth their request.
Within this section, there are two parts:

first, from "At that time, within the great assembly" down to "yet now we do not know where this meaning leads," the author first clarifies that the sūtra’s narrator introduces the fact that the great assembly harbors doubts.

The second section, from "At that time, Śāriputra knew that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts and that he himself had not yet fully understood" up to the third request, is designated as "Śāriputra Properly Conveying the Doubts and Submitting the Request."

Since the Buddha has already taught that he employs the power of skillful means to manifest the teachings of the three vehicles, yet previously did not state that the three vehicles are themselves skillful means, while now suddenly proclaims that the three vehicles are skillful means—this contradicts what was said before. For this reason, Śāriputra raises his doubts and requests a definitive resolution from the Great Sage.
Furthermore, within the scribe’s introduction concerning the doubts of the great assembly, there are two sections:
first, from "At that time, among the great assembly were various śrāvakas" up to "upāsakas and upāsikās," is designated as the scribe’s introduction citing those beings who harbor doubts.

The second section, from "Each had this thought" down to "yet now we do not know where this meaning leads," explicitly presents the points of doubt; these points of doubt concern the two types of knowledge.

Furthermore, within these two sections, each is further divided into two parts. Regarding the introduction by the compiler of the sutra, there are two types of those in the assembly who harbor doubts:
first, the mention of the "one thousand two hundred people," which refers to the doubts held by those beyond training (aśaikṣa);

second, the passage from "and those who have resolved upon the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha" up to "the laywomen (upāsikā)," which sets forth the doubts held by those still in training (śaikṣa).
Within the second section, "Resolving Doubts," there are two parts.
First, from "each had this thought" down to "that which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot attain," the initial doubt is raised: why did the Buddha previously praise the two types of wisdom?
This doubt arises from the first section, which begins with the praise of the two types of wisdom and provides a preliminary opening of the central theme.

The second section, from "The Buddha spoke of the single meaning of liberation" down to "yet we do not know where this meaning leads," clarifies that the great assembly themselves doubted whether the liberation they had attained was ultimate.
"Is it not ultimate?
This doubt arises from the second [section], which clearly distinguishes the three and reveals the one.
Furthermore, regarding the first doubt within the Buddha’s praise of the two wisdoms, there are two parts:

First, "Each [of them] thought: 'Why does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise skillful means? This doubt concerns the aforementioned praise by Śākyamuni for provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna).

The preceding section praised Śākyamuni’s provisional wisdom; when it stated, "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables," one might also wonder why the preceding praise of Śākyamuni’s ultimate wisdom was omitted, though the text is merely abbreviated and does not state it explicitly.

The second section, beginning with "And he spoke these words: 'The Dharma attained by the Buddhas is profound and subtle,'" expresses doubt regarding the previous praise of the two kinds of wisdom of the Buddhas; this sentence specifically expresses doubt regarding the praise of the Buddhas' *tathatājñāna* (ultimate wisdom), as the preceding passage stated: "He addressed Śāriputra: 'The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.'"

Regarding the phrase "The intent of what is spoken is difficult to know," this addresses the doubt concerning the previous praise of the Buddhas' wisdom of skillful means; for it was previously stated that "the gateways of their wisdom are difficult to understand and difficult to enter, such that they cannot be known by any śrāvakas. This present sentence corresponds to that.
"The Buddha speaks of the single meaning of liberation. Below this is the second [section], which directly addresses the doubt as to whether what has been attained is ultimate or not ultimate.

This doubt arises solely from the preceding second [section], where it was clearly explained that "within the One, there are three," and it was stated above: "The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, reveals the teachings of the Three Vehicles."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, from "The Buddha spoke of the meaning of the single liberation" down to "reaching nirvana," which first sets forth the point of doubt;
second, "But now I do not know where this meaning leads," which explicitly clarifies the arising of the doubt.

Now, first we shall explain the two kinds of fruits for those of the three vehicles: first, the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*), and second, the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*). The conditioned fruit consists of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). To illuminate the causes of the triple world and realize their total exhaustion is the knowledge of exhaustion; to no longer undergo future existence is the knowledge of non-arising.

The second is the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*): when those of the three vehicles have exhausted the causes of the triple world, this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; when they have exhausted the fruits of the triple world, this is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

However, these two kinds of unconditioned phenomena exist at one and the same time; the exhaustion of the cause is precisely the time of the exhaustion of the fruit, and the time of the exhaustion of the fruit is the time of the exhaustion of the cause.

Nevertheless, according to the convenience of the meaning, one may speak of a sequence; one may say that "because the cause is exhausted, the fruit is exhausted," but one cannot say that "because the fruit is exhausted, the cause is exhausted."
The questioner said:

"If you say that when the causes are exhausted, the effects are exhausted, then why does the *rūpakāya* (physical body) of an Arhat not perish at the very moment the causes of the three realms are severed through the cultivation of the Path?"
The commentator says: "This reward body (saṃbhogakāya) is so called because it comes to an end spontaneously through the residual force of its causes.
It is like a wheel being turned by means of a staff; though one metaphorically says that the wheel continues to turn even when the staff has ceased, [the momentum remains]."
"The Arhat has exhausted the causes of the three realms; thus, at this time, the residual force of the retribution-body is like a wheel.
The questioner said:
"The liberation of the three families is of one and the same grade; there should not be three different vehicles to receive distinct designations."
The commentator says:

"The reason why the liberation of the three families is of one and the same grade is that they equally take as their object the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) state wherein the causes and effects of the three realms are exhausted. Since this unconditioned state is not distinct, they are all designated as 'one liberation'."

Regarding the parable of the three vehicles and the movement based on the relative superiority or inferiority [of their causes]: this is according to the length or brevity of their functional power. The Śrāvaka, having exhausted all the active afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, is compared to the sheep-cart; the Pratyekabuddha, who has eliminated a small portion of the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), is compared to the deer-cart; and the Bodhisattva, who has completely severed the habit-energies, is compared to the ox-cart.
The questioner spoke again:
"Since there are degrees of superiority and inferiority in the severing of delusions, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) must likewise be unequal. The commentator replied:
"In the past, when establishing their doctrines, [the masters] did not say that one takes birth due to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
nor did they establish the fruit of cessation at the point where habitual tendencies are exhausted, even though such exhaustion occurs.

Nevertheless, all three schools alike take the point where the causes and effects of the triple world are exhausted as the locus for establishing the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*). As for their liberation, the three schools are equal."
Regarding its function, there are distinctions between broad and narrow, as well as differences in length.

To use an analogy, it is like the three vehicles; thus, it is said that the Buddha taught the single meaning of liberation. This liberation consists of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder), which is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*); by citing the fruit, the cause is clarified. In the past, relying on the Buddha's teaching, I practiced the Truth of the Path and realized the fruit of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). Therefore, it is said that the Buddha spoke of the single meaning of liberation, and we too have attained this meaning and reached *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase, "From this point on, I do not know where this meaning leads," the second part correctly clarifies the arising of doubt: "Now I do not know whether the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) practiced by me in the past leads solely to this fruit of liberation?"
"Is there something further toward which he is heading?
All that precedes this is the sūtra-author's narration of the intent of their doubt.

"At that time, Śāriputra knew that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts and that he himself had not yet attained full understanding. From here downward, until the point where [the Buddha] returns after the third request, is the second section clarifying how Śāriputra voices his doubts and makes his petition.
Within this request, there are naturally two sections:

first, from "Śāriputra knew that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts in their hearts and that he himself had not yet fully understood," which clarifies the sūtra author’s introduction to Śāriputra’s intention in voicing his doubts and desiring to make a formal request.
The second section, from "Then he addressed the Buddha" down to the end of the three requests, is designated as the "Formal Request.
Furthermore, within the introduction provided by the compiler of the sutra, there are two parts:
first, the statement "Śāriputra knew that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts"; this is the compiler's introduction indicating that Śāriputra intended to voice the doubts of the great multitude.
The second statement, "I myself have not yet understood," clarifies that the Sūtra author describes Śāriputra as harboring his own doubts.

Within the second section, the formal request, there are five stages: Śāriputra makes three requests and the Tathāgata twice refuses them; these alternating exchanges between guest and host constitute the five stages.
Regarding Śāriputra’s three requests:
the first was a request made by raising a doubt; the second was a request because those of sharp faculties would certainly believe; and the third was a request because he possessed understanding.
Regarding the first inquiry, there are two parts:
first, the prose, and second, the verse.
Furthermore, within the prose itself, there are three layers:

The first doubt concerns the praise of the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas; the second doubt concerns the repeated request of the assembly for an explanation; and the third doubt concerns the praise of Śākyamuni’s two kinds of wisdom.

Now, the first doubt regarding the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas is expressed in the passage: “He addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘For what cause and by what condition do you praise the foremost skillful means of all Buddhas? This, then, is the doubt concerning the praise of the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas.
From the phrase "the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma," this first section praises the profundity of the Buddhas' true wisdom.

From the phrase "Since I have never before heard such a teaching from a Buddha, and now the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts, I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter," this constitutes the second section, wherein the assembly reiterates their doubts and requests the teaching.

From the passage, "Why does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma," this is the third doubt concerning the true wisdom (bhūtajñāna) praised by Śākyamuni. There should likewise be a doubt regarding expedient wisdom (upāyajñāna), though it is omitted from the sūtra text for brevity; since it appears in the subsequent verses, one knows it must have been present in the prose (gadya). However, in the preceding narrative of the sūtra compiler, the doubt regarding expedient wisdom is mentioned while the true wisdom is not, as they are cited alternately to clarify the meaning.
"At that time, Śāriputra spoke in verse. Regarding the first section, the formal invitation, there are two parts: the prose and the verse. What follows is the second part;
the verses consist of eleven lines in total and are further divided into two sections.

The first six and a half lines of verse directly recite the preceding prose. The second section, beginning with "Among all the śrāvakas, the Buddha says I am foremost," consists of four and a half lines of verse which directly express his own doubts regarding what he has attained, rather than reciting the preceding prose.
Some explain it as follows:

"These four lines and a half of verse serve to praise the preceding prose passage, 'The Buddha spoke of the single meaning of liberation,' for the phrasing of 'We too have attained this Dharma and reached Nirvana' is analogous [to the verse]."
I do not think this is so. How is this known?
In the preceding prose section, it was the Sūtra compiler who recorded that at that time the assembly had such doubts; how then could Śāriputra be said to be versifying the compiler’s intent?
Therefore, it is known that this is merely a direct exposition in verse.
Within the prose commentary on these six and a half stanzas, there are originally three parts:
first, doubting the two types of wisdom of all Buddhas; second, repeatedly doubting the request by the assembly for an explanation; and third, doubting the actual wisdom of Śākyamuni.

Now, within these six and a half lines, the first two and a half lines are a verse summary of the third section; the next line is a retrospective verse summary of the first; and the final three lines are a verse summary of the second section.

The first two and a half lines of verse previously versified the third section concerning the two kinds of wisdom of Śākyamuni; now, with the line "The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, after a long time has finally preached this Dharma," the following one and a half lines of verse correctly versify the doubt regarding Śākyamuni’s ultimate wisdom.

Regarding the meaning of this verse, "The Dharma obtained at the site of enlightenment," there is a doubt concerning the provisional wisdom mentioned above; the doubt asks: why is this wisdom praised yet not explained?

Regarding the "Spontaneous Utterance Without Being Questioned," this second verse is a reversal of the first statement above, which asked, "For what reason do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma? While the prose section does not reveal the past causes of the Buddhas, this current verse provides those past causes in its first half and then correctly versifies [the original question] in its second half.

"Those Arhats free from outflows and those seeking nirvāṇa"—the three verses below this constitute the third section, which reiterates the second section above where the assembly, having raised doubts, requested an explanation. Since it was stated above that "I have never before heard such a Dharma from the Buddha," and now the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts, it is known that these three verses are a direct restatement of that point.

There are two parts above: the first verse introduces the request for instruction by the śrāvakas, while the second part, beginning with "Those who seek pratyekabuddhahood," introduces the request for instruction by the pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the statement, "Among all the śrāvakas, the Buddha has declared me to be the foremost," the following four and a half verses constitute the second part of this section; they are titled "Verses Directly Expressing One's Own Doubts Regarding What Has Been Attained."
These four and a half lines consist of two parts.

First, regarding the line "Among all the śrāvakas, the Buddha declares me to be foremost," the following one and a half verses clarify Śāriputra’s own doubt concerning what he has attained: whether it is definitively the cause or definitively the fruit.
The second section, from the three lines of verse beginning with “sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth,” formally concludes the request for the teaching.

The passage below, starting with “At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: ‘Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further,’ ” constitutes the second segment. Within this, the first instance of “stop, stop” intends to convey that if these two types of wisdom were explained in detail, the assembly would collectively give rise to feelings of alarm and doubt; for this reason, there is no need to speak further.

"Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: 'I only pray that you will speak of it; I only pray that you will speak of it. This section below constitutes the second part of the third segment, wherein he requests the teaching because those of sharp faculties will certainly believe. From here on, each of the three segments consists of two parts: a prose passage (*dīrgha-paṅkti*) and a verse (*gāthā*).

Now, [Śāriputra] intends to say: "All those in this assembly possess sharp faculties and are capable of hearing the Buddha’s teaching; why then do you speak of them being startled and filled with doubt?

The passage beginning with "The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra from speaking of this matter" constitutes the fourth section, the second instance of a prohibition. Its meaning is as follows: "If I were to speak of the two kinds of wisdom—the provisional and the ultimate—the members of the assembly would not only give rise to hearts of shock and doubt, but would further produce slander and fall into the evil realms. How, then, should I speak of it?"
"At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I only pray that you will speak!
I only pray that you will speak! This is the third request within the fifth section; it is a request made because there is an understanding [of the teaching]."

"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: 'Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak? From this point down to the end of the *Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training*, there are seven chapters and a half of scripture. These clarify the four original sections of the sutra within the causal stage; what follows here is the third section, the extensive exposition for revealing the One by opening up the Three, thereby severing doubts and engendering faith."
In the preceding inquiry, there were two kinds of doubt:
first, the doubt concerning why the Tathāgata praised the two types of wisdom; second, the doubt concerning the dharma he himself had attained.
Now, the Tathāgata has answered only the second doubt; once this second doubt is removed, it need not be answered separately.

Furthermore, this third section is an expansion of the first part of the "Brief Opening of Three to Reveal One" from the preceding chapter, specifically the section concerning the movement of attachments and the arising of doubt.

Previously, it was explained that the first and second [sections] each open into two, while the third and fourth each open into three. Now, regarding the praise of the third [section], the presence of three layers within the doubt refers to the transformation of individuals with the three faculties into three stages:

The first stage begins from "You have already earnestly requested three times" and extends through the second fascicle to the passage: "Whatever meritorious deeds I possess, whether in this life or past lives, and all the merit of seeing the Buddha, I dedicate entirely toward the Buddha-way. This is designated as the "Dharma-exposition opening of three to reveal one," which transforms individuals of superior faculties such as Śāriputra.
The second section, from "At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!

I now have no further doubt or regret, for I have personally received the prediction of *samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha," through the end of the four chapters up to the "Chapter on Receiving Predictions," is designated as the "Explanatory Teaching Opening the Three and Revealing the One. It is intended to transform those of middle capacity, namely the four great disciples including Kāśyapa and Subhūti.

The third section consists of three chapters of scripture, beginning from the end of the "Parable of the City of Illusion" and extending through the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training. These are designated as the teaching on past-life causes and conditions, which reveals the principle of the three vehicles being one and returning to a single source, thereby transforming those of inferior faculties such as Pūrṇa.
Thus, those of superior faculties, upon hearing the teaching on the meaning of the three-in-one, immediately understand the principle that all paths lead to the same goal;
those of middling faculties, by hearing the meaning of the three-in-one a second time, can awaken to the principle of the common convergence;
and those of inferior faculties must hear the teaching three times before they finally understand that there is no distinction between the three and that they all return to the same source.
However, within the discourse on the Dharma, there is also the meaning of metaphorical discourse, such as the example of the udumbara flower.
There is also the meaning of discourse on past-life causes and conditions, namely the statement: "In the past, I constantly taught and transformed you in the presence of two hundred billion Buddhas."
Although there are parables and explanations, the fundamental main intent is to praise the rarity of the Dharma; thus, it cannot be pointed out or designated.

Although there are accounts of past-life causes and conditions, these merely serve to confirm the realization attained by those of superior faculties; the fundamental main intent of recounting these ancient causes and conditions is not itself the actual cause and condition.

In the second parable, there is both the meaning of the Dharma-exposition and the meaning of past-life causal conditions; therefore, it is stated below that "all these teachings are for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas," which constitutes the meaning of the Dharma-exposition.

However, the phrasing is somewhat insufficient to inspire those of middling capacity. Within the context of the karmic connection between father and son, it was already indicated at the previous seat of Prajñā that there were gold, silver, and so forth; this constitutes the meaning of the discourse on past-life causes and conditions. Yet, this intention is not present within the primary parable itself. At that time, the assembly had already attained realization through the primary parable—just as the impoverished son gained understanding—and it was only upon his realization that these words were spoken; they do not belong to the formal exposition of past-life causes and conditions.

Within the discourse on past-life causes and conditions, there is also an exposition of the Dharma through its underlying meaning; specifically, at the beginning of the "Parable of the Phantom City" (Pūrṇamukha-parivarta), the description of the signs of spiritual resonance through the supernormal powers during the time of previous Buddhas, and the invitation by the Brahmās of the ten directions to turn the Wheel of Dharma—this constitutes the exposition of the Dharma.

Furthermore, the statement "For example, five hundred yojanas" is a metaphorical explanation; although this proclamation is made, its fundamental purpose is solely to clarify the meaning of karmic causes and conditions from past lives.
How is this known?

Furthermore, at the end of the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Four Great Disciples," it says: "I shall now speak of the causes and conditions from our past lives, you and I; listen well! Thereupon, he spoke again for the sake of those of inferior faculties, explaining that in ancient times, he had already transformed them through the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, it says below: "I was among you sixteen [disciples] and have previously taught this for you; because of these original causes and conditions, I now preach the Lotus Sūtra. The general meaning is that one only attains understanding upon hearing this account of past-life causes and conditions; therefore, it is called the "Account of Past-Life Causes and Conditions."

Regarding the reason why there are distinctions among people according to their three faculties and differences in the sequence of their understanding: setting aside the arguments of the teachings and logic, how could it be possible that an Arhat—who has exhausted all afflictions (*āsrava*) of the three realms and attained the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—would fail to understand the principle that [all beings] ultimately return to the same essence, and thus remain ignorant of the distinction between those who possess the Three Refuges and those who do not? Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If a person does not know the single essence of the eternally abiding Triple Refuge, they shall not even attain the stages of Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Bodhisattva; how much less could they attain unsurpassed *bodhi*?"
"If one does not know that the Buddha is eternally abiding, then the fourfold faith will not be accomplished and the five faculties will not be established.
Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"Those who have begun their practice in the three vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma."
Furthermore, it is said: "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know for themselves that they abide on the stage with remainder, yet they will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.

Discussing this according to principle, how could the noble ones of the three vehicles cling to the certainty of their respective vehicles as being distinct, failing to understand that they all converge in the same destination?

If that is so, as for why there are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is because these individuals themselves recognize that the fruit of Buddhahood is to be sought; yet, their own mental resolve is weak and they are unable to renounce their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains to give rise to the mind of vast salvation. Thus, they temporarily act as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to discipline and deliver themselves. Such categories of beings all truly exist.

Now, within this assembly, Śāriputra represents those of superior capacity, while Pūrṇa and others represent those of inferior capacity. If one speaks according to their actual practice, they all practice the secret bodhisattva path internally while manifesting as śrāvakas externally. As for why there are these three types of realization through faith and understanding, they all appear outwardly to be like ordinary persons of shallow knowledge; thus, they adhere to the former teachings on the distinct vehicles of the Three Vehicles or the principle that they ultimately converge. For this reason, the Tathāgata established these three types [of teaching]. At the conclusion of the initial "Teaching by Dharma," those among the external ordinary persons with sharp faculties attained understanding, and Śāriputra manifested as if he had likewise attained it.

When the "Parable" section was concluded, those among the external ordinary persons with middling faculties attained understanding, and Subhūti and others likewise manifested as if they had attained it.

The section on past-life causes and conditions concludes; among those of the outer stage of ordinary beings, those of inferior capacity attain awakening, while Pūrṇa and others manifest as if they have merely attained understanding.
If one sets aside the principle (*li*) to discuss the teaching (*jiao*), even those who have fully attained the state of an Arhat may still harbor such attachments.

Furthermore, if one discusses the principle and the teaching together to establish the distinctions among the three faculties (*indriya*), there are only two types of persons among the external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*):
one type of person is easily turned back, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the stage of "light fur" (*laghupakṣman*).
There is a certain class of people who truly desire to advance.

Now, based solely on the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of those who truly desire to advance, there are three types. Since these three types all arise from the density or thinness of their past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they either confuse principle with teaching or sometimes confuse teaching with principle; thus, it is said that they "hesitate between principle and teaching," and consequently, their realization occurs earlier or later.

Those of sharp faculties have a strong inclination toward grasping at principles and a weak inclination toward doubting the teachings; those of dull faculties have a strong inclination toward grasping at the teachings and a weak inclination toward doubting the principles; those of middling faculties are equally deluded regarding both the teachings and the principles.

Regarding those who cling to principle while harboring many doubts about the teachings: they say that since the principle of non-arising is one, the wisdom that equally contemplates non-arising should likewise be identical.
Since these individuals hold that the principle is one, they wonder why the Tathāgata speaks of three distinct vehicles and three distinct fruits; this is what is meant by doubting the teachings.

Those of dull faculties who cling to the teachings and have many doubts regarding the principles may ask: "Since the Buddha’s teachings state that there are differences between the three causes and three fruits, why must the principle of non-arising observed by the three vehicles be identical?"
This refers to those who cling to the teachings and harbor many doubts while having little understanding of the principle.

Among those of middling capacity, there are times when they cling to the principle and are confused by the teachings, saying: "Since the principle is one, how can the teachings be said to be different?

There are also times when they cling to the teachings and doubt the principle, saying: "Since the Buddha’s teachings already comprise three [vehicles], why must the principle necessarily be the same?"
This refers to harboring doubts based on attachment to either the teachings or the principles.

Now, attaining the Way and becoming a sage must necessarily proceed from the vision of principle; therefore, those of sharp faculties who are largely attached to principle accord with that principle. Consequently, upon hearing the Dharma once, they immediately awaken to the single principle that is without the distinction of three.

Those who are largely attached to the teachings and harbor many doubts while having little grasp of principle do not find their views supported by the principle; consequently, it is only after hearing the teaching three times that they finally awaken to the principle of the One Vehicle which is without the distinction of three.
Those who hold views based on both principle and teaching are situated in the intermediate state and attain understanding upon hearing it again.
However, those who give rise to doubt regarding this principle and teaching include both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, there are those who cling to the teaching and doubt the fruit, of whom there are also three types:

those of sharp faculties have a strong inclination toward clinging to the fruit and a weak inclination toward doubting the teaching; those of dull faculties have a strong inclination toward clinging to the teaching and a weak inclination toward doubting the fruit; and those of middling faculties cling equally to both the fruit and the teaching.

The "fruit" is merely the nirvana of cessation. For those of sharp faculties whose minds are more attached to the fruit and have less doubt regarding the teachings, they personally observe the principle with clear wisdom and see that habitual tendencies still remain; knowing that the severing of delusions is not yet complete, they wonder: "Will my future body be utterly extinguished?"
This refers to those who are attached to the result and have much doubt regarding the teaching, while having little confidence in their own minds;

those of dull faculties who are attached to the teaching and have much doubt regarding the result [think]: "Since it has been said that the divine spirit may be extinguished and that the Buddha’s words are not false, how could one dare not to believe and accept them?"
This is an abundance of adherence to teachings;
it is not yet known whether the Way of the Divine and the Intelligent truly ceases or not—
this is a scarcity of doubt regarding the fruit.

Those of middling capacity may either cling to the fruit while doubting the teaching, or cling to the teaching while doubting the fruit; however, those who harbor doubts specifically regarding the fruit are exclusively those beyond training (aśaikṣas).

Although there are these three types of doubt and clinging, when the three are opened to reveal the one, they are identical. Once the teaching has been fully delivered, they all equally attain awakening and understanding; there is only a difference in sequence and phrasing.
Regarding the first teaching for those of superior faculties, there are four sections within it:
the first, from "You have already earnestly requested three times" to the end of this fascicle, is designated as the teaching of the True Dharma for those of superior faculties.

The second section, from the beginning of the prose and verse of the second fascicle, clarifies how those of superior capacity, such as Śāriputra and others, manifest their understanding in accordance with the teaching.
The third section, from "At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra" onwards, clarifies the manner in which the Tathāgata confirms the realization attained by those of superior capacity.
The fourth section, beginning from "In future kalpas you... and below, bestows predictions upon those of superior faculties.

Furthermore, each of these four sections is divided into two parts; within the first part, which concerns the teaching and transformation of those of superior faculties through the preaching of the True Dharma, there are two sub-sections. The first, beginning from "You have already earnestly requested three times" and continuing through one hundred and fourteen verses, is designated as the teaching and transformation of those of superior faculties through the preaching of the True Dharma.

Since those of superior faculties have already understood that the principle of returning to the same destination is without the distinction of three vehicles, their doubts have been removed. Therefore, the seven lines of verse beginning with "You, Śāriputra, whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas" briefly exhort and encourage those of superior faculties to accept and practice the principle of returning to the same destination.
Furthermore, within these two sections, there are each two types. Regarding the exposition of the True Dharma (saddharma), the two types are the prose (gadya) and the verse (śloka).

Within the second set of seven verses of exhortation, there are two parts: first, five and a half verses exhort those of superior faculties to practice the cause; second, the remaining one and a half verses exhort them to aspire toward the fruit, stating, "The mind gives rise to great joy, knowing for itself that it shall become a Buddha," and so forth.
Furthermore, within the prose section itself, there are two parts:
first, from "You have already earnestly requested three times" up to "I wish to hear it with joy," which is designated as the *nidāna* (circumstantial origin) of the Dharma discourse.
The second section, from "The Buddha said to Śāriputra: 'Such is this wondrous Dharma'" onwards through the prose (*gadya*), is designated as the Exposition of the True Dharma (*saddharma-deśanā*).

Furthermore, within these two sections there are each two parts. Regarding the two parts within the introductory context (*nidāna*): first, the Buddha grants permission to explain the principle that all paths lead to the same destination and the meaning that there are not three vehicles; second, "Śāriputra said: 'So be it, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear it,'" which is designated as Śāriputra’s acceptance of the mandate.
Now, within the first of these [four] permissions granted by the Buddha, there are four layers:

first, the formal permission; second, the injunction to listen attentively; third, the delimitation of the assembly; and fourth, the praise of the assembly worthy of hearing, which serves as a concluding summary of the injunction and permission.
“Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak? This is the first [section], designated as the formal granting of permission.

“Now listen attentively” and below is the second [section], designated as the admonition to listen attentively; this serves to generate the three types of wisdom: by admonishing attentive listening to the teaching, it generates the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
by admonishing careful reflection, it generates the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
"Exhort them to mindfulness so that they may give rise to cultivated wisdom and understanding.

Regarding the passage, "When these words were spoken, five thousand people in the assembly prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew," this is the third instance of distinguishing the assembly. By the Buddha’s spiritual power, those capable of hearing [the teaching] remained, while those incapable departed;

there are four parts to this: first, the explicit clarification that five thousand people prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew; second, the section beginning with "For what reason? which explains their incapacity to hear; and regarding "claiming to have attained what one has not attained," this refers to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) upon the exhaustion of conditioned fruits (*saṃskṛta-phala*).
"Claiming realization when one has not realized" refers to the state of the exhaustion of the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
The third section, "There is such a fault," concludes that [the opponent] is incapable [of the task].
The fourth section, "The World-Honored One remained silent," serves as proof that [the assembly] was incapable [of receiving the teaching].
"He addressed Śāriputra: 'In this assembly of mine now... constitutes the fourth part of the Buddha’s consent, which summarizes and exhorts the assembly by praising them.
Within this section itself, there are three parts:

first, from "Addressing Śāriputra" onwards, it praises the capacity of those who remain; second, from "Such are those of overweening pride" onwards, it clarifies the lack of capacity in those who depart; third, from "You should now listen well" onwards, it provides the formal conclusion.
The questioner said:

"The Tathāgata possesses the two secrets of body and speech; throughout the day he remains seated, yet one does not behold his true countenance, and though one is in his presence, one does not hear him preach the Dharma. Why, then, must he rise from his seat and sweep away the mats before departing?"
The commentator says:

"In this chapter, it is appropriate for the assembly at that time; furthermore, it may be understood as the Buddha’s actual exercise of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*). Intending to praise some members of the assembly and censure others, he causes those who remain to give rise to a mind of reverence and a sense of aspiration, while those who are censured lose the opportunity to hear the Dharma; therefore, they sweep their seats and depart."

Śāriputra said, “Indeed, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear it. Within the *Nidāna* (the introductory section), there are two parts: the first concludes with the Buddha’s granting of permission, and this second part clarifies Śāriputra’s acceptance of that permission.
"The Buddha told Śāriputra: 'Such is this wondrous Dharma. In the prose section (*gadya*), there are originally two parts:
first, the introductory narrative (*nidāna*); second, the formal exposition of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).
From here below is the second part, the formal exposition of the Dharma.
Within the exposition of the True Dharma itself, there are two parts:
first, the broad elucidation of the gates of all Buddhas; second, the broad elucidation of the gate of Śākyamuni.

From the passage "This wondrous Dharma" onwards, the first part broadly clarifies the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one for all Buddhas; this is an extensive treatment of the initial praise of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—of all Buddhas found at the beginning of the preceding chapter.

The reason it is called "extensive" is that, in the first section above, "Faintly Opening the Fundamental Tenet," there was a direct and general praise of the two wisdoms of all Buddhas, stating: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter."
In the second part, the "Brief Explanation," it clarifies only one point, stating: "World-Honored One, after a long time, you must surely speak the truth.
Since this merely offers a general praise of the two wisdoms of all Buddhas without distinguishing them individually, and further clarifies only one point, it is called "brief."
Now, the Buddha is extensively elucidated and his meaning is also extensively elucidated; therefore, it is called "extensive.

Regarding the extensive elucidation of the Buddha: herein, all Buddhas are extensively presented both collectively and individually throughout the three periods of time; thus, the meaning of the extensive elucidation of the Buddha is profound.

Furthermore, regarding the "extensive meaning" (*guǎngyì*): previously, there was a direct praise of the two wisdoms of the Buddhas to manifest their unity; here, however, there are four further meanings, which together with the former make six. First, praising the rarity of the Dharma; second, clarifying that it is not false to stop the slander of sentient beings;

third, clarifying the opening of the three [vehicles]; fourth, clarifying the manifestation of the one; fifth, citing the five turbidities to explain the intent behind first teaching the three and later the one; sixth, distinguishing the true from the false to encourage faith. Since these six meanings are complete, it is called the "extensive meaning. Second, regarding the "extensive explanation of the Śākyamuni gate": this extensively explains the initial, approximate opening of the school and the praise of Śākyamuni’s two wisdoms in the preceding chapter, as well as the meaning of opening the three [vehicles] within the second section on the clear and concise explanation.
Within the gate of Śākyamuni, there is only the broad meaning, but there is no broad Buddha.
Now, it is clarified that within the gates of all Buddhas, four distinct categories naturally arise:
first, a general clarification of how all Buddhas open the three [vehicles] to reveal the one.
Second, by departing from the general category of all Buddhas to specifically address the Buddhas of the past, it clarifies the principle of "opening the three and revealing the one";
third, by departing from the general category of all Buddhas to specifically address the Buddhas of the future, it likewise clarifies the meaning of "opening the three and revealing the one";
fourth, by departing from the general category of all Buddhas to specifically address the Buddhas of the present, it clarifies "opening the three and revealing the one."
Now, first we clarify the general gateway of all Buddhas; herein there should be six points: first, praising the rarity of the Dharma;
second, clarifying its non-falsity; third, clarifying the opening of the three; fourth, clarifying the manifestation of the one meaning.

However, the phrasing is brief and contains only four points; it omits the explanation for why the five turbidities are presented first and the One Vehicle last—a point which only appears in the verses—and likewise lacks a distinction between the true and the false, as well as an exhortation to faith, both of which are omitted.
In the section explaining the gate of Śākyamuni, it can be understood that all six meanings are fully present; however, they are not explicitly set forth because the wording is abbreviated.

Now, when it says, "This wondrous Dharma is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare times, just as the udumbara flower appears but once in a long while," this is the first praise of the rarity of the Dharma.

"Udumbara" is a foreign term; in this land it is called the "Auspiciously Omenous Flower. Only when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world does this flower exist; thus one knows that this flower is rare, and this sutra is likewise so."

“Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are without falsehood. This is the second [point], clarifying that there is no falsehood to prevent others from slandering [the teaching].

From the passage, "Śāriputra, the underlying intentions of what all Buddhas teach according to their suitability are difficult to understand," this is the third section clarifying the opening of the three vehicles.
Within this opening of the three, there are naturally three layers of textual passages:

first, the formal clarification that all Buddhas open the three; second, from the passage, "For what reason? By means of countless skillful expedients," which follows, this cites Śākyamuni Buddha and other Buddhas opening the three.

Why is this? First, because Śākyamuni is counted among the number of all Buddhas; second, because the *Benming* (Fundamental Clarification) explains that the opening of the three [vehicles] by all Buddhas is for the purpose of accomplishing the opening of the three by Śākyamuni.
Third, the statement "only the Buddhas can know this" again cites the Buddhas to conclude the meaning of the Buddhas' opening of the three.

Why is this so? Regarding the passage, “The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do so solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition,” the following section constitutes the fourth [section], which reveals the One.

This “why” serves to explain the meaning of the aforementioned opening of the Three; as for the text itself, it belongs to the subsequent revelation of the One, providing a detailed exposition of the fourfold Oneness: first, the Oneness of the Fruit; second, the Oneness of the Person; third, the Oneness of the Cause; and fourth, the Oneness of the Teaching.

"Clarifying the oneness of the fruit" means that the three fruits of former days are ultimately realized as the single fruit of today; "clarifying the oneness of the person" means that the three types of persons of former days become the single person of a Bodhisattva today; "clarifying the oneness of the teaching" means that the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles of former days become the single teaching of today; and "clarifying the oneness of the cause" means that the practices performed by those of the Three Vehicles of former days constitute but a single cause, corresponding to the single fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, it is said: "The path you practice is the Bodhisattva path."

Among these, there are four "ones" and one "two. Within the two types of wisdom, it is true wisdom that illuminates the object. Regarding the four "ones," there are both commonalities and differences in their meaning. In true wisdom, the illuminated object possesses the "one" of the organic capacity (*indriya*), whereas here [in the context of the four], there is no such "one" of organic capacity. As for why there are four, they are derived by dividing the single principle of oneness into two kinds: the oneness of the cause and the oneness of the fruit.

However, both cause and effect are principles; thus, in that [previous] passage, the unity of the capacity (the *mārga*) was clarified. As for why the unity of the capacity is not clarified here, it is because the previous section clarified the unity of the capacity, whereas this section clarifies the objects illuminated by the two wisdoms (*jñāna*).

In this context, it is explained that the three are unified into one; however, if we were to consider their remote causal origins, one might also argue that the three capacities [of sentient beings] should likewise be unified into a single capacity. Yet, these three capacities are in fact the inherent dharmas of sentient beings themselves, and thus they cannot be unified into one. As for the remaining cases of "three becoming one," these refer to the Buddhas of the past responding to the three capacities; they merely used provisional names to divide the one into three. Now that the capacity for the One Vehicle has matured, the three can indeed be merged and returned to the one.
In this context, the "unity of the teaching" (*ekayāna*) as it is illuminated by actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) differs from the "unity of the teaching" as a mere verbal instruction.

How is this known? The "unity of the teaching" illuminated by actual wisdom refers directly to the illumination of the *Dharmapada-sūtra* (the Lotus Sūtra) as the unity of the teaching. As for the "unity of the teaching" mentioned here [in the provisional teachings], because three vehicles were provisionally established in accordance with the capacities of three types of beings in the past, these three teachings were not one. These three teachings distantly expound today’s single principle; therefore, the convergence of the three provisional teachings of the past ultimately results in today’s single teaching.
In this context, it is clarified that the person who is the subject and the person who is the object illumined by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) are not the same. How is this known?

The object illumined by true wisdom and the person have no distinct essence; because today sentient beings give rise to the wholesome capacity for the One Vehicle, and the person constituted by that single capacity is taken as the "person," all Bodhisattvas are thus collectively regarded as a single object.

Regarding "the one person herein": the capacities for the three vehicles in the past were distinct, yet the culmination achieved by them was not manifold; because the culmination achieved through the virtues of the three capacities is a single excellence and the principle is one, the three types of persons from the past ultimately become the single Bodhisattva-person of today. However, while the name "one person" given in today's teaching is the same as the name "one person" taught in relation to what is illumined by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), the meaning and intent are different.
Herein it is clarified that the "one cause and one fruit" shares the same meaning as the "one principle illumined by true wisdom," though the names differ.
Now, first, regarding the clarification of "one fruit," there are four layers within it:

first, opening the chapter on the one fruit; second, restating the chapter on the one fruit; third, providing a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi) as an explanation of the one fruit; and fourth, concluding the section on the one fruit.

Now, as for the statement, "For what reason? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition," this is the first chapter-gate that initially opens with the fruit.
“Śāriputra, what is meant by ‘all Buddhas’? This and what follows is the second section, which further restates the fruit to provide an explanation.

“The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This and what follows is the third section, which correctly provides a fourfold analysis of the fruit.
Regarding the four phrases of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering," various interpretations of these four phrases differ from one another;
the interpretation of our own school states that the first three phrases refer to the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles.
When the teaching of *prajñā* is given, it is called "showing";
when the *Anantārthasūtra* is preached, it is termed "awakening";
and when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra* is preached, it is designated as "entering."

To understand that "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*) is a name for the fruit of Buddhahood, and to take all myriad practices as the path of this house of knowledge and vision—this interpretation is also excellent.

Now, Master Guangzhai’s interpretation states: Knowledge and vision are simply the future fruit of Buddhahood for a single sentient being. Sentient beings have possessed this future fruit from the very beginning; however, since time immemorial, because the five turbidities have been so powerful and their obstacles so heavy, they have been incapable of hearing the Mahayana. For this reason, it was not preached to them that they possess this future fruit; thus, this future fruit carries the sense of being "closed."

Today, the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened; the five turbidities cannot act as obstacles. To hear today the teaching of the sutra stating that all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood is precisely the meaning of "opening."

To say that the practices undertaken by the three vehicles in the past were all practices for attaining the fruit of a single Buddha-fruit—when sentient beings hear these words, they give rise to the wisdom born of hearing; this is the meaning of "showing."

Furthermore, when those of the three vehicles contemplate and deliberate together, thinking, "In the past this was a skillful means, but now this single cause and single fruit is the reality; we shall all attain Buddhahood in the future," they deeply understand this principle. At that time, the wisdom born of reflection arises, which is designated as "awakening."

Together they realize that they have not yet reached the ultimate stage; thus, they further practice various deeds and cultivate the path of untainted purification (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa-mārga*) to sever the afflictions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). At that time, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises, which is designated as entering the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśanamārga*).

Dharma Master Guangzhai also expounded these four phrases at Shan-she Temple; he interpreted them by correlating the meaning of cause and effect to clarify the four phrases, noting that these four phrases possess the sense of gradual elimination.

Regarding the initial mention of "opening": because this is the most superficial level, it is as previously explained in brief—the opening of the three to reveal the one—which gradually expresses the meaning of the long duration of the Buddha's life and the single fruit; this is the meaning of "opening."

Furthermore, as extensively explained in the "Opening the Three to Reveal the One," which causes one to know the meaning of the single fruit of the long duration of the life-span—this is the meaning of "indicating" (*śāsana*).

Moreover, as briefly clarified later in the "Opening the Near to Reveal the Far," which causes one to know that the Tathāgata’s life-span is long and far-reaching—this is the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhana*).

Furthermore, as explained extensively later, his lifespan is vast and long, and he manifests or conceals his body throughout the ten directions to deliver sentient beings for twice that duration. At that time, the assembly together returns to this cause in order to seek the fruit of a single Buddha; the cultivation and study of these various practices is precisely what it means to "enter."
"Śāriputra, it is for this sole great cause and condition that all Buddhas appear in the world"—this is the first of the four results.
“The Buddha told Śāriputra that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas. This is the second point clarifying the unity of persons.

“Whatever they do is always for one purpose” is the third point clarifying the unity of causes; it clarifies that by cultivating this cause one attains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and therefore it is said that [the Buddhas] manifest and awaken sentient beings solely through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
“Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Below this is the fourth section, which clarifies the unity of the teaching.
Within this unity of the teaching, there are two stages:

first, the formal clarification of the unity of the teaching; second, from the passage “Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas in the ten directions is likewise,” the commonality of the paths of all Buddhas is cited to form the conclusion.

"Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past"—the following section is the second [part], clarifying how the Buddhas of the past opened up the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle. Regarding the three Buddhas discussed below, among the six meanings [of the teaching], they possess only two: namely, opening up the three to reveal the one, while lacking the other four meanings. Now, we shall first clarify the opening up of the three.

The second section, from "These dharmas are all for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle" onwards, clarifies the One; the three Buddhas mentioned below likewise each possess only the three [results] within the clarification of the One, being abbreviated by the absence of the one cause.
The initial statement, "These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle," refers to the unity of the teaching (*śāsana-ekatva*).
The subsequent statement, "These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, reach the ultimate," refers to the unity of the persons (*pudgala-ekatva*).
"All shall attain all-knowledge" (sarvākārajñatā) refers to the first fruit.
The single cause is omitted for brevity.

"Śāriputra, as for the Buddhas of the future"—the following section is the third [part], clarifying that for the Buddhas of the future there is first three and then one; herein, too, there is only the sense of opening up the three to reveal the one. Now, first, the three are opened up.

The second [point], from "These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle," reveals the oneness; herein there is only the three and the one. Now, the statement "Because these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle" constitutes the teaching of oneness.
"These sentient beings have heard the Dharma from the Buddhas to its ultimate conclusion"—this is the first [aspect] of the person.
"They all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)"—this is the first [aspect] of the fruit.
Nor is there a single cause.

"Śāriputra, the present immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in the ten directions"—the following section is the fourth part, which extensively clarifies the meaning that for all present Buddhas, there is first three and then one. This consists of only two points: opening up the three and revealing the one.
This present Buddha-gate demonstrates and explains the meaning of Śākyamuni’s “three first and one last.

Why is this? If even the Buddhas of the ten directions, who are likewise presently existing, still possess the sequence of “three first and one last,” how much more so must it be for Śākyamuni, who appeared in the five turbidities of a degenerate age, not to have followed the sequence of “three first and one last”?
Within this present dispensation of the Buddha, there are naturally three sections.

First, from "Śāriputra" up to "greatly benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings," this first clarifies the meaning of the present Buddha’s sequence of teaching the three vehicles followed by the One Vehicle.
The second section, from "These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means... onwards, correctly elucidates the opening of the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle.
The third section cites the person, the fruit, and the conclusion.
The passage beginning with "Śāriputra, there are currently immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in the ten directions" first clarifies the opening of the three vehicles.

Next, from "These dharmas are all for the sake of the single Buddha-vehicle" onwards, this reveals the one vehicle; herein, there are only three points regarding the one [vehicle]. "These dharmas are all for the sake of the single Buddha-vehicle" constitutes the "one" of the teaching.
"These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, have reached the ultimate"—this is the first "one" (the identity) of the persons.
"They all attain the knowledge of all modes"—this is the first "one" (the identity) of the fruit.
Nor is there a single cause.

From the passage, "Pūrṇa, these Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas," this is the third instance where a person and a fruit are raised together to establish the meaning of what the present Buddha has taught.
