"Śāriputra, I am now also like this. However, within the second section of the prose (長行) which correctly elucidates the teaching by means of the Dharma (法說), there are originally two parts. The preceding extensive explanation regarding how all Buddhas open the three [vehicles] to reveal the one is the extensive exposition of the two wisdoms of all Buddhas from the initial prose of the previous chapter, as well as the completion of the meaning of the Buddhas' revelation of the one within the preceding verses. What follows below is the second part, the extensive explanation of how Śākyamuni Tathāgata opens the three to reveal the one; this is the extensive exposition of the meaning of Śākyamuni's opening of the three, based upon the verses in the initial prose of the previous chapter that praise the two wisdoms of Śākyamuni.
Within this teaching of Śākyamuni, there are only five points:

first, clarifying the opening of the three vehicles; second, clarifying the manifestation of the One Vehicle; third, citing the five turbidities to explain the intent behind first establishing the three and subsequently the one; fourth, distinguishing the true from the false to encourage faith; and fifth, clarifying that this is not deceptive. There is no brief praise for the rarity of the Dharma here, as such praise appears only later in the verses.
By this standard, it should be understood that within a single Buddha-dharma gate, there must be six types of textual passages prepared to mutually illuminate one another.
"I am now likewise so" marks the first section below, which first clarifies the opening of the three [vehicles].
"Those who have various desires" refers to the beginning of the Tathāgata’s teaching, wherein each of the three vehicles has its own particular inclinations.
"That which the profound mind clings to" refers to the point at which one is finally able to practice the various deeds.
"According to their original natures" clarifies that their past habitual tendencies differ.

"Śāriputra, all these shall attain the One Buddha Vehicle"—from here below is the second [section], which reveals the One; within this, there are only three kinds of "One," as the "One of Humans" is omitted.
Now, the statement “all these are for the sake of attaining the single Buddha-vehicle” constitutes the unity of teaching;
the phrase “because of the knowledge of all modes” constitutes the unity of fruit.

"Śāriputra, even in the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions there are not two vehicles, much less three. This clarifies the cause of the "one. By saying "there are not even two vehicles," it means that there are not even the vehicle of the Bodhisattva who practices the six perfections in a partial manner or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, much less the vehicle of the Śrāvaka.
Thus we know that there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle; this clarifies the meaning of "the oneness of the cause.

The passage beginning with "Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities" constitutes the third section, which explains the emergence from the five turbidities and clarifies the intent behind Śākyamuni’s sequence of first [teaching] three and later one. It is precisely because of these five turbidities that they were unable to initially proclaim the oneness.
Within this clarification of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*), there are four sections:

first, the general proclamation of the five corruptions; second, the enumeration of the names of the five corruptions; third, the elucidation of the meaning of the corruptions; and fourth, the formal explanation and conclusion.
Now, the statement, "Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities," is the first general proclamation that there are five turbidities.
The passage beginning with "namely, the turbidity of the eon and the turbidity of afflictions" is the second part, which enumerates the names of the five turbidities in sequence.
The passage beginning with "In this way, Śāriputra, during the period of the kalpa-turbidity" clarifies the meaning of the turbidities;

the passage beginning with "The Buddhas, by the power of skillful means, within the single Buddha-vehicle" is the fourth section, which correctly explains the intent behind first teaching the three vehicles and subsequently the one vehicle.
To explain the meaning of the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*):

the five turbidities are the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). "Turbidity" (*kaṣāya*) has the meaning of being defiled and disordered.

In a general classification of these five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), there should be only the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) and the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Among the ten proclivities (*daśānuśaya*), the five dull proclivities constitute the turbidity of afflictions, while the five sharp proclivities constitute the turbidity of views; these two are the actual substance of the turbidities, whereas the others are discussed as being associated with them.

The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) and the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*) constitute the turbidity of causes; the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kāṣāya*) is the turbidity of karmic retribution; the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*) refers to the persons who obtain the fruit by practicing the cause; and the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kāṣāya*) is named as such because it pertains to the period of time. This kalpa has no separate essence other than these four types occurring within that period of time, which is why it is designated as "kalpa-turbidity. It is just as a year in which there is no food is called a "year of famine," yet the year itself is not the famine; the turbidity of the kalpa is likewise.

It is said that the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) constitute the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). These five dull afflictions arise in all directions and contend with one another, causing practitioners to become bewildered; thus they are called "turbidity.

Sentient beings take these afflictions as their cause, whereby they undergo birth in a state of disarray and without certainty within this world, transmigrating through the three realms and wandering back and forth among the six destinies, receiving births in a state of chaotic confusion. However, it is sentient beings who are the primary agents of this turbidity.

The five views constitute the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). The five views take the body as their basis; if the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) arises once, all other views compete to arise. Because they delude one from the truth and confuse the correct path, they are designated as "turbidity."
The turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) is also a turbidity of retribution.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The six persons and their six consciousnesses attaining continuous birth is termed 'lifespan. Because afflictions serve as the cause for being born within the three realms, drawing forth a lifespan that is experienced as long or short in endless confusion, it is called the turbidity of lifespan."
Since these five turbidities obstruct the capacity for the One Vehicle, they are generally categorized into three types:
the superior grade of the five turbidities corresponds to the turbidities of seeing the truths;
the middle grade corresponds to the turbidities of contemplation.
The inferior grade refers to the five turbidities of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
These three types of five turbidities all obstruct the capacity for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The questioner says:

"These three kinds of five corruptions all obstruct the capacity for the One Vehicle. If an external worldling possesses these three kinds of five corruptions, they should not hear the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, nor should they possess the capacity for the Mahāyāna."

If one considers that the five turbidities also obstruct those with the capacity for the One Vehicle, then there would be no individuals among the seven types of practitioners who possess the capacity for the One Vehicle and would be unable to hear the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

If the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the five turbidities further obstruct those with the potential for the One Vehicle, then Arhats, possessing such habitual tendencies, would likewise lack the potential for the One Vehicle and be incapable of hearing the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The commentator says: "Regarding verses of this kind, all those who have cultivated the Mahāyāna in past lives possess strong karmic conditions for the Mahāyāna; thus, even though the three types of five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) exist, they cannot act as obstacles. Conversely, those who each cultivated the Mahāyāna in past lives but whose conditions were weak may still be obstructed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the five corruptions. Now, to clarify the meaning, we shall discuss this specifically in terms of past cultivation: although ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) may possess all three types of five corruptions, if their past roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the Mahāyāna are strong, these five corruptions cannot act as obstacles. Consequently, the capacity for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) arises, making them fit to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; the same applies to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."

Because the causes and conditions for the Mahāyāna cultivated in past lives are weak, although they may practice with partiality and eliminate the *kleśas* (active afflictions), the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still remain and act as obstacles, such that the capacity for the One Vehicle does not arise.
The questioner asked:
"If all [beings] are caused by their past cultivation of the conditions for the Mahāyāna, what does this have to do with the obstacles of the five turbidities?
The commentator replied:
"Now, let me borrow an analogy to clarify the meaning of 'obstructing the capacity. What is it?

Suppose a person constantly suffers from a chronic ailment; if they are always provided with abundant food and drink, and are kept warm and comfortable at all times with cotton and fur garments as the seasons require, then although this chronic ailment remains fully present, it does not cause affliction."

If this person’s regular food and drink were insufficient and their clothing and bedding were scanty, it would allow cold and heat to take advantage of them, causing chronic ailments from the past to manifest and flare up at that time.
The internal application is likewise: if the nourishment of the roots of goodness is strong, although the perverse diseases of afflictions may exist, they do not manifest;
once the roots of goodness are weak, the perverse diseases of the five turbidities then obstruct the capacity for the One Vehicle.
However, there are three kinds of obstructions:
first, the obstruction of opposition; second, the obstruction of suppression; and third, the obstruction of opportune timing.

What is now called the "obstruction of the five turbidities to the One Vehicle" is designated as the obstruction of opportune timing; it refers simply to those instances when one seizes an opportunity to act as an obstruction.

"Śāriputra, if my disciple claims for himself to be an Arhat"—the following section constitutes the fourth [section], which distinguishes the true from the false to strengthen the faith of sentient beings; those being strengthened are already external ordinary persons (bālapṛthagjana).
Regarding this, there are two sections within the "Discerning the True from the False and Encouraging Faith":

first, the primary discernment of the true from the false; second, from the passage beginning with "Except after the Buddha's extinction" onwards, which explicitly clarifies the encouragement of others' faith.
Within these two sections, each contains three layers. Regarding the first section, which correctly distinguishes the true from the false, there are three layers:
first, clarifying what is not true; second, clarifying what is false; and third, presenting the appearance of a true Arhat as an explanation.
Now, the first section, "If among my disciples there are those who claim for themselves to have attained the state of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha," clarifies at the outset that they are not genuine.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, Śāriputra" constitutes the second part, which correctly demonstrates that these individuals are impostors.
Why is this? Because what was said was not true.

Now it is precisely clarified that this is false: the Arhatship is a fruit of superior attainment (*adhipati-phala*), yet he himself has not actually attained the fruit of Arhatship but claims to have done so. This constitutes conceit regarding a superior state; therefore, it is called "superiority-conceit" (*adhimāna*).

"Why is this so? The following section constitutes the third example of a true Arhat, which serves as a refutation of the aforementioned false claim: if there were anyone who had truly attained Arhatship and yet did not believe in this teaching that reveals the three vehicles as one and shows their common return [to the One Vehicle], such a thing is impossible.

You should know that one who has truly attained arhatship has long since understood that the skillful means within the five states of existence are identical in their ultimate destination. As for your previous statement that those who have attained arhatship do not understand this identical destination, you should know that such a person is not a true arhat.
"Except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa"—the following section constitutes the second part, which correctly exhorts beings to give rise to faith. This also has three layers:
first, the correct exhortation for beings to give rise to faith; second, the explanation of the intent behind this exhortation to faith; and third, the resolution of beings' doubts.

The first statement says, "Except after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa. Once the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the former Buddha has already passed away and the subsequent Buddha has not yet appeared. During this interval, if there is someone who, in a world without a Buddha, practices and attains the stage of Arhat, and for hundreds of thousands of eons no Buddha appears to preach the Lotus Sūtra to that Arhat—showing how all myriad virtues converge in the Way—it is possible that such a person would not understand; it is precisely for the sake of such beings that they are urged to have faith.

"If the Buddha were still in the world, he could have explained for you the principle of our common destination; but now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, who shall explain for you this Dharma Flower teaching on the common destination?"

"You may now take advantage of the Buddha's presence in the world to give rise to a heart of faith and joy, and to receive and uphold the Dharma that leads to the same destination; this is explained from the perspective of the teachings.
However, if we speak from the perspective of principle, whether a Buddha exists or not, one naturally understands it."

At that time, people’s sentiments naturally remained unwilling to believe this; they said to themselves, "Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his disciples have personally mastered the Lotus Sūtra, and after the Buddha's passing, they shall surely expound for us this teaching of the ultimate convergence."

Therefore, in the second section, from "Why is this so? onwards, the Buddha explains this attachment, asking: "For what reason do I exhort you and others to believe and accept [this teaching] while the Buddha is still in the world?"

To speak truly, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the evil age will be full of many hardships; thus, those who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* are difficult to find.
For this purpose, I cause you to believe and accept it today.

However, as for the common understanding of people, they are still unwilling to believe that the Buddha, after his parinirvāṇa, will receive and uphold this sutra and preach the Dharma for them; if such a thing were extremely difficult to obtain, I would have entered nirvana without remainder myself.

Therefore, from the third section beginning with "If one encounters another Buddha," the Buddha explains this doubt, saying that if one encounters another Buddha, one will attain definitive understanding within this Dharma. This meaning specifically states that once a person has attained the fruit of Arhatship, they must hear the Tathāgata preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to know that all myriad virtues converge [in the One Vehicle], and only then can they enter Nirvana; if they do not hear the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* regarding this convergence, they shall ultimately never enter Nirvana.

If an Arhat does not encounter the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* by Śākyamuni in this present age, they must encounter another Buddha in a future world; only by hearing that all myriad virtues converge within this teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* can they enter nirvana, for there is no entering nirvana in the interim.

The sentiments of the people are such that they hear these words of the Buddha and immediately believe and accept them; if it were as you say, we would believe and accept them at once—why wait for other Buddhas before believing and accepting? This would allow even Arhats, from among the ordinary worldlings, who might otherwise be unwilling to believe, to together believe and accept.

"Śāriputra, you all should with one mind believe, understand, receive, and uphold the Buddha’s words. From here below is the fifth section, which clarifies that [the teaching] is not false and serves to stop the minds of beings from harboring slander.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, the clarification of the exhortation to believe; second, from "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas" onwards, the actual clarification that [the teaching] is not in vain; and third, from "There is no other vehicle" onwards, the conclusion of the exhortation by citing the dharma that is to be believed.

"Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse," and so forth. Within the Exposition of the True Dharma (*saddharmavyākhyāna*), there are originally two parts: the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*).
What follows here is the second part, the verses, consisting of one hundred and fourteen lines of verse, which correspond directly to the preceding prose.
In the preceding prose section, there were originally two parts:
first, the causal origin (nidāna), and second, the exposition of the True Dharma, which opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the aspect of ultimate reality.
Now, these one hundred and fourteen verses are likewise divided into two sections:

The first four lines and one verse praise the first section of the preceding prose, the "Origination of the Causes" (nidāna); the second part, consisting of one hundred and nine lines and three verses, praises the second section of the preceding prose, the "Exposition of the True Dharma" (saddharmadeśanā).
However, within the aforementioned *Pratītyasamutpāda*, there are originally two parts:
first, the Buddha’s authorization to explain the meaning of their ultimate convergence; second, Śāriputra’s reception of the Buddha’s clear instructions.
Now, these four lines of verse praise only what the Buddha permitted; they do not praise Śāriputra’s reception of the mandate.

Furthermore, within the Buddha’s permission mentioned above, there were originally four layers: first, the formal permission to speak; second, the admonition; third, the screening of the assembly; and fourth, the praise of the assembly as a concluding summary of the admonition and permission. Now, none of these [first three] are praised; only the fourth is praised.

Now, these four lines and one phrase are divided into two parts. The first consists of three and a half verses which do not correspond to the prose; they are intended to reveal the praise of the "one who abides. Therefore, it first clarifies that the "one who goes" is not [existent]. For without the negation of what is not, there can be no revelation of what is; thus, it first clarifies that the "one who goes" is not [existent].
The following three lines constitute the actual verse.
How is it known that this does not correspond to the prose (gadya)?
Regarding the selection of the assembly mentioned above, those who compiled the sūtras after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa merely recorded the events as they occurred at that time.
How is it that the Buddha now recites the words of the sūtra compiler?
If this is so, why are they similar?
Since both appear in these two places, how could the events at that time not be similar?

Regarding "having deficiencies or leaks in the precepts": violating a single precept is termed a deficiency; committing them in their entirety is a leak, through which one enters the cycle of birth and death.

Regarding "defects" (*kṣata*): "blemishes" (*kṣaya*) refer to the exterior, while "flaws" (*doṣa*) refer to the interior. When one internally violates the precepts yet externally maintains careful deportment, it is therefore said that one "guards and cherishes" [the precepts].

The three phrases from "This assembly has no branches or leaves" to "Śāriputra, listen well" constitute the second formal verse, which is the fourth section: the concluding praise of the assembly and the instruction of permission.
The original text above consists of three parts:
first, praising the listener for possessing the necessary capacity; second, clarifying that those who have departed lack such capacity; and third, the formal conclusion, admonition, and permission.
Here, two lines of verse correspond to the first part, the single line "Śāriputra, listen well" corresponds to the third part, and the second part is omitted from the verse.

"Regarding 'the Dharma attained by all Buddhas'": from this point downward, there are one hundred and nine lines consisting of three-phrase verses. This is the second verse within this section, which versifies the second part of the preceding prose—the teaching of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
However, within the exposition of the True Dharma above, there are originally two parts:

first, a broad clarification of the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one from the perspective of all Buddhas; second, a broad clarification of the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one from the perspective of Śākyamuni.
Now, these one hundred and nine lines of three-verse stanzas are also divided into two parts:
the first consists of seventy-three lines and one verse, which praises how the gates of all Buddhas open the three to reveal the one;
from "Now I am likewise" downward, there are thirty-six and a half lines, which praise the opening of the three to reveal the one at the gate of Śākyamuni.
However, among the aforementioned Buddhas, there are fundamentally four types:

first, all Buddhas generally opening the gates of the three vehicles to reveal the One; second, past Buddhas opening the three to reveal the one; third, future Buddhas opening the three to reveal the one; and fourth, present Buddhas opening the three to reveal the one.
Now, these seventy-three lines and one phrase are also divided into four parts:
first, thirty-four lines and three phrases, which praise the aforementioned general gate of all Buddhas;
second, twenty-seven and a half verses beginning with "Innumerable kalpas past," which praise the second gate, that of the Buddhas of the past.
The third section, from "The future World-Honored Ones" onwards, consists of six and a half verses, praising the gateway of the future Buddhas;
the fourth section, from "Worshipped by gods and humans" onwards, consists of four and a half verses, praising the fourth gateway, that of the present Buddhas.
In general, within the gateway of all Buddhas, there are originally four meanings:
first, praising the rarity of the Dharma; second, clarifying its non-falsity; third, clarifying the opening of the three; and fourth, clarifying the manifestation of the one.

Now, this is not a verse praising the first [point] regarding the rarity of the Dharma; rather, within this verse, there is an extended citation of the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) to explain the intention behind first teaching the three [vehicles] and subsequently the one [vehicle].

Furthermore, these thirty-four lines, consisting of three phrases, are also divided into four parts: the first consists of twelve lines and one phrase, which versifies the third section above concerning the various Buddhas opening the three [vehicles];
the second, from the line "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas" onwards, consists of eleven verses, which versifies the fourth section above concerning the various Buddhas manifesting the one [vehicle].

The third section, consisting of nine and a half verses beginning from "If I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way," is a verse summary of the Buddhas; it explains the meaning of the three [vehicles] first and the one [vehicle] last by citing the five turbidities, a point not present in the preceding prose.
The fourth section, consisting of two verses beginning from "I possess the power of skillful means," summarizes the second point above: that the Buddhas do not speak falsely.

Now, these two lines are analyzed and compared: that which was the second in the preceding prose section—“not false”—is here the fourth; the inversion and omission of the textual sequence are intended to reveal that the six meanings originally possess no fixed order.
In the preceding prose section, there was praise for the rarity of the Dharma, which is now omitted in this verse;

furthermore, while the preceding prose does not contain the explanation of the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) regarding the sequence of the three [vehicles] followed by the one [vehicle], it is present in these verses.
Since these phrases appear and disappear alternately, it is verified that within the gateway of a single Buddha, all six meanings must be fully present.
Above, the general exposition of the three [vehicles] by all Buddhas consists of three main sections:

first, the direct exposition of the three by all Buddhas; second, citing Śākyamuni’s [teaching] while not yet explaining the three as expounded by all Buddhas; and third, concluding by attributing [the teaching] back to all Buddhas.
Now, this [verse] only reveals the first [point], that all Buddhas open up the three [vehicles]; it briefly omits the latter two sections.
In the preceding prose section, only the opening of the three vehicles was shown as being expedient means; here, in this verse, the five vehicles are extensively clarified as being expedient means.
Now, within these twelve lines of one verse, it is appropriate to divide them into two parts:
first, there are eight lines and three phrases of verse which first present the teachings of the four vehicles as skillful means;

second, from the line "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure" downward, there are three and a half lines of verse which separately present the Mahāyāna teachings of the Bodhisattvas as skillful means.
Since [the text] begins and ends with each individual phrase and sentence, it is appropriate to divide it into two parts.
Furthermore, within the fourfold skillful means (*upāya*) emerging from the three-verse stanza of eight lines, there are again two sections:

first, the five lines and three verses that initially present the teachings of the four vehicles; second, the three verses beginning with "I have taught these as skillful means," which properly expound these skillful means, clarifying why the teachings of the four vehicles given in the past were all merely expedient devices.
Furthermore, within these two sections, each contains two parts:

the first consists of four lines and one phrase, which sets forth the teachings for humans, devas, and the two vehicles; the subsequent one and a half lines set forth the teachings for the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Within the first four lines and one phrase, there are four intended meanings:
First, the three phrases beginning with "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" clarify that within the Mahāyāna, one transcends both humans, devas, and the two vehicles;
second, the line beginning with "What is contemplated in the minds of sentient beings" clarifies that the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ.
The third section, "The Buddha, having fully known this," in one line, clarifies that the teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is not singular.

The fourth section, "Or he speaks the Sūtras," in one and a half lines, extensively presents these manifold teachings, which are precisely the ninefold division of the scriptures (navāṅga-buddhavacana).

From "those of dull faculties who delight in the lesser Dharma," there is one line and a half; this is the second emergence of the teachings for the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Although those of the two vehicles are not necessarily dull-witted, they are described as "dull" here because their aspirations are narrow and limited.

Question: "Previously it was stated that if a person encounters suffering and becomes weary of old age, illness, and death; why is it now said that they are greedily attached to birth and death? This is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows."
Alternatively, some explain that there are three kinds of liberation:

first, the liberation from birth-and-death (saṃsāra), which is of two types: the first is the birth-and-death of segmented portions within the triple world (traidhātuka), and the second is the birth-and-death of transformation outside the triple world, which is the ground of abiding in ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi).

When the suffering of the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) realm cuts into one with such intensity that a mind of revulsion (*nirveda*) is manifested, the suffering of the *pariṇāma-vedanīya* (transformative) realm appears comparatively subtle by comparison.

Furthermore, since the teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) of the past did not speak of the suffering of the *avidyāvāsabhūmi* (ground of the dwelling of ignorance), and as those ancient teachings did not mention this suffering of birth and death, there was no sense of revulsion toward it; therefore, it is said that one is "attached through craving" (*abhiniviṣṭa*).

The second interpretation states: Therefore, those such as the initial *srotāpanna* who discuss the limits of seeking the Way still encounter suffering and feel weary of old age, illness, and death; they still possess attachment to wife and children, which constitutes clinging to birth and death.

Either of these two interpretations may be used according to one's preference. Later, it is further stated that if there is a sentiment of weariness within the capacity [of the listener], then there is greed.

Regarding the phrase "I say this is a skillful means," the following three lines constitute the second section, which correctly opens by declaring this to be a teaching of skillful means. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the two verses stating "I say this is a skillful means" initially open up the teachings of the three vehicles—Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva—as being skillful means, asserting that what was taught in the past was the ultimate truth, while what is taught today is the skillful means.

The second statement, “These ninefold teachings of mine,” is a verse that reverses the order to reveal that the teachings for the two vehicles of humans and devas are also skillful means (*upāya*). Therefore, it is said that these sūtras on humans, devas, and so forth are the root, as their fundamental purpose is the Great Vehicle; thus, it is said that this sūtra is taught for the sake of entering the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure," the following three and a half verses constitute the second section, which specifically distinguishes those of the Mahāyāna among the three vehicles.

Within this teaching, there are also two parts: first, one and a half verses that initially present the teaching for those of the Mahāyāna among the three vehicles; "preaching this Mahāyāna teaching" refers to the Mahāyāna within the three vehicles of the past, not the Mahāyāna of the present day. Second, the two verses of the second part correctly reveal these skillful means (*upāya*), which themselves consist of two sections:

first, the one and a half verses beginning with "I bestow this prediction upon such a person" briefly record their attainment of Buddhahood; second, the final half-verse beginning with "The Buddha knows their mental conduct" correctly reveals these skillful means—the Buddha knowing their mental conduct and preaching the Mahāyāna within the three vehicles for them.
"Whether Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas"—the following eleven verses praise the fourth manifestation [of the Buddha's nature] within the general categories of all Buddhas.
Above, there are four: first, the oneness of the fruit; second, the oneness of the person; third, the oneness of the cause; and fourth, the oneness of the teaching.
Now, I shall briefly omit the third cause (hetu) and verse one, and instead recite only verse three and verse one, though not in their original order.
Herein, the single verse beginning with "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas" praises the first person;
the one and a half verses beginning with "In the buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma" praise the fourth teaching.
"Because he speaks of the Buddha’s wisdom. The following eight lines and a half of verse constitute the first of the [three] fruits.
Within these eight lines and a half, there are three sections.

First, from "Because he speaks of the Buddha’s wisdom" downward, there is one line consisting of three phrases of verse; this first section clarifies that before the Buddha appeared in the world, he intended to preach the fruit of the One Great Vehicle for the sake of sentient beings, rather than desiring to grant them the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle.

The second section, beginning with "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom according to the dharmas attained," consists of four lines and three phrases of verse; it clearly demonstrates the desire to bestow the fruit of the One Vehicle since his appearance in the world.

The third section, beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know that I originally established a vow," consists of two lines; it clarifies the desire to bestow the fruit of the Mahāyāna when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past.

Furthermore, among these three sections, the first and the last are not further divided; rather, focusing solely on the second section—concerning the period since the Buddha appeared in the world and his intention to bestow the fruit of the Mahāyāna—there are four stages.
The first, from the three phrases beginning with "As he has attained the Dharma," correctly clarifies that the Buddha is about to bestow the great fruit upon sentient beings.

The second section, consisting of one and a half verses beginning with "Having realized the unsurpassed path for oneself," explains the Buddha’s fundamental intention in appearing in the world: his desire to bestow the great fruit. [He reflects: "If I were to begrudge this great fruit, I would be a person of stinginess and greed; yet, alas, sentient beings lack the capacity for the great fruit. For this reason, he first teaches the three [vehicles].
However, at that time, doubts arose among the assembly. [The Buddha thought: "I wish to bestow great fruits upon sentient beings; who would believe these words of mine?

Therefore, in the third section, beginning with "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha," there is one line and one verse that cite the testimony of superior persons. You say there is no one who believes, yet there are indeed those who believe in the Triple Gem and declare that the Buddha does not deceive. Such people believe that the Buddha constantly desires to bestow great fruits upon sentient beings. At that time, some in the assembly raised a doubt, saying: "If there were absolutely no one who believed in the Triple Gem, who then would believe in the Buddha?"

The fourth verse, "I adorn my body with marks," employs the Buddha’s own meritorious physical characteristics and minor marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) to testify that the Buddha and his great fruit are not in vain. If one were a person lacking majestic power, it might be possible for their words to be untrue; but since the Buddha possesses such physical forms, how could he utter speech that is not true?

"If I encounter sentient beings"—the following nine and a half lines constitute the third section, a verse summary of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) across all Buddha-gates, which was not present in the preceding prose.
Within these five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), there are three sections.

First, the single verse beginning with "If I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way" correctly clarifies that the Buddha appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings amidst the five turbidities, and thus cannot immediately expound the Great Meaning.
The second section, consisting of six lines of verse, sets forth the essence of the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*).

The third section, beginning from "Therefore, Śāriputra" and comprising two and a half lines, concludes by explaining the Buddha’s intention in appearing in the world to teach the *Hīnayāna* for the sake of sentient beings amidst these five corruptions.

Among these three sections, the first and the last are not further subdivided; the second section, which brings forth the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), constitutes five layers. The two lines of verse beginning with "I know these sentient beings" bring forth the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

The verse beginning with “the subtle form of conception” clarifies the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). The verse beginning with “entering the dense forest of false views” brings forth the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Among the sixty-two views, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) serves as the foundation; the non-Buddhists postulate a self, [claiming] that form is the self, or that the self is apart from form, or that the self dwells within form, or that form dwells within the self, and so it is likewise up to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Each of the five aggregates has four types of views, which together constitute twenty views.

Since these twenty views currently exist and arise from causes, there are likewise twenty views regarding the five aggregates of the past. Furthermore, because they project the seeds for the future, there are again twenty views regarding the five aggregates of the future. Combining the twenty views for each of the three periods of time results in sixty views in total.
Although there are sixty types of views, they do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. Why is this so?
If one were to reckon that form is the self, then at a later time one would fall into the view of annihilationism, which is to say, the view of non-existence.
As for the remaining three views, all of them involve conceiving a self apart from form, thereby resulting in the eternalist view; this is precisely the view of existence (*astitva-dṛṣṭi*).

Thus, it should be known that when discussed in general, there are these two views of existence and non-existence (*nāstitva-dṛṣṭi*); when discussed in detail, there are sixty views. Whether taken collectively or individually, there are thus sixty-two views.

"Deeply attached to false dharmas" brings forth the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); "for thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas" (in one verse) brings forth the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

"Therefore, Śāriputra," from here below for two and a half lines, is the third [section], which concludes the intent of all Buddhas to bestow the expedient means of the three vehicles in order to transform sentient beings amidst the five defilements.
Regarding the statement, "I possess the power of skillful means and manifest the teachings of the three vehicles," the following two verses praise the second point above: non-deceptiveness.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, one verse of four lines prefaces the explanation that Śākyamuni, like all Buddhas, is non-deceptive in teaching the three [vehicles] first and the one [vehicle] last.
The second section, from "Now this great assembly" in one line downward, exhorts faith and concludes that [the teaching] is not false.
From "In past incalculable kalpas" below this point, there are twenty-seven and a half verses; this constitutes the second gate among the four gates of the Buddhas: the Gate of Past Buddhas.
In the section on the Buddhas of the Past, there were originally two parts:
first, the opening of the three [vehicles], and second, the revelation of the one [vehicle].
Now, the preceding two lines of verse open the three.
The second section, beginning from "These World-Honored Ones," consists of twenty-five and a half verses, which manifest the One through past Buddhas.
Within these twenty-five and a half verses, there are two parts: first, two and a half verses that teach the One;
second, twenty-three verses beginning from "If there are classes of sentient beings," which present the Three and the One through a triple-layered parallelism.
There is one person, one cause, and one fruit. Regarding the three sections:

the first two stanzas clarify how one attains Buddhahood by practicing while a Buddha is still in the world; the second section consists of twenty stanzas concerning how one attains Buddhahood by practicing after a past Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa; and the third stanza summarizes how one attains Buddhahood through making offerings both while a Buddha is in the world and after his parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the first two lines, concerning those who practiced and attained Buddhahood while past Buddhas were still in the world, there are likewise three aspects:

"if there are sentient beings" constitutes the first [aspect], the person; "practicing the six perfections" constitutes the second [aspect], the cause; and "attaining the Buddha-way" constitutes the third [aspect], the fruit.

The twenty verses beginning with "After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas" constitute the second section, concerning the practice leading to Buddhahood after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Within this, there are four types of offerings: each verse clarifies the offering of gentle and wholesome conduct; the next four and a half verses clarify the offering of building stupas; the following six and a half verses clarify the offering of creating images; and the final eight verses directly clarify the offering of the three karmas (body, speech, and mind).

First, regarding the verse "If a person has a virtuous and gentle mind": since there was no time to perform other offerings, this verse first clarifies the gentle and virtuous mind; it does not yet discuss the actual performance of offerings.

Regarding the four and a half verses beginning with "When the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa," the second section concerns the construction of stupas and offerings, which likewise consists of three unities:
the person is the first unity; the mind of making offerings is the causal unity; and the attainment of the Buddha-way is the resultant unity.

From the verse beginning with "If a person, for the sake of the Buddha," there are six lines and a half of gāthās; this is the third section clarifying the creation of images and offerings, which also possesses the meaning of the three-in-one.

From the verse beginning with "If a person, at a stūpa or temple," there are eight lines of gāthās; this is the fourth section directly clarifying the offerings of the three karmas and so forth, which likewise possesses the meaning of the three-in-one.

The single line of verse beginning with "Regarding all Buddhas of the past, those currently present, or those who have entered parinirvāṇa" is the third section, which collectively clarifies the practice during the Buddha's lifetime and after his parinirvāṇa; it likewise possesses the significance of the three-in-one.
"Regarding 'the future World-Honored Ones,' the following six and a half lines of verse praise the third section above, the Gate of Future Buddhas.
This section itself contains two parts:

first, two and a half lines of verse praise the opening of the three [vehicles] above; second, from 'The fundamental vows of all Buddhas' onwards, four lines of verse praise the manifestation of the one [vehicle] above, which itself contains three parts."
The first line of verse represents one fruit;
the following single verse beginning with "Though the Buddhas of future ages speak hundreds of thousands of billions... represents one teaching;
and the two lines of verse beginning with "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among Two-legged Beings" represent one cause.
"Knowing that all dharmas are eternally without nature" means knowing that the myriad wholesome dharmas do not possess the natures of the three vehicles.

"The Buddha-seed arises from conditions" means that, with respect to the fruit of Buddhahood in relation to the myriad wholesome dharmas, this fruit of Buddhahood is attained through these myriad wholesome dharmas; yet, because the cause is designated as a "condition," it is said that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions.
"Those dharmas abide in the dharma-position" means that all myriad wholesome dharmas abide in the position of the One Vehicle; thus, the dharmas abide in the dharma-position.
"The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding" means that while the world merely grasps at signs, all wholesome dharmas likewise abide in the Buddha-position of the One Vehicle.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation: practicing these ten thousand virtues while remaining in the world, and abiding eternally within the Mahāyāna—what the Teacher spoke of as expedient means is fundamentally but a single cause; it was only in the past that he spoke expediently of three causes. Therefore, one should know that it is indeed but a single cause.
Someone said: "These two verses teach one [principle].
This means: if it were not so, how would one know that this is the cause of one?
To say that "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions" means that the cause is itself the condition.
The following four and a half verses, beginning with "Worshipped by devas and humans," eulogize the fourth section above: the gate of present Buddhas.
In the preceding prose section, there are three parts:

first, clarifying the intent behind opening up the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle; second, formally elucidating the opening up of the three to reveal the one; and third, the concluding summary.
In this present verse, only the first two [sections] are versified, while the third, the "conclusion" (nigamana), is not.

The first line, "Worshipped by gods and humans," constitutes one and a half verses that first versify the Buddhas of the present; because it serves the purpose of the threefold unity, they must appear in the world.

The final three lines of verse clarify the second point: the explicit teaching on the "opening of the three and revealing of the one. In the preceding prose section, the opening of the three was explained first, followed by the revelation of the one; now, within these three lines of verse, they are likewise divided into two parts.
The single verse beginning with "Know the foremost quiescence" first versifies the revelation of the one, specifically versifying the unity of the teaching.
The second section, "Knowing the Various Practices of Sentient Beings," consists of two lines of inverted verse that further elaborate upon the previous three [points].
These two lines of verse themselves have two parts:

first, one line and one phrase clarify how the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present clearly perceive the capacities of those following the three vehicles; second, the three phrases beginning with "By means of various causes and conditions" formally elaborate upon the opening of the three [vehicles].
"Now I am also like this. From this point downward, there are thirty-six and a half verses that versify the preceding "Śākyamuni" section.
Within the preceding prose, there were originally five points:

first, the opening of the three [vehicles]; second, the manifestation of the one; third, citing the five turbidities to explain the intent behind the three followed by the one; fourth, distinguishing the true from the false to encourage faith; and fifth, clarifying that it is not deceptive.
The reason for not praising the fourth [section] here is that it distinguishes the true from the false and encourages faith, while this [section] is intended to extol the rarity of the Dharma.
Furthermore, these thirty-six lines and a half of verse are also divided into five distinct parts;
the first verse transcends and praises the first [section], "Manifesting the One."
Next, there is one verse that retrospectively praises the preceding section on the three [vehicles].
Third, from "Śāriputra, you should know" downward, twenty-seven and a half verses praise the third section on the five turbidities.

Fourth, from "As is the ritual for the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas of the three periods of time" downward, five and a half verses in prose praise the rarity of the Dharma; this is not present in the long prose version.
The fifth [section], from “Do not harbor doubts that I am the King of all Dharmas” down to one and a half verses, constitutes the fifth [point], Non-Deceptiveness.

Now, this is analyzed in three layers: whereas the preceding prose section revealed the first of the two [aspects] of the second [chapter], here, first a verse reveals the one, and subsequently a verse opens up the three, clarifying the sense of their mutual priority and posteriority, as fully explained above.
The fourth section above was intended to distinguish between the true and the false and to consolidate faith; this portion is omitted from the verse.

In the preceding prose, there was originally no praise for the rarity of the Dharma, yet here in the verses, such praise for the rarity of the Dharma is added at length; thus, it serves as a thematic recapitulation.

Therefore, by supplementing what was missing, it again becomes fivefold; however, since within this teaching of Śākyamuni the prose and verse sections appear and disappear alternately, we know that within a single Buddha, all six meanings must be fully present.

For now, let us take the first, second, third, and fifth [sections], excluding only the fourth which praises the rarity of the Dharma. Using these four segments of verse—whether combined, separated, or neither combined nor separated—one may formulate ten types of Dharma-expositions; these serve as the basis for the ten parables within the "Burning House" section below.

The reason the four preceding Buddha-gates are not taken as the basis is that the aforementioned four Buddhas were established for the purpose of fulfilling the meaning of the present Śākyamuni; since those of the future are not the primary subjects, they are not taken.

In this [passage], which is part of the explanation within Śākyamuni’s teaching, one does not take the "marvel at the rarity of the Dharma" as the basis; rather, it clarifies that the "explanation by way of Dharma" (dharmadeśanā) and the "explanation by way of analogy" (aupamyadeśanā) serve as the basis for one another. Since the simile of the udumbara flower exists inherently [within the former], how can the analogy be said to serve as the basis for the analogy?
Therefore, it is not taken [separately].

The first and second sections should be combined into one; the former accords with the intention of all Buddhas to teach "three" first and then "one," which is called the "Identity of the Transformation Master. The latter serves as the basis for the parable of the first householder within the burning house, and is also called the "basis for the general parable."
Furthermore, by excluding the third verse from the five turbidities, it is divided into eight sections to serve as the basis for the eight parables within the burning house.
Additionally, taking the fifth section on "not being false" as neither conjoined nor separated, it serves as the basis for the tenth parable.

Regarding the fact that, setting aside the third verse, the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) serve as the basis for eight types of analogies: first, from the passage "Śāriputra, you should know that with my Buddha-eye I observe," there are four lines of verse. In this context, this is designated as the stage where the Buddha, abiding in the *dharmakāya*, perceives that the sentient beings to be converted are obscured by the five turbidities; this serves as the basis for the second analogy in the "Burning House" parable, where the elder sees the fire. This corresponds to the section in the "Burning House" that says: "The elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides."

The second section, from "I first sat at the site of enlightenment, observing the tree and also walking about," consists of six and a half verses. In this context, it is designated as the Buddha’s inability to convert sentient beings through the Mahāyāna upon his appearance in the world; this serves as the basis for the third analogy in the Burning House regarding the elder’s failure to save his children. This corresponds to the passage in the Burning House that says: "Śāriputra, the elder thought to himself: 'My arms and hands have strength; I should [take them] with a lap-satchel... and so forth.

The third section, consisting of eleven verses beginning from "Recalling the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past," is designated here as the Buddha’s use of the three vehicles to convert sentient beings; this serves as the basis for the fourth analogy in the "Burning House" chapter below, where it says: "At that time, the elder had this thought: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire; if I and my children do not emerge immediately, we will surely be burned by the flames. I must now employ skillful means. This refers to the following passage.

The fourth verse, "Śāriputra, you should know that I see my sons who, with equal resolve, seek the Buddha-way, numbering immeasurable thousands of millions," is here designated as the meaning of the Buddha perceiving those of the three vehicles whose Mahāyāna potential has been awakened. This serves as the basis for the fifth analogy in the Burning House, where it is said: "The elder saw that his sons had safely emerged from the burning house and reached a place of fearlessness, all sitting on the open ground at the crossroads, free from all obstructions."

The fifth section, from "All with hearts of reverence came to where the Buddha was, having previously heard from various Buddhas the Dharma taught through skillful means," contains one verse. In this context, it is designated as the seekers of the fruit among those of the Three Vehicles; what they seek is simply the knowledge of non-arising that exhausts the three realms. This principle serves as the basis for the seventh analogy in the "Fire House" parable—the children seeking their respective vehicles—which is spoken of below when it says: "At that time, each of the sons addressed their father, saying: 'Father, regarding the playthings you previously promised us—the goat carts, the deer carts, and the ox carts—we pray that you will grant them to us now.'"

The sixth [section], "I then had this thought: 'The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to preach the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely the time for it,'" consists of two lines and one phrase of verse. In this context, it is designated as the Buddha’s joy at seeing sentient beings’ capacity for the Mahāyāna awakened; this serves as the foundational analogy for the sixth elder’s joy at seeing his children escape danger within the burning house, as expressed below in the words: "His mind was serene, and he was filled with exultant joy."

The seventh [verse], "Among all bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path"—these three lines are designated here as the Buddha preaching the Mahāyāna for sentient beings; that is, the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This serves as the basis for the eighth analogy, the bestowing of great chariots within the burning house below, which states: "Śāriputra, at that time the elder gave each of his sons an equal, single great chariot. The following passage is that very section.

The eighth verse states: "When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed; the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas. This single stanza is designated here as the meaning of those of the three vehicles receiving and practicing the Mahāyāna. It serves as the basis for the ninth simile in the section on leaving the burning house, concerning the sons obtaining the great chariots and rejoicing; as it says below: "At that time, each of the sons mounted a great chariot, attaining what they had never before experienced—something not originally expected."
The section on the five defilements (*pañcakaṣāya*) has concluded its role as the basis for the eight parables of the burning house.

By employing these eight parables together with the preceding parable of the Master of Transformation, they form nine parables in total. For the tenth, one takes by leaping over to the fifth section, "Not in Vain," which contains one and a half verses stating: "You all should not harbor doubts that I am the King of All Dharmas. This is designated here as "Not in Vain" and serves as the basis for the tenth parable of "Not in Vain" within the subsequent Burning House section, namely the passage beginning: "Śāriputra, what do you think? Would that elder have been guilty of falsehood in giving each of his sons a precious great chariot? This is it.

Therefore, these ten sections—concerning union, separation, and neither union nor separation—are established as the basis for the ten parables within the "Burning House" chapter below; they are also the remote basis for the parable of the "Transformation City," and further, the remote basis for the parable of the "Destitute Son."

The line "Now I am also like this" is a single verse that transcends the preceding [verse] to manifest the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) teaching alone. The following single verse, beginning with "By the power of my wisdom," is a retrospective verse on the preceding "Opening of the Three Vehicles. These two verses together form one section. The former [section] corresponds to the Buddhas of old who first taught the three and later the one; this is designated as the "similarity of the Teacher. The latter serves as the basis for the parable of the "Great Elder" within the burning house—whether it be a kingdom, city, town, or village—and is thus called the "basis for the general parable. It is also termed the "basis for the general parable."

The second section, "Śāriputra, you should know," which comprises twenty-seven and a half lines below this, is a verse commentary on the third part [of the preceding prose], which raises the theme of the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) to explain the meaning of first presenting three [vehicles] and subsequently one [vehicle].

Since it has been divided into eight sections, the four verses beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know" constitute the second of the ten teachings on the Dharma. In this context, they serve as the basis for the analogy of the elder seeing the fire within the burning house below—specifically, the passage that says, "The elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides."
Within these fourteen lines of verse, there are naturally three sections:
first, half a line clarifies the seer; second, three lines present what is seen; and third, half a line clarifies the arising of a compassionate mind.

Now, the half-verse stating, "Śāriputra, you should know that I observe with the Buddha-eye," is the first clarification of the capacity for vision; it shows that while the Buddha abides in the stage of the Dharma-body, he perceives the sentient beings to be transformed as being clouded by the five turbidities.

Below the phrase "seeing the sentient beings of the six realms," there are three lines of verse. The second [line] reveals what is seen; that is, seeing the sentient beings of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) who are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom. This half-verse reveals the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
The second half-verse, "Entering the perilous path of birth and death," clarifies the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
The following one and a half lines, beginning with "Deeply attached to the five desires," specifically cite the latent tendency of greed to clarify the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
The second half of the verse, "Deeply entering into various false views," clarifies the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

The turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is omitted for brevity; it has no separate essence apart from the other four turbidities, as these four turbidities constitute the temporal period, and that period is the turbidity of the eon.

"For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion"—this half-verse is the third [section], clarifying that he perceives both the seer and the seen and gives rise to compassionate pity; it clarifies that the Tathāgata desires to transform sentient beings.

The third section, "I first sat at the site of enlightenment," consisting of the following six and a half verses, is designated here as the point where the Buddha was unable to transform sentient beings through the Mahāyāna; it serves as the basis for the third analogy in the "Burning House" chapter below, concerning the elder's inability to rescue his children. This corresponds to the passage below that says: "Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself: 'My own body and hands possess great strength... and so forth.
Now, within these six and a half lines of verse, there are three parts:

first, the half line clarifies that there is no place where one can transform sentient beings; second, the half line clarifies that there is no time when one can transform sentient beings; third, the five and a half lines correctly clarify that it is impossible to transform sentient beings.
"In the beginning, I sat at the site of enlightenment" (the second half of the line) refers to the first Buddha’s place where he transformed sentient beings through the Mahāyāna.

Regarding "contemplating the tree," one interpretation states that the tree stands as a support for all sentient beings in the world; those who practice the sutra must do so for this very purpose. It is also said that one contemplates repaying the kindness of the tree’s four branches providing shade, thereby establishing a model for sentient beings: if even a tree, being insentient, still repays such kindness, how much more so should a human being!

"During the twenty-one days, he contemplated these matters. This half-verse is the second [section], clarifying the period during which the Buddha was unable to transform sentient beings through the Mahāyāna.

From the line "The wisdom I have attained" below, there are five lines and a half; this is the third section, which correctly clarifies that the Buddha was unable to transform sentient beings through the Mahāyāna. This section itself has three parts:
first, from the second half-line of "The wisdom I have attained is subtle and most supreme," one line clarifies the Buddha’s attempt to adapt by means of the Mahāyāna;

second, from "Sentient beings have dull faculties" below, there are three verses of gāthās, which clarify that the Buddha saw that sentient beings lacked the capacity (indriya) for the Mahāyāna; third, two verses clarify the cessation of his transformative activity.

Within the second category of those lacking the capacity [for the Great Vehicle], there are three parts: the first half-verse, "The faculties of sentient beings are dull," clarifies that there are those with the limited capacities of humans and devas; the latter half-verse, "Those of such a kind," explicitly clarifies that they lack the great capacity; and the two verses beginning with "At that time, the Brahma kings... provide proof of their lack of capacity. It is precisely because the Brahma kings requested [the teaching] that he remained in the world, which serves as evidence that they lacked the great capacity.

Regarding the two lines of verse beginning with "I then thought to myself: 'If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle,'" this constitutes the third section, which clarifies that the Buddha temporarily suspends his teaching of the Mahāyāna.

This section itself has two parts. First, one and a half verses clarify the increase in fear regarding its dangers: if those who lack the capacity for the Mahāyāna are taught only the Mahāyāna, they may give rise to a mind of slander and fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, it is said that they would "sink into suffering."
The second line of the second verse, "I would rather not preach the Dharma," correctly clarifies the cessation of his transformative activity.

The eleven verses following "Reflecting upon the Buddhas of the past" constitute the fourth section; here, this refers to the Buddha employing the three vehicles to transform and save sentient beings. This serves as the basis for the analogy in the subsequent "Fire House" chapter, where the fourth elder saves his children with the three carts. This is what is meant by the later passage: "At that time, the elder thought to himself: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire... and so forth.
Within this passage there are two parts:
first, the eleventh verse, which correctly clarifies that the benefit of using the three vehicles to transform sentient beings is attained;
second, the single verse beginning with "From kalpas of long ago," which explains away the doubts of beings.
Within the first ten lines, there are naturally four sections:

first, six and a half lines clarify the Buddha’s provisional application of the three vehicles; second, one line reveals the capacities of those in the three vehicles; third, one and a half lines show the preaching of the teachings of the three vehicles; and fourth, one line shows the acceptance and practice by those in the three vehicles.

Now, regarding the statement "Recalling the past Buddhas," the six and a half verses that follow constitute the first section: the opening of the three vehicles for provisional instruction. This section itself has three layers:

first, the single verse beginning with "Recalling the skillful means practiced by the past Buddhas" clarifies the search for the teaching for provisional instruction; the first half of this verse is the search for the teaching, while the second half properly clarifies the provisional instruction.
The second section, "When he was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared," spanning four and a half lines, clarifies the praise offered by the various Buddhas.
The third section, "Śāriputra, you should know," consisting of one line, clarifies Śākyamuni’s taking refuge in the Buddhas.

"Furthermore, he forms this thought: 'I have emerged from the turbid and evil world as taught by all the Buddhas. This second verse shows that there are those with the capacities for the three vehicles who are capable of receiving the transformation through the three vehicles.

"Having reflected on this matter, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī"—this one and a half lines constitute the third [section], clarifying that the Buddha immediately preached the teachings of the Three Vehicles at the very time he was establishing the Deer Park.

Regarding the phrase "the quiescent nature of all dharmas," this clarifies that the myriad wholesome dharmas are quiescent; there are no characteristics of the three vehicles to be spoken of, yet they are spoken of as having three vehicles solely for the sake of skillful means.

The line "This is called turning the wheel of Dharma, whereby there is the sound of nirvāṇa" is the fourth. Although followers of the three vehicles receive and practice [the teaching], it is taught that there are three vehicles merely as a skillful means; thus one can only say there is the *sound* of nirvāṇa, but there is no actual substance of nirvāṇa.
Five people attained the Way, and eighty thousand devas attained sainthood; therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states that the Three Jewels thus appeared in the world.
"From kalpas long ago" and the following verse constitute the second resolution of doubts.
The doubt is expressed as follows:

"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni possesses the threefold penetration that illuminates all things; he ought naturally to have understood the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Why, then, must he now further study the Dharma of the Three Vehicles of the Buddhas?"
Śāriputra replied:

"Since the distant kalpas of the past, I have praised and revealed the illumination of the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, and I have already understood the teachings of the Three Vehicles; it is solely because I desire to be equal to all Buddhas."
Another explanation:

At that time, the assembly collectively gave rise to doubt, saying, "If these three vehicles do not exist within the ultimate principle, for what reason does the Buddha intend to preach these three vehicles for the sake of others?"
Therefore, the second verse provides an explanation to dispel doubts:

"From ages long past, he has praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvāṇa. This means that he constantly desires to reveal the Dharma of the causes and effects of the One Vehicle; it is not that there are no sentient beings of the Mahāyāna who are incapable of receiving it.
It is traditionally said that this conveys the meaning of the secret *vidyā* regarding the lifespan; this is the previous explanation.

"Śāriputra, you should know that I see my sons, who are equally resolved to seek the Buddha-way, in numbers of immeasurable thousands of millions"—this single verse is the fifth. Here, it is designated as the Buddha seeing those of the three vehicles whose Mahāyāna capacity has been awakened. Since the awakening of this capacity is the underlying principle (*tattva*), it is called "resolutely seeking. This serves as the basis for the analogy in the "Fire House" section below, where the fifth elder sees his children escape the calamity; the subsequent passage, "At that time, the elder saw that his children had safely emerged from the fire house," is precisely this.

"All come to the Buddha's presence with a heart of reverence"—this verse is the sixth; here it is designated as the "seeking of the fruit" by those of the three vehicles. This, however, serves as the basis for the seventh analogy within the burning house, namely the "sons seeking their carts. The subsequent passage, beginning with "At that time, each of the sons said to their father: 'Father, the precious playthings you previously promised us... and so forth, is that very section.

"I then had this thought: 'This is why the Tathāgata has appeared. This [passage] below consists of two lines and one phrase, which is the seventh [section]. Herein, it is designated as the Buddha’s joy because he perceives that people of the three vehicles have awakened the potential for the Mahāyāna; this serves as the basis for the analogy of the sixth elder’s joy at seeing his children escape danger within the burning house, which appears later in the text where it says, "His mind was serene, and he leaped for joy with exultation. This refers to that section.
Now, these two lines form one verse, which itself consists of two parts:
first, the two verses set forth the cause of the joy; second, the remaining single line explicitly clarifies the joy.
Within the first two lines that set forth the cause of the joy, there are further two sub-sections:
"I then had this thought: 'The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to preach the Buddha's wisdom. This preceding verse clarifies the joy arising from the fulfillment of a favorable matter.

"Those of dull faculties and little wisdom, who are attached to signs and arrogant, cannot believe in this Dharma. This subsequent verse clarifies the joy arising from the removal of an unfavorable matter.
How is this known?
This person was originally of dull faculties, yet now they have become of sharp faculties.
How is it known that this is so?

Although in the past they may have possessed sharp faculties that were subsequently lost and became dull, because they have now given rise to the vast and great mind, they are called people of sharp faculties.
This person was originally of the Small Vehicle and possessed small wisdom, but now has become one of the Great Vehicle and possesses great wisdom;
this person was originally one who clung to signs and was arrogant, but today is no longer one who clings to signs or is arrogant.
"In former times I could not believe in the Mahāyāna Dharma, but today I am able to believe in the Mahāyāna Dharma; for this reason, joy arises.
The single phrase, "Now I rejoice without fear," is the second part, which explicitly clarifies the manifestation of joy.

"Among all bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path"—these three phrases constitute the eighth [section]. In this context, it is designated as the Buddha preaching the Mahāyāna for sentient beings; that is, the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Setting aside" means excluding the provisional teachings of former days; "speaking only of the unsurpassed way" refers to adopting the Mahāyāna teachings of the present day.

This serves as the basis for the eighth analogy of the elder giving great chariots to his sons within the burning house, which is stated below: "At that time, the elder gave each of his sons an identical great chariot."

"The Bodhisattvas, having heard this Dharma, have all cast off the net of doubt. This single verse is the eighth among the five turbidities and the ninth among the ten modes of Dharma-exposition. In this context, it is designated as the point where those of the Three Vehicles together abandon the teachings of the Three Vehicles and attain the realization of the Mahāyāna. It serves as the basis for the analogy of the "lower burning house," the ninth instance where the various sons obtain the great chariots and rejoice; as stated below: "At that time, the sons each mounted a great chariot and experienced unprecedented joy, leaping for gladness."
The verse on the five turbidities concludes.

From "As the Buddhas of the three periods" below, these five lines and a half are a verse praising the rarity of the Dharma within the section on Śākyamuni; they are not found in the prose (long-form) version and do not serve as the basis for the subsequent metaphors.
Now, within these five and a half lines, there are naturally three sections:
first, there is one verse which first sets forth the Dharma that is praised; this is precisely the teaching of the One Vehicle.
The second section, beginning from "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world," consists of two verses which, by means of various difficulties, manifest the rare and marvelous nature of the Dharma.
The third section consists of two and a half lines, which conclude the praise by again relying on the analogy of the udumbara flower.
Another interpretation states:
Within this, there are two parts;
the first verse presents the dharma that is being praised, while the subsequent four and a half lines constitute the actual praise of that dharma.

Regarding the three sections of the praise of the Dharma: the first two verses constitute the discourse on the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*); the next one verse constitutes the discourse by way of analogy (*aupamyadeśanā*); and the final one and a half verses constitute the application of the analogy (*anusandhi*).

The line beginning with "Do not harbor any doubt" comprises one and a half verses. This is the fifth verse within the fifth section, the "Gate of Śākyamuni," concerning the non-falsity [of the teaching]. Within the tenfold discourse on the Dharma, it constitutes the tenth segment. It serves as the basis for the tenth analogy of non-falsity in the "Burning House" section below, which states: "Śāriputra, what do you think? Would that elder have been guilty of falsehood in giving each of his children a precious great chariot? This refers to that passage.
From the passage "You, Śāriputra, whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas" onwards, there are two parts concerning the teaching by means of the Dharma for those of superior faculties.

First, from "You have already earnestly entreated me three times" until the one hundred and fourteen verses above, this is the formal teaching by means of the Dharma for those of superior faculties; through this, those of superior faculties mutually attain understanding of the principle that the three are opened up and the one is revealed, returning to a single source without the distinction of three.
Therefore, the seven verses below this constitute the second part, which briefly exhorts and encourages those of superior faculties.

In the discourse on the sublime Dharma regarding the cultivation of practice and the attainment of the fruit, there are two types of primary statements: prose and verse. Within these seven lines of verse that now serve as an exhortation, there are likewise two parts:
first, five and a half lines of verse which exhort those of superior faculties to cultivate the cause;
second, the one and a half lines beginning with "Since you have already known," which exhort those of superior faculties to aspire toward the fruit.
Exhorting others to practice the causes is precisely transforming others, while exhorting them to aspire to the fruits is precisely self-cultivation; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, within each of these two sections, there are three aspects.

Regarding the threefold structure within the section on "Exhorting the Practice of Causes," there are initially two verses of verse. First, it sets forth the Dharma that is to be propagated, which is precisely this sutra.

Now, the essence of practicing the causes consists solely in propagating the sutra to benefit others while simultaneously cultivating oneself; for this reason, the sutra that is to be propagated is presented first.
The second part consists of two lines of verse that directly exhort and encourage the propagation of the sutra; this constitutes the causal practice (*hetu*).
