The third part, beginning from "Śāriputra, you should know" for one and a half lines, serves as a double conclusion to the preceding two sections.
Furthermore, within these three sections, each contains two layers.
Regarding the first, the emergence of the sūtra that is propagated, there are two parts:
the first line of verse is the primary formal praise of the emergence of the sūtra that is propagated, while the second verse explains and concludes the former.

Regarding the phrase, "One should know that this sublime Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas": this sutra enables people to transcend birth and death and attain nirvana; this is its essential meaning.
Furthermore, that this sublime Dharma has not been taught since the very beginning constitutes its secret meaning.

The single verse beginning with "In this world of the five turbidities" is the second explanation of the meaning of the aforementioned secret essentials. It means that because sentient beings in the world of the five turbidities delight in and are attached to the five sensory objects and the six desires, these classes of beings lack the aspiration for the Buddha-way and cannot be taught this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; this is precisely the meaning of the secret essentials.
Regarding the second part, the correct exhortation to practice the causes [of the teaching], there are two sections:
first, the single verse beginning with "In future ages, wicked people," which admonishes that when practicing these causes, one must not speak of them to the wicked;
second, the single verse beginning with "Those who possess shame and are pure," which exhorts that one should speak of them everywhere to those who are good.
In the third pair of concluding verses, there are two parts:
first, the verse beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know," which concludes the first section on the sūtra that has been propagated;

second, the half-verse beginning with "Those who do not practice will not understand this," which concludes the second section on the proper method for propagating the sūtra—namely, "Do not speak it to those who do not practice. This half-verse directly concludes the first stanza; when concluding the subsequent stanza, the meaning is understood by inversion: one should know that it ought to be explained to those who are able to learn and comprehend it.

"Since you have already known this"—the following one and a half verses constitute the second exhortation for those of superior faculties to aspire toward the fruit; herein there are also three parts:

first, the three lines of verse clarify that those of superior faculties have attained the understanding of the identity of the three and the one; second, the single line "no longer having any doubts" clarifies that the delusions of those of superior faculties and others have been eliminated; third, the latter half-verse "their hearts give rise to great joy" is the actual exhortation to aspire toward the fruit.
The Third Fascicle of the *Fahua yiji* concludes.
The *Yiji* on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Fascicle Four,
composed by the Śramaṇa Fayun of Guangzhai.
Chapter Three: The Parable (Upamāna-parivarta).
This chapter title should not be placed here.
How is this known?

The purpose of the parables was originally to provide analogical explanations for those of medium capacity to open up the three vehicles and reveal the One Vehicle; yet, the teaching through direct discourse (dharmadeśanā) that opens up the three and reveals the one to transform those of superior capacity is still not yet concluded—how, then, can it already be considered a teaching by way of parable?

The reason the title was placed in the middle is that the editor of the scripture divided the fascicles to ensure they were of even length; thus, the remainder of the "Dharmaparyāya" chapter was extracted and inserted here so that no fascicle would be disproportionately large or small. For this reason, the title of the "Parable" chapter was moved to the beginning of the second fascicle.

Regarding the section on the "Chapter on the True Discourse," it begins precisely from the passage where Śāriputra says to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret"; this point marks the beginning of the "Chapter on Parables."
If one employs this method to explain four sections based on the subsequent parables for the transformation of those of medium faculties, they too should comprise four chapters:

the first, the place where the True Dharma is preached, should be called the "Dharmaparyāya Chapter," which is no different from the "Parable Chapter" within the section on the transformation of those of medium faculties.

If this were the section on "Comprehension," it should have been called the "Chapter on Comprehension" (*Viniścaya-parivarta*), no different from the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukti-parivarta*) for those of medium faculties taught below.

If this were the section on "Expressing Sincerity," it should have been called the "Chapter on Expressing Sincerity" (*Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-parivarta*), no different from the "Chapter on the Herbs" (*Oṣadhi-parivarta*) for those of medium faculties taught below.

If this were a chapter specifically on the bestowal of predictions, it should have been titled "Chapter on the Bestowal of Predictions"; there would otherwise be no distinction from the "Chapter on the Prediction for the Four Great Disciples" within the section on those of medium capacity among the inferior teachings.
Regarding why the current "Discourse on the Dharma" (Fashuo) consists of four sections yet lacks such a chapter [as the "Chapter on the Fourfold Array"], there are three reasons and conditions.

First, the underlying intention is to use the lower to categorize the higher. Since the intermediate section of the parable already contains four chapters, one may now seek the same meaning by using the lower to categorize the higher. Conversely, if one were to use the higher to categorize the lower, the lower would likewise lack four chapters. Therefore, through this mutual illumination of presence and absence, the intended significance is naturally revealed.

According to the second interpretation, because the text consists merely of dharmas and its phrases are few, it does not further establish four categories; according to the third interpretation, it may also be that the compiler of the sutra, having deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent, established only twenty-seven chapters.

At that time, the assembly was moved to realization according to what was appropriate; yet, had they been removed and replaced by others, it would have been of no benefit to the assembly. Furthermore, other regions and different lands are far more than twenty-seven categories.

However, in the "Exposition of the Dharma" (Fashuo), which opens the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle for those of superior faculties, there are originally four sections. From this point downward, the entirety of the verses constitutes the second section, clarifying how those of superior faculties, such as Śāriputra and others, attained realization and understanding.

Among the four sections previously determined for the "Teaching of the Dharma" (dharmadeśanā), each was exemplified as being divided into two; now, within this section on "Receiving and Understanding" (prativedha), there are likewise two parts: first, the passage where the Sūtra narrator describes the manner in which Śāriputra attained understanding; second, the actual words of Śāriputra’s reception and understanding.
Furthermore, within these two sections, each is further divided into two parts. Regarding the first section, where the sūtra-narrator provides the account, there are two sub-parts:

first, the narrator describes the internal joy of the mind; second, the narrator describes the external manifestation of reverence, which begins from the passage "He immediately rose and joined his palms" and continues below.

The phrase "and addressed the Buddha, saying" marks the beginning of the second section, the formal expression of realization (*prativedha*), which also consists of two parts: first, the prose (*gadya*), and second, the verse (*śloka*).

Now, within the prose section itself, there are three distinct parts: first, the formal explanation of how Śāriputra himself expresses his joy because he has attained understanding; second, from the passage "This was our fault, not the World-Honored One's" down to "contemplating and attaining realization," which is designated as the repentance and self-reproach.
The third section, from "Since the past" down to the end of the prose, serves as a summary and conclusion of the understanding.

Furthermore, within each of these three sections, two sub-sections are opened; and within each of those two sub-sections, the first instance generally remains unopened, while the second instance is again divided into two.

Now, regarding the two parts within the first section: the first is the formal comprehension and understanding; the second, from "Why is this? onwards, cites the manifestations of grief from the past to explain the joy of the present. Because there was previously both regret and doubt, one was constantly in grief; because doubt and regret have now been eliminated, one is therefore joyful.
Regarding this second interpretation, the principle of "opening up both" applies throughout: the first section cites past remorse, while the second cites past doubt.

From the words "For what reason? down to "lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision," the first part designates the citation of past remorse as a formal explanation for today’s joy; this thus reveals the characteristics of attaining understanding today.
How do we know this was so?

Formerly, during the assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, I personally witnessed bodhisattvas receiving instruction in the Mahāyāna and receiving predictions of their attainment of Buddhahood; yet I was not included among them. To regret not having taken up the Great Vehicle is both deeply moving and tragic.
"Immeasurable knowledge and vision" is precisely the fruit of Buddhahood; however, this fruit of Buddhahood was not accepted in the past, and it is a matter for which one should feel regret.

From "World-Honored One, I have always dwelt alone" down to "and have been delivered," this is the second section, which raises former doubts regarding outward form to explain today’s joy. Since there truly exists the Dharma of the Mahāyāna and we have equally entered the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*), why did the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna while delivering others by means of the Mahāyāna?
This means that because one is deluded by principle regarding the teaching, this doubt arises.

Regarding the second part, "repenting and reproaching oneself," there are two points; the first, "However, this is our own fault, not the World-Honored One's," is the primary general repentance and self-reproach.
The second section, beginning with "For what reason," provides a specific explanation for the general meaning of the confession of transgression.

Previously, it was constantly said that we have all equally entered the *dharmatā*; why then has the Tathāgata delivered us by means of the *Hīnayāna* while delivering others by means of the *Mahāyāna*?
I have always harbored resentment toward the World-Honored One for lacking an impartial mind;
today I finally realize that it was because I myself lacked the capacity from of old to receive the Mahāyāna, which caused the Tathāgata to employ skillful means to teach the Hīnayāna.

However, within this explanation there are two examples: first, clarifying the regret for not having previously taken up the Great [Vehicle]; second, clarifying the regret for having taken up the Small [Vehicle].
Now, the first concerns the regret for not having taken up the Great [Vehicle] in the past.

From the passage beginning with "Why is this so? down to "one will necessarily attain the Great Vehicle and achieve liberation," the "cause" (hetu) refers to the fact that, in view of the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, the myriad practices are the causes belonging to the family of that Buddha-fruit.
Furthermore, if we consider the myriad practices in relation to the Mahāyāna teaching, the Mahāyāna teaching is precisely the cause of those myriad practices. How is this known?

It is solely because of the Mahāyāna teaching that the myriad practices arise; and because of the myriad practices, the fruit of Buddhahood is realized. Thus, what is here referred to as the "cause" is simply a designation for the Mahāyāna teaching as the cause.

Nevertheless, the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles are also presented sequentially: the Four Noble Truths were taught at the Deer Park, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination were taught in Rājagṛha, and later the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* was taught.

Śāriputra said to himself: "Why did I not wait for the Tathāgata to preach the Mahāyāna teachings? Had I practiced therein, I could have attained the realization of the Mahāyāna; instead, I hurriedly accepted the minor teachings of the three vehicles."
This, then, is the regret for not having accepted the Great [Vehicle] in the past.
Now, from "We did not understand the skillful means" onwards is the second [section], the regret for having accepted the Small [Vehicle] in the past.
If I had understood that the Tathāgata’s teaching in the past was a skillful means, how could I have again accepted the Lesser Vehicle?
It is precisely because I did not understand the Tathāgata’s former skillful means and provisional teachings that I continued to believe and accept them as the truth.
This constitutes the regret for having chosen the lesser path in the past.
Regarding the third section, the summary of understanding, there are two parts: first, from "Since the distant past" down to "I constantly reproach myself," which summarizes the former anxieties.
The second section, beginning with "Now, from the Buddha," concludes the joy resulting from the attainment of understanding today.

This also has two parts: first, from "Now, from the Buddha, I have heard what I have never heard before" up to "I have swiftly attained peace and security," which refers to the joy arising from the departure of evil matters.
The second section, beginning with "Today I finally know that you are truly sons of the Buddha," is designated as joy arising from the arrival of good news.

Previously, it was said that those of the two vehicles would certainly not attain Buddhahood and were unable to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas; therefore, they were not considered sons of the Buddha.
Now, since it is stated that the path you practice is the bodhisattva path and that you will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas, you are called true sons of the Buddha.

"Then he spoke in verse. Regarding what was previously mentioned as the correct comprehension, there are two parts: the first is the prose (gadya), and this following section is the second, the verse (śloka).
However, in the original prose section above, there were fundamentally three parts:
first, the direct statement of having attained understanding; second, the repentance and self-reproach; and third, the conclusion summarizing the realization.

Now, within these twenty-five and a half verses, they are divided into four sections. The first consists of eleven and a half verses, which versify the first part of the preceding prose—the direct statement of having attained understanding.
The second section, beginning from "I formerly adhered to false views," consists of five lines of verse; it praises the preceding second part on repentance and self-reproach.

The third section, beginning from "When I first heard what the Buddha taught," consists of six and a half lines of verse; its meaning emerges from these verses, which do not correspond to the preceding prose.
In the preceding prose section, it directly clarifies that the doubt and regret of the past take on the form of joy today, but it does not state that new doubts have been removed today;
this present passage of six and a half lines of verse, however, precisely clarifies the removal of doubts today. Therefore, we know that this does not serve as a summary of the preceding prose.

The fourth section, consisting of two and a half verses beginning with "Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice," praises the third part of the preceding prose: the summary of understanding and realization.
Furthermore, within the first part of the preceding prose—the primary account of one's own attainment of realization—there are originally two sections:
first, the direct account of one's own attainment of realization; second, citing the sorrow of former times to illustrate the joy of the present day.
Now, within these eleven and a half verses, the text is further divided into two parts:
the first consists of two and a half verses, which versify the first section, the "Correct Comprehension and Understanding.
The second part, beginning with "I dwell in mountain valleys," comprises nine verses, which versify the second section, citing the form of past sorrow to explain the joy of the present.
Now, within these first two and a half verses, there are three stages:

the first consists of three lines that directly correspond to the aforementioned understanding and realization, which states: "He addressed the Buddha, saying: 'Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy at having attained what I have never experienced before.'"
The second section, beginning with "The net of doubt has been entirely removed," further contains three lines that clarify the extinction of delusion and the arising of understanding.

Since the extinction of delusion and the arising of understanding must necessarily depend upon the Buddha, the third line—the single verse "The Buddha’s voice is most rare"—praises the Tathāgata to conclude the attainment of this understanding.

Regarding the nine verses beginning with "I was situated in a mountain valley," these praise the second section: citing the forms of past sorrow to explain the present joy. However, within the preceding prose commentary, there are originally two parts:
first, citing past remorse; second, citing past doubt.
Now these nine verses of practice are also divided into two parts:
the first six verses praise the former repentance;
the second three verses praise the former doubts.
Now, within the first six lines of verse concerning repentance, there are three stages:
the first one and a half verses first establish the basis for repentance and provide the formal verses of repentance itself;
the second consists of three verses, which set forth the dharmas repented of in the past.
The third section consists of one and a half lines, which conclude by describing the arising of remorse.
Previously, in the first part, it simply stated "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*), but it was not known at what time or place this doubt and remorse arose.

Now that this has been explained extensively in the present verse, the specific location where the doubt and remorse originated is revealed: while he was practicing the path in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*) within mountain valleys and forests, at that time, the mind of doubt and remorse arose, giving rise to feelings of resentment and lamentation.
How is this known to be so?

Because in the past, the Tathāgata only spoke of bodhisattvas receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, and did not say that śrāvakas would attain Buddhahood; for this reason, they gave rise to doubt and regret. Thus, there was both doubt and regret among the great assembly, as well as in the mountain valleys. They regretted, "I did not seek the Mahāyāna," and they gave rise to doubt, saying: "Since we have equally entered the *dharmatā*, why does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna while delivering others by means of the Mahāyāna?"
Since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is identical, there should be no distinction between small and great; this, however, is to confuse principle with teaching.
Furthermore, since the Tathāgata personally taught that there are distinctions among the three vehicles of instruction, why must the principle of the nature of phenomena be identical?
This, then, is using the teaching to delude the principle.

Now, according to what I have heard from the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*, when one is amidst the great assembly, seeing with one's own eyes and hearing with one's own ears the superior deeds of a Bodhisattva, and hearing the exaltation of the Great Being’s lofty virtue and far-reaching conduct, since one is not included among those in such a situation, at that time one can only give rise to regret and remorse; there is no leisure for the thought of doubt to arise.
However, if one is in a mountain forest or a quiet place, at that time many doubts and suspicions will likely arise.
"We too are sons of the Buddha, equally having entered the dharma of outflowlessness. Below this are three lines of verse; these constitute the second emergence of the dharmas previously regretted.
There are three intentions here:

the first verse clarifies the arising of the benefit of preaching the Dharma; the next verse clarifies the arising of internal and external merits such as the thirty-two marks; and the final verse clarifies the arising of internal and external merits such as the eighty minor characteristics.

Regarding the passage beginning with "When I was walking alone," there is one and a half verses; this is the third instance where, both in a secluded mountain valley and amidst the great assembly, he gives rise to a mind of remorse. This indicates that even in a secluded place, one can give rise to remorse.
Regarding the three lines of verse beginning with "I constantly, throughout day and night," these praise the aforementioned raising of former doubts about form and explain today’s joy.

These three lines of verse are further divided into three stages: the first verse directly praises the existence of former doubts; the second verse sets forth the matters formerly doubted; and the third verse clarifies that because liberation was attained today, the former doubts have been eliminated.
Now, in the first case, one confuses the teaching with the principle; therefore, it is said that [the teaching] is lost.
At other times, one may confuse the principle with the teaching; therefore, it is said that [the teaching] is not lost.

Therefore, it is said that one may be confused by principle regarding the teaching, or confused by the teaching regarding the principle; lingering between principle and teaching, one thus speaks of whether there is loss or no loss—this is precisely what is meant.

The verse beginning with "I have often seen the World-Honored One praise all bodhisattvas" constitutes the second point, which clarifies the matter giving rise to doubt. It is precisely because, when the Tathāgata was teaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he exclusively praised the bodhisattvas for their lofty virtue and beautiful conduct, stating that they shall all attain Buddhahood; it is on account of this matter that the doubt arises.

The single verse beginning with “Now I hear the Buddha’s voice” is the third [section], clarifying that liberation has been attained today; thus, the doubts of the past are removed. This involves two meanings: the first half-verse clarifies the opening of the three, while the second half-verse clarifies the manifestation of the one. This meaning reveals that in the past, it was correct to let principle delude the teaching and incorrect to let the teaching delude the principle. Now, through the power of the inconceivable outflow-free state, sentient beings have reached the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); this statement indeed accords with the past principle that let the teaching be deluded by principle.
"I originally held wrong views"—the five stanzas following this constitute the second part of the second section, which is the repentance and self-reproach for doubt.

However, within the preceding prose (long-form) commentary there were originally two parts; the first was a general confession, which is not recited here, while only the second—raising specific points to explain the general—is recited.
However, within the preceding explanation there are two parts: first, the regret that he did not take up the Great [Vehicle] in the past, which is not recited here;
second, the regret that he took up the Small [Vehicle] in the past, which is now being recited.

The preceding statement—“Yet we did not understand that these were teachings spoken according to expedient means suited to the occasion, and instead we immediately accepted them with faith, contemplated them, and sought realization”—is now divided into three parts within these five lines of verse. First, there are two lines of verse which directly eulogize the previous regret for having grasped the Lesser Vehicle;
second, from “But now I have awakened for myself” onwards, there are two lines of verse clarifying the attainment of understanding today;
third, the single line beginning with “The Buddha, amidst the great assembly,” clarifies the extinction of evil.
Regarding the second part, "Attaining Understanding Today," there are two sections:
first, the half-line beginning with "Only now do I realize that this was not true extinction," which clarifies the understanding of the provisional;
second, the one and a half lines beginning with "When I attain Buddhahood," which clarifies the understanding of the revelation of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "Hearing for the first time what the Buddha has taught," there follow six and a half verses; this constitutes the third meaning, which does not correspond to the preceding prose. How is this known?

In the prose section, it clarifies that there were doubts in the past, but it does not clarify that new doubts have been removed today; the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter clarified that expedient wisdom is difficult to fathom and true wisdom is profoundly deep.
Furthermore, it was said that "the Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifested the teachings of the three vehicles," which gave rise to a mind of doubt;
however, upon hearing this extensive explanation above regarding the opening of the three to reveal the one, this doubt is removed.

Within these six lines and a half of verse, there are naturally two sections. First, the single verse beginning with "Now that I have heard what the Buddha has taught, my heart is not startled or doubtful" sets forth the mind of doubt;
second, the five lines and a half beginning from "The Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions," extensively clarifies the removal of that doubt.
Now, within these five and a half lines, there are three stages:
first, one line of verse correctly and generally clarifies the removal of doubt;

second, the three lines beginning with "The Buddha spoke of the immeasurable Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa" cite the Buddhas of the three periods of time as all following the sequence of three [vehicles] followed by one [vehicle], specifically presenting the teaching that removes doubt.
The third section, "The World-Honored One Speaks the True Path," consisting of one and a half verses, summarizes the removal of doubts.

"Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice" and the following two and a half verses constitute the fourth section, which is a verse summary of the third conclusion of understanding found in the preceding prose.
However, in the prose section above, there were originally two parts:
the first was the conclusion of past sorrows, which is now omitted from the verse; only the second part, the conclusion of present joy, is versified.
However, regarding the joy mentioned above at the conclusion of today’s discourse, there are fundamentally two stages:
first, joy because evil matters have departed; second, joy because auspicious matters have arrived.
Now, these two and a half lines of verse are also divided into two parts.

First, the line and a half beginning with "Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice" praises the first [point]: joy because evil matters have departed. The preceding text stated that one now hears such a Dharma from the Buddha, which cuts off all doubts and regrets.

The second line of the subsequent verse says: "Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha; born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, I have obtained a share of the Buddha-Dharma."

"At that time, Śāriputra": in the "Teaching of the Dharma" (*dharmadeśanā*), which opens up the three vehicles to reveal the one vehicle for the transformation of those of superior faculties, there are originally four sections; this following section is the third, clarifying the signs by which the Tathāgata confirms the attainment of understanding by those of superior faculties.

Within the four sections of the fundamental discourse, this is further divided into two parts. Herein, there are two: first, "The Buddha said to Śāriputra," which recounts the past; second, the account of the present, beginning from the passage: "I now wish to cause you to recollect your original vow."
"Śāriputra, in a future age... From here below is the fourth section, which bestows a prediction of enlightenment upon those of superior faculties. Within this, there are two parts:

first, from the end of the preceding verse until this point, it is the actual bestowing of the prediction upon Śāriputra; second, from where the great assembly sees Śāriputra receive the prediction, they give rise to sympathetic joy and offer worship, through which their own rejoicing may be inferred.
However, Śāriputra’s prophecy consists of both prose and verse; focusing on the prose alone, there are eight sections:
first, the record of the causal practices;
second, from "He shall become a Buddha" onwards, the record of his two names, the general and the specific.
The third section, "The land is named Vimalā," describes the realm;
the fourth section, "The Tathāgata Padmaprabha also teaches sentient beings through the three vehicles," explains the doubts regarding the objects [of the teaching];
and the fifth section, "That eon is named Mahāratnavyūha," describes the persons.
The sixth section, "The Lifespan of Śāriputra and Flower-Light Buddha," records the length of their respective lifespans;
the seventh section, "After Twelve Minor Kalpas of the Tathāgata Flower-Light," records the subsequent Buddhas;
and the eighth section, "After the Parinirvāṇa of Flower-Light Buddha," records the Semblance Dharma and the True Dharma.

The fourth section above resolves doubts regarding phenomena. A doubt is raised: if the land of the Buddha Flower-Light is purely pure and all those transformed by him are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, then these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would never have heard the names of the three vehicles; why, then, is it said here that he teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the three vehicles?
The commentator says:

"The beings transformed by the Buddha Flower-Light are in fact bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the reason he speaks of the three vehicles is that this accords with the intention harbored by those who occupy the rank of mahāsattva."

Why is this? The mind of a bodhisattva should preach the Four Noble Truths to those for whom the Four Noble Truths should be preached; it should preach the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination to those for whom the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination should be preached; and it should preach the Six Perfections to those capable of hearing the Six Perfections.
"Now, because the Buddha Flower-Light expounds the function of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, it is said that he 'preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles by virtue of his original vow.
"At that time, the fourfold assembly"—from here below is the second section, clarifying how the various devas rejoice upon seeing Śāriputra receive his prediction.

The reason for my joy is precisely that the mind is impartial; now that Śāriputra has received his prediction, I hope that I too shall be included in this same category, and for this reason I am joyful.
Within this, there are both prose and verse. Furthermore, within the prose itself, there are two parts: first, clarifying that the great assembly saw Śāriputra receive his prediction;

second, correctly clarifying their joy. Within this [second part], there are three sections: the phrase "their hearts were greatly filled with joy" clarifies the joy of the mental faculty (*manas-karma*); the passage beginning with "each and every one removed the upper garment they were wearing" clarifies the offering of the physical faculty (*kāya-karma*); and the passage beginning with "and spoke these words" clarifies the praise of the vocal faculty (*vāk-karma*).

Within the verses, there are three and a half verses that clarify rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma; next, two lines of verse clarify the joy arising from seeing the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); and finally, one verse clarifies dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Second, since the Tathāgata has already prophesied above that those of superior faculties will attain Buddhahood—having formerly been śrāvakas and now becoming bodhisattvas—the virtues of a bodhisattva must necessarily involve two types of resolve: seeking the fruit of Buddhahood through one's own practice, and extensively saving sentient beings through the transformation of others. To fully encompass these two intentions, he again requests the Buddha to speak for the sake of those of middling and inferior faculties.
Now, within these two sections, each is further divided into three parts.

Regarding the three aspects of the "request": first, as he intends to request the Buddha to preach again for the sake of those of middling faculties the meaning of "opening the three to reveal the one," he first personally articulates his own understanding; because his understanding correctly accords with the principle that all paths converge, he receives the prediction of attaining *bodhi*.
The second [section] cites those who have not yet attained understanding; from the passage "these twelve hundred" onwards is the third [section], which serves as the conclusion of the request.

The second [point] clarifies that these practitioners are all people who have not yet understood, and they are by no means limited to twelve hundred; however, for the purpose of initiating the request, only this specific number is cited here.
“Being free from the view of self” refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
“As well as the views of existence and non-existence” refers to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism (*uccheda* and *śāśvata*).
“And so forth” refers to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

When these people heard the Buddha open up the three vehicles to reveal the One, they all together confused the principle with the teaching and the teaching with the principle; doubting for themselves whether what they had attained was right or wrong, it is said that "they all fell into doubt and confusion."

The passage beginning with “Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be free from doubt and regret” constitutes the third request.

From the point where the Buddha says to Śāriputra, “At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra,” the following is the third response, which also consists of three sections. The first is the illustrative discourse on dependent origination (*nidāna*). The second, from the passage beginning with “If there is a kingdom, city, or village” and extending through the one hundred verse stanzas, is precisely the illustrative discourse that reveals the One Vehicle within the teaching of the Three Vehicles to transform those of medium capacity; it shows that once followers of medium capacity understand the principle of the common return [to Buddhahood], they know for themselves that they will certainly attain Buddhahood. The third section, from “You, Śāriputra, this seal of my Dharma” and extending through sixty-five verse stanzas at the end of the chapter, is the exhortation and encouragement for those of medium capacity to accept and practice the teaching.
Furthermore, within each of these three sections, two parts are distinguished.
Regarding the two parts within the section on Dependent Origination:
the first part, ending with "all for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas," addresses Śāriputra and rebukes ordinary persons of middling faculties.
The second [section] permits the use of analogies to demonstrate the principle of ultimate convergence.

As for why the first [section] first employs censure, it is to arouse a sense of indignation in those of middling faculties, thereby causing them to open themselves to the teaching through that very indignation.
Now, all those who possess mind and consciousness alike return to becoming Buddhas; yet, in principle, there is only this single consistency, with no threefold distinctions.
What has been explained above clarifies everything—what is there not understood? Regarding this first [section], there are three internal points:

the passage beginning with "by means of various causes and conditions" clarifies the unity of the teaching; "are they all for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? clarifies the unity of the fruit; and "all that has been taught is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas" clarifies the unity of the person.

If one were to reprimand them too severely, they might feel shame or give rise to thoughts of retreat and decline; thinking, "Because I am a disciple of the Buddha, I have been subjected to this censure. Therefore, the second part begins with: "Śāriputra, I shall now further clarify this meaning through a parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables. This clarifies that the Buddha permits the use of parables to demonstrate the principle of ultimate convergence.

Although human faculties differ in being sharp or dull, and there are distinctions in the sequence of realization and understanding, you have not yet understood; I shall provide further analogies for you.

Regarding this second section, there are two parts: from "However, Śāriputra" onwards, the text formally grants permission for the parable; next, from "Those who possess wisdom" onwards, it praises those of middle capacity.

The Sage perceives the nature of things with profound insight; therefore, he grants or denies according to the proper timing, and his intention in first rebuking and later permitting is precisely this.
Within the second section, the "Actual Simile," there are two parts:
the first is the prose narrative (*gadya*), and the second is the hundred verses of the *geya* (repeated verse).
In the third section, the exhortation for those of middling capacity consists of two parts.

First, the intent of the exhortation is to clarify that by propagating this sutra to benefit others and practicing it oneself to transform others, one plants the causes for the ultimate convergence [of all beings] and realizes the fruit of the most perfect and wondrous state. Therefore, the first part—consisting of the single verse beginning with "O Śāriputra, this Dharma-seal of mine"—first identifies the sutra to be propagated, which is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Second, from the verse "Wherever you travel, do not proclaim it recklessly" until the end of the chapter, there are sixty-four verses that properly exhort the reception, practice, and propagation of the sutra to benefit sentient beings.

Previously, while transforming those of superior faculties among humans, I exhorted them to practice the causes and further encouraged them to aspire toward the fruits; however, at the end of this fascicle, I exhort only the practice of the causes and do not encourage aspiration for the fruits. This is because the mind that aspires toward the fruits arises easily, whereas the intention to practice the causes is difficult to establish.
How is this known to be so?

For example, among people in the world, there are none who do not covet and delight in high offices, important positions, autonomy, wealth, and pleasure; yet all such things are fruits of retribution that do not arrive without cause, necessarily being evoked by prior causes. As for the practice of asceticism and the cultivation of the Way, they hardly need mention. Therefore, I exhort only the performance of the causes; the underlying intent is as such.

"Śāriputra, if in a kingdom, city, village... From this point downward, ending with the one hundred lines of verse, is the second section, which provides a parable specifically for those of middling faculties to reveal the One by opening up the Three. This also consists of two parts, as previously explained: the first is the prose (*gadya*), and the second is the verse (*śloka*).
Now, within this extended prose exposition, there are naturally two sections:
first, the opening of the parables; second, the application of the parables.
Within the opening of the parables, ten parables are presented in total, which correspond to the ten types of dharma-teachings in the "Expedient Means" chapter above.
Regarding the ten analogies:

the first, from "If in a kingdom, city, or village" up to "or as many as thirty are within this house," is called the analogy of the householder. It is also designated as the comprehensive analogy (*sāmānya-upamāna*), for it comprehensively illustrates how all Buddhas discourse vertically through the three periods of time and horizontally across the ten directions; hence it is termed "comprehensive."
The remaining nine similes clarify only Śākyamuni.
If it were as such, there would be only two similes; however, by combining the general and the specific, there are ten similes in total.
Regarding the current first point concerning the substance of the "house," my present intention is not as [previously] stated.

This refers to the two lines of verse following the passage in the "Expedient Means" chapter that reads, "Now I am likewise so, for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. These verses clarify that Śākyamuni, like all Buddhas, first employs the three vehicles and subsequently the one vehicle, thereby elucidating the principle of the purpose of transformation.

The second section, from "The elder saw this great fire" to "had no intention of seeking an escape," is called the Parable of the Elder Seeing the Fire. This serves as an analogy for the four verses in the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know that I, observing with the Buddha-eye," which clarify that while the Buddha abides in the stage of the Dharma-body, he perceives sentient beings obscured by the five turbidities.

The third section, from "Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself, 'My hands and body possess great strength'" up to "he merely looked at his father," is titled "The Parable of the Elder Failing to Save His Sons. This illustrates the meaning of the six and a half verses in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṛiccheda*) chapter beginning with "When I first sat upon the site of enlightenment," clarifying how the Buddha employed the Mahāyāna to transform sentient beings but was unable to do so [at that time].

The fourth section, from "At that time, the elder had this thought: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire'" up to "striving to exit the burning house," is designated as the parable of the elder using the three vehicles to save his children; this corresponds to the eleven verses in the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter beginning with "I then recalled the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past," which clarifies how the Tathāgata uses the three vehicles to transform and deliver sentient beings.

The fifth section, from "At that time the elder saw his sons had safely emerged without further hindrance," is designated as the parable of the elder seeing his sons escape danger; it corresponds to the fifth line of the verse in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "Śāriputra, you should know that I see the sons of the Buddha who are intent on seeking the Buddha-way. This clarifies how the Tathāgata perceives that sentient beings' obstacles of the five turbidities have been removed and their capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened.

The sixth [section], consisting of the two phrases "his mind was serene, joyful, and leaping with delight," is designated as the elder’s joy upon seeing his son emerge from danger; this is thus transposed to serve as the seventh analogy within the "Expedient Means" chapter.

The preceding statement, "I then had this thought as to why the Tathāgata appeared," is followed by two lines and one phrase of verse, which clarifies that the Tathāgata rejoices because he perceives that sentient beings in the five turbidities have awakened the capacity for the Mahāyāna.

The seventh section, from "At that time, each of the sons said to their father: 'Father, please grant us at this time the goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts which you previously promised,'" is designated as the Parable of the Sons Requesting Carts; it serves as the sixth parable within the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter.

The preceding verse, "All with hearts of reverence have come to where the Buddha is," clarifies the intention of those of the three vehicles who seek fruits and undergo transformations; this shall be explained below.

The eighth section, from "At that time, Śāriputra, the elder gave each of his sons an equal great carriage" onwards, is designated as the Parable of the Elder Bestowing Great Carriages. This illustrates the three lines of verse from the eighth [section] of the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paryāya*) chapter: "Among all bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path. It signifies that the Buddha preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for those of the three vehicles and bestows upon them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.

The ninth section, from “At that time, the sons each mounted a great vehicle and attained what they had never before experienced, which was not what they had originally expected,” is designated as the parable of the sons’ joy at obtaining the great vehicles. This corresponds to the ninth passage in the preceding “Expedient Means” chapter: “When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed; the twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas. This clarifies the meaning of those of the three vehicles receiving and practicing the Mahāyāna.

The tenth section, beginning from "Śāriputra, what do you think? and below, clarifies how the elder first promised small chariots but now bestows great chariots; this is called the Parable of Non-Deception. It illustrates the one and a half verses from the tenth section of the "Expedient Means" chapter, "Do not harbor doubts that I am the King of the Dharma," which clarifies that the Tathāgata’s teaching is non-deceptive: initially promising small [vehicles] but ultimately bestowing the great. This involves the intention of deception and non-deception regarding the vehicles, which shall be explained below.

Now, regarding the first analogy of the householder, which is also termed a comprehensive analogy, it clarifies that Śākyamuni, like all Buddhas, employs a teaching of "three first and one later" to transform sentient beings in the five turbidities. Categorized by their commonalities, there are six points, which constitute six stages: first, the formal clarification of the commonality of the householder;

second, the commonality of the place of transformation; third, the commonality of the gate of transformation; fourth, the commonality of the persons to be transformed; fifth, the commonality of the matters to be rescued; and sixth, the commonality of those who receive the transformation.
What is meant by this?
First, it clarifies that Śākyamuni, like all Buddhas, is the Lord of Transformation; this is the meaning of being a "householder.

Second, it clarifies that the locus of transformation is the same: while this Lord of Transformation should likewise appear within the triple world, this triple world is actually under the dominion of the Tathāgata; this is the meaning of a householder possessing a great mansion.

Third, regarding the identity of the gateways of transformation: when sentient beings of the five turbidities reverse their flow and exhaust the source, they must rely upon the verbal teachings of the Tathāgata. The function of these teachings is able to lead sentient beings out of the abode of the ocean of suffering and to the place of wondrous bliss; this is precisely like the elder’s house having only a single gate.

The fourth point clarifies that those to be converted are identical [to the previous analogy]: the beings to be taught are the sentient beings of the five destinies; this is the meaning of the "five hundred people" within the elder’s house.

The fifth point, regarding the fact that those rescued share the same circumstances, is as follows: sentient beings within the three realms are all tormented by the five turbidities and the eight kinds of suffering; this is equivalent to the fire within the elder’s house.

The sixth point clarifies that those who receive transformation are identical [in nature]. Among the sentient beings of the five destinies, those who can properly receive transformation possess the root-natures (*gotra*) of the Three Vehicles; these Three Vehicle root-natures are precisely the meaning of the "thirty sons" and are no different [from them].
Although there are five hundred people, they do not all share the same nature as the elder; as for those whose natures are related to his, there are thirty people.

Now, among these six meanings, only that of the householder is common [to both]; this is present in the aforementioned discourse on the Dharma (dharmadeśanā), whereas the remaining five meanings exist only now in this discourse by way of analogy (aupamyadeśanā).

First, to clarify the householder: it is explained in general that the Buddhas of the ten directions all transform sentient beings within the five turbidities; this constitutes the meaning of "the one elder."
Now, within the first parable of the burning house, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the name of the elder and his dwelling place; second, formally introducing the master of the house; and third, praising his virtues.
Furthermore, within these three sections, the first and the last each contain three points, while the middle one contains only one.
Regarding the three points in the first section:

first, it clarifies that the elder is renowned throughout a single kingdom; second, it clarifies that he is renowned throughout a single district; and third, it clarifies that the elder is renowned throughout a single village.
The questioner asked:
"Why do you not proceed from the narrow to the broad, yet now proceed from the broad to the narrow?
The commentator replied:
"Because one wishes to proceed from the remote to the intimate, one proceeds from the broad to the narrow.

For example, a person may gain a reputation in a single country, yet that fame spreads abroad merely as a sound; it does not compare to knowing their true character within a single gate or district. Furthermore, though a good name may be broadcast throughout a province or commandery, it does not compare to knowing their virtue within a single neighborhood or village."

Regarding the internal synthesis as the meaning: horizontally, it encompasses the ten directions of the world and the six paths of the four modes of birth; vertically, it spans from the Avīci Hell above to the Vajra Realm below. Thus, the Tathāgata’s virtue covers all sentient beings and his grace nourishes all living things, just as an elder possesses great merit within a kingdom.

If one were to consider only the reach of the single path of transformation and response of the Buddhas of the ten directions—such as Śākyamuni’s domain of a trichiliocosm—it would be like a wealthy elder possessing virtue within a single town.
Furthermore, it specifically discusses how the Tathāgata benefits the southern continent of Jambudvīpa within this Sahā world, just as there is a virtuous person in a village.
"There was a great elder" refers to the second protagonist who actually departs from his house.
"One is not necessarily called an elder (*sthavira*) simply because one's years have worn away; it is only by virtue of possessing moral excellence and virtuous conduct that one is so designated.
The section beginning with "his years having declined" constitutes the third eulogy of the elder’s virtues, which itself contains three parts:
first, a eulogy of the elder’s internal virtues; second, a eulogy of his external virtues; and third, a eulogy of his retinue.
Now, the first phrase, "his years have declined and he is advanced in age," praises the internal virtue of the elder.

Generally, an old man must possess extensive knowledge; this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s threefold penetration illuminates all things and knows them all. However, since it specifically takes extensive knowledge of the past as its primary focus, "decline in age" is used as the principal metaphor.

Next, the statement "his wealth is immeasurable and he also possesses fields and houses" constitutes the second praise of the elder’s external virtues. This clearly demonstrates that his seven treasures are abundant and provide shelter for the solitary and the poor; it illustrates that the Tathāgata’s virtue of external transformation is inexhaustible. Therefore, he employs the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to guide people and saves all beings with compassion.

Now, sustaining life is likened to a field, and securing one’s person is likened to a dwelling. It is clear that the Tathāgata can produce the merit and wisdom of sentient beings like a field, and he demonstrates the methods for beings to practice cultivation like a dwelling. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"To establish all sentient beings in the five precepts and the ten wholesome karmas"—this is precisely what is meant.
"And his various servants": this is the third praise of the householder's retinue; śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have narrow minds and short aspirations, being like servants.
“The house is vast and extensive”: this is the second meaning, clarifying the elder’s residence.

A residence has the sense of providing a place for the body to dwell. The Tathāgata should reside within the triple world (*tridhātu*); since the triple world is bound to the Tathāgata, that which is transformed [by him] serves as his residence. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
“Sentient beings are the pure land of a bodhisattva,” clarifying that the sentient beings transformed by a bodhisattva constitute his very land.

Now, it is clarified that the Tathāgata transforms the triple world (tridhātu) and takes this triple world as his dwelling; thus, because the triple world is exceedingly vast, it is described as "extensive. "There is only one gate" is the third meaning:

although the dwelling is extensive, there is only a single gate through which people enter and exit. Now, the Buddha's teaching is called the gate; for sentient beings within the triple world who seek to reverse the flow [of saṃsāra], they must rely upon the Tathāgata’s verbal instruction before they can transcend birth and death and inevitably reach Bodhi. Thus, the verbal instructions of the five periods constitute the gate without distinction, and therefore it is said to be "one."

"The great multitude of people"—the following constitutes the fourth meaning, clarifying that within the elder’s house there were more than five hundred people; internally, this corresponds to the five destinies of sentient beings within the three realms, categorized according to their common nature.
"The hall and pavilion are dilapidated" is the fifth meaning; it clarifies the matter of what is to be rescued, clarifying that there is fire within the elder’s house.
To apply this internally as a doctrinal meaning, it clarifies that within the triple world, the five turbidities and eight sufferings are fully present, scorching and pressing upon sentient beings.

Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying that fire arises by first describing the objects to be burned; second, correctly clarifying the transmission of fire through fuel with the sentence, "Suddenly, fire breaks out all around at once. Now, the first part clarifies that the desire realm is like a hall, while the form and formless realms are like upper stories.
However, all sentient beings within the three realms are oppressed by the impermanence of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and thus they are said to be "decayed and worn out.

The four great elements serve as the walls for these sentient beings of the three realms; yet because these bodies composed of the four elements arise and perish moment by moment, they are said to be "collapsing."
Life is like the foundation of a pillar; since this life is summoned by roots of goodness, it is impermanent from moment to moment, and thus it is said to be "rotting.

Consciousness is like the ridgepole and beams; those who possess consciousness are called sentient beings, and thus sentient beings take consciousness as their master. Yet this consciousness, in grasping its conditions, also arises and perishes in each kṣaṇa, and thus it is said to be "tipping and precarious."
From "simultaneously on all sides" onwards, this second section correctly clarifies the arising of fire.

Regarding "simultaneously on all sides," it means that within the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), there are universally the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the eight sufferings (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*).
The phrase "suddenly a fire broke out" precisely clarifies that the fire has ignited.
As for the meaning of the external analogy, it is precisely because the elder was absent that the fire was allowed to break out within the house.

In the following verse, the phrase "it has not been long since that person first emerged" corresponds internally to the Tathāgata having already transformed this sentient being by subduing their afflictions (*kleśa*). At that time, the conditions for their deliverance were already established; however, because the karmic conditions [of the Buddha's presence] have now exhausted, the Tathāgata is teaching and transforming them in another region. Yet, the sentient beings again give rise to the afflictions of the three poisons, which was not what was originally intended. Therefore, it is said that "suddenly a fire breaks out."

"The sons of the elder": this marks the sixth meaning below, clarifying that among the five hundred people, there were those whose natures were related to the elder's; there were thirty sons, which internally corresponds to the clarification that among those transformed by the Tathāgata, there are three types of *gotra* (dispositions) who enter into the triple world.

"Seeing this great fire rising from all four sides," and continuing down to "having no intention to seek escape," constitutes the second analogy of the elder seeing the fire. This corresponds to the four lines of verse in the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means) beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know that I, observing with the Buddha-eye," which clarify how the Tathāgata, abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, perceives sentient beings obscured by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
However, within the "Expedient Means" chapter, there are three sections:
first, clarifying the seer; second, clarifying the seen; and third, giving rise to a heart of compassion.
In this present parable, three sections are likewise established to correspond to the three sections above;

first, the statement "the elder saw" clarifies the capacity for seeing, which corresponds to the passage in the "Expedient Means" chapter above: "Śāriputra, you should know that I observe with the Buddha-eye."

"The great fire arises from the four sides" refers to the second aspect of what is seen; it is an analogy for the aforementioned "seeing the sentient beings of the six realms impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom. This fully clarifies that the Buddha perceives the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) within the five realms; now it clarifies that sentient beings of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) are likewise possessed of the five turbidities and all give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), which is why it is said that [the fire] "arises from the four sides."

"He was immediately seized with great alarm and fear. This marks the third stage, clarifying that once the elder saw the fire break out within the house and the children being tormented by its flames, he gave rise to a heart of alarm and fear. This corresponds to the third stage within the preceding parable in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*) chapter, which states: "For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)," clarifying that once the Tathāgata sees sentient beings obscured by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), he gives rise to a heart of pity and compassion.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the single phrase "was immediately seized with great terror" serves as a direct metaphor for great compassion;
second, from "and had this thought" down to "safely emerged," clarifies that he did not act for his own sake;
third, from "but the sons" down to "terror," identifies those for whom he acts.

Regarding the current statement, "he was immediately struck with great terror": the sense of compassion suddenly arose, which caused him to be startled. Internally, this corresponds to how the Tathāgata had previously, at the sites of twenty trillion Buddhas, already taught and transformed sentient beings; at that time, he had already established the causes for their deliverance. Yet from then on, they again became greedily attached to the five sensory objects and extensively gave rise to afflictions, thereby losing the understanding they had gained in the past. Because of this loss regarding the matter of the compassionate intent, it is said that he was "startled."

It is not merely that they lose their understanding; it is also feared that sentient beings will extensively give rise to afflictions, sever their roots of goodness, and become icchantikas, falling into the three miserable realms to suffer for kalpas upon kalpas—hence the word "fear."
The phrase, "And he thinks to himself: 'Although I am able to emerge safely from this burning gate,'" indicates the second point: being afraid yet not acting for oneself.
"The previous statement designated Buddhism as a 'gate'; why then is this gate being burned? He replied: "That was merely a designation of Buddhism as a gate;

it did not say that this Teaching itself is being burned. Rather, it is the sentient beings transformed by the Teaching who are being burned. Thus, it is like establishing a great university gate for a single entrance—how could one not speak of reading books and explaining their meaning through both panels and double doors?"
Thus we know that those within the One Gate understand the meaning and study the scriptures.

As for "peacefully and securely emerging," this clarifies that in the past the Tathāgata personally relied upon the teachings of the Mahāyāna to depart from the three realms and the eight sufferings, thereby accomplishing the awakening of the seeds; hence it is said that he "peacefully and securely emerged."

"The sons" and so forth refers to the third category of those for whom fear is produced. Because sentient beings are greedily stained by the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), it is said they "delight in and cling [to them]. Since they spend their entire days engaged in the activities of the three karmas (*tri-karma*) without a single meritorious record, it is said they "play."

They do not realize that they are oppressed by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings; if they were to realize that these ninety-eight latent proclivities (anuśaya) are a loss, they would then fear the sufferings of the three miserable realms. It is precisely because they do not realize this that they neither know nor are struck with terror.

"Śāriputra, this elder thought thus," from here until "he merely looked at his father," constitutes the third illustration clarifying how the elder could not save his sons; it corresponds to the six and a half verses beginning with "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment" in the third chapter, the "Expedient Means" (Upāya-paṛiccheda), which clarify that the Tathāgata was unable to transform sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna.

However, within the preceding analogy, there are three sections. The first, consisting of half a verse stating, "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I gazed at the tree and also practiced walking meditation," clarifies that there were places where the Tathāgata could not transform sentient beings using the Mahāyāna; this [section] is not being used as an analogy here.

The second statement, "For twenty-one days he contemplated these matters," constitutes half a line; it clarifies the period during which the Tathāgata employed the Mahāyāna to transform sentient beings when he was unable to do so, and here, too, no analogy is provided.

Only the third [case] can be properly used as an analogy for transforming sentient beings through the Mahāyāna; however, this meaning fundamentally does not involve verbal teachings, but rather precisely clarifies the Tathāgata’s intention regarding the methods for the path of transformation through the Mahāyāna.

The third section above, "The Correct Transformation Failing to Reach the Middle," originally consists of three parts: first, employing the Mahāyāna as a provisional teaching; second, the absence of a karmic capacity for the Mahāyāna; and third, the cessation of Mahāyāna transformation.
Now, this passage also serves as a complete analogy for these two sections; however, since the intent of the analogy is already exhaustive, it is appropriate to divide it into two parts:
the first constitutes the exhortation, and the second, from the words "I shall speak to you of things that cause fear" onwards, constitutes the admonition.

Although the Tathāgata, while in the world, filled the three thousandfold world-system with his words and pervaded the six realms with his form, when considered on a grand scale, he did not transcend the two paths of admonition and exhortation. Therefore, at the very beginning of his appearance in the world, he stated: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Practicing all that is good is the Great Compassion that exhorts one toward goodness; committing no evil is the Great Benevolence that admonishes one against evil. Thus, benevolence desires to bestow happiness and exhorts one to perform good deeds, while compassion is able to uproot suffering and admonishes one to sever evil. Consequently, as previously explained, the two truths of Suffering and its Origin constitute the Great Compassion that admonishes against evil, while the subsequent clarification of the two principles of Cessation and the Path constitutes the Great Benevolence that exhorts toward goodness.
The meaning of this present parable is likewise so.

Within these exhortations, there are three sections each, all corresponding to the three sections of the original parable: first, the preliminary exhortation and instruction; second, the clarification that the sons lack the capacity to receive such exhortation; and third, the cessation of the exhortation and instruction.

Now, to clarify the appropriateness of the exhortation and instruction: it is analogous to what was said in the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter, where [the Buddha] stated, "The wisdom I have attained is subtle and supreme," using the Mahāyāna as the appropriate teaching.

The preceding section clarified only wisdom; now, within this analogy, both wisdom and its object are explained in detail. Thus, regarding this correspondence, there are two parts within the analogy itself.

First, as for "the elder thinks to himself: 'My hands and body possess strength,'" this first clarifies how the elder uses his hands and body to provide relief. Internally, this corresponds to the Tathāgata’s contemplation that the Dharma-body possesses the efficacy of responding to beings, and that wisdom possesses the power to rescue and deliver them.

The second statement, "One should take him out of the house using a garment-sack or a small table," precisely clarifies that his compassionate mindfulness has reached its utmost limit; he wishes to wrap the child in a garment-sack and wishes to lift him up with a small table. This internally corresponds to the Tathāgata’s actual application of the Mahāyāna teachings as a provisional expedient: the garment-sack is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna cause, and the small table is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna fruit. It is intended to clarify that since the Tathāgata possesses the hands and body of wisdom, he bestows the Mahāyāna cause upon sentient beings and wishes to bestow the Mahāyāna fruit upon them so that they may emerge.

"Furthermore, he reflects again"—this is the second [point], clarifying that the sons lack the capacity to be receptive to his exhortation; it corresponds to the second stage in the "Expedient Means" chapter above, concerning those classes of sentient beings whose faculties are dull, who are attached to pleasure, and blinded by ignorance—how can such as these be delivered?
In this passage there are two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Great Teaching is of no use to such a person; second, it properly clarifies that they lack the capacity for the Great [Vehicle].

Regarding the first point, the phrase "this house has but one door, which is moreover narrow" clarifies that at that time, the door of the Mahāyāna teaching did not enable beings to be transformed and attain liberation from the three realms; thus, the teaching was of no use to them, and its inability to accommodate them is what is meant by "narrow."
The questioner said:
"The gate itself is narrow and small, preventing the sons from passing through and escaping; how does this concern the sons' refusal to come out?
The commentator replied:
"The scripture itself states that the sons were young and lacked understanding, and thus refused to go out through the gate;
if they had possessed discernment and knowledge, how could they have remained inside the gate to be burned by the fire?"
"However, at that time, the Mahāyāna teaching was of no use to sentient beings, and its meaning was thus established as narrow and limited.
From the passage "The sons were young and immature" onwards, the second section correctly clarifies the lack of spiritual capacity (*anabhavyatā*).
Within this, there are two points:
first, "the children are young" clarifies that sentient beings possess the minor capacities for the five precepts and ten wholesome actions of devas and humans.
Second, "they have no discernment" is the primary meaning, which correctly clarifies that sentient beings lack the capacity for the Mahāyāna; therefore, it says they have no discernment.
If one does not mention its smallness, there is no way to manifest its lack of greatness.

The preceding section, beginning with "At that time, the Brahma kings," was intended to provide a middle-level analogy; the subsequent section, from "At that time, the various Brahma kings" onwards, cites scriptural evidence to prove the absence of a great capacity, and thus no further analogy is made here.

"Attached to the place of play": the following section is the third, clarifying the elder’s cessation of his exhortations. This corresponds to the third stage in the "Expedient Means" chapter above: "I then reflected to myself: 'If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma. Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms. It would be better for me not to preach the Dharma at all, and to quickly enter nirvana.'"

Regarding the phrase "or they may fall and be burned by fire," this clarifies that since sentient beings lack the aspiration for the Great Vehicle, if one were to forcibly convert them using the Mahāyāna, they might instead give rise to slander and fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, it is said they will be "burned by fire."

"I shall speak to you of matters of fear; this house is already burning, you should quickly exit at once, lest you be harmed by the fire. From here below begins the second section, which constitutes the Mahāyāna admonition and instruction; however, the meaning of "admonition" (kai) is that one urges [the listener] by speaking words of suffering.

This section consists of three parts, which likewise correspond to the three parts in the preceding discourse on the Dharma: first, the initial use of admonitions and instructions to prepare the way; second, the clarification that the sons lack the capacity to receive such admonitions; and third, the clarification that the elder ceases his instructions and commands.

Now, regarding the term "provisional suitability" (niyi): it refers back to the first statement in the "Expedient Means" chapter above, which says, "The wisdom I have attained is subtle and most supreme," clarifying that the Tathāgata employs the Mahāyāna as a provisional means to suit sentient beings.
Within this, there are two stages:

first, it clarifies the elder’s contemplation and the instruction he issues as a warning; second, it clarifies the Tathāgata’s contemplation and his desire to preach for the sake of sentient beings that within the triple world there are the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, and that they are oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death, so as to cause them to feel weary of them.
The second section clearly explains the intended application.
The questioner says:

"The Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes penetrates the conditions of sentient beings; responding to their capacities and meeting their needs is a matter of a single moment. Now, you speak of 'contemplation'—will this not contradict the clarity of his knowledge of all modes and diminish the illumination of his threefold mastery?"

The commentator says: "If one discusses the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is fundamentally beyond words and images; yet, based on the traces [of the Buddha's manifestation] which involve form, this meaning is not non-existent.

If one were to find it strange that the Tathāgata would further contemplate and issue instructions of admonition and exhortation, one should likewise find it strange that he possesses a body sixteen feet tall, and one should likewise doubt his contemplation during the three periods of seven days."
Since you have never harbored doubt regarding the sixteen-foot [image] or the thirty-seven [auxiliaries], for what reason do you suddenly treat them with strange suspicion and issue this admonition?

This intention clarifies that the Tathāgata’s great compassion is inexhaustible and his heart to gather and rescue beings is ever more profound; he ensures a good beginning and a good end, always acting for the sake of the Mahāyāna.

"Having formed this thought, he informed his sons in detail according to what he had contemplated, saying: 'You all must come out quickly! From here below, the text correctly clarifies how the elder employs admonitions and instructions as a provisional means; internally, it corresponds to the correct clarification of how the Tathāgata employs the admonitions and instructions of the Mahāyāna as a provisional means for sentient beings.

"Although the father feels compassion," and so forth, constitutes the second section, which clarifies that sentient beings lack the capacity to receive instruction and admonition. This section has two parts: first, "Although the father feels compassion and uses kind words to entice and instruct them," which cites the preceding phrase; second, "Yet the sons were unwilling to believe or accept it, neither startled nor afraid," which properly explains the absence of great capacity. This corresponds to the previous analogy of sentient beings whose faculties are dull, who are attached to pleasure, blinded by ignorance, and of such a kind—how can they be saved?
There was no capacity for the Mahāyāna;
nor was it intended as an illustration to provide scriptural evidence.
"He merely ran about here and there, playing and looking at his father"—this is the third teaching, which consists of instructions given when [the son's] agitation has subsided.

North and south constitute the vertical, while east and west constitute the horizontal. If the mental activity of sentient beings were to accord with the Great Principle, it would be like the verticality of north and south; however, because sentient beings do not realize the True Principle amidst birth and death, they employ their minds according to the horizontal principle, which is like east and west.
To gallop amidst the five sensory objects is called "running"; though one may further engage the three karmas, if there is no hope for goodness, it is termed "sport.
Only when there is the capacity to be moved by the vision of the sixteen-foot [Buddha] body is it said that one "beholds the father."
Because there were no sentient beings with the capacity to understand the teaching of the Mahāyāna, he spoke only in words.

From the passage, "At that time, the elder had this thought: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire,'" down to "striving to exit the burning house," is the fourth section, which clarifies the analogy of the elder using the three vehicles to save his children. This corresponds to the eleventh line of the fourth section of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*), which clarifies how the Tathāgata uses the three vehicles to transform and deliver sentient beings.

However, within the original text of the preceding analogy, there are two sections: the first consists of ten lines of verse that correctly clarify how the Tathāgata uses the three vehicles to transform and deliver sentient beings; the second, beginning with "From kalpas long ago," consists of a single verse that resolves doubts.
I shall not now provide an analogy for the Śrāvakas; rather, I shall provide an analogy solely for those who are converted through the correct application of the Three Vehicles.
Within this section on the correct application of the Three Vehicles for conversion, there are originally four parts:

first, the provisional application of the Three Vehicles; second, observing the capacities of those of the Three Vehicles; third, preaching the teachings of the Three Vehicles; and fourth, the single line—"Thereupon there were sounds of Nirvāṇa, as well as the distinct names of Arhats, Dharma, and Saṃgha"—which clarifies how those of the Three Vehicles receive and practice them.

In this present parable, all four preceding sections are likewise complete.
