The statement, "In the same way, the Tathāgata likewise possesses power and fearlessness, yet does not employ them," constitutes the second [section], which correlates with the third external analogy mentioned above.
The section beginning with "But by means of wisdom and skillful means" constitutes the third [section], which correctly corresponds to the fourth analogy.

Now, as we are about to correlate the fourth [analogy] through a fourfold analysis, the reason for citing the third analogy is to demonstrate the intention of the Sage in appearing in the world—an intention centered upon the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the reason for citing the fourth analogy is to demonstrate the Tathāgata’s intention in employing the provisional path (*upāyamārga*).

However, sentient beings lack the capacity to receive the Mahāyāna; thus, having no other recourse, he employs the transformation through the Three Vehicles. This is why the meaning of the fourth analogy is cited here.

The reason for restating the eighth external analogy is to demonstrate the intention of beginning well and seeing it through to the end; although the practice in the interim may be small, the intent remains fixed on the great. Therefore, the eighth is restated here to manifest the meaning of its correspondence with the Great [Vehicle].

As for the reason for joining the third [section] together: since it has already been joined above and is now held by the formal document (*nyāya*), the third is therefore joined to it so that it belongs to the preceding.
As for the reason for not joining the eighth: it is joined by the text itself below, so what need is there to join it here?
Now, the third section precisely corresponds to the fourth analogy of saving the children; however, within the preceding analogy there were originally four stages:

first, employing the three vehicles as a provisional means; second, seeing that the children possessed a mind of prior affinity; third, preaching the three vehicles for them; and fourth, the children receiving and practicing them.

This section also comprises four parts; the current phrase, "But by means of wisdom and skillful means," corresponds to the first part, in which the elder employs the three vehicles as a provisional measure.

The Sūtra says: "At that time, the elder had this thought: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire; if I and my sons do not exit immediately, we will surely be burned by the flames. I must now employ an expedient means.'"

"Delivering sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world"—this single phrase is the second [part], which corresponds to the second [point]: seeing that the sons possess a latent affinity for the Dharma.

The preceding statement, "The father knows that each of his sons has a prior inclination toward various marvelous and extraordinary things, and their hearts will surely delight in them," refers to the teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
This section below is the third [section], which combines with the aforementioned third point to constitute the teaching of the three carts (*trivihaga*).
However, in the previous discourse on the three vehicles, there were four stages:
first, praising the three vehicles; second, indicating the location of the three vehicles; third, encouraging the taking of the three vehicles; and fourth, guaranteeing that they are not in vain.

Now, this [passage] likewise possesses all four stages, though they are not in their proper order: first, it combines the second stage by indicating the location of the three vehicles; second, it skips ahead to combine the fourth stage by assuring that [the gift] is not in vain; then it returns to combine the third stage by exhorting the taking of the three vehicles; and finally, it follows up by combining the first stage through praising the three vehicles.

Regarding the current statement, "He speaks for them of the three vehicles," the following four and a half lines first correspond to the second section above, which indicates the location of the three carts; that is, it shows that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of those of the three vehicles exist outside the triple world.
The preceding statement, "Such various goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate for you to play with," refers to this. The phrase, "I now guarantee this matter for you;

it shall never prove false," directly corresponds to the fourth point above—the guarantee that the three carts are not false—which is to say, the guarantee that the people of the three vehicles will attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). This corresponds to the preceding statement: "Whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you."

From the two phrases, "You should simply cultivate diligence with earnest effort; the Tathāgata uses these skillful means to entice and advance sentient beings," one returns to and merges them with the third exhortation to take the three vehicles.

The previous statement, "You should all quickly come out from this burning house," is an exhortation for those of the three vehicles (triyāna) to practice so as to attain the fruits of the three vehicles.

The subsequent passage, "Furthermore, you should know that these teachings of the three vehicles are all praised by the sages," spanning the following three and a half lines, corresponds back to the first praise of the three carts; that is, it is a praise of the three vehicles.
The preceding statement says: "He told them, 'These things you may enjoy are rare and difficult to obtain; if you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later.
An Arhat has severed all fetters of the three realms and is no longer constrained by delusions; therefore, he is said to be 'autonomous'."
If there were afflictions that could bind one to the three realms, they would exist; however, since afflictions have already perished, it is said that he is "unbound.

Previously, when he had not yet attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he had dependence and seeking; now that he has realized the ultimate fruit of the virtue of no-more-learning, it is said that he has "nothing upon which to depend or seek."

Regarding the phrase "riding these three vehicles," for an Arhat at that time, the two knowledges of *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) and *anutpādajñāna* (knowledge of non-arising) constitute the fruit. As for why they are called "vehicles," it is because at the moment of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one is spontaneously carried by the power of these knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; therefore, there is the sense of a "fruit-vehicle. The phrase "thereby attaining immeasurable peace and happiness" refers precisely to the bliss of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
"Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within," from this point downward, it corresponds to the fourth section above concerning the sons' acceptance and practice.
This refers to what was stated previously: "At that time, the sons, having heard what their father spoke regarding the rare treasures and playthings, found them to accord with their wishes."

However, regarding the four stages within the Middle [Vehicle] that the sons above have received and practiced, these are now fully combined with the four stages above; yet their applications differ. In the preceding [section], the analogy directly established four stages collectively for those of the Three Vehicles. Now, here, one proceeds through each individually, establishing four stages for each of the Three Vehicles respectively, which constitutes a perfect correspondence. Subsequently, an external analogy is raised to provide a further correspondence, thereby forming three layers of four stages, which precisely corresponds to the subsequent correspondence.

Now, first, regarding the four stages established according to the Śrāvaka-yāna, the initial statement, "Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they receive it with faith," corresponds to the first [stage] above: "The minds of each were courageous and sharp," which gives rise to the roots of goodness of the external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana).
The phrase "diligent and energetic" corresponds to the second stage above, "mutually pushing one another," which gives rise to the roots of goodness of the internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

"Wishing to quickly exit the triple world and seek nirvāṇa for oneself" constitutes the third stage; it corresponds to the third stage above, "rushing together in competition," wherein followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, enter into the practice of signlessness (*animitta*), and through the path of seeing and contemplation (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*), they eliminate the fetters.

"This is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle" refers to the fourth stage; it corresponds to the aforementioned fourth stage, wherein one "emerges from the burning house through dispute" and attains the fruit of Arhatship.
The passage beginning with "Just as those sons" below is the citation of the external analogy to provide a formal correspondence.
The section beginning with "If there are sentient beings" constitutes the second part; herein, regarding the Pratyekabuddhayāna, another four stages are established for the formal correspondence.

The initial statement, "Hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they received it with faith," corresponds to the first point, "each heart being courageous and sharp," referring to those of the Pratyekabuddhayāna who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, give rise to the roots of goodness of an external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana).

“Diligent and energetic effort” corresponds here to the second point, “mutually pushing one another forward,” which refers to the arising of the roots of goodness in those at the stage of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

“Seeking spontaneous wisdom” corresponds to the third point above, “rushing together in competition,” clarifying how followers of the Middle Vehicle, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, enter into the practice of signlessness (*animitta*), contemplate the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*), cultivate the path, and sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The reason it is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*) is that the realm of the two truths is spontaneous; now, since wisdom receives its name from this realm, wisdom itself is termed "spontaneous.
This is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, which corresponds to the fourth section, "Emerging from the Burning House," wherein one realizes the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
The passage beginning with "Just as those sons" below serves to cite an external analogy and apply it to the case at hand.
The section beginning with "If there are sentient beings" refers to the third category, those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle; this is further divided into four stages to provide a precise correspondence.

The initial statement, "Hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, one receives it with faith," corresponds to the first stage, "the minds of each being becoming courageous and sharp," which gives rise to the roots of goodness of the external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana).

“Diligent and earnest effort” is the second [stage], which combines with “mutually encouraging one another” to clarify that when Bodhisattvas hear the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, they give rise to the roots of goodness of the inner ordinary beings (ārya-prthagjana).

"Seeking all-knowledge": this is the third section below, which combines with the preceding "rushing together in competition. When Bodhisattvas hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, they enter into the practice of signlessness (*animitta*), perceive the truths (*satya*), and sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) through contemplation.
"Buddha-wisdom" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood within the Three Vehicles.
"Self-existent wisdom" is as explained previously.

"Teacherless wisdom" correctly clarifies that when the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) are completely severed, one achieves the fruit of Arhatship; thus, the wisdom of an Arhat is termed "teacherless wisdom."

"This is called the Mahāyāna" is the fourth [section], which combines with the preceding "quarreling and exiting the burning house" to testify to the realization of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*).
From "like those sons" onwards, external analogies are presented to provide a formal correspondence (*pratirūpaka*).
"Śāriputra, it is just as that elder saw his sons safely emerge"—this section below constitutes the fifth segment, which combines and superimposes the fifth and eighth analogies.
The reason for combining these two analogies is that, since they do not apply to the sixth and seventh [stages], the two analogies are presented side by side.
This is precisely because, upon perceiving the awakening of the Mahāyāna capacity, one immediately teaches the Mahāyāna.
Now, within this section, it is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the two external analogies proposed by the opponents; second, the formal application of those two analogies.
First, the fifth external analogy is cited; next, from the passage beginning with "I reflect upon my wealth," the eighth external analogy is cited.

"Thus it is with the Tathāgata as well," and so forth, marks the second section, which correctly correlates the two parables. Now, first, the analogy of seeing the son emerge from distress is correlated to clarify the awakening of the potential for the Mahāyāna.
In the preceding analogy, there are originally two parts:
first, clarifying how one severs delusions, exits beyond the triple world, and attains the fruit of no-more-learning; second, correctly clarifying the arousal of the Mahāyāna potential.
Now, the two layers are combined.

From "The Tathāgata is also like this" up to "emerges from the perilous path of the suffering and terrors of the triple world," this corresponds to the first section above: "seeing his sons safely emerge."
"Attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa" corresponds to the second section, which clearly elucidates the arousal of the Mahāyāna capacity.

Previously it was said that "they all sit in the open air at the crossroads without further obstruction"; now it says "attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa. This bliss of nirvāṇa is the fruit of those possessing the wholesome capacity for the Mahāyāna; here, by citing the fruit, one indicates the cause, or rather, one speaks of the fruit within the context of the cause.

If one were to argue based on principle, since it transcends both kinds of birth-and-death, it ought to be the eternally abiding nirvana; however, as this teaching has not yet clarified that principle, it is therefore named "nirvana" by doubling the aforementioned number.

"At that time, the Tathāgata... and below this is the formal application of the eighth parable, "The Elder Bestowing Great Chariots upon His Sons," which clarifies the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
However, within the preceding section on the "Opening of Similes," there were originally two parts:
first, the simultaneous opening of the two chapter-gates; second, the simultaneous detailed explanation of the two chapter-gates.

In that preceding section on the opening of similes, each textual passage was treated according to its beginning and end, which should properly be combined into two sections. Now, within this current section on the "Correspondence of Similes," there are both correspondences and non-correspondences, as well as instances where the sequence is not maintained; therefore, it is appropriate to re-open this into six sections.
What are they? First is the chapter-gateway of the equality of mind;
second is the chapter-gateway of the single great vehicle.
The great, single carriage is three.
The explanation of the great carriage is four.
The broad mind of equanimity is five.
The sixth [point], the broadening of the mind through equanimity (*samacitta*), is not included here. Previously it was said: "Why is this?
Because even if I were to distribute these goods throughout the entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted; how much less so for my sons. This [previous point] is not included here either.

Although the remaining five stages are combined, they are not in sequential order; first, the first stage is combined with the fourth, and by the force of that, it is combined with the fifth, after which one returns to combine them with the first, second, and third stages respectively.

Now, from the statement "At that time, the Tathāgata had this thought" up to "the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas," this corresponds to the fourth explanation, which elaborates upon the single great carriage. The previous remark, "Why is this? Because this great elder possesses immeasurable wealth, and his various treasuries are all overflowing," has its full meaning already explained above.

The passage from "All these sentient beings are my children" down to "and bring them to parinirvāṇa" corresponds to the fifth point above, the broad mind of equality. This refers to what was stated previously: "I have formed this thought: 'My wealth and goods are infinite; I ought not to give inferior, small carts to my children alike. Now these young children are all my sons, and my love for them is without partiality.'"

"These sentient beings who have escaped the triple world shall all receive [it]"—this refers back to and merges with the first chapter on the equality of the mind. Previously it was said, "He bestowed equally upon his sons," and now it says, "all shall receive. "All shall receive" is precisely the meaning of equality.

"The various Buddhas' implements for entertainment, such as meditative concentration (dhyāna), liberation (vimokṣa), and so forth," corresponds to the second chapter on the bestowed gifts, namely the aforementioned "one great carriage."

"All are of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the noble ones, and capable of producing pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss"—this corresponds to the third [section], the extensive description of the single great carriage, specifically the passage above that begins with "those carriages are high and wide," and so forth.
"Śāriputra, just as that elder first used the three vehicles to entice his children"—the following constitutes the sixth section, which corresponds to the tenth "Non-Deceptive" parable above.
However, in the previous analogy, there were originally three sections:
first, the Tathāgata provides the analogy of non-falsity and questions Śāriputra, which does not correspond here;
third, the Tathāgata confirms and completes Śāriputra’s statement, which also does not correspond here.
"Only a name"—this second response by Śāriputra correctly clarifies that [the teaching] is not false;

now, this analogy shall be applied. This section should be divided into four parts: first, a restatement of the three preceding analogies; second, the actual application; third, the explanation of the application; and fourth, the conclusion of the application.

First, regarding the citation of the three preceding parables: "Śāriputra, like that elder" cites the first parable; "initially using the three vehicles to entice the sons" cites the fourth parable; and "thereafter giving only the great vehicles" and following cite the eighth parable.

"The Tathāgata is also like this. The following section constitutes the second part, the "correct application" (*saṃyoga*). Above, Śāriputra looked up and answered the Buddha, clarifying that [the teaching] is not in vain; however, within that previous answer, there were originally two parts: first, a general answer clarifying that it is not in vain, and second, a specific answer clarifying that it is not in vain.
Now, the statement "The Tathāgata is likewise thus, without any falsehood" corresponds to the preceding "No, World-Honored One," collectively clarifying that [the teaching] is not false.

"First, the teaching of the three vehicles"—the following section consolidates the previous detailed explanation of how [the Buddha's words] are not in vain. Within this, there are originally three types; they are now consolidated in sequence.
"First, the teaching of the three vehicles" consolidates the first point above: that the granting of the heavy was not in vain because it superseded the light.
Next, the statement "guiding sentient beings" corresponds to the second [point]: that one's original resolve is not in vain.
"Thereafter, he delivers them by means of the Mahāyāna alone" corresponds to the third [point]: that what is bestowed exceeds their expectations and is not in vain.
“For what reason? From here below is the third explanation, which provides the synthesis.
“Śāriputra, by these causes and conditions” from here below is the fourth, which is the final conjunction.

"Then he spoke in verse. This allegorical exposition, which opens the three to reveal the one for the sake of those of middle capacity, originally consists of four sections; however, within the first section—the primary allegory itself—there are two parts: first, Śāriputra’s request, and second, the Tathāgata’s response to his previous words.
Each of these two sections contains three parts, and within the Buddha’s response there are likewise three, as previously detailed.

First is the *nidāna* (the introductory context); second, from "In whatever kingdom, town, or village" through the one hundred verses, is the primary parable; third, from "You, Śāriputra, this seal of my Dharma" onwards in sixty-five verses, is the exhortation to accept and practice it.
A previous commentary further explains:
within these three sections, each is divided into two parts. Regarding the two aspects of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the first is the censure and the second is the permission.

Within the formal exposition (*uddeśa*), there are two parts: the first is the prose (*gadya*) and the second is the verse (*gāthā*); from this point downward, the one hundred lines of verse constitute the second round of verses (*anugāthā*).
In the preceding prose section, there were originally two parts: the first was the opening of the parable, and the second was the application of the parable.
Now, within these one hundred verses, they are likewise divided into two:

the first consists of sixty-five and a half verses which eulogize the opening of the parable; the second consists of thirty-four and a half verses beginning with "I am also like this, Śāriputra," which eulogize the application of the parable.
In the preceding prose section, ten similes were presented; here, only nine are versified, with the tenth simile—of being non-false—omitted for brevity. Why is this so?
The ancient commentary states:

"The reason the tenth [verse] is not recited is that the preceding analogy of non-falsity was originally composed by Śāriputra; since the present verses are spoken by the Buddha, how could one use verses spoken by the Buddha to recite the words of Śāriputra?"

Now, the school we follow does not employ this interpretation; for how could there be any limit to such instances? Thus, in the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), the Buddha, acting as a physician, poses a non-false analogy to Maitreya.
Maitreya answered the Buddha that his explanation was not false; this serves as an analogy for when Maitreya later returned to his residence and likewise declared it was not false.

Furthermore, as in the prose section of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" where the Buddha speaks, and the verse recitation by Maitreya follows accordingly, such instances of correspondence are truly numerous.

The reason why the tenth analogy of non-falsity is not versified here is to clarify that the intent of "non-falsity" is fundamentally to enable sentient beings to attain genuine understanding. Since the assembly has already attained faith in the meaning of non-falsity, the intent is naturally revealed; therefore, the tenth analogy of non-falsity is omitted from the verses.
Now, these sixty-five and a half lines of verse, consisting of nine similes, are further divided into nine sections:
the first comprises thirty-three lines of verse, which correspond to the first simile of the householder, also known as the general simile.
The second section, from "At that time, the householder stood outside the gate" onwards, consists of two lines of verse, praising the second analogy of the elder seeing the fire.

The third section, "Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house," consists of six lines of verse, praising the third analogy of the elder being unable to rescue his children.

The fourth [section]: "At that time, the elder had this thought: 'These sons of mine cause me such distress and sorrow,'" followed by seven and a half lines, which constitutes the verse on the fourth analogy: the elder rescuing his children.
The fifth section, "The Elder Sees His Sons Escape from the Burning House," contains three lines of verse, praising the fifth analogy of seeing the sons emerge from the calamity.
The sixth section, "Sitting upon the Lion Throne and Speaking Words of Joy," contains four lines and one phrase, praising the sixth analogy of the elder’s rejoicing.
The seventh section, beginning with "At that time, the sons knew their father was sitting at ease," contains three verses of gāthā, praising the seventh parable of the sons requesting vehicles.

The eighth section, beginning with "The elder was immensely wealthy, possessing many treasuries," contains seven and a half verses of gāthā, praising the eighth parable of the bestowal of great vehicles.

The ninth section, beginning with "At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness," consists of one and a half verses; it is a verse summarizing the ninth analogy, which illustrates how the sons rejoiced upon receiving the chariots.

The first consists of thirty-three verse stanzas; the second, two verse stanzas; the third, six verse stanzas; the fourth, seven and a half verse stanzas; the fifth, three lines of verse stanzas; the sixth, four lines and one line of verse stanzas; the seventh, three verse stanzas; the eighth, seven and a half stanzas; and the ninth, one and a half stanzas.

In the preceding section on the "Master of the Dwelling," there were six meanings in total within the main text; here, only four meanings are versified, as the third single gate and the sixth thirty sons are omitted for brevity.

Now, these thirty-three lines are divided into four sections: the first line praises the first elder; the second consists of three lines and one phrase praising the second, the great house; the third consists of half a line praising the fourth, the five hundred people; and the remaining twenty-nine lines of verse praise the fifth, the outbreak of fire within the house.
Regarding the three sections within the "Exalted Householder" (Śreṣṭhin):
first, "In a kingdom, town, or village" indicates the location of his status;
second, "There was a great householder" explicitly clarifies the householder himself.
The third section, beginning with "His years have advanced," praises his virtues.
Now, the single phrase "For example, like an elder" is a verse summary of the passage "There was a great elder."
The names, positions, locations, and praises of their virtues are omitted from this verse. The line "There was a great house" and the following three lines and one phrase praise the great house;

many people use this verse to describe kingdoms, cities, and villages, but that is not the case here. It correctly praises the phrase "that house was vast," for while the parable itself simply states "that house was vast," this second section provides a detailed description of the characteristics of the great house. However, the phrasing is similar to the fifth section’s description of the fire's characteristics; though they are similar, they are not the same, as there will be separate phrasing below specifically praising the arising of the fire.
Since the three realms are taken as a dwelling, it is "great.

Because every moment within the three realms is impermanent, they are "suddenly dilapidated. The form and formless realms are like halls, while the desire realm is like a house; yet, as there is no peace within the three realms, they are said to be "lofty and precarious."
Life is like the base of a pillar, impermanent from moment to moment; therefore, it is said to be "crumbling and decaying.
Consciousness is like the beams and rafters, arising and ceasing from moment to moment; therefore, it is said to be "slanting and leaning."
Since karma serves as the foundation and both ignorance and delusive appearances are falsely constructed and arbitrarily created, it is said that they are "ruined.
Since the four great elements are like walls and are all destroyed by impermanence, it is said that they are "collapsed and split apart."
Since form, fragrance, taste, and touch are all impermanent from moment to moment, it is said that "the plastered coating falls away.

Because the four modes of deportment are not upright or correct, it is said that "the thatched roof collapses in disorder"; furthermore, it is said that hair, teeth, and nails are what adorn the body.

The five consciousnesses no longer correspond to their objects, and since their substance arises and perishes moment by moment, one perceives that "the rafters and eaves are out of alignment"; this also refers to the five sense organs.
The Sage, through his swift and penetrating wisdom, contemplates this realm of impermanence; therefore, he says it is "completely obstructed and winding.
"Winding" means being thoroughly detailed and exhaustive.
"Five hundred people dwell within it"—this half-line constitutes the first five hundred [beings] of the third verse.

"Owls, crows, vultures, and eagles"—the twenty-nine lines following this constitute the fourth verse, which describes the fifth fire arising; it refers to what was stated above: "The halls and pavilions are decayed and old, the walls have collapsed," up until "all around, suddenly at once, fire breaks out."

However, while the preceding prose did not explicitly mention the three realms (*tridhātu*), the present verses provide a detailed account; therefore, they specifically clarify the outbreak of fire within the three realms.

Now, these twenty-nine lines of verse are divided into four sections. The first consists of twenty-two lines, which clarify the outbreak of fire within the house—that is, the outbreak of fire in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The second section, from "wild beasts and venomous insects" downward, consists of three and a half verses; it clarifies that fire breaking out within the cave refers to the arising of fire in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

The third section, consisting of two and a half verses following the line on "centipedes and millipedes," clarifies that fire arises in empty space; this refers to the arising of fire in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The fourth section, "That house is thus most terrifying," consists of one line that summarizes the outbreak of the fire.
Within the preceding three sections, each has four stages clarifying the meaning, whereas the fourth section contains only one and is not further divided.
Now, regarding the preceding twenty-two lines which clarify that the arising of fire in the desire realm has four stages:
first, seventeen and a half verses list the sentient beings who are to be burned;
second, the single verse beginning with "This dilapidated old house belongs to one person" clarifies the cause for the arising of fire in the desire realm.
The third section, "Suddenly a fire breaks out in the house," consists of two lines of verse, which specifically clarify the outbreak of the fire;
the fourth section, "The various spirits and ghosts raise their voices and cry out," consists of one and a half lines of verse, summarizing the signs of being consumed by the flames.

Furthermore, within the preceding seventeen and a half verses, there are three distinct sections. The first consists of six verses, which first separately identify sentient beings with the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*).
The second, beginning from "In every place" (*sarvatra santi*) and comprising ten verses, separately identifies sentient beings with the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
The third section, consisting of one and a half verses beginning with "yakṣas and hungry ghosts," summarizes the sentient beings who are being burned.
Within the first two stages, there were two sub-categories each; here, in the third, they are not further differentiated.

Regarding the fact that there are two [sections] within the six lines: first, five and a half lines of verse separately identify sentient beings with the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*); second, half a line summarizes these sentient beings with the five dull afflictions.
Now, by explaining five and a half lines, it is shown that sentient beings with the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) constitute five stages:

first, half a line explains the affliction of pride (*māna*); second, one and a half lines explain the affliction of anger (*pratigha*); third, one line explains the affliction of delusion (*moha*); fourth, two lines explain the affliction of greed (*rāga*); and fifth, two phrases explain the affliction of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
First, the second half-line of "owls, crows, eagles, and vultures" clarifies sentient beings driven by the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*).
Next, the one and a half lines beginning with "vipers, snakes, and scorpions" clarify sentient beings driven by the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣa-anuśaya*).

Next, the line following "The place stinking with excrement and urine" clarifies that ignorance drives sentient beings; it uses excrement and urine as metaphors for the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Thus, sentient beings' greedy attachment to the five sensory objects is like that of dung beetles and the like, who greedily crave excrement and urine.

Regarding the two lines below, "foxes, wolves, and jackals," these clarify how sentient beings are driven by the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*). Here, "corpses" and so forth serve as metaphors for the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); because sentient beings compete to seize the five objects—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—it is said they "gnaw" upon them.
They plunder one another and seize by force in a manner devoid of the Way; hence it is said they "tread upon" [one another].

The two phrases, "quarreling and contending, snarling and barking," clarify that doubt causes sentient beings to ponder whether the principle of cause and effect exists or does not exist; their views remain undecided, like two dogs whose dispute has not been resolved.
"The house is so terrifying and its manifestations are such as these"—this second half-line summarizes the second category: sentient beings of the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nivaraṇa*).

"In every place there are *chimei* and *wangliang* spirits"—the following ten lines constitute the second section, specifically identifying the sentient beings of the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*). This also has two parts: first, this half-line verse provides a general clarification of the sentient beings of the five sharp afflictions; second, the remaining nine and a half lines specifically identify the sentient beings of the five sharp afflictions.

However, while the preceding section clarifies sentient beings with the dull afflictions (*dauṣṭhulya-kleśa*) by first explaining them individually and later collectively, this section on the five sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) explains them first collectively and later individually.

From the passage "yakṣas and evil spirits" below, for nine and a half lines, is the second part, which specifically enumerates sentient beings with the five sharp afflictions. Since these five sharp afflictions constitute five stages, the first three lines clarify false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); the next two and a half lines clarify the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); the next one and a half lines clarify the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the next half line clarifies the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and the final two lines clarify the two views of annihilationism and eternalism (*uccheda- and śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), which constitute the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the three lines beginning with "yakṣas and evil spirits," this first clarifies sentient beings of wrong views who slander the non-existence of cause and effect; yet cause and effect are precisely the Four Noble Truths. To slander the non-existence of the causes and effects of cessation and the path is like [the description] "devouring human flesh."

The section beginning with "the class of venomous insects" clarifies the absence of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*). Within this, first one line lists suffering and its origin, followed by one and a half lines that explicitly clarify the denial [of them].

"Conceiving and nursing" as the cause constitutes the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya), and "giving birth" as the result constitutes the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya); since both suffering and origination are distinct and unrelated, it is said that they are "each separately hidden and protected."

"Yakṣas compete to come"—this one and a half lines below constitutes the second section, which correctly explains how sentient beings with false views slander the causes and effects of suffering and its origin.
Because their bonds of false view have reached the highest degree, it says, "their evil minds burn ever more fiercely."
Because they rely on heterodox doctrines and deviant meanings, it is called "the sound of strife.
Since this will inevitably invite the sufferings of the three miserable realms, it is said to be "most terrifying."

"Kumbhāṇḍa ghosts"—the following two and a half verses constitute the second stage, clarifying those sentient beings who cling to precepts; that is, those who observe the precepts of chickens, dogs, and deer.

A small elevation on level ground is called a "mound of earth" (tǔduǎ). This is intended to clarify that sentient beings who cling to precepts and rituals subdue the causes for rebirth in the three miserable realms and are born among humans or devas, just like a mound of earth.

At times, one may grow weary of the suffering of the desire realm and, by suppressing the fetters of the desire realm, temporarily take birth in the form realm, as if rising one foot above the ground.

At other times, one may grow weary of the suffering of the form realm and, by suppressing the fetters of the form realm, temporarily take birth in the formless realm, as if rising two feet above the ground.

The subduing of rebirth-linking in the form and formless realms is like lighting a fire; it is a temporary suppression rather than a permanent one, for one eventually regresses back to the three miserable destinies, which is why it is said to be "reversal."
These sentient beings who cling to precepts do not apply their minds according to the Dharma; therefore, they are said to be "heedless.
Their efforts are in vain and yield no merit; therefore, they are said to be "sporting.
Regarding the phrase "seizing the dog by its two hind legs and throwing it down until it loses its voice," some explain it as follows:
Sentient beings in the realm of form slander the formless realm as being without cause and without effect, like seizing a dog by its two hind legs.
Furthermore, they slander the realm of desire as being without cause and without effect, like placing their feet upon their own necks.
At first glance, this appears to be a superficial examination that fails to ascertain the truth.

Now, it is clarified that there are ten latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) among sentient beings in the desire realm; since there is a separate scriptural passage below [this] clarifying the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how can it be said that this refers to the form realm?

Now, as for the phrase "seizing the dog by both hind legs and striking it until it loses its voice," this refers to slandering the truths of suffering and its origin, thereby severing the principle of cause and effect so that it no longer holds; hence, it is said that it "loses its voice."
Regarding the phrase "placing his foot upon the dog's neck and taking pleasure in terrifying it," this refers to slandering the two truths of the Path and Cessation (*nirodha*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it refers to slandering the absence of karma and afflictions as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya*); thus, it speaks of seizing the dog by its two hind legs and so forth.
Furthermore, they slander [the teaching] by claiming that there is no suffering as a result; thus it is said that they "place their feet upon the necks" of others and so forth.

The passage beginning with "There are certain ghosts whose bodies are tall and large," spanning one and a half lines below, clarifies the perception of sentient beings through the view of self (ātman).
"My body is large and my form is small," thus he speaks of being "large and tall.
Because he lacks shame and remorse, he is said to be "naked.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "There are other ghosts whose throats are like needles," this half-verse clarifies those sentient beings who cling to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); they are unable to reflect upon themselves, yet they claim to have realized their own views as truth while asserting that all others are false speech.

"Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like those of oxen. The following two lines clarify sentient beings who hold the two views of annihilationism and eternalism; the ox's head has two horns, which serves as a metaphor for how these two views—annihilationism and eternalism—necessarily accompany one another.
From the line "yakṣas, pretas, and various evil birds and beasts" for one and a half lines, this is the third summary of the sentient beings being burned; it is not further elaborated upon.
The realms of form and formlessness are like looking up at the light of the upper stories through a window or skylight.
"This dilapidated old house belongs to one person"—this single line is the second clarification regarding the origin of the fires arising in the desire realm.

It was solely because the elder was temporarily away that a fire broke out within the house; internally, it was as if the Tathāgata had already converted these sentient beings in the past, so that for a time their afflictions were subdued and did not arise—no different from when the elder was present and the fire had not yet started.

Once the conditions for his manifestation have been exhausted, the Tathāgata departs once more for other regions; yet these sentient beings consequently give rise to even greater afflictions, which blaze forth like a dense, raging fire. Thus, it is said that this is the origin from which the fire arises.

"Subsequently, a fire suddenly broke out in the house. These two lines below constitute the third section, which correctly clarifies the outbreak of fire in the desire realm; they are the direct verse-commentary on the phrase "a fire suddenly broke out."

"The various ghosts and spirits raise their voices and cry out loud"—this subsequent one and a half lines of verse constitute the fourth summary of the signs of the sentient beings of the desire realm being burned.
Regarding the three and a half verses beginning with "Evil beasts and venomous insects," this is the second section clarifying the outbreak of fire in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Within this, there are also four stages: first, the initial verse clarifies that sentient beings of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) are tormented by the eight sufferings of the afflictions; consequently, they remain subject to the fetters of the Desire Realm while taking birth in the Form Realm, which is described as "hiding in holes and burrows."
The second statement, the single phrase "because of meager merit," clarifies the cause from which the fire arises.
The third statement, the single phrase "burned by the fire," precisely clarifies the arising of the fire in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The fourth section consists of two lines, which clarify the signs of the burning of sentient beings in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The following two lines of verse, beginning with "centipedes and millipedes," constitute the third part, clarifying the arising of fire in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which likewise has four stages. First, the initial line clarifies how sentient beings of the form realm, having subdued the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form realm, are born into the formless realm.

The second statement, "The kumbhāṇḍa spirits take whatever they encounter and eat," clarifies in this half-verse the cause by which the fire arises: because people with false views there are taught [to do so] and thus take it, it is said that they "take whatever they encounter and eat."
The third statement, "Furthermore, fire burns upon the heads of all hungry ghosts," this half-line precisely clarifies that fire arises from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The fourth, "Tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they wander about, obstructed and distressed," this half-line clarifies the characteristics of being burned.

"The house is thus extremely terrifying"—this single line below constitutes the fourth major section, which summarizes the outbreak of fire in the three realms and does not provide further elaboration.

"At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate. These two lines of verse below eulogize the second analogy above, that of the elder seeing the fire. Within this analogy, there are originally three sections:
first, the one who sees; second, that which is seen; and third, the arising of a heart of sorrowful compassion.
In this present passage, the arising of a compassionate mind is not explicitly versified; yet, even though the compassionate mind is not versified, the structure still consists of three parts.

Above, it was stated directly that the elder saw the fire burning, but the location where he saw it was not specified. Here, however, the location is specifically added; by supplementing what was omitted with this addition, the structure is ultimately completed as three parts.

Regarding the three sections: the first half-verse indicates the place where the fire is first seen; the second single verse-line is that which is able to see; and the third line and verse-line are that which is seen.
Now, the first statement says, "At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate," which is the place where he first emerged and saw the fire.

Standing, however, is a sign of being about to move; thus, the Tathāgata, while abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, is about to respond by coming to the triple world to guide and transform sentient beings, just as the elder is about to enter the gate.

Regarding the phrase "I have heard someone say": this single line constitutes the second [verse], which corresponds to the aforementioned capacity for seeing. Since the previous passage stated "the elder saw," whereas here it says "heard," this substitutes hearing for seeing.

The former is an analogy for the vision of the Way; this clarifies that the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom that illuminates the capacities of beings. Herein, "hearing the Way" refers to the capacity to respond to the Sage; yet, the capacity to move the Buddha to appear in the world comes to engage the Sage’s wisdom, just as it is when one hears someone speak.

"O you, my sons"—this following line is the third [verse], which summarizes what was seen in the second [verse] above. Previously it was said, "This great fire breaks out from the four sides," and just now it was mentioned that one hears someone speak; what, then, is being said?
The Buddha spoke thus: "You sons, you previously entered this house because of your play.
Some explain this by saying:
"Because they flowed from outside the triple world and entered into the triple world, it is said that they 'entered this house.'"

What is currently practiced is not so; in the past, under twenty-two billion Buddhas, they have already received the transformation of the Mahāyāna. This constitutes the relationship of father and sons; therefore, it says, "You, my sons."

Regarding the phrase "having previously entered this house for the sake of play," it is as clarified in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching): those who have not yet been delivered have all already established the conditions for their deliverance.

Formerly, when one possessed the understanding of the Mahāyāna, at that time and in that state, the mind was entirely intent upon transcending birth and death; later, by giving rise to afflictions and losing that Mahāyāna understanding, one immediately fulfills the condition of entering into birth and death.
The meaning of their coming and entering is intended in this way.

As for "the young and small," at that time those of the Mahāyāna have weak understanding; thus they are called "young and small. Precisely because their understanding is weak, they lose their comprehension and give rise to afflictions; therefore, they are called "ignorant."
"After the elder had heard this," there follow six lines of verse, which recapitulate the third parable, "The Failure to Rescue the Sons.

In the preceding parable, there were originally two sections: the admonition and the exhortation; within each of these two sections, there are three stages, namely: the provisional application of the teaching, the lack of receptive capacity [in the listeners], and the cessation of the transformative activity.
Now, within this section as well, the three stages for each of the two preceding segments are fully set forth, though the methods differ.

Regarding these differences in method: among these six lines, they are divided into three parts. First, the five lines beginning with "The elder, having heard it" eulogize the tentative approaches of the two families; next, two lines eulogize the lack of spiritual capacity in the two families; and finally, two lines eulogize the cessation of their transformative activity by the two families.

From the passage "Having heard this, the elder... onwards, each of these three sections contains two parts. The first part consists of one verse that first summarizes the exhortation regarding the appropriate course of action for the household, which corresponds to the section beginning with "His hands and body possess strength."

Second, the four lines of verse beginning with "Admonishing the sons" are a restatement of the instructions regarding the household strategy; these correspond to the passage beginning with "I shall now speak of matters that cause fear."
The two lines following "The sons are ignorant" constitute the second [section], which simultaneously summarizes the lack of capacity in both families.

Regarding the presence of two [families]: first, the single line "The sons are ignorant" summarizes the lack of capacity in the family that was exhorted; within the aforementioned lack of capacity, there were originally two [types]. Now, the first—the Great Vehicle teaching being useless for them—is not summarized, namely: "This house has but one door, and it is moreover narrow. Only the presence of the Small Vehicle and the absence of the Great Vehicle are summarized here. Thus, this single line "The sons are ignorant" generally summarizes the aforementioned presence of the Small Vehicle and absence of the Great Vehicle, which corresponds to: "The sons are young and have not yet attained any knowledge."

The second phrase, "Although he heard his father’s instruction," corresponds to the lack of affinity for the admonition at home; it is equivalent to the passage: "Though his father felt compassion and enticed him with kind words."

The third couplet of verses describes the cessation of the teaching by the two schools; as for the "two" themselves, the first line specifically praises the cessation of the teaching by the school of exhortation, namely, "clinging to the place of play."

Second, the single phrase "never ceasing his play" corresponds to the admonition to cease teaching within the household; it refers to what was stated above: "running and playing here and there, looking only at his father."
Furthermore, another interpretation states:

the three sections of the exhortation for householders are not versified; only the two sections of the admonition for renunciants are versified. The first five lines of verse correspond to the suitability [of the teaching], while the final line of verse corresponds to the lack of receptive capacity; it does not versify the cessation of the transformative activity.
The "Proposed Plan" (*yīnguǐ*) consists of two parts: first, contemplating the method for rescuing the sons; second, the actual proposed plan.
This section is further divided into two: the first verse contemplates the method, while the subsequent four verses beginning with "He exhorted his sons" constitute the actual proposed plan.
"At that time, the elder had this thought. Below this are seven and a half lines of verse, which summarize the fourth analogy: how the elder saves his children by means of the three vehicles.

However, within the central parable above, there are originally four sections: first, using the three vehicles as a provisional means; second, seeing that the sons possess the inclination of former affinity; third, preaching the three vehicles for them; and fourth, the sons receiving and practicing them.

Now, in this context, the second point—the sons' long-standing preferences—is omitted from the verse. This is because it was already stated above: "The father knows that each son’s former mind has its own particularities and strange objects to which his heart is surely attached."
Now, within these seven and a half lines, there are three sections that correspond to the three preceding sections [of the prose].

The first three lines first summarize the first section, the provisional application of the three vehicles; the next three lines skip ahead to summarize the third section, the preaching of the three vehicles; and the final one and a half lines summarize the fourth section, the sons' acceptance and practice.

Now, from "At that time, the elder had this thought" onwards, the first three lines of verse concern the provisional application of the three vehicles; this refers to the passage beginning with "At that time, the elder immediately had this thought: 'This house has already been consumed by a great fire.'"

"Addressing all you sons," etc.—the following three lines constitute the third *atiśloka* (interpolated verse), which describes the provision of the three vehicles. In the previous description of the three vehicles, there were originally four stages; now, these three lines fully versify them:
one line versifies the first stage, three phrases versify the second, another three phrases versify the third, and half a line versifies the fourth.

Now, the single line beginning with "I tell you, my sons," is a verse praising the first [offering], the three chariots; it corresponds to the preceding statement: "And he said to them: 'These toys which you may enjoy are rare and difficult to obtain; if you do not take them, you will surely feel regret later.'"

Next, regarding "the goat-drawn carriage and the deer-drawn carriage," these three lines below constitute the verse for the second stage, indicating the location where the three carriages are displayed; this refers to the previous statement: "These various kinds of goat, deer, and ox-drawn carriages are now outside the gate."

"Come forth, all of you! This phrase also consists of three parts, which correspond to the third exhortation to take the three vehicles mentioned above; it refers to the previous statement: "All of you should quickly come forth from this burning house."

Next, "Whatever you desire, you may enjoy as you please" is this half-line which versifies the fourth point above, "providing [what is] not in vain"; it corresponds to the previous statement, "I shall give you all that you wish."

"The sons hear such words regarding these various chariots"—this one and a half lines [of verse] praises the fourth stage, the sons' reception and practice. Within the aforementioned reception and practice, there were originally four stages; now only three stages are praised, as the second stage, their mutual pushing and shoving, is omitted.

First, the half-line, "The sons heard it said that such chariots were [prepared]," prefigures the verse on the "courageous and keen minds" of those practicing as external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

The six characters, "immediately rushed and vied with one another," correspond to the verse on "vying and rushing together," representing the practices of those who have realized the truths (*satyadarśana*), those in the path of cultivation through reflection (*bhāvanāmārga*), and those in the path of cultivation (*mārgabhāvanā*).

The two characters "chū" (出) and "shutsu" (出) at the end of the lower line of the verse correspond to the phrase "leaving the burning house through contention," signifying the attainment of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, another interpretation states that the first two [stages] are omitted from the verse, and only the latter two are recited.
"The elder sees his children emerge from the burning house. The following three lines constitute the verse for the fifth analogy, "seeing the children emerge from the calamity.

Within the preceding analogy, there are two parts: first, clarifying how one abandons afflictions, emerges from the triple world, and attains the fruit of *aśaikṣa*; second, properly clarifying the arousal of the Mahāyāna capacity.
The first two lines first praise the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The line "dwelling at the crossroads" correctly praises the arousal of the Mahāyāna capacity.
From "sitting upon the lion throne" below, there are four lines and one phrase which praise the sixth point above: the Elder’s joy.
Now, within these four lines of verse, there are three distinct sections. The first three lines properly versify the "joyful leaping for joy.
The subsequent three lines, beginning with "These sons," explain the cause of their joy; they rejoice because they have escaped from peril.
"Therefore, all you people, we are now joyful"—this half-verse is the third summary of joy.

"At that time, the sons knew their father was sitting at ease"—the three verses below this praise the seventh section, wherein the sons request vehicles, clarifying how those of the three vehicles seek their respective fruits.

Within these three verses, there are four stages: half a verse clarifies the time of requesting the vehicle; one full verse is the actual verse for the request; one full verse clarifies the Tathāgata’s words at that time granting the vehicle; and half a verse concludes the verse on the request.
Now, from the phrase "At that time, the sons knew their father was sitting at ease" down to this half-line, this first section clarifies the time when they sought the vehicle.

It simply refers to the moment they knew their father was sitting at ease; internally, it clarifies that when the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings’ Mahāyāna potential arise, it accords with the Tathāgata’s original intention, and thus he is said to be "sitting at ease."
"All went to where their father was"—the following line is the second verse, which correctly restates the previous request for the chariots.
"Just as previously promised"—this one line is the third, which restates the Tathāgata’s words at that time granting the chariots.
"Right now is the proper time"—the second half of this line constitutes the fourth section, which is the concluding verse requesting the vehicle.

"The elder is greatly wealthy"—the seven and a half lines following this constitute the eighth section, the parable of bestowing the great vehicles, which is the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The preceding section contained two parts: first, the simultaneous opening of the two chapter-gates; second, the simultaneous detailed explanation of those two chapter-gates.

Now, these seven and a half lines are likewise divided into two: the first seven lines first versify the second part—the detailed explanation of the chapter-gates—while the remaining half line subsequently versifies the opening of the two chapter-gates.
Furthermore, within this expanded verse, it only expands upon the single great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and does not expand upon the equality of the mind.

However, regarding the great vehicle itself, there are originally two aspects: first, the expansion of the primary meaning (*mūla-vistara*), and second, the expansion of the explanation (*vyākhyāna-vistara*).
Now, first, there is one verse and a half that precedes the explanation of the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*), namely: "For what reason? Because this elder possesses immeasurable wealth."

"Adorned and magnificently decorated"—the following five lines and a half are a retrospective verse praising the aforementioned great and vast chariot, as previously stated: "That chariot was high and wide, adorned with various jewels."

"By means of these wondrous chariots"—this second half-line constitutes the second [section], which is a recapitulative verse (anusarga) summarizing the two preceding chapter-headings; this single phrase first recapitulates the chapter-heading on the "Great Chariot."
Next, the single phrase "equally bestowing upon all sons" is a retrospective verse summarizing the topical heading of the equality of mind.

The following one and a half lines of verse, beginning with "At that time, all the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness," summarize the ninth analogy: the sons' joy at obtaining the great chariots.
The preceding passage states: "At that time, the sons each mounted great vehicles and attained what they had never experienced before.
The tenth point, "not in vain," is omitted from this verse summary.

From the line "I am also like this, Śāriputra" below, there are thirty-four and a half verses; this constitutes the second section, which summarizes the second part of the prose commentary, the "Section on the Combined Parables."
Furthermore, in the section on "correspondence" (*saṃgraha*) above, only seven analogies are corresponded, while the sixth, seventh, and ninth are not.
Although seven analogies are corresponded, because the fifth and eighth analogies are combined together, the textual sections consist of six parts.

Now, within this section, seven parables are combined into verses, resulting in seven textual segments. Although the names of these seven are the same as those previously mentioned, their underlying significance differs.
The prose section above did not combine the sixth and seventh parables, nor are they combined here;
however, the first, second, third, fourth, and tenth parables were combined in the prose above, and they are likewise versified here.
Above, the fifth and eighth similes were combined; now, only the eighth simile is being versified.
Previously, the fifth was combined but the ninth was not; here, according to the meaning, the ninth is versified and combined, while the fifth is omitted from the verse.
Now, within these thirty-four and a half lines, they are further divided into seven sections:
first, there are four lines of verse, which correspond to the general analogy of the householder;
second, the two lines of verse beginning with "The Tathāgata has already left the burning house of the triple world" correspond to the analogy of seeing the fire.
The third section, "Now, this place is full of many perils and hardships," also consists of two lines of verse, corresponding to the third simile of being unable to save the children;

the fourth section, "Therefore, by means of skillful expedients, he speaks of the three vehicles," consists of four lines of verse, corresponding to the fourth simile of successfully saving the children;
and the fifth section, "If you all can believe and accept these words," also consists of four lines of verse, corresponding to the eighth simile of bestowing the great chariots.

The sixth section, beginning with "Having obtained such a vehicle, he causes his sons... and so forth, consists of three lines of verse-meaning, which corresponds to the ninth parable of the sons' joy upon obtaining the chariots.
The seventh section, beginning with "He says to Śāriputra, 'You all... and so forth, consists of fifteen and a half lines of verse, which corresponds to the tenth parable of non-falsity.

The first consists of four-line verses; the second consists of two-line verses; the third consists of two-line verses; the fourth consists of four-line verses; the eighth consists of four-line verses; the ninth consists of three-line verses on the meaning; and the tenth consists of fifteen and a half lines of verses.

The preceding section, which provides a general analogy for the first type of householder, corresponds precisely to the meaning of the single elder; within that meaning, it further allows for the inclusion of the remaining five meanings.
Now, these four lines of verse provide a summary that encompasses all five meanings, though they are slightly abbreviated in that they do not specifically praise the single gate.
Now, the line "I am also like this" corresponds to the Elder [Sudatta] mentioned previously; the preceding statement "The Tathāgata is also like this" does the same.
The phrase "Father of the World" corresponds to the passage "He is the father of all the world."

"All sentient beings are my children": this entire passage combines the two meanings of the preceding verses. The initial phrase "all sentient beings" corresponds to the verse concerning the five hundred people;
the subsequent three lines, beginning with "are all my children," correspond to the verse concerning the thirty sons.
The verse beginning with "There is no peace in the three realms" summarizes the meaning of the great house as a whole.
The line beginning with "Constantly subject to birth and old age" summarizes the meaning of the fire within the house.

The two lines beginning with "The Tathāgata has already transcended" constitute the verse that combines the second simile of seeing fire; the preceding line states, "He sees all sentient beings [afflicted] by birth, old age, sickness, and death."
However, in the preceding analogy, three aspects are provisionally correlated: first, correlating the seer; second, correlating the seen; and third, correlating the arousal of a mind of compassion.
Now, these two lines only achieve the combination of verse for the seer and the seen; they do not combine the mind of compassionate pity in verse.
Nevertheless, it still forms three sections.
How is this known to be so?
It is precisely because [the verse] first presents the place where the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings.

Now, regarding the line "The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world," the first half-verse first presents the place where he perceives sentient beings; the next half-verse corresponds to the first [point], the capacity to perceive; and the subsequent half-verse corresponds to the second [point], the objects perceived.

Now, the first line clarifies the locus where [the Tathāgata] perceives sentient beings. Because the Tathāgata has long severed the burdens of the triple world, it is said that he is "already detached.
Because he dwells serenely in the state of the Dharma-body, it is said that he "abides in tranquil seclusion."
The "forest" refers to the forest of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*).

With the spirit dwelling in the realm of the Dharma-body and acting with freedom beyond the sphere of obstructions and impediments, it is therefore said that one "abides peacefully in the forest wilds."
However, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is not the same as the eternally abiding [body]. There are two interpretations:

first, it is said that the prolongation of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) so that it remains long in the world constitutes the Dharma-body; second, it is said that this correctly clarifies the mutual relationship among all Buddhas throughout the ten directions. Thus, we know that Amitāyus is currently teaching in the West for those of the future here; from the perspective of those here looking toward him there, he is precisely the Dharma-body.

However, while the response body (nirmāṇakāya) inherently possesses form and image, the dharma-body (dharmakāya) inherently lacks form and image. Since the Buddha has not yet come to this world, he is here without form or image; this is precisely the dharma-body.

If it comes to this world, then in relation to this world, it is the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya); if one looks toward this world from another direction, then in relation to this world, it is the Dharma Body (dharmakāya).
Now, this half-line, “The three realms are all mine,” is the second part of this section; it corresponds to the first [part] above, namely, the seer.
This half-line, “All sentient beings therein are my children,” is the third part of this section; it corresponds to the second [part] above, namely, that which is seen.
"Now, in this place"—the following two lines constitute the verse that combines the third analogy above, "Failing to Rescue the Sons.

However, within the original opening of the analogies, there were two sections—admonition and exhortation—each of which also had three parts. Upon reaching the combination of the analogies, these are divided into three segments: first, the combined application of admonition and exhortation; second, the combined cases where both families lacked the capacity for response; and third, the combined instances where the Buddha ceased his transformative activity for both families.

Now, these two verses only praise the combined admonition regarding the extremes; however, the original central section of the admonition has three parts. Here, the central part is omitted and not praised, nor is the combined admonition regarding the cessation of transformation. Only the combined admonition regarding the suitability of the teaching for those without the capacity is praised.

Now, the statement, "At present, this place is full of many perils and hardships, and I alone am able to provide protection," constitutes one line of verse that appropriately summarizes the admonition; it corresponds to the previous remark: "Having seen this, the Buddha thought to himself, 'I am the father of sentient beings; I ought to uproot their suffering and distress.'"

"Although they were instructed and exhorted, they did not believe or accept"—this single line summarizes the preceding warning regarding the lack of spiritual capacity (*agotra*). The preceding passage, "If I were to rely solely on my supernormal powers... and so forth, refers to this; now, the statement "although they were instructed and exhorted, they did not believe or accept" reveals their lack of capacity. If one attempts to penetrate this through supernormal powers, there is no one who believes or accepts it. The following lines provide the explanation: "Because their attachment to the defilements of desire is profound."
"By means of skillful expedients"—the following four lines constitute the verse summarizing the fourth analogy of rescuing the children.
In the previous summary of the fourth analogy, there were originally three sections; the first, which first cited three external analogies, is not versified here.

The second point, "The Tathāgata is also like this: although he possesses powers and fearlessness, he does not employ them," corresponds directly to the third external analogy; it is not recited here as a verse either.
Only the third section of the verse properly corresponds to the fourth analogy. However, within the aforementioned correspondence to the fourth analogy, there were originally four sections;

here, for brevity, the second section—the meaning of observing the capacities of sentient beings to rescue them from the burning house of the triple world—is omitted and not versified. Within these four lines, there are two layers: the first three lines directly versify the aforementioned three sections, while the second line combines those three into one to conclude the preceding meaning. This [concluding layer] is a matter of interpretive elaboration and does not correspond to the original text above.

Now, within these three types of practice, the first line of verse corresponds to the first [section], which uses the three vehicles as a provisional teaching; the next line and a half of verse correspond to the third, which teaches the three vehicles; and the subsequent one and a half lines of verse correspond to the fourth, concerning how the sons receive and practice them.

The current phrase "by these skillful means" (以此方便) is a verse summarizing the first application of employing the three vehicles as provisional measures, which was previously stated as "merely by means of wisdom and skillful means" (但以智慧方便).
"To preach the Three Vehicles"—this subsequent line and phrase constitute the second part of the verse, which summarizes the third point mentioned above: "preaching the Three Vehicles."

In the preceding exposition of the Three Vehicles, there were originally four stages; now, this single line and single verse can only correspond to one stage, namely the point that demonstrates the three fruits.

The preceding statement, "You shall quickly emerge from the triple world and attain the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle," indicates the fruit and destination for those of the three vehicles.
The remaining three stages are omitted here and not included in this verse.

"If these sons have their minds resolved"—the following one and a half lines constitute the third part of this verse; that is, it summarizes the fourth section above, "The Sons Receiving and Practicing. However, whereas in the previous summary of the parable each of the three vehicles was treated separately with four stages, here too the summary is made according to the three vehicles, yet it does not fully correspond to all four stages, but only provides a summary for the fourth stage of each of the three types of persons.
Now, this one and a half lines consists of two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific.

The current statement, "If these sons have a resolute mind," constitutes the first half-line, which generally clarifies that those of the three vehicles all attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa*; this is precisely the meaning of "resoluteness."

The next line separately clarifies that those of the three vehicles attain the fruit of no-more-learning; the initial statement, "endowed with the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers," constitutes this half-line as the definitive fruit of the śrāvaka. This verse corresponds precisely to what was stated above as the "śrāvakayāna," which is the illustration of "striving to exit the burning house."

The phrase "there are those who attain the pratyekabuddha" corresponds to the aforementioned "this is called the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. The fruit of the *aśaikṣa* stage of the pratyekabuddha corresponds to the metaphorical expression "striving to exit the burning house."

The single phrase "non-retrogressive bodhisattva" is a verse that summarizes the above; it is called the Bodhisattva Vehicle, which is the attainment of the fruit of no-more-learning, and it also illustrates the passage from the parable concerning "leaving the burning house."
"The line 'O Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings'—the second [part], which combines three into one, concludes the preceding meaning.
This line is an explanatory gloss (artha-nirdeśa) and does not constitute a verse (gāthā), yet it still belongs to the preceding section."

"If you all can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the path of Buddhahood. Below this are four lines, which constitute the verse summarizing the eighth parable, the Bestowal of the Great Chariots.
However, in the preceding section, while the eighth analogy was further expanded into six stages, only five stages were correlated and the sixth stage was not.

Now, these four lines are divided into two segments; in this first line of verse, two stages are correlated through the meter, namely the passage above: "All these sentient beings who have escaped the three realms are fully endowed with the meditative concentrations and liberations of all Buddhas," which signifies the equality of mind and the nature of the gifts bestowed.

The three lines beginning with "This vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme" correspond to the aforementioned "vast and great chariot. The preceding passage states: "All are of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the sages, and capable of producing the pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss."
Therefore, these four lines only correspond to the third stage of the verse.

The following three lines, beginning with "Having obtained such a vehicle, all the Buddha-sons," constitute a thematic summary that combines with the ninth [stage], the parable of the sons' joy upon obtaining the great chariots.
In the preceding prose section, this ninth [verse] was originally not included; it is now added here as a verse of meaning.
Nevertheless, among these three verses, the first two are verses of primary meaning that correspond to the preceding explanation of how one cause produces one fruit, and thus they establish joy.
The second section, beginning with "For this reason," in one line clarifies that there is no other cause.

Now, regarding the first point, "Riding this precious vehicle straight to the place of enlightenment," it clarifies that since the Tathāgata has bestowed predictions upon those of the three vehicles that they will attain Buddhahood in the future, the assembly at that time collectively resolved their minds to purchase the fruit of future Buddhahood through cultivation and progress; this is precisely "riding this precious vehicle," which is the vehicle of the [ultimate] realm.

Regarding the phrase "reaching the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): although all myriad practices lead to the site of enlightenment, it is specifically at the stage of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) that one attains proximity to Buddhahood and practices until reaching the adamantine state; this is the meaning of "reaching the site of enlightenment."
"Addressing Śāriputra and all of you," followed by fifteen and a half verses, together with the preceding summary verse, constitutes the tenth analogy, "Not in Vain.

Within the initial summary of the analogies, there are four sections: first, the citation of the three preceding external analogies; second, the formal application (*saṃgraha*); third, the explanation of the application; and fourth, the concluding synthesis.
