However, within this detailed exposition, there are originally two sections: first, the opening of the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and second, the application of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Now, these seventy-one and a half verses are also divided into two parts:

the first forty-one verses provide the illustrative parable (*udāharaṇa*), and the second, beginning with "The Buddha is also like this," consists of thirty and a half verses that provide the application of the parable (*upanaya*).
In the preceding section on analogies, there were originally nine; now, based on these forty-one lines of verse, they are likewise divided into nine sections:
first, thirteen lines of verse praise the first analogy, that of the father and son losing each other;
second, seven and a half lines of verse beginning with "Hiring out labor in succession" praise the second analogy, that of the father and son meeting each other.
The third section, "He immediately commanded the messenger," consists of three verses, praising the third analogy of being unable to call the son;
the fourth section, "He then employed skillful means," consists of three verses, praising the fourth analogy of successfully calling the son;
and the fifth section, "The elder, at the window," consists of five and a half verses, praising the fifth analogy of instructing him to act as a son.
The sixth section, "Showing Him the Gold and Silver," contains two lines of verse, which eulogize the sixth analogy of entrusting property;
the seventh section, "The Father Knowing His Son’s Mind Has Gradually Become Vast," consists of the latter half-line of verse, which eulogizes the seventh analogy of seeing the son’s great resolve;
the eighth section, "Wishing to Give Him Property," contains four and a half lines of verse, which eulogize the eighth analogy of entrusting the family estate.
The ninth section, consisting of two lines of verse titled "The Son Recollects His Former Poverty and Inferior Aspirations," praises the joy of the ninth son.

Now, to further explain: thirteen lines of verse praise the first; seven and a half lines praise the second; three lines praise the third; another three lines praise the fourth; five and a half verses praise the fifth; two lines praise the sixth; half a line praises the seventh; four and a half lines praise the eighth; and two lines praise the ninth.
In the first of the four analogies concerning the loss of father and son, there are four stages:
first, the son departs from his father; second, the father seeks his son; third, the son returns to be near his father; and fourth, the father’s anxiety and longing grow ever deeper.
Now, these thirteen lines also fully comprise these four sections, though they do not follow the original order and contain some omissions.

Here, one and a half lines constitute the first section; next, six and a half lines constitute the second; next, two and a half lines skip ahead to constitute the fourth; and finally, two and a half lines look back to constitute the third.
The line and a half beginning with "For example, like a young child who is immature and ignorant" first summarizes the first son’s departure from his father.

In the original account of the elder son’s departure from his father, there were two sections: first, it was said that "he turned his back on his father and went away," and second, it was said that "he headed toward the kingdom and returned."
These current one and a half lines only praise his departure from his father; they do not praise his journey toward the kingdom and his return.
From the line "His father was filled with anxious concern" below, the following six and a half lines praise the second section above: the father’s search for his son.

In the middle section of the "Father Seeking His Son," there were originally two stages: first, the failure to find the son; second, the statement that "one should not abandon the great affairs of the household because of the suffering caused by losing one son. Now, this is fully expressed in verse as "the father, filled with anxiety, searches in all four directions. This half-line of verse refers to the failure to find the son, while the preceding line states that "the father had previously sought him but could not find him."
The six lines beginning with "Having exhausted his search" correctly versify the second section above concerning the great matter of not losing the family estate.
The two and a half verses beginning with "Noble and wealthy, possessing such great power" skip ahead to versify the fourth section, where the father’s anxiety grows ever deeper.
The preceding passage originally had two stages: first, the suffering of losing one's child; second, the hypothetical contemplation of the joy of obtaining a child.
Now, I shall not versify the hypothetical contemplation of the joy of obtaining a child, but only versify the contemplation of the suffering of losing a child.
The preceding passage states: "The father constantly thinks of his son with whom he has been separated for over fifty years.

The two and a half lines of verse beginning with "At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing" are a retrospective summary of the third section above, concerning the son drawing near to his father.
The section on the elder son approaching his father also consists of two parts: first, the causes and conditions for his approach; second, the actual clarification of his approach.
Here, too, the verses are complete: the first two lines of verse clarify the reasons for his approach, while the subsequent half-line verse clarifies the actual approach itself.

Regarding the preceding passage on the circumstances of the father’s proximity, it says, "At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities," and so forth; because he went from one set of five precepts to another set of five precepts, it is said that he went "from village to village."
From the ten wholesome paths of action to the ten wholesome paths of action, it is therefore said that one goes from land to land.

Regarding the phrase "there may be something attained or nothing attained": practicing the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths in this present life and thereby receiving retribution upon the transition of this body is called "having something attained."
That which is produced through the influence of past karma and received as a subsequent retribution is called "having nothing to obtain.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
that which is accomplished through the influence of karma for the duration of a single lifetime is called "having something to obtain."
Those who do not achieve [the path] experience a state of mere dependence, which is termed "having nothing to obtain.
Because wholesome dharmas fail to sustain the body and are perpetually insufficient, they are said to be "emaciated.
Not only are they devoid of wholesome dharmas, but they are also fully possessed of the ninety-eight proclivities (anuśaya); therefore, it is said that "sores and scabs grow upon their bodies."

The half-verse, "Gradually passing through until reaching the city where his father dwells," explicitly clarifies the act of approaching his father; it corresponds to the previous statement, "He encountered the city where his father resided."
"By means of successive employment, he eventually reached his father's house. The following seven and a half verses praise the second analogy, that of the father and son meeting.
In the preceding analogy, there were originally two sections: the first clarifying the son seeing the father, and the second clarifying the father seeing the son.
Now, the first section consists of six and a half verses concerning the son seeing his father.
The line beginning with "At that time, the elder" (長者) constitutes one verse regarding the father seeing his son.

Within the preceding section on the son seeing his father, there are originally four stages: first, the causal conditions for seeing the father; second, the location where he sees the father; third, the explicit description of seeing the father; and fourth, the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance.

Now, this is also complete in verse: the first line of verse corresponds to the first [section], the next line corresponds to the second, the next two and a half lines correspond to the third, and the next three and a half lines correspond to the fourth.
The phrase "wandering from one place of labor to another" praises the first cause and condition: seeing his father.
The phrase "finally arriving at his father's house" praises the second location: where he saw his father.

The previous passage stated, "He eventually arrived at his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate"; now, it mentions only the father’s house without mentioning the side of the gate, for the meaning is self-evident.

The two and a half lines beginning with "At that time, the elder was inside his gate" constitute the third [section], the actual seeing of the father. As for the previous statement, "He saw his father from afar sitting upon a lion throne," and so forth, and the phrase "some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects": because there are both detailed and abbreviated descriptions, the word "calculating" is used.
Because it is spoken to others, it is called "external.
Because the merit of transformation is attributed to oneself, it is called "internal.

As for the phrase "notes, records, vouchers, and commentaries," this clarifies that by discerning the cause one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); therefore, they are called notes, records, vouchers, and commentaries.

The three and a half lines beginning with "The impoverished son saw his father, noble, wealthy, and majestic" eulogize the fourth stage mentioned above: the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance. This refers to the previous statement: "When the impoverished son saw his father’s great power and influence, he immediately felt terror and regretted having come here."
Regarding the verse beginning with "At that time, the elder," which summarizes the four sections of the father seeing his son, this [verse] now only summarizes the first and second.
The first half of the line summarizes the first stage, the place where he sees his son; the preceding text states, "At that time, the wealthy elder was upon the lion throne."

"From afar he saw his son and silently recognized him"—this half-line praises the second point, the actual seeing and recognizing of the son. The preceding statement, "seeing the son and immediately recognizing him," omits the praise of the third point, the great joy in his heart, and likewise omits the praise of the fourth point, the thought of being relieved and at ease.
"Immediately he commands the messenger"—the following three lines of verse praise the third analogy, that of failing to find the son.

In the preceding analogy, there were originally three sections: first, the acceptance of exhortation and the proposal of suitability for those lacking the capacity; second, the acceptance of admonition and the proposal of suitability for those lacking the capacity; and third, the cessation of both forms of transformation.

Now these three lines of verse also correspond to three sections: the first three phrases correspond to the first section, the next one line and one phrase correspond to the second, and the following one line corresponds to the third.

Now, regarding the first of these three lines of verse, which exhorts those who are unsuitable for the [ultimate] teaching: the half-line of verse exhorts those who are suitable, while the subsequent line acknowledges those who are unsuitable.

Within the preceding section on "suitability," there are two parts: first, acknowledging and exhorting them to act; second, formally acknowledging their suitability. This current half-line only versifies the acknowledgment and exhortation to act, as stated above: "He immediately sent an attendant to pursue him urgently and bring him back."

This does not summarize the formal reception and the appropriate application; the preceding statement, "At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him," and the single phrase, "The impoverished son cried out in alarm," summarize the second section: the exhortation to receive [the teaching] when there is no receptive capacity.
Regarding "there is no superior capacity, but there are two within the middling": first, there is the small; second, there is the absence of the great.

The current mention of the three characters "the impoverished son was startled" (*qióngzǐ jīng*) is a verse summarizing the presence of the small capacity mentioned above, which refers to the phrase "the impoverished son was struck with alarm" (*qióngzǐ jīng'è*).

The single word "shouting" in this verse indicates that there was no great capacity [for enlightenment]. The preceding statement, "Crying out in resentment, 'I have not offended you; why do you seize me? clarifies that there was no great capacity.
"Confused and distressed, he fell to the ground. This subsequent line and phrase summarize the second section above: the suitability of the instruction and the lack of receptive capacity.
Within the aforementioned suitability and lack of receptive capacity, there are two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the suitability; second, the lack of receptive capacity.
Now, I do not provide a verse summary for the "Proposing the Appropriate" section; I only provide a verse summary for the "Admonishing the Absence of Capacity.
Within the "Absence of Capacity" section above, there are two parts: first, the absence of greatness, and second, the presence of smallness.
Now, in the preceding verse there is the small [vehicle], while in the subsequent verse there is no great [vehicle].

The single line, “confused and fainting, he fell to the ground,” contains the small capacity; it refers back to the earlier statement, “becoming even more terrified, he fainted and fell to the ground.”

"This person thinks, 'I shall certainly be put to death'"—this single line precisely summarizes the aforementioned lack of great capacity; the preceding passage states: "At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself: 'Though I am innocent, I have been imprisoned and seized; this must surely mean death.'"
"The elder knew his son was foolish and narrow-minded"—this single line summarizes the third section, which concerns both the cessation of conversion and the transformation [of the son].

Within the preceding section on the cessation of conversion, there were originally two parts: first, the desire to cease conversion; second, the actual cessation of conversion. Here, the second part—the actual cessation of conversion—is not summarized; only the first part—the desire to cease conversion—is summarized.

The superior desire to cease his transformative activity also has two stages: first, clarifying the desire to cease his transformative activity; second, explaining the desire to cease his transformative activity. The preceding passage beginning with "The father saw him from afar and told the messenger, 'There is no need for this man; do not force him to come'" refers to the contemplation of the desire to cease his transformative activity, which is not recited here.
Only the second verse explains the intention of ceasing the manifestation [of the Buddha-body], as stated above: "Why is this?
Because the father knows that his son's disposition is inferior, and he himself knows that his own nobility and wealth are difficult for the son to accept."
"By means of skillful expedients"—the three verses below this praise the fourth analogy, that of calling the son and finding him.
Within the preceding analogy, there are two parts: first, the father calls the son; second, the son responds to the call.
In the first two lines of verse, the father calls his son; in the subsequent line, the son responds to the call.

Within the father’s call, there are originally four sections: here, one line of verse summarizes the first section, three lines summarize the second, the next three lines summarize the third, and the final line summarizes the fourth.

The single phrase "thereby employing skillful means" praises the search for a person who can be employed; that is, the search for a teaching of skillful means, which corresponds to the previous statement: "At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised skillful means."

The three lines beginning with "Furthermore, he sent other persons" eulogize the second point: obtaining persons who can be dispatched, which refers to obtaining the teaching of skillful means; this corresponds to what was stated above regarding "secretly dispatching two persons."
The "squinting eye" is a mark of irregularity; it signifies that the teachings of the Two Vehicles are not the truly authentic teaching, and is thus named "Squinting Eye.
Because the teachings of the Two Vehicles do not fully explain the marks and signs of majestic virtue, they are said to be "without majestic virtue."
"You may speak to him"—the following three lines constitute the verse on the third point, the instruction to employ a messenger; this refers to the method of applying skillful means (*upāya*).
The previous statement, "You may go to him and speak gently to the impoverished son," indicates the place where the action is to be performed.

The phrase "I shall give you double the price" corresponds to the fourth stage of the messenger’s mission: the actual execution of the command to summon the son. This clearly illustrates how the Tathāgata employs skillful means (*upāya*) to accommodate sentient beings; it refers to what was stated above: "At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son."

"Upon hearing this, the impoverished son... This single line of verse concerns the second stage of the son’s response to the call. Within the preceding section on the call, there were also four stages; here, three of those stages are not versified, and only the third stage is versified. Regarding the first stage above, "Having already obtained it," there was the capacity to hear; regarding the second stage, "He fully recounted the previous matters," there was the capacity to receive; and the fourth stage, "The father saw his son and felt pity and wonder," is not versified here.

The third section above states: "At that time, the impoverished son first took the wages and immediately began clearing away the filth and cleaning the various rooms. Now, only this portion is versified.
Regarding the phrase "purifying all rooms": the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are like rooms; because one is undefiled amidst these six sense-objects, it is called "purifying all rooms."
"The elder, at the window"—the following five lines and a half of verse praise the fifth instruction regarding the analogy of employing laborers.

In the preceding analogy, there were originally three sections: first, the causal conditions for the instruction on employment; second, the actual instruction on employment; and third, the laborers performing their work in accordance with the elder's intentions.

The first two verses of the stanza teach the causal basis for the action; the next two and a half verses correctly teach the performance of the action; and the final remaining verse expresses the approval of the elder’s intention.

Regarding the reasons for the aforementioned instruction, the original text consists of three sections: first, the elder seeing his son; second, discarding the attire of a nobleman; and third, donning the clothing of a lowly person.
These two verses only praise the first and third [points], but do not praise the second: the meaning of discarding the attire of a noble person and donning the Dharma-body.
The initial verse praises the first point—seeing the son; the subsequent verse praises the third point—donning the clothing of a lowly person.
However, within the middle section of "The Father Seeing His Son Above," there are further three segments; here, we do not versify the first, but only versify the second stage.
The first line of the aforementioned section, "Furthermore, on another day," clarifies the time when he saw his son, which is not versified here.

The second part states, "Within the window," clarifying the place where he clearly sees his son; here, the first line of the verse corresponds precisely to this second stage, while the following three lines correspond to the third stage, the actual seeing of the son.

Regarding this verse, "Thereupon the elder put on tattered and soiled garments": it praises the third stage mentioned above, the receiving of the clothing of a lowly person. Within that aforementioned reception of the lowly person's clothing, there are three stages; here, the second stage is not praised, and only two stages are praised.
The first half-verse praises the first [point] above, clarifying the absence of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); the second half-verse praises the third [point] above, the absence of wisdom.

From "Skillful means approaches" (*upāya-sannidhi*) onwards, there are two and a half lines, which praise the second [point] above, the actual instruction for practice. Within that original instruction for practice, there were four sections; now they are fully versified: one half-line praises the first, one line praises the second, one line and one phrase praise the third, and half a line praises the fourth.

"Using skillful means, he approaches and speaks to them, urging them to work diligently. Now, this first half-line of verse corresponds to the first stage, specifically the third exhortation to take the three carts; it is thus an exhortation to diligence. As stated above: "He says to the laborers, 'All of you, work diligently.'"

The phrase "I have already increased your wages" corresponds to the second part of the second section concerning the pointing out of the three vehicles; it refers to what was stated above: "Later he further addressed them, saying, 'Ho, men! You shall always work here and not go elsewhere.'"

The single line and phrase, “and applying oil to the feet,” praises the third [category] of the aforementioned praise for the implements, which corresponds to the first praise for the three vehicles. Previously it was said, “the jars, vessels, rice, and flour you require”; now, the application of oil to the feet serves as a substitute for the aforementioned aged and infirm servants. These aged and infirm servants are merely supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Here, the application of oil to the feet serves as their substitute;

for in foreign lands, the use of oil to anoint the feet enables one to walk upon water as if upon the ground. The drinking [of oil] serves as a substitute for the flour, and the eating [of oil] serves as a substitute for the rice. Therefore, the *Śāstra* states that there are two kinds of "lump food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*): first, coarse, and second, fine. Rice and the like are called coarse, while drinks and the like are called fine.
The mats serve as a substitute for the upper vessels used to contain things; this clarifies that "or" (*ming*) may be like the mats.

Furthermore, the half-line "speaking with gentle words as if [he were] my own son" praises the fourth point of the preceding section, namely that what is received is necessarily not in vain. The preceding statement, "Rest your mind well; I am like a father to you," conveys the meaning of providing security and non-deception.

"The householder, being wise, gradually causes him to enter and exit"—this single line constitutes the third [verse], which summarizes the third point above: that the person acts in a manner pleasing to the householder.

The preceding section was deemed acceptable; that original text consists of four sections, which correspond to the four sections within the passage on receiving and practicing the Three Vehicles mentioned above. Now, only the third section is versified, while the others are not.
The first is: "When you constantly act, there are no five kinds of evils. This illustrates the meaning of "each mind being courageous and sharp," which is not chanted here.

Second, regarding the phrase "from now on, like a son born of oneself," which refers to ordinary people within the community who resemble noble ones, this is not praised here; only the third [category] is praised.

At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer; for this reason, he was constantly made to clear away dung for twenty years. Because he perceived the Truth, contemplated it, and practiced the path of cultivation, it is said to be "twenty years."
The fourth verse, "After this, with minds characterized by mutual trust," does not praise the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship.
The following two lines, "Showing him gold and silver," are a verse on the sixth preceding analogy, that of entrusting the property.
The preceding analogy has two parts: first, the father’s entrustment, and second, the son’s reception.
Within the father’s entrustment, there are three stages; none of these are recited here, and only the son’s reception is recited.
Within "the son receives [the inheritance]" there are again three parts; however, only the second and third are versified, while the first—the initial acceptance of the command—is not.
The line "showing him the gold and silver" versifies the second part, "the formal acceptance," which was previously referred to as "taking charge of and knowing the various goods."
The line "still remaining outside the gate" is a verse summarizing the third point: "yet having no intention to seek even a single meal, nor being able to abandon one's base mind."
"The father knows that his son’s mind has gradually become vast" constitutes the seventh [section]; this half-verse summarizes the seventh analogy above, that of seeing the son's great resolve.
"He wishes to give him wealth and goods"—the following four and a half verses constitute the eighth; they summarize the eighth analogy, that of entrusting the family estate.

In the middle version of the above parable, there are four sections; however, only the first section—concerning the time when he was about to pass away and entrusted his family estate—is not versified, while the remaining three sections are all versified.
The single verse beginning with “Desiring to give wealth and property” establishes the assembly for the second collection.
The two and a half verses beginning with “In this great assembly he says, ‘This is my son’” establish the natural affinity between father and son in the third chapter.
Those of twenty years are vessels for receiving the Way among humans and devas.
"Whatever I possess"—this one-line verse marks the fourth section, the formal entrustment of the family estate.
"Thinking of my former poverty, my resolve was base and inferior"—these two lines below praise the ninth analogy above, that of the sons' joy.
From "The Buddha is also like this" onwards, there are thirty and a half verses which constitute the second [section], praising the nine analogies above by condensing them into eight segments.
The single line "The Buddha is also like this" corresponds to the first parable of the father and son losing each other;
next, the line "Knowing that I [perceived] their delight in inferior teachings" corresponds to the second parable of the father and son meeting;
and finally, the latter half of the verse, "Never having said to them, 'You shall become Buddhas,'" corresponds to the third parable of failing to find the sons.
Next, the second half-line, "And we declare that we have attained all the outflows-free [dharmas]," corresponds to the fourth simile of calling the sons to receive [the inheritance].
Next, the second half-line, "Accomplishing the disciples of the Śrāvaka-vehicle," corresponds to the fifth simile of instructing the laborers.
Next, the eighteen and a half lines beginning with "The Buddha commands us" correspond to the sixth simile of entrusting the property.
Next, the three lines beginning with "Like a wealthy elder" combine the seventh and eighth similes into a single verse;
next, the seven lines beginning with "Today we have attained what we never had before" combine the ninth simile, that of the son’s joy, into a single verse.

Furthermore, regarding the eight stages: one line of verse praises the first; one line of verse praises the second; half a line of verse praises the third; half a line of verse praises the fourth; half a line of verse praises the fifth; eighteen and a half lines of verse praise the sixth; three lines combined praise the seventh and eighth; and subsequently, seven lines of verse praise the ninth, the "Joyful Parable."
Now, regarding the single phrase "The Buddha is also like this," it corresponds to the first analogy of the father and son who have lost each other.

Within that, there were originally two lines; here, we obtain only the verse for the great wealthy elder being the Tathāgata, while the line "We are all like sons of the Buddha" is omitted from the verse.

The single phrase, "Knowing that I delight in the small," corresponds to the second section on the mutual recognition between father and son. The previous statement in the parable, "The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons," refers to the discourse from beginning to end; whereas the present statement, "Knowing that I delight in the small," is discussed in terms of the moment when he illuminates the capacities of the disciples.
The half-line, "I have never said that you shall become Buddhas," corresponds to the third analogy of calling out to one's children but not finding them.

In the preceding section on the correspondence of analogies, there were originally two parts: the absence of great capacity and the presence of small capacity; here, only the absence of great capacity is versified.

The preceding statement, "We, because of the three kinds of suffering, undergo all manner of feverish afflictions, confusion, and ignorance within birth and death," indicates that since there was no great capacity [for the Mahāyāna], it was said, "I have never spoken to you of your becoming Buddhas. This is a brief omission of the meaning concerning those with small capacities who delight in the Lesser Dharma.
The half-line, "And we say that we have attained all the outflows-free [dharmas]," corresponds to the fourth analogy of calling the sons to attain [the goal].
In the preceding analogy of attainment, there were originally two sections: first, the father’s calling; second, the sons’ receiving of the call.

Within the section concerning the father calling his son, there are naturally four parts. Of these, the preceding correspondence with the parable only corresponds to the fourth stage—the phrase "at that time the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son. The preceding correspondence with the parable states, "The World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate and eliminate the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all dharmas," which is not recited here.

Within the "The Son Responds to the Call" section, there are originally four parts; it corresponds only to the third part: "At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately began clearing away the filth. The preceding allegory states: "Among these, we diligently applied ourselves with vigor and obtained the day’s wage of nirvana. Now, this verse merely recites this specific line, hence it says: "And it is said that we have attained all the outflows-free [dharmas]."
"Accomplishing the disciples of the Śrāvaka-vehicle of the Hīnayāna" constitutes half a verse; this is the fifth instruction on the analogy of making a person.

In the preceding extended analogy, there were originally three parts: first, the causal conditions for the instruction on making [the person]; second, the actual instruction on making; and third, clarifying that the person so made accords with the householder's intention.

In the previous section on the three stages of correspondence with the parable, all were corresponded to, though some were omitted for brevity; now, only the fourth stage within the third stage is versified, while the others are not.

Why is this? Within the three [sections] concerning the causes and conditions for the aforementioned teaching, the preceding analogy only corresponds to the third section and not the other two. The preceding correspondence to the third stage begins with "First he knew that we were deeply attached to and obscured by desires" and concludes with "he did not distinguish the portions of the treasure-store"; now, none of these are recited here.

In the second section, the analogy within the "Correct Teaching" (samyag-deśanā) consists of four parts; however, in the application (*yoga*), only the second and third stages are applied. The preceding application of the words, "The World-Honored One, by the power of skillful means, speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," corresponds to "I shall increase your price," and it may also correspond to "whatever you require. Now, these [two points] are likewise not versified here.

The third section, "Acting in a manner that accords with the elder’s wishes," consists of four parts; the preceding [section] corresponds only to the fourth stage, stating: "After this, their minds accord in mutual trust, and they enter and exit without difficulty" (referring to the fruit of arhatship). The previous correspondence with the parable stated: "We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day's wages for nirvana, which we consider a great gain. Now, the statement "accomplishing the disciples of the Hīnayāna śrāvakas" precisely corresponds to this verse.
"‘The Buddha commands us’—from here below, for eighteen lines and a half, this verse corresponds to the sixth parable of entrusting property.
In the preceding extended parable, there are two parts: first, the father’s entrustment; second, the son’s acceptance."
Regarding the "Father's Entrustment" (*pitṛparīndanā*), there are three sections; the preceding [text] did not correspond [to them], and thus they were not versified here either.

Regarding the "Son’s Acceptance" (*putrapratigraha*), there are likewise three sections; since the preceding [text] fully corresponded to these three sections, the present verses on the "Acceptance" also fully versify the three sections of the "Son’s Acceptance. Within these eighteen and a half stanzas, one stanza corresponds to the first section, the next five stanzas correspond to the second, and the subsequent twelve and a half stanzas correspond to the third.

The first line, "The Buddha commanded us," refers to the sons receiving the instruction; in the opening of the analogy, the first statement says, "At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the command"; and in the application of the analogy, it says, "We, moreover, rely upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom."

The five lines beginning with "I, receiving the Buddha’s teaching, for the sake of the great bodhisattvas" correspond to the second section, the actual turning of the teaching, which concerns "receiving and knowing the various objects, gold, silver, and precious treasures"; this is equivalent to the statement in the preceding analogy, "opening up and proclaiming [the teaching] for the great bodhisattvas."

From the phrase "Just like that impoverished son" onwards, there are twelve and a half verses. These verses correspond to the third section, "Yet he himself has no aspiration for this," which clarifies the meaning of not seeking [the Dharma]. Within these, some lines provide a direct correspondence while others provide an explanatory correspondence; now, these twelve and a half verses are divided into two parts: first, eleven and a half verses correspond directly to the lack of seeking; second, the single verse beginning with "The guide saw him abandon [him]" corresponds to the preceding explanatory lines.
Within these eleven and a half verses, there are naturally three sections. First, the single verse beginning with "Just like that impoverished son" prefaces the external analogy of not seeking;
second, the verse beginning with "Although we preach the treasure-trove of the Buddha-dharma" internally correlates with the meaning of not seeking.

The third section, beginning from "We [have attained] internal extinction," consists of nine and a half verses that correctly recite the theme of "not seeking. This is an extensive commentary on the first three sections of the preceding chapter—namely, the three segments on "not seeking, yet it is spontaneously accomplished"—beginning with "We [have attained] internal extinction. First, the four lines beginning with "We [have attained] internal extinction" extensively explain the first point: not seeking because one already stands at the head of the Saṃgha. Second, the four verses beginning with "We, throughout the long night," extensively explain the second point: not seeking because one considers oneself to have already attained *nirvāṇa*. Third, the one and a half verses stating "Although we are sons of the Buddhas... extensively explain the third point: not seeking because one's years are advanced and decrepit.
"The Teacher has abandoned us"—this single line is the second [verse], which explains the aforementioned phrase "not seeking.
The passage beginning with "Why is this?
For the Buddha knows that our minds delight in the Lesser Dharma" follows from there.

"Like a wealthy elder"—the following three lines constitute the seventh [section], which combines the verse for the parable of the son’s great ambition (the seventh) and also combines the verse for the parable of entrusting the family estate (the eighth).
Within this, it is further divided into two parts: the first one and a half lines cite four external parables, and the second one and a half lines apply these parables to the teaching.

"Just as a wealthy elder knew his son’s inferior disposition" cites the fourth parable, the calling back of the son; "by the power of skillful means" cites the fifth parable, teaching him to work as a laborer; "he subdued his mind with gentleness" cites the seventh parable, the aspiration for greatness; and "only then did he entrust him with all the wealth and treasures" cites the eighth parable, the entrustment of the family estate.

“The Buddha is also like this”: these one and a half lines constitute the second section, correlating four external metaphors. The first two phrases correlate with the fourth [metaphor]; the following two phrases, “knowing those who delight in the small,” correlate with the fifth; “taming their minds” correlates with the seventh; and “then teaching great wisdom” correlates with the eighth.

"We have today attained what we have never before had. The seven lines of verse below this constitute the eighth stanza, which combines with the ninth section on joy; therein are three parts: first, one verse that correctly clarifies the joy itself; second, half a line that cites an external analogy to apply it by way of correspondence; and third, five and a half lines that extensively clarify the characteristics of joy.

"The Great Kindness of the World-Honored One"—the thirteen verses following this constitute the second part of the "Correct Comprehension," wherein he praises the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay because [the Dharma] has come from the Buddha, thereby concluding the preceding section on comprehension.
Within the section on "Correctly Receiving and Understanding" there are three parts; specifically, the prose and the verse constitute two.

Within this current section, there are two parts: first, six and a half verses that directly praise the Buddha’s profound kindness which is difficult to repay; second, the six and a half lines beginning with "The Buddhas are rare," which describe the characteristics of the Buddha’s kindness.
Furthermore, within these two sections, each contains two parts. Regarding the two parts in the first section:
the first consists of one line that initially clarifies the Buddha’s grace, which is to say, the opening of the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle.
From "For immeasurable billions of kalpas" down to the fifth line and a half, it clarifies that there is no one who can repay [this kindness].
Within this second section, there are three parts:
first, the initial half-line provides a general clarification that no one can repay it;
The second section, "Providing Hands and Feet," consisting of the following four lines, specifically clarifies that worldly offerings cannot repay [the debt];
the third section, "Such matters as these," consisting of one line, summarizes that nothing can repay it.

"Rare are the Buddhas"—the following six and a half lines clarify the characteristics of the Buddha’s grace, which also consists of two parts: first, two lines clarify the benefits of the physical body (*kāyakarma*); second, four and a half lines clarify the benefits of the verbal activity (*vākkarma*), which is the meaning of the provisional and ultimate two wisdoms opening the three to reveal the one.

Chapter Five: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs. In this chapter, three types of grasses and two types of trees are employed as metaphors; however, because the name is derived from the predominant element, it is called "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs."

The second part, the "Parable" (Upamā), which explains the teaching that reveals the One by opening the Three for those of middle capacity, consists of four sections. First, the first chapter, "The Parable" (Upamā), provides the actual parables to explain the teaching that reveals the One by opening the Three for those of middle capacity.
Second, the "Resolute Belief" (Adhimukti) chapter records the understanding and realization of those of middle capacity.

Now, this third chapter, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (Oṣadhī-parivarta), clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment of the meaning of the understanding attained by those of middle capacity.
The fourth is the "Bestowal of Prophecy" (*Vyākaraṇa*).
Within these four sections, each is generally divided into two parts; specifically, within the section on the parable, there are two: first, Śāriputra’s request, and second, the Tathāgata’s response.

There are two parts to this "comprehension and understanding": first, the sūtra author describes the manner in which the four great śrāvakas attained understanding; second, it consists of the actual words of comprehension and understanding spoken by the four great śrāvakas.
This present chapter explains the meaning of how those of middling faculties attain understanding; it consists of two parts: first, the prose (long passage), and second, the verse (stanzas).

However, within the words of the four great śrāvakas’ formal comprehension, there are originally three sections: first, a brief comprehension; second, a preliminary inquiry of the Tathāgata before wishing to provide a detailed comprehension; and third, the detailed comprehension itself.
Now, the Tathāgata merely restates and confirms the extensive understanding [of the first part], omitting the brief restatement of the preceding two sections.

However, within the third section, the extensive confirmation of understanding, there are originally two parts. First, from "Suppose there were a person" down to the end of the verses—comprising seventy-three and a half verses—is divided into nine analogies, which confirm the Tathāgata’s clarification of the meaning that the three vehicles are opened up to reveal the one, all returning to the same destination.

The second section, from "The Great Kindness of the World-Honored One" onwards, consists of thirteen lines of verse that praise the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay, thereby concluding the exposition of understanding.

Regarding this prose commentary (*dīrghapada*), it is likewise divided into two parts, which correspond to and confirm the two preceding sections: first, from the beginning of the chapter up to "whatever is spoken is not in vain," the second point—that the Buddha’s kindness is profound and difficult to repay—is confirmed by anticipation; second, from "In all dharmas, through wisdom and skillful means" until the end of the prose, the first point—the actual employment of nine parables to lead [the disciples] to understand the Tathāgata’s seven meanings of opening the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle—is confirmed by retrospective narration.

Furthermore, within each of these two sections there are three sub-sections. In the section describing how the Buddha’s profound kindness is difficult to repay, the first is the formal exposition; the second clarifies that which has not yet been fully explained; and the third cites the Dharma King to demonstrate that what the Tathāgata has spoken is not in vain.

What is this? From the beginning of the chapter until the words "It is truly as you have said," this is the first section, which completes the formal exposition and subsequently praises the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay. Regarding your previous statement, "Even if one were to provide for him with hands and feet and pay homage by bowing one's head for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would still be difficult to repay his kindness"—this is indeed exactly as you have praised.

However, because sentient beings give rise to doubt upon seeing the Tathāgata describe how the four great śrāvakas praise the Buddha’s profound and unrepayable kindness, they may say that the Tathāgata’s virtuous conduct and deep grace are entirely exhausted by what these four śrāvakas of shallow wisdom have praised. Therefore, from the passage "The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merits" down to "cannot be fully described," it is designated as "expounding what was previously left unsaid."

However, those thirteen preceding verses of yours that praise the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay merely extol a small portion of what is taught from one perspective; they speak directly only of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful means and reality, and his grace in benefiting sentient beings.
As for that which you have not yet praised, there are furthermore immeasurable, boundless, unspeakable, and incalculable deep graces and heavy virtues that benefit sentient beings in manifold ways.

This is the resolution of doubts. However, within this second layer, the common understanding still gives rise to further doubt, questioning: "The essence of the Tathāgata is exhausted; he possesses only provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to benefit beings through skillful means, and real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) to expound principles and deliver people. Although the Buddha is fully endowed with all virtues, if one examines them through the lens of the provisional and the real, they do not exceed these two paths. Why, then, is it said that there are furthermore immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* merits?"
In this case, the internal contradictions between the preceding and following sections would be so sharp as to make it difficult to accept the text as authoritative.

Since such doubts exist, the third section—from "Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas" down to "all is not in vain"—cites the title of Dharma-King to clarify that what the Tathāgata has spoken is not false.
Those who lack self-mastery have things to fear, and thus the words they utter in teaching are mostly unreal;
since Your Majesty’s nature dwells at the ultimate pinnacle of the sovereign body, abiding in a state of mastery, how could there be an edict issued from such a source that is false?
To clarify that the Tathāgata is the King of the Dharma and that his spoken words and teachings contain no false or empty pronouncements, this third section exists.
However, the first section is precisely the fulfillment of the preceding praise, stating that the Buddha’s kindness is profound and difficult to repay; the latter two sections resolve doubts.
Within these three sections, each contains two stages.

Regarding the first stage, which correctly describes how the Buddha’s profound grace is difficult to repay, there are two parts. The first part, from "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa" down to "true merit," describes and praises the four great śrāvakas; it is a statement of principle that skillfully expresses "Excellent! by saying, "Very good, very good."
"Along with the great disciples" refers to Subhūti, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kātyāyana, and others.

The second phrase, "Truly as you have said," describes the reality underlying the words previously spoken; whereas the preceding section clarified the skillfulness of the words regarding the principle, this subsequent section clarifies the reality of the principle underlying the words. This pair together constitutes the first formal exposition, wherein the four great śrāvakas, through thirteen lines of verse, praise the Buddha’s profound kindness which is difficult to repay.

The second part, "Explaining that which was not yet fully stated," contains two sections. First, the statement, "The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits," directly presents the dharmas that were not yet fully explained; it means that beyond what has already been said—namely, the thirteen lines of verse praising the Buddha’s profound kindness that is difficult to repay—there are further immeasurable merits that cannot be described or numbered.

Second, the statement, "If you were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you could not exhaust them," clarifies that they cannot be fully spoken. This pair together constitutes the second section explaining what was not yet fully stated, and it also serves to resolve the doubts of sentient beings, as the nature of those doubts was explained previously.

The third section, "Clarifying that [the Tathāgata’s words] are not in vain," contains two parts. First, from the passage "Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas," he first cites the Dharma-king as the starting point for demonstrating that his words are not in vain.
Second, the statement "Whatever he says is entirely not in vain" directly clarifies that they are not in vain.
This pair, taken together, constitutes the third clarification that [the teaching] is not in vain, and also serves to resolve doubts—the nature of which is as previously described.

From the passage beginning "By means of wisdom and skillful means regarding all dharmas" onwards is the second section, which retrospectively explains how the first [section] correctly received and understood the Tathāgata’s meaning of opening up the three and revealing the one.

Within this second section, there are three parts. First, from "By means of wisdom and skillful means regarding all dharmas" up to "revealing all wisdom to all sentient beings," prior to the actual exposition of the conclusion, he first sets forth the dharmas previously mastered; this is precisely the meaning of the two wisdoms—expedient and real—opening the three to reveal the one.

The second section, from "For example, as in the trichiliocosm" down to "Therefore, he did not immediately preach all-encompassing wisdom," clarifies that the understanding attained today was preceded by an explanation of how the four great śrāvakas failed to understand the meaning of the three-in-one in the past. It describes how they clung to the fixed distinction of the three vehicles and were deluded regarding the principle of their common return [to the One], just as grasses and trees receive the moisture of heaven and grow, yet each is unaware of the specific characteristics of its own growth and nourishment. This clarifies the nature of their lack of understanding in the past resulting in their attainment of understanding today.

The third section, from "O Kāśyapa, it is most rare indeed" down to the end of the prose, correctly describes the fulfillment of the purpose of attaining liberation today by opening up the three and revealing the one.
Within these three sections, there are two parts each.

Regarding the first section, which presents the dharmas to be realized, there are two: first, the simultaneous opening of the two chapter-gates; second, the simultaneous detailed exposition of the two chapter-gates.
Regarding the two chapter-headings: "Expounding all dharmas through wisdom and skillful means" is the chapter-heading for provisional wisdom;
"The teachings he expounds all reach the ground of omniscience" is the chapter-heading for ultimate wisdom.

Now, to explain the meaning of the chapter on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*): "Regarding all phenomena" refers to the Buddha-fruit and Buddha-wisdom; knowing all phenomena is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the myriad virtues are the causes for this knowledge of all modes.

Regarding the phrase "expounding it through wisdom and skillful means," this clarifies that the Tathāgata, upon the causal dharmas of the house of omniscience, employs skillful wisdom to manifest the teachings of the three vehicles; therefore, it is said that he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means.

Regarding the phrase, "The teachings he expounds all reach the ground of omniscience," this is an explanation of the topical heading for true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). As for "the teachings he expounds," it refers to the myriad wholesome dharmas previously taught by his skillful means (*upāyajñāna*).
Because these principles of the ten thousand virtues can bring about the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is said that they "all reach the ground of all-knowledge.
From the words "The Tathāgata observes and knows" onwards is the second section, which extensively elaborates upon the two preceding topical gateways.
The preceding extensive section on the categories of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) consists of two parts: first, the recognition of the medicine; second, the knowledge of the illness.

Now, when it says, “The Tathāgata observes and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena,” this is the first point clarifying the meaning of the Tathāgata’s recognition of the medicinal dharma, which is the objective realm illuminated by expedient wisdom.
When it says, “He also knows the profound mental activities of all sentient beings with unimpeded penetration,” this is the meaning of knowing the illness.

Regarding the phrase "knowing the deep-seated inclinations and practices of all sentient beings," this clarifies that the Tathāgata knows the capacities and appropriate dispositions of those belonging to the three vehicles: thus, for those with the capacity of a śrāvaka, it is appropriate to practice the Four Noble Truths; for those with the capacity of a pratyekabuddha, it is appropriate to practice the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for those with the capacity of a bodhisattva, it is appropriate to practice the Six Perfections.

Regarding "thorough penetration" (*tongda*): "thorough" (*tong*) has the meaning of being unobstructed, and "penetration" (*da*) has the meaning of arrival. It clarifies that according to the capacities and dispositions of those of the three vehicles, their practice must sever afflictions without obstruction; this is the meaning of "thorough."

To clarify that the faculties and dispositions of those of the three vehicles are appropriate for their respective paths, and that through practice they will surely reach the state beyond the triple world where the wisdom of the exhaustion of birth arises—this is the meaning of "attainment.
As for "unimpeded," it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the faculties and dispositions of those of the three vehicles is exhaustive; this is what is meant by being "unimpeded."

Now, by raising what is appropriate for practice and attaining thorough penetration, he clearly demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the capacities and natures of the three vehicles is exhaustive; therefore, it is said that he knows the practices of the deep minds of all sentient beings with unobstructed penetration.

The section beginning with "Furthermore, one thoroughly and clearly understands all dharmas" constitutes the second part, which extensively elaborates upon the preceding chapter on true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Within this, there are two sections: first, identifying the medicine; second, diagnosing the illness.

Now, the statement "furthermore, thoroughly exhausting and clearly understanding all dharmas" refers to the first meaning of the medicinal dharma of consciousness (*vijñāna*). This clarifies the object illuminated by the wisdom of the reality of consciousness; because the Tathāgata’s wisdom of reality knows everything within each cause and each effect, it is said to be "thoroughly exhausted and clearly understood."

"To manifest all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings" refers to the second [aspect of] knowing the illness; the meaning of "knowing the illness" is simply to know that sentient beings possess the capacity for the Mahāyāna, and thus to bestow upon them the prediction (vyākaraṇa) that they shall all attain Buddhahood in the future—hence it is said, "to manifest all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings."
This means that one must know the medicine as before and recognize the illness as after, so as to provide the appropriate medicine for the specific illness and enable its application.

"Kāśyapa, it is like the trichiliocosm" — from here until "therefore I do not immediately teach the knowledge of all modes" — constitutes the second section. This intends to describe what has already been understood today; first, it states that previously [the disciples] did not understand the meaning of the three-in-one, just as insentient grasses and trees receive the moisture of heaven and grow, yet do not themselves know the distinctions of their growth.
Within this, there are also two sections: the first is the opening of the analogy (*upamā*), and the second is the application of the analogy (*upanaya*).

Each of these two sections contains two parts. Regarding the two parts within the opening of the analogy: the first, from "For example, as in a trichiliocosm" down to "flowers, fruits, and seeds flourish," is designated as the analogy of receiving moisture and growing.
The second section, from "Although the sentient beings of a single ground... down to "...each has its own distinction," is titled the "Parable of Not Knowing for Oneself.

It clarifies that the three types of grass and two types of trees receive the moisture of heaven throughout the day and grow, yet each is unaware of the specific characteristics of their growth and differentiation. This is internally correlated to clarify that the four great śrāvakas formerly received the teachings of the three vehicles in person and practiced them, yet they were unaware that what they practiced was in fact but a single vehicle, ultimately returning together at the end to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, within the first analogy concerning growth through receiving moisture, three sub-analogies are further distinguished. First, from "For example, like the trichiliocosm" down to "name-and-form are each distinct," the recipient is first presented; this recipient is the grasses and trees.
Second, from "dense clouds spread everywhere" down to "its moisture universally saturates," there is further the manifestation of what is received; that which is received is the dense clouds.
The third section, from "the grasses, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs" down to "the flowers, fruits, and seeds," correctly clarifies how [beings] receive the moisture and grow.

The preceding section clarifies that those who receive [the moisture] are the grasses and trees; the following section clarifies that what they receive is the clouds and rain; and the subsequent section correctly clarifies the growth resulting from receiving this moisture.
By internal analogy, those who receive and accept the teaching are the four great śrāvakas, while that which they receive is the benefit provided by the Tathāgata’s form and voice.
Regarding "clearly elucidating the increase through receiving the transformative moisture," this clearly elucidates how the four great śrāvakas received the teachings and practiced them.
Within these three parables, there are respectively two stages.

Regarding the ability to receive [the analogy] as having two parts: this refers to having both a root and a branch. It simply clarifies that grasses and trees are the branches; these grasses and trees must have a root, and that root is the earth.

From the passage beginning with "For example, the three thousand [worlds]" up to "mountains, rivers, streams, valleys, and land," these five types constitute the fundamental basis for those capable of receiving [the teachings].

The second section, from "the grasses, trees, and forests that grow therefrom" up to "their names and forms are each distinct," correctly presents those who receive [the teaching], namely the three types of grasses and two types of trees.

To correlate this internally with the treatise: that which is capable of receiving [the moisture] is the family root, namely the past habitual causes and roots of goodness of sentient beings; that which is the grasses and trees capable of receiving it is the sentient being formed today by the fruits of wholesome practice. Since one now wishes to take the grasses and trees but not their root, in the subsequent correlation of the parable, only the grasses and trees are correlated and not their root.
The questioner said:

"Sentient beings are of many kinds: there are those formed by the cause of evil habitual tendencies, those formed by the cause of evil retributive results, those formed by the cause of wholesome habitual tendencies, and those formed by the cause of wholesome retributive results. Now, which of these causes formed beings do you intend to take?"
The commentator says:

"One does not take sentient beings produced by two types of unwholesome causes as those capable of receiving [the teaching]. Rather, among those produced by two types of wholesome causes, only those produced by the cause of wholesome practice are capable of receiving it; those produced by the cause of wholesome retribution are not taken as being capable of receiving it."
Why is this so? Because the cause of the retribution of goodness lacks the sense of increase, it is not taken [as the recipient];
whereas the sentient beings produced by the cause of the practice of goodness possess the sense of increase, and for this reason they are taken as those who can receive [the teaching].
The questioner spoke again:

"Now, taking sentient beings accomplished through the causes of wholesome cultivation as those who receive [the teaching], does this mean one should simply take those for whom the causes of wholesome cultivation possess the sense of increase?"
"Those sentient beings who are thus accomplished also possess the sense of growth.
The commentary further states:
"Sentient beings are provisional designations; as provisional designations they have no separate substance, for their substance consists of dharmas."

Now, the causes and conditions of practice that are wholesome are real dharmas; these dharmas constitute sentient beings. It is only that the causes and conditions of practice which are wholesome undergo increase; as for "sentient beings," they are merely provisional designations and should not be said to increase or not increase—they possess only the function of a name.
The questioner spoke again:

"If sentient beings have no separate essence and take only the causes of habitual cultivation—namely, goodness—as their essence, then once those causes of habitual cultivation increase, how could sentient beings not also increase?"
If one says that sentient beings do not increase, then one should not say that they take the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) as their substance.
The commentary further states:

"I originally said that dharmas of provisional designation (*prajñapti-dharma*) have no substance, yet they take the wholesome habitual cause as their substance. If you now object that sentient beings increase separately, then dharmas of provisional designation must also have a separate substance; how then can you say they take something else as their substance?"

The general meaning here is as follows: in brief correspondence with the four great śrāvakas, because the present *nirvāṇa* concerns the five vehicles, the three types of grass and two types of trees are borrowed as metaphors for those who receive the teaching. There are three kinds of grass—superior, middling, and inferior—and two kinds of trees—large trees and small trees.
The subsequent scripture further states:

"Regarding large and small trees, although grasses and trees themselves are numerous in kind, we now take only those capable of serving as medicine. This internally corresponds to the fact that although sentient beings—whether ordinary or sagely—are numerous, we select only those of the five vehicles who are capable of cultivation for the purpose of being 'medicine.'

Those who ride the vehicle of humans and those who ride the vehicle of devas—these two types of persons are likened to minor medicinal herbs; śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—these two types of persons are likened to medium medicinal herbs; and among the three vehicles, bodhisattvas are likened to superior medicinal herbs.

In the Mahāyāna, the internal ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) bodhisattvas are illustrated by small trees, while bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward are illustrated by great trees. As for the reason why humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are collectively illustrated by small grasses, and why *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are further combined and illustrated by medium grasses: it is because one now wishes to address these people specifically. Although they received the Tathāgata’s scriptural teachings in the past, they did not understand the principle that the provisional and the real both converge in their function; therefore, humans, devas, and the two vehicles are grouped together and likened to small grasses.
As clarified in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, those termed "beings who have not heard the Dharma" are thus disparaged for their former ignorance;
the same principle applies to those who conform to the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The questioner said:
"Since Bodhisattvas and others already know for themselves that the provisional and ultimate teachings of the Tathāgata share the same underlying meaning, why do they speak of them as inferior?
The commentator said:

This has already been explained as before; it merely addresses the partial comparison with the four great śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others regarding nirvāṇa, and with bodhisattvas. If one takes the meaning of "equally receiving" the increase of roots of goodness through hearing the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, then both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practitioners experience such increase—just as the metaphor of the three types of grass and two types of trees all flourish by receiving the moisture of heaven.
If, however, one takes the meaning of "knowing versus not knowing," the general intent refers only to the four great śrāvakas; therefore, it concerns nirvāṇa and other [Hīnayāna] individuals.
The questioner spoke again:

"If you maintain that the Bodhisattva has the sense of growth and thus uses the analogy of the two trees, then I, a Śrāvaka, also possesses the sense of growth and thus use the analogy of medicinal herbs; it is not that I lack knowledge, for which reason I would use the analogy of medicinal herbs."
The commentator further said:

"This chapter was originally intended to describe and establish the four great śrāvakas; today they have attained understanding, whereas previously it was stated that they did not understand, and thus the simile of the grass was employed."
It is said that because they do not know the source of their own moisture, the Śrāvakas and others abide in the extreme of non-knowing, while the Bodhisattvas abide in the extreme of growth.
Within this second analogy for what is received, there are two parts: first, the fundamental nature of that which receives; second, the actual emergence of what is received.

“The dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the three thousandfold world system”: this is the fundamental basis of the family from which he first received his lineage; its original nature is that of a cloud.
Internally, the application of this analogy is as follows: the physical form and vocal teachings of the Tathāgata are likened to clouds.

"At one time, they rain down equally, their moisture universally soaking all" refers to the second point, which correctly identifies what is received; that which is received is the rain. This is used to illustrate the Dharma proclaimed by the Tathāgata’s vocal teachings, which is like the rain from heaven falling upon grasses and trees. This merely clarifies that while these grasses and trees alike receive the heavenly rain and grow, there are differences in their degree of growth; likewise, while sentient beings alike listen to the Buddha preach the Dharma and increase their roots of goodness, there are distinctions in the excellence of their progress.

"Flowers, trees, and forests"—the following constitutes the third section, which correctly clarifies the analogy of receiving nourishment and growing. This also has two parts: first, from "flowers, trees, and forests" down to "each receives its share," is called the analogy of receiving moisture.
The second section, from "the rain showered by a single cloud" down to "flowers, fruits, and seeds flourish," is called the analogy of growth.

The preceding part clarifies receiving moisture; this latter part clarifies growth. Internally, this corresponds to sentient beings who, upon first hearing the Buddha’s teaching, all receive it with joy and acceptance—just as grasses and trees receive moisture from a single downpour of heavenly rain.

The subsequent explanation of "increase" clarifies that after sentient beings heard the Buddha preach the Dharma in the past, they collectively increased their roots of goodness. Although the preceding analogy states, "being born in a favorable realm, they experience happiness through the Way," this explains how a causal retribution leads to a resultant retribution; it is not that there is no causal retribution. However, here, in discerning the meaning of "increase," we restrict ourselves to the habitual cause and habitual result to clarify the specific sense of increase.
Within each of these two similes, there are two stages.

Regarding the two stages within the simile of receiving moisture: the first begins from "the grasses, trees, groves, and various medicinal herbs" and concludes with "according to superior, middling, and inferior. This section cites the phenomena that receive moisture—namely, the roots, stalks, branches, and leaves of the three types of grasses and two types of trees—which serve as metaphors for the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the five types of people previously described.

The second statement, "each has that which they receive," precisely clarifies the meaning of receiving nourishment. Internally, it clarifies that in the past, sentient beings heard the Buddha’s teachings and each received and upheld them; therefore, it is said that "each has that which they receive."

Regarding the second stage of increase within the analogy, there are two levels. First, the phrase "the rain from a single cloud" initially cites the cause of increase; this "cause" refers to the cloud and rain. Internally, this corresponds to the reason why sentient beings are able to cultivate and increase their roots of goodness: it is because of the presence of the Tathāgata’s form and voice.
The second statement, "in accordance with their lineage," and the following three phrases explicitly clarify growth; these three phrases also arise in successive order.

The first phrase, "in accordance with their lineage," first cites the categories of growth, using as an analogy that the faculties and natures of those belonging to the five vehicles each have their own specific types through which they attain growth; this is what explicitly clarifies growth.
"Flowers, fruits, and seeds flourish" explains the characteristic of growth; for if there were no growth, how could one speak of the reality of flowers, fruits, and seeds?
"Though born from the same soil"—from this point below is the second section, clarifying the analogy of not knowing oneself.

The three types of grass and two types of trees receive the moisture of heaven all day long, yet they do not know the distinct characteristics of their growth; likewise, the four great śrāvakas personally received the Tathāgata’s teachings on the three vehicles in the past, but they clung to the fixed distinction of the three vehicles and were deluded regarding the principle of the single convergence, failing to realize that the beginning and end of what the three vehicles practice is in fact only the One Vehicle, tending toward the same single fruit.

Furthermore, regarding the analogy of "not knowing for oneself," there are also two stages. First, the phrase "though born from the same earth and moistened by the same rain" first presents the reason why they do not know for themselves.

Second, the statement "yet the various grasses and trees each have their differences" correctly clarifies this lack of self-knowledge; although there are distinct characteristics, they do not know the reason why these differences exist. This corresponds internally to the four great elements and the śrāvakas of the past who received the Tathāgata’s distinct teachings of the three vehicles and each attained a distinct fruit. At that time, those of the three vehicles each claimed that they were different from one another, yet they did not know for themselves that from beginning to end they all return to the same place and arrive together at the ultimate fruit.
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this. From here below is the second part, the application of the analogy (*upanaya*).
In the preceding opening of the analogy, there were originally two parts: first, the analogy of receiving moisture and growing; second, the analogy of not knowing [it] oneself.

Within this current application of the parable, there are likewise two sections: first, from "The Tathāgata is also like this" down to "fully receiving the moisture and each attaining growth," which corresponds to the parable of receiving the dew and growing;
second, from "The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is of a single characteristic and a single flavor" onwards, which corresponds to the parable of not knowing [the source] oneself.
Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the detailed and specific application; second, the citation of external analogies to provide a parallel application.

Regarding the detailed and specific application: although the preceding analogy of receiving moisture originally consisted of three parts, each of these three contains two sub-elements. Now, they are combined into a single essence, which should be expanded into five.
The reason they do not constitute six [sections] is that, in the preceding opening on the capacity for receiving instruction, there were two parts: first, the root, and second, the branches.
Now, only the branches are combined while the root is not; therefore, it forms five sections.
Furthermore, the sequence is not correct; now, first clouds are joined, second, grasses and trees; third, rain; fourth, receiving moisture; fifth, growth.
However, the grasses and trees were originally first, while they are now in the second position.
Regarding the sequence described above: first there are grasses and trees, and only then do clouds arise and rain fall, whereby they receive moisture and grow;
in this present case, however, clouds first arise to shade the grasses and trees, and only then does the rain fall to cause them to receive moisture and grow.

Within the analogy of the clouds, there are two layers: first, comparing the Buddha’s physical form to the clouds; second, comparing the Tathāgata’s vocal teaching to the clouds. Both the Buddha’s form and his voice pervade everywhere, and both are likened to clouds.

However, within the first layer—comparing the Tathāgata’s form to the clouds—there are further two stages: the first is the direct comparison of the Tathāgata’s form to the clouds; the second, by the phrase "like a great cloud arising," employs an external analogy to provide a supplementary correspondence.

"With a great voice"—the following section constitutes the second [part], which compares the Tathāgata’s vocal teaching to clouds; this also has two layers: first, the general comparison to clouds, and second, the specific comparison to clouds.
Each of these two sections contains two parts.

Regarding the first part, which presents the general synthesis of the clouds: the first statement, "With a great voice that pervades devas, humans, and asuras," precisely presents the general sound-teaching as being like the clouds.
The second statement, from "Just like those great clouds" down to "the trichiliocosm," presents the external analogy and applies it to the teaching.

From the passage beginning with "In the midst of the great assembly he uttered these words" onwards, the second section presents the distinct vocal teachings in conjunction with the clouds; this second section also contains two parts.
There are also two parts: first, the formal presentation of the distinct teachings by name; second, the exhortation for the assembly to come and listen to the Dharma.
Within the first part, the formal presentation of the distinct teachings by name, there are six types of such teachings.
First, from the passage "In the midst of the great assembly he uttered these words" onwards, it first clarifies that the Tathāgata possesses the virtues of the ten titles.
The second section, from "causing those who have not crossed over to cross over," clarifies the virtue of the Four Great Vows.

The third section, from "knowing the present life and future lives as they truly are," clarifies the virtue of the Threefold Clarity; here, "the present life" refers to the present world, while "future lives" refers to both the past and the future worlds.
If one looks back from the present toward the past, this is the "later life";
if one turns away from the future toward the past, then that future is precisely the meaning of the "later life."
The fourth statement, "I am the omniscient one," clarifies the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Because one knows all phenomena, it is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajña); this refers to designating the wisdom by means of its object.
The fifth statement, "the one who sees all," clarifies the virtue of the five eyes.

From the sixth statement, "the one who knows the Way," onwards, it clarifies the virtue of being a guide.
