Regarding "the one who opens the way": to speak of opening the three vehicles is a provisional teaching; since the Dharma of the three vehicles is in fact the single vehicle of Dharma, it is said that he possesses the virtue of a guide.
"O you gods, humans, and asuras"—the following section is the second exhortation to come and listen to the Dharma.

From "At that time, there were countless thousands of myriads of kotis of kinds" down to "come to listen to the Dharma," this corresponds to the preceding passage on grasses and trees; above it was said, "the various herbs and trees that have grown."
"Coming to the place where the Buddha is to listen to the Dharma": what was previously presented as a metaphor is now explained according to its actual meaning.

"At that time, the Tathāgata observes these sentient beings": from this point downward is the third section, which correlates with the rain above; the previous passage spoke of "pouring down equally at one time."

Regarding the phrase "various and immeasurable," the following constitutes the fourth section, which synthesizes the aforementioned "receiving moisture. Within this synthesis, there are two parts, corresponding to the two points mentioned above. The previous statement, "according to superior, middling, and inferior," is now precisely synthesized as "various and immeasurable," which corresponds to "according to superior, middling, and inferior."
"Causing all to rejoice and swiftly obtain excellent benefit" corresponds to the preceding "each having that which they receive.

"When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma," from here below is the fifth section, which corresponds to the preceding "increase"; above it was said, "the rain from a single cloud accords with their respective natures."

Now, within this combined analogy there are two parts: the first clarifies the fruit of retribution, which is: "When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will be secure and at ease in the present life and be reborn in a good realm in future lives."
"Furthermore, they are able to hear the Dharma": the following constitutes the second section, clarifying the attainment of the fruit of cultivation.
"Like that great cloud" and below constitute the citation of an external analogy to provide a parallel application.

However, there are two ways in which the application of the analogy is received: first, the sequential and direct application; second, the application through the presentation of five external analogies, which follows below.
"Like that great cloud" refers to the application of the first analogy, that of the cloud.
"Raining upon all" corresponds to the preceding analogy of rain.
"Grasses, trees, thickets, and forests" corresponds to the second preceding point concerning grasses and trees.
"According to their respective lineages, they fully receive the moisture" corresponds to the metaphor of receiving nourishment.
"Each attains growth" corresponds to the fifth metaphor, that of increasing.

"The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor. This section below constitutes the second part, which correlates [the analogy] with the inability to know for oneself.
Within this correlation, there are five stages:
first, the presentation of the dharma that cannot be known.
Second is not knowing the correct synthesis;
third is not knowing the analysis of forms, as for example, the Tathāgata knows the analysis of all dharmas while the followers of the two vehicles do not;
fourth is citing external analogies to apply them to the synthesis.
Fifth, it returns to employing the Tathāgata’s knowledge for synthesis.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has a single characteristic and a single flavor," there are first two aspects to the dharmas that were previously unknown; this sentence establishes two topical headings (*dvāra*):
"single characteristic" refers to the topical heading of the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
"One flavor" (ekarasa) refers to the category of the conditioned (saṃskṛta).

It clarifies that the Dharma of the three vehicles taught by the Tathāgata in the past results, from beginning to end, in the same single fruit of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and the single conditioned; therefore, it is called "one characteristic and one flavor."

The second explanation first interprets the section on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through three phrases. The phrase "namely, the characteristic of liberation" (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*) directly clarifies the two kinds of unconditioned states at the point where cause and fruit are exhausted. The following two phrases explain them specifically: "the characteristic of detachment" (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*) clarifies the exhaustion of the cause, and "the characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) clarifies the disappearance of the fruit.
"Ultimately reaching all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*) explains the section on the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛtaphala*).
"If there are sentient beings who hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma"—from this point downward is the second [section], which correctly addresses how those of the two vehicles do not know for themselves.

"Why is this so? Only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings. From here below is the third section, which explains that while the Tathāgata knows their forms, the two vehicles do not. This is divided into three stages. First, "Only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings" and following, correctly clarifies that the Tathāgata knows the faculties and natures of sentient beings; this is precisely the meaning of "knowing the illness."

The second section, beginning with "What does he keep in mind," clarifies that the Tathāgata knows the dharmas required according to the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings; this is precisely the recognition of the medicine. Why is this so?

It is because, as in the case of the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth, there are various different ways of entering the Path depending on the circumstances and companions.

The third section, beginning with "Sentient beings abide in various states," again cites the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings to summarize how the Tathāgata knows their illnesses and recognizes the appropriate medicine.

Now, regarding the first point, "knowing the categories, characteristics, and essential natures of sentient beings," this clarifies that the Tathāgata knows that the lineages of the three vehicles are distinct and not the same, their manifest signs differ, their capacities for benefit and dullness are unique, and their habitual tendencies are not one and the same.

The second point, "clearly knowing the dharmas required according to the faculties and natures of sentient beings," means that the mental activities of sentient beings do not exceed the three types of wisdom; therefore, by citing these three wisdoms, it is shown that the dharmas required by them differ accordingly.

Within this, there are naturally four stages. First, the three phrases—“What should one contemplate? What should one reflect upon? What should one cultivate?”—clearly demonstrate that the required objects of focus differ and the ways of entering the Path vary accordingly.
The second section, "What is mindfulness? What is reflection? What is cultivation?"—these three phrases arise from the differences in the methods of practice currently employed by sentient beings.

The third section, consisting of the three phrases—"by what dharma does one mindfully attend, by what dharma does one contemplate, and by what dharma does one cultivate"—clarifies that the past causes of practitioners in the present are not identical.
The fourth section, "By what dharma one obtains what dharma," consists of these two phrases which clarify that for a practitioner of the present, the future fruit is also indeterminate.
When composing this well, [one asks]: by means of what dharma of mindfulness does one obtain what dharma?
By means of what dharma does one contemplate to obtain what dharma?
By means of what dharma does one cultivate to obtain what dharma?
Although the phrasing is brief, the meaning may be inferred.

The passage beginning with “Sentient beings abide in various states” constitutes the third section, which summarizes how the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the illness and his recognition of the medicine are clear and unimpeded.

The section beginning with “Just as those herbs, trees, and forests” combines the fourth illustration from the analogy of not knowing oneself—the illustration of not knowing external things—and applies it to the present context.
“The Tathāgata knows this single characteristic. This section below constitutes the fifth [part], which cites the Tathāgata’s knowledge as the synthesis.

“You, Kāśyapa, are truly rare. This section below is the third, the formal exposition of the fulfillment; having attained understanding today, one has fully realized the opening of the three to reveal the one. However, this text is abbreviated and speaks only of the opening of the provisional.
Within this third section there are also two parts: first, the formal exposition of the understanding of the provisional; second, from "Why is this so? onwards, the explanation.

"And he spoke in verse," meaning that this chapter consists of two sections: the prose and the verse as the second. From here on, there are fifty-four and a half lines of verse, which constitute the second round of versification.

However, in the original prose section above, there were two parts: first, from the beginning of the chapter until the passage "whatever is spoken is not in vain," which first clarifies the formal confirmation (*anumodanā*) wherein the four great śrāvakas praise the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay. This portion is not versified here; the reason it is not versified is that while praising the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay is the primary intent of the formal confirmation and understanding (*anumodanā-parijñā*), this secondary meaning [of the śrāvakas’ own realization] is incidental, and for this reason it is omitted from the verses. Only the second part—the formal confirmation and understanding itself—is versified.

However, within the second section, which correctly describes the accomplishment of the realization of understanding, there are originally three parts. The first part, from "By means of wisdom and skillful means regarding all dharmas" up to "manifesting all wisdom to all sentient beings," intends to accomplish the description of the realization of understanding; first, it sets forth the dharmas that were realized.

The second section, from "For example, like the trichiliocosm" down to "therefore he did not immediately preach it," is titled "Clarifying the Lack of Understanding in the Past to Contrast with the Attainment of Understanding Today."
The third section, beginning with “O Kāśyapa, you are truly rare,” precisely describes the realization attained today.
This passage of fifty-four and a half lines is also divided into three parts: first, there are four lines of verse which praise the first [section], the Dharma that has been realized;
second, from “Kāśyapa, you should know it is like a great cloud” onwards, there are forty-seven lines of verse which praise the second [section], the former lack of understanding.

The third section, beginning with “Kāśyapa, you should know that by means of various causes and conditions,” consists of three and a half lines of verse. This constitutes the third part, which correctly explains and confirms the realization.

Regarding the first part above, where the fundamental dharma realized is presented, there are two sections: the first has two lines that open two topical gates, and the second provides an explanation of those topical gates.
These four lines of verse are also divided into two parts: the first two lines open the thematic gates, and the second two lines provide the second explanation of those thematic gates.

Within the former two verses, the first verse corresponds to the thematic gate of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and the latter verse corresponds to the thematic gate of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

Now, this single verse beginning with "Is there perhaps a Dharma King? eulogizes the preceding statement, "He expounds all dharmas through wisdom and skillful means," which is precisely the opening of the gate of skillful means.
Now, when it says "the Dharma King who destroys existence," it refers to the Dharma King who destroys the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
"In accordance with the desires of sentient beings" means in accordance with the desires of the capacities and natures of the three vehicles.

This verse, "The Tathāgata holds it in high esteem," praises the preceding section on the chapter of True Wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Previously, it was stated that "the Dharma he teaches all reaches the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

Now, it is said that "the Tathāgata holds wisdom in high esteem, profound and far-reaching"; for a long time he has remained silent regarding this essential point of ultimate convergence, not being intent on expounding it hastily.
The two verses beginning with "If those with wisdom hear" eulogize the second section above, which explains the two chapter-gates.
The first verse eulogizes the explanation of the gate of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and the latter verse eulogizes the explanation of the gate of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

In the preceding explanation of provisional and ultimate wisdom, there were originally two phrases; the first stated, "The Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation is that to which all dharmas converge. This refers to the dharma of consciousness, wherein one knows that the various dharmas of the three vehicles converge in the One Vehicle. This is not recited here.

Furthermore, it is said: "He also knows the practices of the deep minds of all sentient beings, penetrating them without obstruction. This refers to the wondrous discernment of the faculties and natures of those of the three vehicles; now, this single line of verse celebrates this very point.
"Therefore, Kāśyapa, he teaches according to his capacity"—this verse praises the preceding explanation of ultimate wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).

Within that preceding explanation of ultimate wisdom, there were originally two lines; the first, "Furthermore, he thoroughly understands all phenomena," concerns the meaning of identifying the medicine for the afflictions and is not praised here.
The subsequent statement, "to reveal all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings," is now being versified by this single verse alone.

From the words "Kāśyapa, you should know" below, there are forty-seven lines which constitute the second section; this specifically versifies the second point mentioned above: that [the disciples] did not understand in the past.
In the preceding prose section, there were originally two parts: first, the opening of the analogy (*upamā*), and second, the application of the analogy (*upanaya*).

Now, within these forty-seven lines of verse, they are likewise divided into two: the first ten and a half verses constitute the opening of the analogy, and the second part, beginning with "The Buddha is also like this," consists of thirty-six and a half verses that constitute the application of the analogy.
The preceding opening analogy consisted of two parts: first, the analogy of receiving moisture and growing; second, the illustration of not knowing it for oneself.

Now, proceeding with the ten verses and a half, these are likewise divided into two: the first nine and a half verses in verse form illustrate receiving moisture and growing, while the final one verse illustrates not knowing it for oneself.

However, regarding the increase through receiving the moisture as explained above, there are originally three elements: first, that which receives; second, that which is received; and third, the actual clarification of the increase through receiving the moisture.
Now, these nine and a half stanzas are also divided into three parts, though they do not follow the sequential order.
First, there are four stanzas which transcend [the standard sequence] and correspond to what is received in the second [section].
The second section consists of two and a half lines, which again returns to verse the first [section] concerning the recipient of the teaching.
The third section consists of three lines, which verse the third [section] that correctly clarifies the receiving of grace and its increase.
However, regarding what was received above, the analogy of clouds and rain serves as the basis for both the beginning and the end;
first, there is one verse concerning the clouds, followed by one verse concerning the rain, which begins with "That rain is universally equal."

The analogy of the rain-cloud above illustrates two matters: form and sound. Now, the three lines of verse are likewise divided into two parts: the first line of verse praises the analogy of the cloud of form;
the subsequent two lines, beginning with "The cloud of wisdom contains moisture," praise the analogy of the cloud of sound.

Within these two lines, the first line is the actual verse that uses the metaphor of clouds; the second line, "The sunlight is obscured," is the second meaning, clarifying the characteristics of the rain-bearing clouds, which itself contains three points. First, regarding the phrase "The sunlight is obscured": this one clause intends to clarify that before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, non-Buddhists used false teachings to transform people, like the sunlight in a drought-stricken sky.

Now, it is explained that when the dense clouds of darkness disperse, the sunlight immediately appears; internally, this corresponds to the time when the Tathāgata of Radiance appeared in the world. Although he had not yet proclaimed his verbal teachings, the heterodoxies and false doctrines were thereby utterly extinguished.

Next, the statement "the ground above is cool and refreshing" constitutes the second meaning. Since the dense clouds have spread everywhere and the ground above is cool and refreshing, this clarifies that among sentient beings, there are none who do not rejoice upon beholding the Tathāgata.

The two lines following "Massing and hanging down" constitute the third meaning: upon first beholding these clouds, they appear like mountains or stones, yet ultimately they cannot be grasped or seized by hand. This internally corresponds to the fact that although the Tathāgata’s form appears identical to the body of an ordinary person, when sought through the truth of wisdom, the Buddha-body is none other than the Dharma-body.
Form is itself formless, and sound is itself soundless.
"Its rain is universally equal"—this line of verse refers to the rain mentioned above, which states that "at one time it pours equally, its moisture universally soaking all."
"Mountains, rivers, and steep valleys"—the following two and a half lines again praise the first category, the "recipient.
Within the recipients, there are originally two parts; the first is the recipient as the physical land itself, which is now first praised with this half-line.
Second, that which correctly emerges and is able to receive [the moisture] refers to the three types of grasses and two types of trees; the remaining two lines now generally summarize this.
"That which is emitted by the clouds"—the following three lines summarize the aforementioned correct reception of the moisture and subsequent growth.
The superior [roots] correctly receive the moisture; herein, there are fundamentally two aspects: first, receiving the moisture, and second, increasing.
Now, regarding these three lines of verse, the first line praises the receiving of moisture, while the latter two lines praise the increase.
The first section on "receiving moisture" originally consists of two parts: first, the cause by which moisture is received; second, the explicit explanation of the meaning of receiving moisture.
Now, within this single line, the half-line beginning with "That which the clouds produce" first versifies the cause by which moisture is received;
the subsequent half-line then directly versifies the aforementioned reception of moisture.
In the section on "Increasing" (*vṛddhi*), there are originally two parts: first, the explicit explanation of increasing; second, the explanation of the characteristics of increasing.
Now, within these two lines, the first line—“All trees, superior, middling, and inferior, etc.”—is the direct verse that praises the aforementioned increasing.
The line "roots, stems, branches, and leaves" summarizes the characteristics of growth mentioned above.
The line beginning with "according to their essential nature and appearance" constitutes the second verse, which summarizes the analogy of being unaware of oneself.
The preceding section contains two parts concerning the middle [truth]: first, not knowing the cause by which one comes to be; second, the explicit clarification of this lack of self-knowledge.
This present single verse summarizes both of these points.
"The Buddha is also like this. From here below, there are thirty-six lines and a half of verse which summarize the preceding analogies.
Within these thirty-six lines and a half, there are also two sections: the first consists of thirty-five lines, summarizing the analogy of receiving moisture and growing;
the latter one line and a half summarizes the analogy of not knowing it for oneself.
The preceding section on "harmonizing through analogy" is divided into two parts: first, the sequential and distinct harmonization; second, the application of external analogies for harmonization.
Here, we do not recite the application of analogies, but only the preceding sequential and distinct harmonization.

In the preceding section on the sequential and combined analogies, five points were further distinguished: first, the combination of clouds; second, the combination of grasses and trees; third, the combination of rain; fourth, the combination of receiving moisture; and fifth, the combination of growth. Now, we shall again follow the three sections established in the sequential analogies and proceed according to the order of the combined analogies.
Now, regarding these thirty-five lines: the first consists of thirteen and a half lines, which summarize the content received;
the second consists of two lines, which summarize the recipient of the teaching;
and the third consists of nineteen and a half lines, which summarize the actual reception and the increase of its benefit.
Now, these thirteen and a half lines are divided into two parts: the first seven and a half lines correspond to the simile of the clouds;
the second six lines correspond to the simile of the rain.
Now, first, the verse correlates this with the simile of clouds.
In the preceding prose correlation, there are two parts: first, correlating the physical form with clouds; second, correlating the sound with clouds.
Within these current seven lines and a half of verse, the first line correlates the physical form, while the subsequent six lines and a half correlate the sound.

Regarding the "raising of the form" (*ākāra-udgraha*) within the middle [section], there are two parts: first, the formal raising of the form; second, the application of an external analogy as a corroboration (*pratisaṃyoga*).
Now, the latter half of the verse, "The Buddha is also like this," constitutes the formal corroboration, while the subsequent half-verse presents an external analogy as a corroboration.
Regarding the phrase "having already appeared in the world," there follow six and a half lines of verse which illustrate the correspondence between the sounds [of the teaching] and the clouds.
Within the preceding section on the correspondence of sounds, there are two parts: first, the correspondence of the general sound-teaching; second, the correspondence of the specific sound-teachings.
Now, of these six and a half lines, the first line corresponds to the first [section], and the remaining five and a half lines correspond to the second.

Above, the general sound-teaching was raised for correspondence, which contains two parts: first, the formal raising of the general sound-correspondence; second, the raising of an external analogy as a supplementary correspondence.
Now, regarding this single line, "Having already appeared in the world," it only praises the primary correspondence and omits the secondary correspondence.

Above, in citing the specific scriptural teachings within the section on correspondence, there are two parts: first, the actual citation of the specific scriptural correspondence; second, the exhortation for the assembly to come and listen.

Within these five and a half verses there are also two parts: the first three and a half verses directly praise the presentation of the distinct sounds combined; the subsequent two verses praise the exhortation to listen to their combination.

However, when one mentions the specific term "Buddha" within the context of sound, it inherently possesses six kinds of virtues that are integrated with that sound. Now, within these three and a half lines of verse, the first two lines following the phrase "Great Sage, World-Honored One" eulogize the virtues of the ten titles.
Next, the one and a half lines beginning with "Pervading and moistening all" eulogize the virtues of the four great vows;
the remaining four virtues are omitted from this eulogy.
The two lines beginning with "The assembly of devas and humans" constitute the second exhortation to come and listen to the Dharma within the combined and separate verses.

The six lines beginning with "For the sake of the great assembly" correspond to the preceding analogy of rain and are divided into four sections: the first two lines directly correspond to the analogy of rain; the next two and a half lines, beginning with "I observe all," clarify the equality of the mind; the following single line, beginning with "Constantly expounding the Dharma," clarifies the absence of weariness; and the final half-line, beginning with "Satisfying the world," provides an external analogy as a corroboration.
The two lines beginning with "Noble and base, high and low" constitute the second [section], which combines the verse with the analogy of those who receive instruction.
The nineteen and a half lines beginning with "All sentient beings who hear my Dharma" constitute the third [section], which combines the verse with the growth resulting from receiving nourishment.

Within these nineteen and a half lines, the text is divided into two parts: the first eleven lines of verse correspond to the section on "receiving nourishment," while the latter eight and a half lines correspond to the section on "growth.

Within the eleven lines, they are further divided into five segments. First, the second half-line beginning with "All sentient beings" corresponds to the various immeasurable phrases; that is, it corresponds to the section on sentient beings who receive nourishment.
Next, the second half of the line beginning with "according to their capacity" (*yathābala*) correctly praises the harmonious reception of moisture.

Next, the seven lines beginning with "or dwelling among humans or devas" extensively cite the three types of grasses and two types of trees to clarify that sentient beings differ in how they receive this moisture.

Next, the one and a half lines beginning with "The Buddha’s impartial teaching" clarify that while the Buddha’s mind is impartial, the moisture received by sentient beings differs according to their own capacities.
Next, the one and a half lines beginning with "The Buddha uses this analogy" clarify that this is an illustration of only a small portion [of the truth].

Now, returning to the extensive exposition of the three types of grass and two types of trees within the seven modes of practice: the first four lines clarify the three types of grass, while the latter three lines clarify the two types of trees.

Regarding the four lines that clarify the three types of grass: the line beginning with “In some places, humans, devas, and wheel-turning sage-kings” clarifies that humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles constitute the small grass.
The two lines beginning with "Knowing the untainted dharmas" clarify that the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas constitute the middle and inferior grasses.

The line beginning with "Seeking the state of the World-Honored One" clarifies that the external ordinary beings and the bodhisattvas who practice the six perfections in a partial manner constitute the superior grasses.

Regarding the three lines clarifying the two types of trees: the first one and a half lines beginning with "There are some sons of the Buddha" clarify that the bodhisattvas at the stage of inner ordinary beings (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*) are small trees.

The next one and a half lines beginning with "Abiding securely in supernatural powers" (*abhijñā*) clarify that the bodhisattvas in the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*) from the stage of constant abiding (*sadāsthita*) upward are great trees.
"I rain down the rain of Dharma. From here, the following eight lines and a half constitute the verse on "concordant increase" (*anurūpa-vardhana*).
This is divided into four sections: the first line is a brief verse on concordance;
the second line presents an external analogy to illustrate the concordance.
The third [section] consists of one and a half lines of verse, which combines the parable;
the fourth consists of five lines, which combine the parable according to the five types of persons.
Within the first line, there are two parts: the first three lines beginning with "I rain down the rain of Dharma" combine the parable regarding the cause of growth.
The next line correctly praises the increase.

"Just as that forest" and the following line constitute the second section, which cites an external analogy and applies it to the teaching; this also has two parts. First, the three lines beginning with "Just as that forest" cite the essential nature of the increase, which is the phrase "according to their lineage."
The next line also praises "increase.
From the words "The Dharma of all Buddhas" below, there is one and a half lines; this is the third, which extensively praises the "conformity.

The first three lines directly praise the phrase "one characteristic and one flavor"; the next line praises the phrase "swiftly obtaining excellent benefit"; and the following two lines praise the phrase "being born in a good realm in future lives."
Regarding the passage "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas," there are five lines below this that extensively enumerate the five classes of people to clarify their growth, though it is not complete.
First, the one and a half lines beginning with "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" initially present the followers of the two vehicles, who are the medium-sized medicinal herbs.
Next, the one and a half lines beginning with "If there are bodhisattvas" that emerge from the small trees refer to bodhisattvas at the stage of the foremost of faith (*śraddhā-adhimukta*) and above.

Next, the two lines beginning with "Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna and have attained supernatural powers" that emerge from the large trees refer to bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi (*prathamā-bhūmi*) and above.
"Thus, Kāśyapa"—this following one and a half lines constitutes the second verse, which combines [the preceding] with the analogy of not knowing oneself.
"Kāśyapa, you should know"—this following three and a half lines constitute the third section at the end of the prose, which confirms the understanding of the present day.

The above has already explained the provisional (open the provisional); the explanation of the manifestation of the one (reveal the real) is omitted for brevity. Since the opening of the provisional has been described, the revelation of the real is naturally evident.

Now, this verse extends further to clarify the meaning of revealing the real: the first two and a half lines directly versify the aforementioned opening of the provisional, while the subsequent line extends the explanation of revealing the real.

However, within the aforementioned exposition of the provisional (*upāya*), there are two parts: first, the formal description of the interpretation that reveals the provisional; second, the explanation.
Now, these one and a half lines of verse only recite the formal descriptive portion and do not recite the explanatory portion.

Chapter Six: The Chapter on Bestowing Predictions (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta).
In this chapter, predictions regarding their future fruition are bestowed upon four individuals; thus, it serves as the title of the chapter.

If one speaks of "receiving" a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), the meaning pertains to the bodhisattva; if one speaks of "bestowing" a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), the meaning concerns the Tathāgata. Thus, "receiving" carries the sense of taking, while "bestowing" carries the sense of giving.
There are, however, two kinds of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): first, that which predicts, and second, that which is predicted.

That which predicts is the Tathāgata’s verbal teaching, which is the very essence of prediction; that which is predicted refers to the future fruit of Buddhahood and the names of the lands of the Bodhisattvas, which are also called "prediction" because they receive their name from another [source].

However, in the parable that opens up the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle, there are originally four grades among those of middle capacity; these constitute four sections. Now, this following section is the fourth, which bestows a prediction of enlightenment upon those of middle capacity.

Furthermore, the previous commentary explained that within the four sections, each is divided into two parts. Now, regarding these two parts within the section on the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*): the first is the actual bestowal of predictions upon these four great disciples; the second, the single verse at the end of the chapter, further grants permission to explain the principle of the common destination for those of inferior faculties.

Within the section on the formal conferral of predictions, there are three parts: first, the initial prediction conferred upon Mahākāśyapa; second, the subsequent predictions conferred upon three other śrāvakas; and third, the general predictions conferred upon five hundred disciples.
"At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana... From here below is the second section, which further bestows predictions upon three śrāvakas.
Because they had specifically requested them, this is treated as a separate section.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the request for a prediction from the three śrāvakas, including Maudgalyāyana; second, the Tathāgata bestowing predictions upon each of the three individuals, which constitutes three stages.
" My disciples are endowed with majestic power"—the following one and a half lines constitute the third section, which bestows predictions upon five hundred disciples.
"I and you all"—this single line is the second section within this chapter, which is the promise to teach those of inferior faculties.

Chapter Seven: The Parable of the City of Illusion. This seventh chapter, "The Parable of the City of Illusion," clarifies the third section within the causal stage—the extensive exposition on opening up the three vehicles to reveal the one vehicle. It consists of three internal sections, which correspond to the transformation of those with the three types of faculties into three stages.

From here until the end of the "Chapter on the Prediction for Those in Training and Those Beyond Training," there are three sūtras. This third section clarifies the causes and conditions of past lives to explain the principle of revealing the One by opening the Three, thereby transforming those of inferior faculties.

However, among those of superior and middling faculties, there are respectively four sections each; now, if this transformation for those of inferior faculties were to follow the preceding examples, it should likewise have four sections. Yet, as the meanings follow one another, there are only three points: first, the existence of past-life causes and conditions; second, the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); and third, the comprehension and realization—there being no section on "reiteration and confirmation" (*anumodana*).
Although there are three meanings, there are only two sections.
How is this known?

In the section on "Receiving Understanding and Entering the Prediction," since the prose and verses are already integrated and straightforward, they are clearly divided into two parts: first, this "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter correctly clarifies the causes and conditions of past lives to teach those of inferior faculties; second, the remaining two chapters bestow predictions upon those of inferior faculties.

The general meaning is this: I have already previously, at the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, when I was among the number of the sixteen princes, expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for you; now I am expounding it for you once again. Why is it that you do not understand it after hearing it three times?

Therefore, the text of the subsequent sutra states: "I was among those sixteen and have previously taught this for you; by virtue of these fundamental causes and conditions, I now preach the Lotus Sutra. However, those of inferior capacity cling to this, merely hearing these accounts of past causes and conditions and taking them as their mutual understanding and realization.

Within this chapter, the text is broadly divided into two sections. The first, from the beginning of the prose up to the end of the verses, clarifies how the Buddha’s wisdom can perceive events of the distant past.
The second, from "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus" at the start of the prose down to the end of the verses, correctly elucidates the explanation of causes and conditions from previous lives.
Furthermore, within these two sections, each contains two layers, both consisting of prose and verse as the two layers.
Now, regarding the preceding prose section which clarifies how the Buddha’s wisdom can perceive events from the distant past, there are three stages therein:
first, an account of the events of the past, namely those of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
The second section, from "Monks, since that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa" onwards, uses the three-thousandfold world system as ink to provide a metaphor for the vastness of remote antiquity.

The third statement, "By the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I observe that which is remote as if it were today," precisely clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to perceive events from the distant past.
"And he spoke in verse," from here below is the second section, the verses. In the preceding prose, there were three parts; now these seven lines of verse are likewise divided into three:
the first verse praises the first [section].

The second section, beginning with "As if a person were to grind the three thousandfold world-system with their strength," consists of four lines; this verse summarizes the second preceding analogy concerning the vast duration of time.

The third section, beginning with "The Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom knows that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa," consists of two lines of verse; it praises the preceding third point by clearly demonstrating that the Tathāgata’s wisdom can perceive past events.

"The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus"—from this point down to the end of the chapter constitutes the second section, which correctly elucidates the causes and conditions of past lives. This section also has two layers, namely, the prose and the verses, which form the two parts.
Within this extended narrative, there are naturally two stages:

first, from here down to the passage "abiding in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas," the text first clarifies the causes and conditions for establishing a karmic connection in the past.

The second section, from "At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration" through the end of the prose narrative, correctly elucidates the forming of karmic conditions.
Furthermore, within these two stages, there are two parts each.

Regarding the causes for establishing a karmic connection (*karmapratyaya*), there are two: first, from this point down to the passage "The Brahmās of the ten directions requested the turning of the wheel of Dharma," the text first clarifies the distant origins of the establishment of connections in the past.

The second section, from "The Greatly Penetrating Buddha accepted the invitation of the Brahma Kings" up to "entering meditative concentration," clarifies the proximate causes for establishing karmic connections in the past.
Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions for establishing this karmic connection (*kalyāṇamitra*), there are four stages within each of the two levels.

Now, concerning the first level, the four stages of the remote causes for establishing the connection are as follows: first, clarifying how the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū practiced the path and attained Buddhahood; second, clarifying how the sixteen princes requested him to turn the wheel of the Dharma; third, clarifying the signs of the supernatural manifestations that moved others after the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained Buddhahood; and fourth, clarifying how the Brahmās of the ten directions requested him to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, within each of these four distinct sections, there are three specific differences.

Regarding the first, which clarifies the three differences in how the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū practiced the path and attained Buddhahood: first, it clarifies the nature of the difficulty of attaining the Buddha-way as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū practiced that path;

second, from the passage "At that time, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" onwards, this clarifies how the various devas constantly made offerings during the interval before Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained Buddhahood.

Third, from the passage "The bhikṣus, after ten intermediate kalpas had passed since the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... onwards, this correctly clarifies that the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained the Way of the Buddha; these three distinct elements combined constitute the remote conditions.
Among the four stages, the first clarifies how the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū practiced the Way and attained Buddhahood.
"Before that Buddha had left the household life" marks the beginning of the second stage: the sixteen princes requesting him to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Among these, there are also three stages: first, it clarifies how the princes came to the Buddha’s presence for the purpose of making a request;
second, from “Having arrived, they prostrated themselves at his feet” onwards, it clarifies that once they had reached the Buddha’s presence, they performed offerings through the three karmas;

third, from “At that time, the sixteen princes, having praised the Buddha with verses, exhorted the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma” onwards, it properly clarifies the princes’ request for the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
These three sections taken together constitute the distant cause; specifically, the second stage clarifies how the prince requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma.

From the passage "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus" onwards is the third section, clarifying the signs of the supernatural manifestations that moved others after the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained Buddhahood.
Within this, there are also three stages:
first, clarifying how the Buddha’s supernormal powers cause the earth to tremble;
second, from the passage "In the midst of that land, in places of darkness and obscurity" onwards, clarifying the manifestation of the universal radiance of light.
The third section, beginning with "Furthermore, as for that realm," clarifies how the two signs—the Buddha’s light and its movement—reach as far as the celestial palaces.
The fourth section, beginning with "At that time, in the eastern direction," clarifies how the Brahmās of the ten directions entreat the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Within this, there are also three parts: first, it clarifies how the Brahmās of the two directions—the east and the southeast—request the turning of the wheel of the Hīnayāna;
second, from the south down to the nadir, the Brahmās of seven directions request the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Mahāyāna;
third, it clarifies how the Brahmās of the single direction above collectively request the turning of the wheels of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Regarding the first section, the invitation by the Brahmās of the eastern and southeastern directions, there are two parts:
first, the invitation by the Brahmās of the eastern direction; second, the invitation by the Brahmās of the southeastern direction.
Regarding the various Brahmās in one direction, there are generally seven points:
first, to clarify how the light of that Buddha shines upon them and causes them wonder;
second, to clarify their collective deliberation on the reason for this light.
The third clarifies that among the various Brahmā assemblies, there were those who were intelligent and thus provided a grand interpretation of the meaning of the light;
the fourth clarifies that the various Brahmās and others followed the light to the Buddha’s dwelling;
the fifth clarifies that once the various Brahmās had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they paid homage through the three karmas.
The sixth [section] clearly explains the request for the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma;
the seventh clarifies that the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
The same seven points apply to the Brahmās from the southeast as well.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣus in the south... This section below constitutes the second part, clarifying how the Brahmās of the seven directions requested the turning of the Great Vehicle Dharma-wheel. This also has two sections: first, a detailed explanation of the seven meanings concerning the Brahmās in the south;
second, from the southwest onwards, a general reference to the six directions, which is applied identically to the south.

"At that time, from above" marks the third section below, which clarifies how the various Brahmās from the upper realms collectively requested the turning of the Dharma wheels of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. This section contains only six points; the seventh point—the Tathāgata’s silent assent—is absent.

Why is this? At that time, the invitation had already been completed, yet the Buddha still accepted the invitation to preach the Dharma; therefore, there was no need for him to grant permission through silence.

However, within the two verses of the sixth request for the preaching of the Dharma, the former verse requests the teaching of the Hīnayāna, while the latter verse requests the turning of the Mahāyāna wheel of Dharma.
Within these four stages, there are three layers each; together, these constitute the distant causes for establishing karmic connections.

"At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted [the offerings] from the Brahma Kings of the ten directions"—from here below is the second section, clarifying the proximate causes for establishing karmic connections in the past.
Within this, there are also four stages:
first, it clarifies how the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahmās and turned the wheel of Dharma for the followers of the two vehicles;
second, it clarifies how the sixteen princes at that time requested the Buddha to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The third [section] clarifies how the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the princes' invitation to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;

the fourth clarifies that after preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū again entered meditative concentration and withdrew from his seat as the reason for delivering a "re-exposition" (*puna-vyākhyāna*), for if he had not entered meditative concentration, how could there have been a re-exposition?
Furthermore, within these four stages, there are three layers each.

Regarding the first stage—receiving the invitation from the Brahmās of the ten directions to preach the Dharma wheel of the Two Vehicles—there are three layers: first, the initial acceptance of the invitation;
second, the section beginning with "At that time, the three turnings," which enumerates the characteristics of the Dharma wheel of the Two Vehicles.

Third, from the passage "When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans," the following describes the signs of realization experienced by the assembly at that time.

Regarding the second section, which lists the two wheels of Dharma for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas: first, the Four Noble Truths are presented; subsequently, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are presented. Within each of these two wheels of Dharma, there are two enumerations of the Four Noble Truths.
Second, the first [enumeration] generally clarifies the three turnings and twelve aspects, namely: showing, encouraging, and realizing.
The second section, beginning with "That which is called suffering," separately sets forth the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the second point, the listing of the twelve links of dependent origination, the first part, from "and the detailed exposition of the twelve links of dependent origination" onwards, clarifies the forward-order explanation (*anuloma*), while the second part, from "because ignorance ceases" onwards, clarifies the reverse-order explanation (*pratiloma*).

"At that time, the sixteen princes all left home as youths"—the following section constitutes the second part, clarifying how the princes at that time requested the Buddha to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Within this, there are also three stages: first, it clarifies that the sixteen princes left home for the purpose of making the request;
second, from "They all addressed the Buddha, saying" onwards, they formally request the Buddha to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
third, with the words "At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King," it clarifies that the king and his retinue also left home.

“At that time, that Buddha accepted the request of the śrāmaṇeras. Below this is the third section, which clarifies how the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, having accepted the request of the princes, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This also consists of three parts: first, it properly clarifies that the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the princes’ request to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
second, from the passage “Having preached this sūtra,” it clarifies the differences in realization among the assembly at that time;

third, the repeated statement “The Buddha preached this sūtra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing” clarifies that the duration of the preaching of this sūtra lasted for such a number of kalpas.

"Having spoken this sutra"—the following section constitutes the fourth stage of the proximate causes. It clarifies that after the Tathāgata had finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Because the Prince delivered a recitation based on the Buddha’s entry into absorption, there are likewise three stages: first, "having spoken this sutra, he immediately entered his quiet chamber," which first clarifies the signs of entering absorption;
second, "abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*)," which properly clarifies his remaining in absorption;
third, "eighty-four thousand *kalpas*," which clarifies the duration of the Buddha’s stay in absorption measured in *kalpas*.

From the beginning of this chapter up to this point, the first section within the prose narrative—the explanation of the causes and conditions for establishing a karmic connection in the past—is concluded.

From the passage "At that time, the sixteen bodhisattvas knew that the Buddha had entered his room" onwards, the second section of the prose narrative—the formal explanation of the establishment of the karmic connection—is completed.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the discourse on the Dharma (dharmadeśanā), and second, the discourse through parables (aupamyadeśanā).
Within the first, the discourse on the Dharma, there are three stages:
first, the formal clarification of the establishment of karmic conditions in the past; it then proceeds to state that today, at their third meeting, he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The second section clarifies the general purport of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s teachings from the beginning to the end, spanning from the time after he had established karmic connections with sentient beings until the present moment of our meeting.
Furthermore, within each of these three stages, there are four successive layers.
The first section, "Correctly Clarifying the Establishment of Connections in the Past," consists of four parts.

First, the passage beginning with "At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration" clarifies the intention behind the princes' ability to deliver the secondary exposition; this was solely because the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had entered his room for eighty-four thousand kalpas, and at that time, the Dharma seat could not be left empty.
Therefore, the second part, from "Each ascended to the Dharma seat" onwards, correctly clarifies the secondary exposition itself.
The third section, "Each and every one was delivered," and those following, clarify the extent to which the audience attained awakening during the previous lecture;
the fourth clarifies that after eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū emerged from meditative concentration and praised the princes.

From "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus" onwards, the second section summarizes the general purport of the teaching from beginning to end; it also consists of four parts. First, from "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: these sixteen bodhisattvas constantly delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*" onwards, it correctly clarifies that after establishing the conditions for future connection in the past, they have constantly encountered one another until their meeting today.
Second, from "Bhikṣus, I now tell you" onwards, it clarifies that the sixteen princes, who were previously taught in secret, have already manifested the realization of Buddhahood.
Third, from "At that time, those who were converted" onwards, it harmonizes and connects the past with the present.

The fourth section, from "After my parinirvāṇa" onwards, clarifies that those who encounter [the teaching] today but do not understand it will eventually meet it in future lives; this elucidates the principle that a karmic bond formed on a single day remains indestructible throughout kalpas.
"O bhikṣus, if the Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived"—the following section clarifies the third stage, namely the meeting with him today.
Within this, there should also be four layers; however, the text contains only three, omitting the third layer, which may also be due to an error by the transmitter.
Although it was not present [in the original], its meaning emerges today. How do we know this?
Because it exists within the subsequent analogy.
Now, regarding the fourfold structure of this profound work:

first, from the passage beginning with "The bhikṣus" up to "entering deeply into meditative concentration," it first clarifies how the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened within sentient beings;
second, it concerns the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Third, it clarifies that [the Buddha] was unable to accommodate them through the Mahāyāna; this is precisely what constitutes the emergence of the present meaning.
Fourth, he preached the Hīnayāna for them.

Now, first, it clarifies the arousal of the Mahāyāna capacity (*gotra*): when it says, "O Bhikṣus, if the Tathāgata knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived," since the teaching of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was not far removed from the time the Tathāgata preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the Mahāyāna capacity had already been aroused while he was still preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he therefore said, "the time for parinirvāṇa has arrived."
Furthermore, another interpretation states:

When the capacity for the Mahāyāna is about to be awakened, the Tathāgata’s transformative work through the three vehicles is on the verge of ceasing; therefore, it is said that "the time for nirvāṇa has arrived.
As for the phrase "the assembly is again pure," this specifically clarifies that the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened.

If the five turbidities of the past had obstructed the capacity for the Mahāyāna, that capacity would not be pure; however, when the capacity for the Mahāyāna arises such that the five turbidities no longer act as obstructions, this is called purity.

Regarding "firmness in resolute belief" (*adhimukti*): although one may have had faith in the past, it was not yet perfected; now, the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened, giving rise to Mahāyāna faith.

When the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened today, there arises Mahāyāna understanding (*adhimokṣa*); this understanding is wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, faith, wisdom, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) mutually support one another, and by this power, the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened.
"Thoroughly comprehending the dharma of emptiness" clarifies that the dharma of signlessness from the past is what is meant by "thoroughly comprehending the dharma of emptiness.

"He then assembled all the bodhisattvas"—the following section constitutes the second part, the formal exposition of the Mahāyāna, namely the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. "He then assembled all the bodhisattvas" signifies that at that time the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly.
The statement, "In the world there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction (nirvāṇa)," is the opening of the door of skillful means.
The statement, "Only by the single Buddha-vehicle does one attain extinction," is the revealing of the true reality.

Below this, there should have been a third application [of the analogy] using the Mahāyāna to illustrate that it is impossible to transform sentient beings; however, now it is cryptically presented as being applicable to what follows. What follows constitutes the basis for the analogy of indolence and regression.
"Monks, you should know the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means. This section below is the fourth, clarifying how the Tathāgata uses the three vehicles to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Regarding this fourth section on converting sentient beings through the teaching of the *Hīnayāna*, there are four passages within it.
The first states, "The Tathāgata’s power of skillful means penetrates deeply into the nature of sentient beings," which first clarifies the provisional application of the three vehicles.

The second statement, "knowing that their aspirations and inclinations lie in the lesser Dharma and that they are deeply attached to the five desires," clarifies that the Tathāgata perceives those with the capacities of the Hīnayāna.
"For their sake, he speaks of nirvāṇa" constitutes the third [point]: correctly teaching the doctrine of the three vehicles for the sake of sentient beings.
The fourth statement says, "If this person hears it, they will immediately believe and accept it. This clarifies that those of the three vehicles receive and practice [the teaching].
The questioner asks:

"In the 'Burning House' parable, it was shown that the Mahāyāna transformation could not be achieved; only after that were the transformations of the three vehicles successful. Subsequently, the capacity for the Mahāyāna was aroused, and at the time that capacity was aroused, the Mahāyāna was preached."

"Now for what reason is there no Mahāyāna capacity [for them] such that a Great Sūtra is preached for them, yet subsequently they do not receive the Mahāyāna transformation while receiving the Hīnayāna transformation?
The commentator says: "This meaning is so because of the correspondence between causes and conditions of the past and the present."
In the past, when I was one of the sixteen princes, I already knew that you possessed the capacity for the Mahāyāna, so I immediately gave a supplementary lecture on the Mahāyāna for your sake.

At that time, you had already attained an understanding of the Mahāyāna as a causal condition; today, as your Mahāyāna capacity has been awakened, I have accordingly preached this Mahāyāna sūtra for you, and you must not fail to believe it.

Regarding the sequential arrangement within the burning house: at the beginning of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, he originally intended to preach the Mahāyāna sūtras; however, at that time there were no beings with the capacity for the Mahāyāna. Since I could not effect their transformation by employing the Mahāyāna as appropriate, and it was not permissible to let these sentient beings sink forever into long-term suffering, the Tathāgata therefore used the three vehicles to teach and gather in sentient beings. Only when the capacity for the Mahāyāna later arose did he then preach the Mahāyāna sūtras.

In the subsequent parable, it again follows the original sequence: those who cannot be transformed by the Mahāyāna can be transformed by the three vehicles; subsequently, when the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened, the Mahāyāna is taught to them.

Now, regarding the aforementioned teaching on the Dharma, each of the three sections contains four stages—namely, taking up, discarding, combining, and separating—which are maintained as five types of Dharma teachings. The former corresponds to the "Parable of the Poor Son" and the "Fire House" chapters of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*, while the latter serves as the basis for the five types of parables.

The five kinds of analogies are: first, the analogy of leading the way; second, the analogy of weariness and retreat; third, the analogy of establishing a conjured city; fourth, the analogy of knowing when to rest; and fifth, the analogy of approaching the place of treasure.

Within the second of the three sections of the *Dharmapada*, there are four stages summarizing the essential meaning of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s teachings from beginning to end; these are now all discarded and not adopted. Within the third section, "Meeting Today," there are four stages; these are now all adopted.

First, in clearly elucidating the causal conditions established in the past, there are four stages involving both inclusion and exclusion. We do not include the first stage, which clarifies the intention behind the "covered lecture" (fùjiǎng), nor do we include the fourth stage, in which the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arises from meditative concentration to praise the princes.
It is only by taking the second statement, "each ascended the Dharma-seat," that the lecture is correctly covered;
and by taking the third stage, "each and every one was delivered," those who heard the lecture and its commentary at that time obtained benefits that were profound and vast.
How is this known to be so?

The master who presides over the review lecture corresponds to the meaning of the Teacher of the Path; the fact that at that time the benefit obtained is profound and vast corresponds to the meaning of the multitude of people being led. Therefore, these two stages are combined to form a single section.

The first section corresponds to the passage in the "Rich Man Seeking His Poor Son" chapter concerning the mutual loss of father and son; the second corresponds to the general analogy of the householder in the "Burning House" chapter; and it also remotely corresponds to the "Now I am likewise" passage in the "Expedient Means" chapter, clarifying that Śākyamuni, like all Buddhas, acts as a master of transformation to transform sentient beings in the five turbidities. This serves as the basis for the first analogy of the "Guide."

Third, regarding the clarification that among those encountered today there are four stages, all of whom are recipients [of the teaching]: first, the passage beginning with “The Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived and the assembly is pure” clarifies the *mārga* (capacity) for the Mahāyāna. This corresponds above to the seventh of the nine similes, where the father perceives the son’s great resolve; it also remotely corresponds to the fifth simile in the *Fire-House* chapter, where the elder sees his sons escape from calamity. Furthermore, it remotely corresponds to the fifth section of the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paryāya*) chapter: “Śāriputra, you should know that I see my sons who equally seek the Buddha-way, numbering immeasurable thousands of millions. This clarifies that the *mārga* for the Mahāyāna has been awakened within the assembly at this time. Below, this serves as the basis for the fourth simile, that of knowing when to rest.

The second section, “He then assembled all the bodhisattvas and preached this sutra for them,” corresponds above to the eighth analogy of entrusting the family estate in the *Parable of the Rich Man’s Son*, and it also remotely corresponds to the eighth analogy of the elder bestowing great carts in the *Parable of the Burning House*. Furthermore, it remotely corresponds to the eighth statement in the "Expedient Means" chapter which says, “Among all bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path,” which is precisely the preaching of the *Lotus Sutra*. Below, it serves as the basis for the fifth analogy of destroying the conjured city so that one may reach the place of true treasure.

Regarding the third statement, that "the Mahāyāna transformation cannot mutually produce [results]," this above corresponds to the third analogy in the section on the impoverished son’s realization—where the father calls for his son but cannot reach him—and it also remotely corresponds to the third analogy in the "Fire House" chapter—where the elder attempts to save his sons but cannot do so. Furthermore, it remotely corresponds to the meaning in the third part of the "Expedient Means" chapter—"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment"—concerning the Buddha’s inability to transform sentient beings through the Mahāyāna alone. Below, it serves as the basis for the third analogy regarding indolence and regression.

The fourth statement, “The Tathāgata’s skillful means penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings,” clarifies that he transforms and gathers sentient beings through the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Above, it corresponds to the fourth illustration in the *Parable of the Rich Man’s Son*, where the son is finally recognized as his own child, and the fifth illustration, where he is employed as a laborer; it also remotely corresponds to the meaning in the *Parable of the Burning House*, where the fourth illustration shows the elder using the three carts to rescue his children. Furthermore, it remotely corresponds to the meaning in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*), where the fourth line—“Reflecting upon the power of the skillful means practiced by past Buddhas”—describes the Buddha’s use of the three vehicles to transform sentient beings. Below, it serves as the basis for the third illustration, the Parable of the Phantom City.

This, then, corresponds only to the meanings of the first, third, fourth, and fifth sections—along with the eighth—among the ten sections consisting of both the Dharma-explanation and the Simile-explanation; it does not correspond to the meanings of the remaining five sections.
"Suppose it were five hundred yojanas"—from here below begins the second illustrative explanation (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Within this illustrative explanation there are also three sections: first, the opening of the illustration; second, the application of the illustration; and third, the citation of an external illustration to provide a concluding summary.

Within the section on providing analogies, there are five distinct analogies that correspond to the five types of dharmas explained previously as the basis: first, the analogy of the guide; second, the analogy of weariness and retreat; third, the analogy of establishing a conjured city; fourth, the analogy of knowing when to rest; and fifth, the analogy of leading one to the place of treasure.

Regarding the first analogy of the guide: this is primarily intended to clarify the two stages within the context of establishing karmic connections in the past, corresponding to the general analogy of the master of the first house in the "Burning House" parable.

Within the burning house, there were originally six meanings; now, in this analogy, these meanings follow one another such that there are four meanings, as the single gate and the five hundred people have been omitted for brevity.

Regarding the phrase "for example, five hundred yojanas," this is based on the analogy of the burning house: the Desire Realm is like one hundred, the Form Realm like two hundred, and the Formless Realm like three hundred; the residual habits of the three realms to be severed by the [first] seven stages are like four hundred, and the afflictions of the *avidyā-āvasthā* (ground of ignorance) to be severed from the eighth stage up to the Diamond-like Mind are like five hundred.

"Perilous and difficult paths, vast and desolate, devoid of people, and places of terror" refers to the meaning of fire within the house; these are all grounds of birth-and-death (saṃsāra), and are therefore called perilous and difficult paths.

We see directly that within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) of sentient beings cannot simply be non-existent; why, then, do you now say there is no person (*pudgala*)?
The commentator replies:

"The reason we say there is no person is that those who go against the current within birth and death are, for the most part, not worth mentioning. It is not that there are not one or two individuals capable of going against the current; rather, because such people cannot be designated by the word 'person,' we say there is no person."

"If there are many assemblies" and so forth—this constitutes the meaning of the "thirty sons," which corresponds to the third stage mentioned above, "each and every one is delivered. This section clarifies that those in the audience obtain benefit.

"There is a guide" refers to the meaning of the elder, which is an analogy for the second master of the covered lecture mentioned above. His knowledge that sentient beings attain understanding upon hearing the Dharma and thereby subdue their afflictions is the meaning of "knowing the passage. That they lose correct understanding and again give rise to afflictions is the meaning of "obstruction. At that time, he causes the multitude not to sink into birth and death but to seek the fruit of Buddhahood from afar; this is the act of leading the multitude across these difficulties.

"The multitude of people being led"—the following section constitutes the second simile of indolence and retreat; it corresponds to the third point within the previous "meeting today," namely that those for whom the Mahāyāna is appropriate lack the karmic capacity (*indriya*) for the Mahāyāna.

If one says "midway," it would imply that among the five hundred, they should have severed half of the afflictions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception; however, in reality, this is not the case.
Generally, there are two types of falling back:
first, falling back after having already traversed half the path; second, conceiving a mind of regret once the covenant has already been finalized.

Now, judging by what follows, the meaning of "at that time" clearly indicates that the assembly at that moment intended to transcend five hundred yojanas—the intent being to cross over the two kinds of birth-and-death—but they instead lost their correct understanding and lacked the aspiration for Buddhahood; this is precisely the meaning of "retrogression."
The following section consists entirely of discourse based on principle (*yukti*).

Within it, there are two parts: first, a single line that directly clarifies the regression; second, from "and addressed the Guide" onwards, which explains the three causes and conditions for regressing:
first, extreme exhaustion; second, fear; and third, the distance of the path.

"The Guide possesses many skillful means"—the following constitutes the third analogy of the constructed city, which illustrates the preceding statement: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings," whereby he gathers sentient beings through the transformation of the three vehicles.
The preceding section contained four analogies; here, too, there are four corresponding to those above.

First, it clarifies how the Guide employs the "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura) as a provisional expedient. Second, it clarifies that the Guide perceives the people of the time have a desire for the transformed city. Third, he establishes the transformed city for them. Fourth, it clarifies that the exhausted multitude immediately enters the transformed city.
The statement that "the Guide possesses many skillful means" refers to the primary meaning of employing the three vehicles as appropriate expedients.

The passage beginning with "He then thought, 'These [beings] are to be pitied'" constitutes the second point: the intention to manifest the city of the *śrāvaka* (the "city of peace"), which corresponds to the aforementioned meaning of perceiving those with the capacity for the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

"What is meant by 'discarding great precious jewels'? This refers to the desire to retreat due to a lack of the capacity for the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), which implies the presence of the capacity for the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

"Having had this thought," from here below is the third section, where the transformation city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) is actually established as a teaching. This section itself contains two parts; first is the preliminary contemplation on creating the transformation city. This is a metaphorical elaboration not present in the original [text]: the two types of knowledge—the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—originally transcend the three realms, which is precisely the meaning of "passing beyond three hundred *yojana*."

"Addressing the multitude," from this point downward is the second section, which properly establishes the provision of the conjured city. This contains four phrases that derive from the original parable; if expanded, they are analogous to those found within the "Burning House" chapter.

The initial statement, "Do not be afraid; whatever you desire shall all be granted to you," is precisely the guarantee that it will not be in vain; this corresponds to the subsequent illustrative phrase: "I now guarantee this matter for you, and it shall ultimately not be in vain."
"Do not turn back" is the second [phrase], which is the phrase for diligent exertion; it means, "You should all come out quickly from this burning house."

"This great city now" marks the third section below, which indicates the locations for the three vehicles; it corresponds to the preceding statement: "These carts drawn by goats, deer, and oxen are now outside the gate, where you may play."

"If one enters this city"—the following section is the fourth [section], which corresponds to the previous praise of the three vehicles. It refers to the earlier statement: "Those things you may find pleasing and rare, difficult to obtain—if you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later."
The combined analogy states: "You should know that these vehicles of the Threefold Dharma are all phrases praised by the Sages.

At this point, the "exhausted multitude" below refers to the fourth instance of the exhausted multitude entering the city of transformation; this corresponds to the aforementioned people receiving and practicing [the teaching]. Within this section, there are four meanings, which, when compared to the original analogy, correspond extensively to the impoverished son and the burning house.

The beginning refers to the practice of the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), which carries the meaning of "each mind being courageous and sharp"; this is what is meant by "the assembly, exhausted at that time, felt great joy in their hearts."
Next, the practice of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is clarified by the phrase "mutually pushing and shoving," which begins from the words "We, at this time... and so forth.

Next, the entry into the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that treats the truths seen (*satyadarśana*) is clarified by the meaning of "rushing together in competition," which consists of the five characters beginning with "Then, before the multitude... and so forth.
Next, the attainment of the fruit of no-more-learning is explained as the meaning of emerging from contention; this corresponds to the section beginning with "Entering the City of Transformation.
The natural exhaustion of causes is "the thought that birth has been transcended," and the natural disappearance of effects is "the thought of dwelling in peace and security."

"At that time, the guide knew this multitude of people"—the following constitutes the fourth analogy for knowing when to rest, which illustrates the awakening of the capacity for the Mahāyāna. The passage beginning with "O Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived" likewise refers, from a distance, to the meaning of the awakening of the capacity for the Mahāyāna expressed in the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means) as "I see the sons of the Buddha," and so forth.

"Immediately extinguishing the conjured city": the following section constitutes the fifth [section], clarifying the parable of approaching the treasure place. Above, the Buddha assembled all the bodhisattvas to preach the Mahāyāna *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; here, the statement "the place of treasure is near" signifies the revelation of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). This corresponds to the aforementioned "only by means of the single Buddha-vehicle does one attain extinction," and it also extends back to the meaning of the unsurpassed path taught solely in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*) chapter.
