From the passage below, "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed their respective assemblies of bodhisattvas," the tenth section elucidates how the Buddhas of the ten directions, having been illuminated by the light, consulted with their bodhisattvas regarding their desire to come.

"At that time, the Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity. The following section is the eleventh, clarifying how Śākyamuni Tathāgata transformed his land three times to accommodate the various emanation Buddhas; at that time, it was solely through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power that the land was transformed, and thus the compiler of the sutra records it.
The reason for the three transformations is to clarify the shattering of the minds that cling to the three vehicles.
Thus, the land is transformed from the narrow perspective of the two vehicles into a vast one; this is also echoed in the following verse.
"At this time, all the Buddhas dispatched messengers"—the following section is the twelfth, clarifying that once the Buddhas had assembled, they sent envoys to inquire after Śākyamuni.

"At that time, the Muni Buddha saw that all the emanated Buddhas had already assembled. This section below is the thirteenth, clarifying that once Śākyamuni Tathāgata had received the mutual inquiries and desired to open the jeweled stupa, he immediately rose into the air and opened the stupa.
The section beginning with “At that moment, the entire assembly here” is the fourteenth, in which the scribe describes how the great multitude beheld the signs of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.

The section beginning with “At that time, the fourfold assembly, having seen the past [Tathāgata]” is the fifteenth, clarifying that once the great assembly had seen the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, they scattered flowers as an offering and spoke these words.
Some interpret this by saying:
"At that time, there was speech from the assembly, but the sutra text is abbreviated and does not record it in full.
I maintain that this is not the case; this passage simply takes up the words of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praising Śākyamuni.

"At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna divided his seat within the jeweled stupa"—the following section is the sixteenth, clarifying how Prabhūtaratna offered half his seat for Śākyamuni to sit upon.

"Immediately, this was Śākyamuni Buddha. The following section is the seventeenth, clarifying that Śākyamuni took his seat. The reason it says that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna is together with Śākyamuni is that since the Buddha who has entered parinirvāṇa is already seated here, it signifies that Śākyamuni, though unborn, manifests birth. As for Śākyamuni sitting side-by-side with Prabhūtaratna, this clarifies that his passing between the twin trees was not a real extinction.

"At that time, the great assembly saw the two Tathāgatas. From here below is the eighteenth [section], clarifying that once the great assembly had seen the two Tathāgatas in the sky, they further wished to remain in the sky.

"At that moment, Śākyamuni, by means of his supernatural power... from here below is the nineteenth section, clarifying how the Tathāgata used his supernatural power to receive the great assembly into the air.

From "With a great voice" until the end of the prose section is the twentieth segment, which properly proclaims the search for those who will propagate the sutra; the following verses also chant upon this.

"Then he spoke in verse. This chapter consists of two sections, namely the prose and the verse. From this point downward, there are forty-eight lines of verse, which constitute the second section, the versified summary.
The prose version originally contained twenty sections; here, only four sections are versified:
three and a half lines verse the fifth section, three lines verse the seventh, five and a half lines verse the eleventh, and thirty-six lines verse the twentieth section.
Now, at the beginning, there are three and a half verses following the fifth section above.
The fifth section states that the Buddha answered Mahāpratibhāna regarding the purpose for which Prabhūtaratna has come.

From the words "Furthermore, my emanated bodies... below, there are three verses corresponding to the seventh section of the prose; this seventh section clarifies the Buddha’s answer to Mahāpratibhāna, stating: "If you wish to see the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, you should now assemble all the emanated Buddhas."

"For the sake of the seated Buddhas. Below this are five lines and a half of verse, which correspond to the eleventh section of the prose (the first part of the eleventh). It states that at that time, the Sahā world immediately transformed into purity; this clarifies that because Śākyamuni wished to accommodate all the manifested Buddhas, he underwent the transformation of his appearance three times.
The preceding section was the sūtra-author’s narration of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power; now, these five and a half lines are likewise verses spoken by the sūtra-author.

"Addressing the great assembly after my parinirvāṇa"—the remaining thirty-six lines of verse below this are a summary of the prose section's twentieth chapter. The previous statement, "With a great voice, he universally addressed the great assembly," refers precisely to the person who correctly transmits the sūtra.
Within these thirty-six lines, there are naturally six sections:
first, the statement "He addresses the great assembly" consists of one and a half lines that directly versify the preceding prose;
second, from "That Buddha Prabhūtaratna," there are three lines that briefly exhort the assembly of the time to make vows for the universal propagation of the sutra.

The third section, consisting of four lines of verse beginning with "Those who are able to protect this sutra-dharma," states that those who can propagate this sutra are thereby making offerings to the Tathāgata.
The fourth section, consisting of eighteen lines beginning with "All good sons, each contemplate this carefully," extensively addresses various difficulties to encourage the propagation of the sutra.

The fifth section, consisting of three and a half lines beginning with "I, for the sake of the Buddha-way," is Śākyamuni’s own recounting of his past propagation of the sutra to exhort the assembly of his time.

The sixth section, from "This sutra is difficult to uphold; if one upholds it even briefly" until the end of the chapter, consists of six lines and exhorts the assembly at that time to propagate the sutra by citing its karmic rewards.

Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Upholding (Dhāraṇī-parivarta). This chapter clarifies that five types of persons receive, uphold, and propagate the sutra; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Upholding."

The four chapters on the distinct circulation of the teaching consist of three sections. The preceding two chapters constitute the first section, which commands those who transmit the sutra; this chapter, the second, clarifies how the transmitters of the sutra receive their mandate to propagate it.
There are five types of persons who take a vow to master the sutra in five sections. First, the chapter clarifies Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and Mahāpratibhāna; these categories are twofold:
first, the various great bodhisattvas who personally vow to master the sutra.
The second clarifies that among the assembly, five hundred śrāvakas received predictions of enlightenment by vowing to master the sūtras.
The third clarifies that those in training and those beyond training who received predictions likewise vowed to master the sūtras.
Since those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have already severed the fruits of the three realms, how can they dwell in a pure land to propagate the sutras?
The explanation states:

"For those beyond training, there is in reality no birth in either the pure or impure lands; however, for the sake of propagating the sutras, they manifest through a semblance of non-outflow karma (anāsrava-karma) and take birth within the three realms. If one discusses this retribution in truth, it is not actually the fruit-retribution of the three realms."
The fourth section, beginning from "At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt... and following, clarifies how the assembly of nuns vowed to master the sutra.

From "At that time, the World-Honored One looked upon eight hundred trillion... until the end of this chapter constitutes the fifth section, clarifying how the eight hundred trillion great bodhisattvas made vows to propagate and disseminate the sutra.
Although there are five types [of practitioners], when categorized by their commonalities, they should be understood as three groups:

first, it clarifies that the Bodhisattvas of Great Practice circulate [this teaching] in the defiled lands; second, the middle three types clarify that the Śrāvakas circulate it in the pure lands; and third, the final one clarifies that this sutra is circulated in both the pure and defiled lands alike.

Chapter 13: On Peace and Bliss (Anle-pin) In this chapter, it is clarified that a bodhisattva who propagates this sutra possesses four kinds of practice; by means of these, they are able to leave danger behind to attain peace, and distance themselves from suffering to obtain bliss. For this reason, the compiler of the sutra has designated this as a chapter title.

The previous commentary states: The fourth section specifically circulates the meaning of "opening the three to reveal the one. Although there are four chapters of scripture, they are divided into three segments. First, the two chapters—the "Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇaka*) and the "Vision of the Jeweled Stūpa"—first clarify that the merit of those who transmit the sutra is profound, and that those who receive and uphold it shall attain long life; they seek out such individuals to transmit the sutra. Second, the single chapter of the "Upholding" (*Parīndanā*) clarifies the assembly of those who delight in merit and goodness, who together before the Buddha take vows and receive the mandate to transmit the sutra, all declaring that they do not cherish their own bodies or lives, but instead treasure the Unsurpassed Way.

However, while they were still in the process of mastering the "Dharani" chapter before having fully mastered the sutra, there was the fault of slander and the anxiety for their lives; thus, these bodhisattvas of inferior grade, though originally intending to take a vow to master the sutra, upon seeing the many hardships of this evil age, gave rise to thoughts of regression and abandoned their intention to master the sutra.

Therefore, this chapter is the third; because the Tathāgata employs the Practice of Peaceful Conduct (*sukha-vihāra*), it addresses those of inferior capacity who would otherwise fall back. It states that if one can fully possess these four practices, then even celestial Māras cannot obstruct them; thus, within this evil age, they sacrifice their bodies to save sentient beings and give their lives to deliver others. This is how those of inferior capacity may, by means of this, give rise to the resolve to propagate the sutra and further develop the intention to ferry others across.
Previously, it was further explained that among these three sections, the first and the last each contain two parts, while the middle one itself has five distinct divisions.
Now, regarding the two parts within this [middle section]: the first is Mañjuśrī’s question, and the second is the Tathāgata’s answer.
Now, within the inquiry itself, there are two stages:
first, a preliminary praise of those capable of penetrating the sutras; second, from the words "World-Honored One" onwards, the actual posing of the questions.
The Buddha said: The following is the second section of this chapter, clarifying the Tathāgata’s response.
This section consists of four parts: first, the proclamation of the number of the four practices;

second, from "This one is abiding" onwards, the exposition of the essence of the four practices; third, from "After my parinirvāṇa" onwards, one and a half lines of general exhortation to cultivate these four practices; and fourth, at the end of the chapter, twenty-one and a half lines that comprehensively clarify the signs of the blissful fruition attained through the four practices.
The explanation of the meaning of the four types of blissful ease consists of four stages:

first, the correct determination of their essence; second, clarifying that wisdom and merit constitute their practice; third, clarifying that one's own practice and external transformation constitute their practice; and fourth, clarifying the stages of these four practices.

First, regarding the correct identification of their essential natures: among the four kinds of bliss, the first has wisdom as its essence; the second has the preaching of the Dharma as its essence; the third has the elimination of faults as its essence; and the fourth has a mind of compassion as the essence of its practice.

Regarding the second clarification concerning the merit of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*) as previously judged: since the second [category] is likewise wisdom, and the "wisdom of desire" (*chanda-prajñā*) is present in its exposition, the second is also wisdom.

The third and fourth are identical in being meritorious qualities; therefore, within the gate of wisdom, the teaching of the Dharma is distinguished, while within the gate of merit, compassion is distinguished—thus there are four practices.

Regarding the third [section], the classification of self-cultivation and external transformation: the first and third are self-cultivation, while the fourth is likewise external transformation. Generally, the methods for interpreting the sutras do not exceed these two categories of self-cultivation and external transformation.
The reason for these four practices is that self-cultivation and the transformation of others are each divided into two.

Self-cultivation is divided into two because there are two meanings: first, the first [practice] is the understanding that illuminates the two kinds of emptiness—of the provisional and the real; this is the gate of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*). Third, it clarifies the departure from faults; this is the gate of severance (*prahāṇa-mukha*). Therefore, self-cultivation must clarify these two.

Regarding the second meaning: wisdom refers to the illumination of objects; from this, the practice of goodness that takes up the side of departing from faults is precisely the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*). Since there is thus a distinction between cessation and practice, they are divided into two.

The reason external transformation (*bahirdhā-vinaya*) is divided into two aspects is as follows: if one speaks of compassion (*karuṇā*), one discusses its root; if one speaks of preaching the Dharma, one discusses its branch. If there were only the knowledge of preaching the Dharma without compassion, it would be like indeterminate speech (*avyākṛta-vāk*).

If there were only compassion without preaching the Dharma, the practice of bestowing happiness and extracting suffering could never be accomplished. Therefore, for the sake of external transformation, these two must be clarified.

The fourth section clarifies the determination of these four stages of practice. At the outset, they begin at the initial stage of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), prior to reaching the state of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
For what reason is the determination of their stages restricted to this point?
The commentator says:
"These four practices are fundamentally intended for external ordinary beings and bodhisattvas; they must not be taken too deeply.
Now, one should abide in these four dharmas; this is the first general enumeration.

"First, abiding securely"—from this point downward is the second section, which sets forth the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the four modes of peaceful conduct (*caturvidha-sukhavihāra*), thus forming four parts.

Furthermore, regarding these four practices, the phrasing differs: in the explanation of the first two practices, each has three sections of interpretation, whereas in the explanation of the latter two practices, each has two textual passages.
Now, to clarify that within the initial practice there are three parts:
first, from "From this" downward through twenty-three verses, there is the correct explanation of the essential characteristics of the initial practice;
second, the four and a half verses beginning with "If there is a bhikṣu," clarify the characteristics of the peace and bliss of attaining the fruit.
The third section, "Mañjuśrī is this Bodhisattva," consists of one line and one phrase, which concludes this initial practice.
Now, regarding the first [part], the correct explanation of the primary essence and characteristics, there are two internal divisions:
first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (gāthā).
Now, within the prose section itself, there are two distinct parts:
first, a passage of about one line that initially establishes two topical headings based on the prose;
second, an explanation of how this sutra can be propagated during the evil age to come.
"Mañjuśrī, how is it that a bodhisattva... and so forth constitutes the second section, which correctly explains the two topical headings (*dvāra*) but does not explain the meaning of "circulation.
The two topical headings are the topical heading of the essence of practice (*caryā-svabhāva*) and the topical heading of skillful means (*upāya*).

"Abiding securely in the sphere of the bodhisattva's practice" constitutes the topical heading for the chapter on the essence of practice. This practice takes the understanding that both provisional names and substantial dharmas are empty as its essence; since these two types of emptiness—of the provisional and the substantial—are now the objects perceived by the mind of understanding, it is called the "sphere of practice."

The "Points of Intimacy" constitute the gateway to the second chapter; that is, the path of skillful means for realizing the two kinds of emptiness. Next, regarding the phrase "being able to preach this sutra for the sake of sentient beings," it correctly clarifies that when a bodhisattva who has newly entered the practice seeks to propagate this sutra during the evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they must necessarily understand the mind and abide in the two kinds of emptiness—conventional and ultimate—as well as the path of skillful means. One who treats enemies and kin with equality and encourages both the good and the evil alike will be unable to be harmed by devas, Māras, or externalists; such a person leaves danger behind to attain peace, and leaves suffering behind to attain happiness.

"Mañjuśrī, how is it that a bodhisattva... This is the second section, the correct explanation of the two chapter-headings. First, the chapter-heading on the sphere of practice and realization of the two kinds of emptiness is explained; subsequently, the chapter-heading on the spheres of intimacy for the two families is explained.
Now, within the section on "Practice through Understanding," there are three parts:
first, the general outline; second, the detailed explanation of the two practices; and third, the summary.
The present statement, "What is the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva? constitutes the first general heading. The section beginning with "If a bodhisattva...

is the second part, the detailed explanation; herein there are two sub-sections: first, the explanation of the sphere of practice that is empty of conventional designations (*prajñapti-śūnya-gocara*); second, the explanation of the sphere of practice that is empty of phenomena (*dharma-śūnya-gocara*).
Now, regarding the explanation of the two types of practice for the emptiness of conventional designations (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*), one interpretation states:

"The Bodhisattva dwells on the ground of patience, gentle, compliant, and harmonious. This single phrase clarifies the attainment of the emptiness of conventional designations; therefore, there are no four faults in speech.
“Without being violent” (the second phrase) indicates the attainment of the emptiness of conventional designations; thus, there are no three types of unwholesome karma of the body.
“The mind is also not startled” (the third phrase) clarifies the attainment of the emptiness of conventional designations; thus, there are no three types of unwholesome karma of the mind.
These three phrases all clarify the characteristics of the emptiness of conventional designations by way of their application.

If one examines provisional emptiness by means of this passage, it is inherently difficult to perceive; therefore, it is known through the sphere of practice of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) below that what preceded was provisional emptiness.

Since the subsequent explanation of the sphere of practice of the emptiness of phenomena states, "Furthermore, regarding phenomena," we know that what preceded was the emptiness of provisional names (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*).

In the subsequent verses that extensively expound upon the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it further states, "Nor does one perceive them as male or female. Therefore, we know this refers to the emptiness of conventional designations (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, the interpretation of the three phrases explains the sphere of practice regarding the emptiness of conventional designations (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*). This refers to the person to manifest the characteristics of the emptiness of conventional designations; the first phrase is based on the external circumstance that when evil comes, one does not give rise to evil.
The latter phrase refers to the fact that when encountering wholesome objects, my mind is not startled.
How is this known?
The phrase, "When hearing the Sage speak of non-self and emptiness, my mind is not startled, and in the interim there is no sudden violence," specifically refers to my inner mind.
If one does not attain provisional emptiness, it is not as described here.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "Moreover, there is no practice with respect to dharmas," the following three phrases clarify the sphere of practice regarding the emptiness of dharmas; this specific phrase clarifies that one possesses the wisdom that understands dharmas and does not engage in the objective realm with a mind that treats them as real.
The second phrase, "observing all phenomena as they truly are," clarifies the wisdom that understands the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
The third phrase, "neither practicing nor discriminating," clarifies that at the time of attaining the emptiness of phenomena, there is no sense of discriminating between self and other.

In the past, before one had attained the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*), one would form the mental conception that "I alone am capable of practice while others are not," harboring a sense of distinction between self and other.
Today, having attained the emptiness of dharmas, there is only the single characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*); there is no longer any differentiation between self and other.
"This is called the sphere of practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is the third summary of the two spheres of practice.
From "What is called the sphere of intimacy? onwards is the second section, which explains the spheres of intimacy according to the two schools.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the section heading "What is meant by the 'proximate bases'? and second, the formal explanation. Within the latter, there are again two parts:

first, the explanation of the provisional designation of the "proximate bases of emptiness," and second, the explanation of the "proximate bases of the emptiness of phenomena. These constitute the paths of skillful means for the two schools.
Regarding today’s explanation of the "Proximity to the Emptiness of Designations," there are three sections:
first, clarifying the objects that should not be approached; second, clarifying the objects that should be approached; and third, the conclusion.

If one discusses the essence of skillful means (*upāya*), it is precisely the period from when one has transcended provisional names regarding actual dharmas until before the attainment of true contemplation that constitutes the essence of skillful means; for now, however, we speak in this way by employing external conditions as skillful means.
Within the explanation of the places one should not associate with, there are eight types.
First, it clarifies distancing oneself from the conditions of power and influence:

this refers to the passage beginning, "A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not associate with kings. Second, it clarifies distancing oneself from the conditions of false views; this refers to the section beginning, "He does not associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas)."
The third clarifies the distancing from the conditions of unwholesome karma; this begins with "Nor does he associate with... and so forth.

The fourth clarifies the distancing from the conditions of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); this begins with "Furthermore, he does not associate with those who seek the state of a Śrāvaka... and so forth.
The fifth clarifies the conditions for being free from the defilement of craving; this is the section beginning with "Mañjuśrī.
The sixth clarifies the conditions for being free from the lack of resolve; this is the section concerning "the five kinds of non-males."
The seventh clarifies the conditions for avoiding reproach, beginning from "not entering alone" below.
The eighth clarifies the conditions for avoiding distraction, beginning from "delighting in keeping young [attendants]" below.
"Always delighting in seated meditation" marks the second section, which correctly clarifies the places to be frequented.
"Mañjuśrī," and so forth, constitutes the third section, which serves as the conclusion.
"Furthermore," from here below is the second section, which clarifies that there are three aspects to the locus of the cultivation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*):
first, the preliminary clarification of the locus to be cultivated; second, the formal clarification of the essence of the cultivator; and third, the concluding summary.
That which is the object of close approach is the realm of the two truths.
That which is capable of close approach is the wisdom that contemplates.
Within the clarification of the object of close approach, there are two [aspects]:
The first clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the second, from "It exists only by way of causes and conditions" onwards, clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Within this clarification of the ultimate truth, there are three parts:
first, the single phrase "Contemplating all dharmas as empty, their true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*)" correctly clarifies the principle of the ultimate truth.
The second section, from "non-inverted" (*aviparyāsa*) onwards, consists of six phrases that clarify the cessation of the mind's sphere of activity;
the third section, from "the path of all speech is cut off" (*sarva-vāk-patha-vicchinna*) onwards, consists of eleven phrases that clarify the severance of the path of speech.
The two lines beginning with "It exists only by way of causes and conditions" constitute the second [section], which clarifies conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

From the phrase "One should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena," this is the second [point] within the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), clarifying the wisdom that is capable of contemplation.
"This is called 'the proximate abode'" is the third summary verse.
"And he spoke a verse" marks the beginning of the second verse section.
However, within the preceding prose (gadya), there are originally two parts:
First, the initial section establishes two chapter-headings and subsequently clarifies how this sutra can be circulated during the evil age that follows;
second, the main body provides a formal explanation of these two chapter-headings, but does not explain the meaning of "being able to circulate" it.
Now, these twenty-three lines of verse are also divided into two parts:
the first one and a half lines of verse summarize the first section on conduct into two topical headings;
the subsequent twenty-one and a half lines of verse constitute the second part, which provides the formal explanation.
The first section has two parts:
first, the establishment of two topical headings; second, the clarification of those capable of circulating this sutra.

Here, one line of the verse is inverted to first recite the second part—the clarification of those capable of circulating it—followed by half a line to retrospectively recite the first two topical headings.
In the second preceding explanation, there were two parts: first clarifying the sphere of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), and subsequently clarifying the sphere of intimacy (*sevā-bhūmi*).

Now, in this verse, one must not directly judge it according to those three sections; rather, the first part consists of thirteen and a half lines, which first versifies the sphere of intimacy regarding the emptiness of conventional designations (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*);
next, there are two and a half lines, which retrospectively versify the two spheres of practice.
The third section consists of five lines and a half; this verse concerns the locus of proximity to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Regarding the preceding explanation of the two loci of proximity, there were two parts:
first, the presentation of the topical headings (*uddāna*), which is not versified here; now, only the second part, the actual explanation, is versified.
Regarding this provisional designation of "emptiness" as the place of practice, there are originally three parts:
first, clarifying those places not to be practiced; second, correctly clarifying the place to be practiced; and third, the concluding summary.

Now, the second place of association is not versified; within these thirteen and a half verses, the first twelve and a half verses versify the first [place], that which is not to be associated with, while one verse summarizes the third.

However, regarding the eight types of places that one should not associate with mentioned above, these twelve lines and a half can only be understood as a general verse and cannot be divided; thus, this is called the summary verse for this section.
However, while the *Upāyikā-śāstra* [deals with] the proximate locations (*upapatti-sthāna*), why is the location of practice (*caryā-sthāna*) presented here?
The explanation states:
"Because this presents the location of practice as being proximate, it is placed at the beginning."
Regarding these two locations: this proximate location is the second, and the previously mentioned location is the first; thus, there are two paths.
Furthermore, the phrase "nor does one practice" and the following two and a half lines constitute the second section, which summarizes the two locations mentioned above.
The original text consists of three parts:
first, the presentation of the topical outline; second, the formal explanation; and third, the concluding summary.
Here, the first part is not versified, and only the latter two sections are versified. The first two lines verse the formal explanation, while the subsequent half-line verses the conclusion.
However, above, we first explained the practice of the emptiness of conventional designations, followed by the practice of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*).

These two practices are presented here in reverse order in the verse: the first line first summarizes the practice of the emptiness of phenomena, and the second line subsequently summarizes the practice of the emptiness of conventional designations.
"This is what is called" marks the third conclusion for the preceding half-line verse.
From "all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*) below, these five lines and a half constitute the third verse’s section on the locus for approaching the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The original text above consists of three parts:

Now, these five lines and a half are directly divided into six sections:
The first section consists of one and a half lines, which briefly summarizes the first point of "approaching" mentioned above.

The second section, beginning with "Discriminating erroneously whether phenomena exist or do not exist," consists of one line; this cites what is incorrect as being correct—something absent from the preceding prose—to clarify that such a person is unable to practice the contemplation of approaching the emptiness of phenomena.

The third section, "dwelling in a secluded place," contains half a line which correctly versifies the second point above, the "place where one can draw near," namely, the phrase above: "always joyfully contemplating such characteristics of phenomena."

The fifth [verse], "Observing that all phenomena are non-existent," consists of one line and three phrases, which inversely recite the aforementioned practice of the emptiness of phenomena.
The sixth section consists of one sentence; it concludes the third point above concerning the approach to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

First, regarding the initial statement: the reason for clarifying the avoidance of evil herein is that one who expounds the Dharma must necessarily purify themselves to transform sentient beings and deliver them throughout their lives; therefore, in order to clarify pure preaching of the Dharma, one first clarifies the departure from all faults and evils.

Regarding the second intention: herein, first the avoidance of evil is clarified, and subsequently the actual teaching of the Dharma is clarified. In the third line below, the initial clarification of avoiding evil is presented. Regarding the third intention:

within the subsequent verses, the teaching of the Dharma is first versified, followed by the versification of avoiding evil; therefore, it is verified that the essence [of this section] is precisely the teaching of the Dharma.

Now, to clarify the three sections within the avoidance of evil: first, the two lines beginning with "If one proclaims with the mouth" clarify the timing of preaching the Dharma; second, the section beginning with "Not delighting in speaking of others" correctly clarifies the avoidance of evil; and third, the single line "Because of skillfully cultivating such a mind of peace and happiness" is the concluding sentence.
Regarding the second [category], avoiding evil, there are generally six kinds of avoidance:
first, the statement "one does not delight in speaking of people," which clarifies that one does not speak of the faults of those who recite the sutras.
Second, regarding the phrase "and the faults of the scriptures," this clarifies that one does not correctly understand the words and phrases of the sutra texts.

Third, regarding "separation," it means that what constitutes a thorough understanding of the scriptures for others is not considered a thorough understanding of the scriptures for oneself; this refers to the section beginning with "nor should one be contemptuous."
Fourth, regarding the phrase "not speaking of others' likes and dislikes, strengths and weaknesses," one may say that it refers to not speaking of others' shortcomings.
Why, then, does it also mention not speaking of others' strengths?
The commentator’s original statement says:
"In this context, the Elder Madhyantika originally intended to expose their shortcomings.

Fifth, from the passage beginning with "Regarding the śrāvakas," it clarifies that he did not criticize the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as such; rather, in this instance, it simply clarifies that he did not employ the name of the Small Vehicle.
Regarding the phrase "if there are those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle," it may also be called "arrogance by name.
Sixth is the statement: "Nor does one give rise to a mind of resentment or aversion."
The section beginning with "All those who listen" is the second part, which correctly elucidates the essential nature and characteristics of this practice.
This section itself contains two parts:
first, it clarifies that one should not oppose the intentions of those who come to listen in silence.
The second section, from "When there are questions and inquiries" onwards, clarifies that when there are consultations, one does not oppose their intent.

From "And he spoke these verses" onwards is the second part; it consists of eleven and a half lines of verse in total, which are now divided into two segments. The first segment comprises six and a half lines, which first recapitulate the second part of the preceding prose—the primary exposition of the essence of practice. The subsequent five lines are a reverse recitation of the first part of the preceding prose—the avoidance of evil.
However, within the second section of the preceding prose, there are originally two parts: the first clarifies silent listening, and the latter clarifies questioning and debate.
Now, these six lines and a half should be divided into three sections:
the first consists of two lines and a half which clarify the method of preaching the Dharma; this is something not present in the preceding prose.
The second section, "If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs," consists of two lines; it corresponds to the first point above, regarding those who come silently to listen.
The third section, "If there are difficult questions," consists of two lines; it corresponds to the second point above, regarding those who raise difficult questions.
"Eliminating the mind of indolence": the following five lines constitute a verse on the first [topic], the abandonment of evil.
However, while the original text above contained three "existences," these five lines do not verse the first and the third, but only the second.
In the second section above, there were originally six lines; now it is appropriate to divide them into two parts:

the first two and a half lines clarify the abandonment of the evil of indolence, while the subsequent two and a half lines, beginning with "robes and bedding," clarify the abandonment of the evil of craving and longing.

The phrase "After my parinirvāṇa" introduces the third section, which consists of five lines and clarifies the characteristics of the peace and bliss of attaining the fruit. This section itself has two parts; the first three lines clarify the meaning of being free from peril and suffering.
The second section, "The wise person is thus," consists of two lines below, which precisely clarifies the characteristics of the peace and happiness attained.

Next, the third practice is elucidated; this practice takes the avoidance of evil as its essence. As for the two sections, these consist of the prose (chángxíng) and the verses (jì) as the two parts.
Now, within this extended discourse, there are naturally three sections:
first, the primary clarification of abandoning evil;
second, from "One should [behave] toward all sentient beings" onwards, the clarification of cultivating goodness, for without cultivating goodness, there is no way to abandon evil.
The third section, from "Mañjuśrī" onwards, clarifies the characteristics of the bliss of attaining the fruit.
Now, within the context of abandoning evil, six kinds of evil are generally abandoned:
the first is "jealousy."
Second is "flattery" (śāṭhya): this person is truly able to practice virtue, yet does so solely to please others.
Third is "deception" (māyā): this person has no genuine practice within their inner mind.
4. "Furthermore, do not disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way.
5. From "If there be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs" for the following five lines, this refers to not slighting those who study the Hīnayāna.
Sixth: "Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous conceptualization regarding all phenomena nor contend with them.
The section beginning with "One should [act] toward all sentient beings" clarifies the second point, the cultivation of goodness, which itself comprises four kinds of goodness.
The first is: "To give rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings."
Second is the section beginning with "Toward all Tathāgatas";
third is the section beginning with "Toward all Bodhisattvas";
and fourth is the section beginning with "Toward all sentient beings."
"Mañjuśrī," from here below is the third section within the prose, which clarifies the perception of the bliss of attaining the fruit.

The third section, "The third dharma is thus," consists of one line of verse, which summarizes the third point above: the characteristic of peace and happiness.
Next, the fourth "Peaceful and Joyful Practice" is explained. This practice clarifies that compassion is its essence; within it there are also two sections, namely the prose and the verse.
Now, within the prose section itself, there are two parts:
the first clarifies the essence of practice; the second, beginning with "Mañjuśrī," clarifies the characteristics of the peace and bliss of attaining the fruit.
Furthermore, within these two sections, each contains two parts.
Within the first section, there are two:
the first briefly clarifies great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
The second section, from "Regarding those who are not bodhisattvas" onwards, extensively elucidates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

"Not hearing" refers to the failure to achieve the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) in the past; "not knowing" refers to the failure to achieve the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) in the past; and "not awakening" refers to the failure to achieve the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) in the past.
How is this known? The final three phrases constitute the explanation.

"Not having heard" explains the preceding phrase "not having heard. Had one been able to hear these Three Vehicles in the past, then the meaning of "hearing" would have been fulfilled; it is precisely because one did not hear them in the past that the meaning of "hearing" was not realized.

The phrase "lack of faith" immediately explains the aforementioned point of "not knowing"; it is precisely because they previously lacked faith and spoke of three vehicles by differentiating what is in fact the One Buddha Vehicle that they do not understand the principle that all paths return to the same destination.

The phrase "not understanding" immediately explains the preceding term "not awakening. If one had previously understood the meaning of "returning to the same," one would have immediately awakened to the meaning of "the absence of three.
From the words "Mañjuśrī" onwards is the second section, which correctly elucidates the characteristics of peace and bliss; this also has two parts:
first, the correct elucidation of the characteristics of peace and bliss, and second, the immediate explanation thereof.
However, within the primary clarification of the characteristics of peace and bliss, there are two parts:
first, the prior clarification of human affection; second, from the words "the various devas" onwards, the clarification of divine protection.
Thus, the Tathāgata’s sūtra-dharma resides within the embrace of such a person; for this reason, humans and devas constantly protect people for the sake of the Dharma.

"The reason why" introduces the second section, which explains the characteristics of peace and happiness (*anābādha-lakṣaṇa*); this also has two parts: first, the explanation by means of the Dharma (*dharma-deśanā*), and second, the explanation by means of a simile (*upamā-deśanā*).
Furthermore, within these two sections, there are two parts each.

Regarding the first section on the Dharma-exposition, the first part clarifies that this sutra is the secret treasury protected by all Buddhas; the second part, beginning with "Mañjuśrī," clarifies that this sutra should be revered based on the fact that it is difficult to hear and yet has been attained.
"Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful wheel-turning sage-king," and so forth, is the second simile.

That the characteristics of peace and bliss are explained as being twofold refers to these two similes; they constitute two sections, serving as similes for the two aforementioned types of Dharma teachings.
However, the first analogy itself contains both an opening and a closing.

From the passage "Mañjuśrī was like a wheel-turning monarch who saw the assembly of bhikṣus" onwards is the second analogy; it likewise has two parts, namely an opening and a closing, which constitute two sections.

However, within the application of the analogy itself, there are three parts: first, the direct application; second, from the words "Mañjuśrī" onwards, the citation of the external analogy as a commentary; and third, again from "Mañjuśrī" onwards, the synthesis of these elements.

The first is the teaching by way of Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), which itself contains two sub-sections: first, the secret treasury of all Buddhas; second, the persons who have attained this Dharma. In the two preceding analogies, each had both an opening and a closing; however, these present ten lines and a half should be divided into only two parts:

first, four lines which first cite the two external analogies from the verse; second, six lines and a half beginning with "The Tathāgata is also thus," which cite the two internal applications (inner *saṃgraha*) from the verse. Within the initial four lines, three lines constitute the verse for the first external analogy, while the single line beginning with "Suppose there were a brave and vigorous [man]" constitutes the verse for the second external analogy.

Within the subsequent six lines and a half, the first three lines beginning with "The Tathāgata is likewise" constitute the internal application of the first simile; next, the three lines beginning with "Having known that sentient beings have obtained its power" constitute the internal application of the second simile.

Regarding the phrase "after my parinirvāṇa," there are four sections within the Buddha’s response; this following one and a half lines constitute the third summary, exhorting the practice of these four modes of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*).

"Those who read this sutra"—the following twenty-one and a half lines constitute the fourth section of the Buddha’s response, which generally clarifies the characteristics of the peace and bliss resulting from [this practice].

However, herein the primary aim is to clarify the characteristics of obtaining the peace and happiness of the three types of retribution. Within these twenty-one and a half lines, there are naturally four sections:
first, there is one line that initially clarifies the attainment of peace and happiness through present retribution.
The second section, "Not being born into poverty," consists of three and a half lines, which clarifies the attainment of happiness as a result of the present life.
The third section, "If, in a dream," consists of sixteen lines, clarifying the attainment of happiness as a result of future lives.
The fourth line summarizes the three preceding explanations.
Regarding the third section, "Now, based on the signs of retribution in dreams," there are five parts:
first, one and a half lines clarify listening to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma;
The second section, "Manifesting oneself as a person preaching the Dharma," also consists of one and a half lines;
the third section, "Furthermore, seeing all Buddhas" and below, consisting of six and a half lines, clarifies receiving the prediction of Buddhahood and preaching the Dharma;
the fourth section, "Furthermore, seeing oneself" and below, consisting of one and a half lines, clarifies practicing the causes for the fruit of Buddhahood.

The fifth section, “The Bodies of All Buddhas Adorned with Golden Complexions and the Marks of a Hundred Blessings,” consists of five lines of five-character verse and clarifies the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Within this fifth section on attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, there are two intentions:
first, one line initially cites and enumerates the preceding four dreams; second, the subsequent four lines properly clarify the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood.
First, regarding the preliminary citation of the four dreams: the first two phrases up to "hearing the Dharma" cite the first dream;
the three characters "for others to preach" cite the second dream.
The phrase "I constantly have such auspicious dreams" summarizes the third and fourth dreams.
The following four lines, beginning with "Furthermore, I dreamt of becoming a king," correctly clarify the second point: the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood.
"If, in a future evil age... This subsequent line constitutes the fourth summary of the three types of retribution.

Chapter 14: The Emergence from the Earth. The title of this chapter should not be placed here; it ought to follow immediately after the preceding dialogue, as its textual content is brief. It has been inserted at the beginning of this chapter for convenience.
It is named after its position following the preceding section; thus, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence" (*Nyorubun*).

In total, fourteen chapters and a half of the sutra constitute the second main exposition (*shōsetsu*), which is itself divided into two segments. The first segment consists of the twelve preceding chapters, which open up the three vehicles to reveal the one vehicle (*kai-san ken-ichi*) in order to clarify the meaning of the cause (*in-gi*). From this point onward, up to the middle of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" (*Funbetsu Kudoku-bun*), there are two chapters and a half of the sutra; these constitute the second segment of the main exposition, which opens up the near to reveal the far (*kai kin ken en*) in order to distinguish the meaning of the fruit (*ka-gi*).
Within the section clarifying the causes and distinguishing the effects, each part is further divided into four; herein, there are four:
first, from the beginning of this chapter down to the verse "One should practice with diligence and single-mindedness," is the specific introduction concerning the lifespan;

second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses" down to "I have, for a long time, taught and transformed these multitudes," is the brief exposition that reveals the near to manifest the far, thereby shaking fixed attachments and giving rise to doubt.

The third section, from "At that time, Maitreya and the others felt doubt and marveled at this unprecedented event" to the end of the chapter, clarifies how the great assembly harbored doubts and offered their request;

the fourth section, beginning from the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* and extending through the first one and a half chapters up to the *Guṇaparikīrtana-parivarta*, extensively elucidates the long duration of the Buddha's lifespan in order to sever doubts and engender faith.
Now, within these four sections, the first and the last are each divided into three parts, while the two middle sections are separately divided into two.
Within the first, the "Separate Introduction," there are three parts:

the first, which occupies approximately two pages less, is designated as the "Introduction of Opening and Elucidation"; the second, from "Maitreya Bodhisattva" onwards, consisting of slightly more than one page, is named the "Introduction of Inquiry"; and the third, from "The Buddha told Maitreya" onwards, is named the "Introduction of Exhortation."
Now, first, regarding the introduction to the opening, there are two parts:
the first is the reason for the opening, and the second, from "At that time the Buddha said... onwards, is the actual clarification of the opening.
Regarding the reason for stating that [the teaching] was revealed: because the attendant bodhisattvas of the transformation Buddhas from other lands requested its circulation, the Buddha simply said:
"In my Sahā world, there are bodhisattvas who can circulate it themselves; there is no need for you."
Therefore, there is the cause for the emergence of this exultation.
Furthermore, within these two sections, each contains two stages.
Regarding the two aspects of the cause for its manifestation:
First, the request for the circulation [of the teaching] by bodhisattvas from other directions is clarified;
second, the Buddha’s response. From the passage "When the Buddha had spoken these words, in this Sahā world... onwards is the second section, which correctly clarifies the unfolding [of the event];

herein there are also two parts: first, the sūtra-master’s description of the signs of the bodhisattvas’ emergence; second, from "Among this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders... onwards, which clarifies the dialogue between the emerged bodhisattvas and the Buddha.
Now, within the sequence of the sūtra’s description of the manifestations of emerging from the earth, there are eight stages:
first, the enumeration of the manifestations of emerging;
second, from the passage "The bodies of these bodhisattvas were all golden" onwards, the description of the physical characteristics of the bodhisattvas.
The third section, beginning with "Previously they were all here," describes the origins from which the bodhisattvas have come.

The fourth section, beginning with "These bodhisattvas, hearing the voice spoken by Śākyamuni, emerged from below," records the reasons for their emergence as provided by the narrator of the sutra: because Śākyamuni told the bodhisattvas from other quarters that they were not needed and that his own Sahā world possessed bodhisattvas capable of circulating this sutra, they emerged upon hearing these words.
The fifth section, beginning with "Each individual bodhisattva," is the sūtra-author’s narration of the retinues of the bodhisattvas who leaped forth.
The sixth section, beginning with "Having emerged from the earth, each went into the void," clarifies the threefold offering performed by the leaping bodhisattvas after they had emerged.

The seventh section, beginning with "These bodhisattvas, from their initial emergence," describes the number of kalpas that elapsed during the time of their emergence as recorded by the narrator of the sutra.

The eighth section, beginning with "At that time, the fourfold assembly, also through the Buddha’s spiritual power," describes how the fourfold assembly saw all the bodhisattvas everywhere, as recorded by the narrator of the sutra.

"Among this assembly of bodhisattvas, there are four leaders. From here below, the main body of the exposition is correctly developed; it consists of two parts, and from this point onward is the second section, which clarifies the fourfold dialogue between the emerging bodhisattvas and the Buddha. This can be understood as consisting of four segments.
"At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... and below this is the second section, the introduction to the inquiry. Within this introduction to the inquiry, there are also two parts:

first, it clarifies Maitreya Bodhisattva’s own questioning of Śākyamuni; second, from "Questioning the Buddhas of other directions who have manifested their bodies" onwards, it clarifies the Bodhisattva’s own questioning of those manifested Buddhas.
Within Maitreya’s inquiry itself, there are two parts:
first, the sūtra-master’s narration of Maitreya’s intention to inquire; second, the actual presentation of the verses of inquiry.
Within these nineteen and a half lines of verses that constitute the formal inquiry, there are three sections:
The first line of verses is a preliminary request for the Buddha’s response before the formal inquiry;
the second section, beginning with "From where have you come? and comprising thirteen verses, constitutes the formal inquiry;
the third section consists of the remaining five and a half lines, which serve as the concluding request.
In the twenty-third verse, the formal inquiry consists of two parts:
first, two verses inquire about the person of the Bodhisattva who has leaped forth; second, the twenty-first verse inquires about the teacher of the Bodhisattva who has leaped forth.

Regarding these two verses, there are two intentions and four textual passages concerning the human body. First, the single phrase "From where have they come? asks about their place of origin. Second, the single phrase "By what causes and conditions do they assemble? asks why they gather in one place and appear simultaneously. Third, the line beginning with "A massive body and great supernormal powers" is a praise of this bodhisattva that concludes the second question.
The fourth line, "From where have they come? concludes the first question.
The following eleven lines, beginning with "Each and every bodhisattva," constitute the second question: who is the teacher of these bodhisattvas?
Within this, there are two parts:

first, nine verses that enumerate the number of the Bodhisattvas' retinues, ranging from those with retinues as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers down to those who have no retinue at all;
second, the two lines beginning with "These [Bodhisattvas] of Great Majestic Virtue," which formally inquire after and seek out the teacher of the Bodhisattva who has leaped forth.

"Such is the great power of knowledge and the supernormal knowledges of these bodhisattvas"—the following five and a half verses constitute the third request for clarification within the formal inquiry.

"Then the Buddhas who are emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha," and so forth, constitutes the introductory section of the inquiry; herein there are two parts, and this below is the second question. From "the emanation Buddhas" onwards, the Bodhisattvas themselves inquire regarding the emanations, and within this, the response to the inquiry is presented in two stages.
The third section, the "Exposition of the Exhortation," contains two parts:
first, from "Śākyamuni says to Maitreya, 'Excellent! onwards, the formal description of Maitreya’s ability to inquire;
second, the exhortation to believe.
The exhortation to faith consists of two parts: prose and verse.
Within the prose section itself, there are two further divisions.

First, from the passage "You all should with one mind" onwards, is the actual exhortation to faith. Specifically, not accepting external heterodoxies is called "donning the armor of diligence," and guarding the path of goodness for oneself is called "arousing a firm resolve."
The second section, concerning the principles of what is to be believed, naturally consists of two parts:

first, there are two lines intended to clarify the meaning of opening up the near to reveal the far; second, there are three lines intended to manifest the benefits for sentient beings through supernatural powers across the three periods of time.
The phrase "the Tathāgata now wishes to reveal" clarifies the opening of the near [teaching], showing that for eighty years the Buddha was not the ultimate Buddha.
The phrase "proclaiming the wisdom of all Buddhas" clarifies the meaning of the distant [teaching], which is twice the aforementioned number.

Regarding the latter three phrases: "The power of the Buddhas' sovereign supernormal abilities" clarifies the Tathāgata’s past power of supernormal abilities for benefiting sentient beings; "the power of the Buddhas’ lion-like springing forth" clarifies the Tathāgata’s present power for benefiting sentient beings; and "the power of the Buddhas’ fierce and great majesty" clarifies the Tathāgata’s future power for benefiting sentient beings.
Within this, these three points of meaning concerning the secret mantras are only fully revealed in the "Life Span" chapter.

From the passage beginning "At that time, the World-Honored One," which constitutes the second verse encouraging faith, there are four lines, each representing one of four intentions: the first verse encourages diligence; the second verse encourages faith; the third verse admonishes against harboring doubt; and the fourth verse admonishes one to listen with a single-minded focus.
"At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken this verse," refers to the second brief exposition on the long duration of his lifespan, which dispels attachments and resolves doubts.
Within this section there are two parts: namely, the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*).
Within the prose section itself, there are two parts.
Regarding Maitreya’s questions above, there are three stages:
first, one verse requesting the teaching by way of inversion; second, thirteen lines constituting the formal inquiry; and third, five and a half lines concluding the request.
Now, I shall answer only the second stage of the primary inquiry.
Within this primary inquiry, there are originally two parts:
first, two lines of verse inquire about the body of the Bodhisattva who has emerged; second, eleven lines inquire as to who his teacher is.
Now, first I shall answer the second question.
Within that question there are two parts:
first, an inquiry regarding the number of his retinue; second, the primary inquiry concerning the teacher himself.
Now, not answering the first [question], he answers only the second: "Who is this teacher?
The Buddha now replies:
"I alone am that teacher."
"These bodhisattvas all [reside] beneath this Sahā world," and so forth, is the sequential response to the first question, which concerns their physical bodies.
The original text above contains two intentions and four passages; here, the latter two stages are not answered. "Beneath this Sahā world" answers the first question.
The question above asked: "From where have they come?"
"Ānanda," from this point downward, he answers the second question posed above. The question asked was:
"By what causes and conditions do these bodhisattvas assemble in one place and simultaneously leap forth?"

"Then he spoke in verse. The following constitutes the second section of verses. However, while the preceding prose (*dīrgha-pada*) originally consisted of two parts, these eight and a half lines of verse now comprise three sections: one line with three phrases praises the first part, "I am his teacher";

the next two lines with three phrases praise the second part, the answer regarding the human body; and the subsequent four lines beginning with "The power of his resolve and mindfulness is firm" praise both preceding parts collectively.
Within the second set of two lines and three phrases, there are four points that correspond to Maitreya.
The phrase "The world is the basis" answers the first question: "From where does it come?"
The line "Constantly practicing the dhūta austerities" answers the second question, "By what causes and conditions is it gathered?
The line "All such sons as these" answers the third question, "Praising all bodhisattvas."
The second half of the verse, "In the Sahā world," answers the fourth question, "From where have they come?

The section beginning with "At that time, Maitreya and the others felt doubt and wonder at this unprecedented event" constitutes the third part, clarifying how the great assembly conceived doubts and offered their request.
Within this section there are two parts:
first, the narrator describes how the great assembly harbors doubts;
second, from the words "They addressed the Buddha, saying" onwards, is the formal request, which itself consists of two parts: the prose and the verse.
Within the long prose section itself, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of doubt; second, the formal request.
Furthermore, each of these two sections is further divided into two sub-sections.

Regarding the clarification that there are two aspects within "doubt": first, from "He addressed the Buddha, saying, 'World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was a prince'" onwards, he clarifies doubt by means of the Dharma;
second, he employs the analogy of the father being young and the son being old, clarifying doubt by means of an illustration.

"Although we have faith in the Buddha’s teachings as he has spoken them according to his needs"—the following constitutes the second part, the formal request, which also has two sections: first, Maitreya describes his own understanding; second, from "However, those who have newly resolved their minds," below, he formally requests [the teaching] for the sake of those who do not yet understand.
"Then he spoke in verse. The fourteen verses below eulogize the preceding section on harboring doubts and making a formal request.
The preceding section consists of two parts:
first, the clarification of the doubts; second, the formal request itself.

Now, these fourteen lines of verse are also divided into two parts: the first eleven lines of verse praise the preceding section on doubt; the second part, consisting of the three lines beginning with "We have heard from the Buddha," praises the preceding section on the formal request.
However, within the aforementioned doubts there are two types:
first, doubts regarding the explanation of the Dharma; second, doubts regarding the explanation of the analogies.
Now, within these eleven verses, they are likewise divided into two parts:
The first five lines of verse constitute the explanation by way of the Dharma (dharmadeśanā), while the remaining six lines constitute the explanation by way of analogy (aupamyadeśanā).
"We have heard from the Buddha" and the following three lines constitute the second part of the verse, which corresponds to the second section of the preceding prose: the formal request.
However, within the original text of the formal request (*adhyeṣaṇā*), there are two parts:
first, Maitreya’s own account of his own understanding; second, the formal request on behalf of those who do not yet understand.
Now, these three lines are also divided into two parts:

The first half-verse praises the first section, which clarifies that Maitreya has already attained understanding; the second part, consisting of two and a half lines, praises the second section above, which is the formal request for instruction on behalf of those who have not yet understood.
Chapter Fifteen: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata. This chapter clarifies that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is measured by the sands of the Ganges; hence it is called the "Lifespan Chapter."

From this point down to the halfway mark of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," this constitutes the fourth section, which extensively explains the long duration of the lifespan in order to sever doubts and engender faith.
Within this fourth section, there are also three parts:

first, this very chapter, which extensively and correctly elucidates the long duration of the lifespan; second, the initial prose section of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," which bestows predictions upon the assembled multitude; and third, Maitreya’s delivery of verses, which expresses his understanding in accord with the Buddha’s prose exposition.
Furthermore, within these three sections, one additional meaning is clarified: there are two points in the first section, three in the second, and four in the third.
Now, regarding the first [section], the primary and extensive explanation of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are two parts:
first, the clarification of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); second, the actual extensive explanation.
Within the section on dependent origination, there are three stages:
First, from "You all should believe the Tathāgata’s words of truth and sincerity" onwards, it clarifies that the Tathāgata first issued three admonitions;

second, from "At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas" onwards, it clarifies that Maitreya and others received the Tathāgata’s command four times, expressing their sole wish for him to speak;
third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, it clarifies that the Tathāgata again issued a further admonition.

"Regarding 'all worlds,' from here until the end of this chapter is the second section, which extensively explains the vastness of his lifespan. Within this, there are two parts: the prose and the verse."
Now, within this prose section itself, there are two parts:
first is the "explanation by way of the Dharma" (dharmadeśanā), which clarifies how [the Buddha] benefits beings over a long duration;
second, from "For example, like a skilled physician" onwards until the end of the prose section, is the "explanation by way of analogy" (aupamyadeśanā).
Now, within the discourse on the Dharma, there should originally be four sections; however, as the text is abbreviated, there are only three.
I shall now explicitly set forth the third section, thereby making it four sections in total.
How is this known? It is fully present in both the subsequent analogies and the verses; therefore, we know that there must be a third section within the prose exposition (*gadya*).
As for the names of the four sections:

First, it clarifies how Śākyamuni Tathāgata benefited sentient beings through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) in past lives; this corresponds to what was stated above in the Introductory Exhortation as "the power of the sovereign supernormal faculties of all Buddhas.

Second, from the passage beginning "Good sons, the Tathāgata sees that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings" onwards, it clarifies how the Tathāgata benefits sentient beings through his supernormal powers in the present; this corresponds to the aforementioned "power of the lion’s majestic stride of all Buddhas. Third, one should clarify how the Tathāgata will benefit sentient beings through his supernormal powers in future lives;

this corresponds to the aforementioned "power of the fierce and great might of all Buddhas. This [third point] was not explicitly mentioned in the preceding Dharma-discourse; it is now brought forth implicitly to correspond with the subsequent parables and verses.

The fourth section, beginning with "Furthermore, son of good family, the dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are thus," universally addresses the concealment and manifestation across the three periods of time; it clarifies that the benefiting of sentient beings is not false and stops the minds of sentient beings from harboring slander.
Within each of these four sections, there are three parts.

Now, regarding the first of these three parts within the section clarifying how the supernatural powers benefit beings in the past, it explains that although the lifespan of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) Buddha is exceedingly long, those who are deluded claim it is short; this is precisely the opening of the meaning of "nearness."

The second section, beginning with "In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable and boundless," clarifies the characteristic of the long duration of the lifespan of the fundamental body (*mūlakāya*) of the *nirmāṇakāya* (the manifested body); that is to say, it reveals the meaning of "remoteness."
The third section, beginning with "From that time onward," correctly clarifies how he benefited sentient beings through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) in past lives.
Within these three sections, there is an increase in the number of meanings explained: the first has one, the second has two, and the third has three.

Now, regarding the statement, "All the world says that Śākyamuni has only now departed from the palace of the Śākyas," this section below is the first, clarifying that although his attainment of Buddhahood was in fact long ago, those who are deluded believe it occurred recently; this first segment is the only one that remains unopened.

"However, good son," from this point downward is the second section, which clarifies the fundamental nature of the family of those who should [attain Buddhahood], and the characteristics of the long duration since he himself attained Buddhahood.
Within this second section, there are two parts:
first, an explanation through the Dharma regarding the extreme length of his lifespan;
The second section, beginning with "For example, five hundred thousand ten-million nayutas," clarifies the use of analogies for the sake of longevity.
Within this analogy, there are three parts:

first, the opening of the analogy of longevity by questioning Maitreya; second, Maitreya’s immediate response that it is indeed long for the Buddha; and third, the Buddha’s synthesis of the analogy of longevity.

"Since that time, I have always been here. This section below constitutes the third part, which correctly clarifies how he benefited sentient beings through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) during past lives.
Within this third section, there are three sub-parts:
first, it clarifies the locations where he benefited sentient beings in the past.
The second section, from "In the meantime" onwards, clarifies that the names for benefiting sentient beings in the past were different;
the third section, from "If there are sentient beings who come to my place" onwards, correctly clarifies the actual benefiting of sentient beings.
Furthermore, within each of these three layers, there are three stages.
Regarding the first, which clarifies the locus of benefit, there are two parts:
first, the statement "Since that time, I have constantly been in this Sahā world" specifically indicates the locus where beings are benefited.

The second statement, beginning with "Furthermore, in other places, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions" and ending with "guiding and benefiting sentient beings," summarizes the benefits for beings in other locations mentioned below.
The second section concerns the different names used for the Buddha’s past acts of benefiting sentient beings, which consists of two stages:

First, it states, "In the interval between these, I spoke of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others, and further mentioned their entry into *nirvāṇa*. This directly presents the difference in the names used for his past acts of benefiting beings, implying that Dīpaṃkara and Ratnarcis were none other than Śākyamuni himself.

Second, it states, "All such [names] are distinguished through skillful means (*upāya*). This explains why the names differ: the underlying intention is precisely to benefit sentient beings through skillful means; therefore, there are simply differences in their names.

From the passage beginning, "Good sons, if there are sentient beings who come to me," and following, the third section correctly elucidates the benefiting of beings. Within this, there are two parts; the four intentions are combined into two pairs, forming two sections:
first, it clarifies the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus; second, it correctly elucidates how the physical form and the teachings benefit beings.

Now, regarding the first pair: "If there are sentient beings who come to me" clarifies that these are the conditions for resonance; "I observe their faculties, such as faith, with my Buddha-eye to discern whether they are sharp or dull" clarifies that this is the wisdom that illuminates those conditions.
Regarding the second pair:

first, from "In accordance with those to be saved, he speaks his own name differently in each place," it is explained that he benefits beings through his physical form; this clarifies benefiting beings by manifesting birth.
Then, "He also manifests the statement that he shall enter nirvana," this clarifies benefiting beings by manifesting extinction.

From the passage "Furthermore, by means of various skillful methods" onwards, it clarifies the benefit of teaching sentient beings. First, it correctly clarifies the differences in the preaching of the Dharma; second, the phrase "able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy" clarifies the attainment of benefits.

"Good sons, the Tathāgata perceives that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings. This is the second section, clarifying how the Tathāgata benefits beings through his supernormal powers in the present age.
Within this, there are also three stages:
first, by reducing four lines, it clarifies how the King’s palace [the Buddha] does not arise yet manifests arising;
second, from the passage "Thus, since I attained Buddhahood, a very long time has passed" onwards, it clarifies how the twin trees [the Buddha] do not perish yet manifest perishing.

The third section in the middle, beginning with "Good sons, as for the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata," clarifies how he benefits sentient beings through supernormal powers after his manifestation in this world and before his parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, within these three stages, there are four layers each:

regarding the first stage, which clarifies that although there is no arising, there is an appearance of arising, there are four points: first, clarifying that the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings who possess the capacity for responsive arousal; second, clarifying the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s birth; third, clarifying that in reality there is no birth; and fourth, explaining the reason why he manifests birth despite being unborn.

Now, when it says, "Good sons, the Tathāgata perceives that sentient beings delight in inferior dharmas, their merit is meager, and their defilements are heavy," this first point clarifies that he perceives the capacity of sentient beings to respond; it is precisely because they delight in inferior dharmas and possess meager merit and heavy defilements that sentient beings move the Buddha to appear in the world.
From the passage, "For this person's sake, I said that by leaving home for a short time, I attained *sambodhi*," this second section clarifies the Tathāgata’s manifestation of birth.
From the passage, "Yet, in reality, it has been a vast period of time since I truly attained Buddhahood," this third section clarifies the meaning of his actual non-birth.

From the passage "But by means of skillful means he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way" onwards is the fourth section; it explains why he manifests birth despite being unborn, which is solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

"O sons of good family, the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata"—from here below is the second section, clarifying the supernormal powers used to benefit sentient beings during the interval after Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s manifestation in this world and before his parinirvāṇa.
Within this section there are also four parts:

first, one and a half lines clarify how the teaching benefits sentient beings; second, from "Or he manifests his own body" onwards, clarifies how his physical form benefits sentient beings; third, the single phrase beginning with "All that he speaks" concludes that the benefit through teaching is not in vain; fourth, from "Why is this so? onwards, provides a general explanation of both the benefits of physical form and teaching.
Furthermore, within these four stages, the first, second, and fourth each have two sub-stages, while the third does not.
Regarding the first teaching, which has two sub-stages:

the first states, "All sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the sake of liberating sentient beings. This general gate clarifies that the teaching benefits all things; every word uttered and every teaching set forth is entirely for the benefit of all beings.
The second statement, "Or speaks of one's own body," refers to the following two lines which clarify the benefit of the teaching according to a specific perspective.
