"Or speaks of one's own body" means speaking of one's own body as another's body;
"or speaks of another's body" means speaking of another's body as one's own body.

Why is this? When it is now said, "or one speaks of one's own body," it means speaking of oneself as another; therefore, we know that this body of mine, sixteen feet in height, is a partial emanation of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, and thus this body does not belong to me.

Regarding the phrase "or speaks of another's body," this means that he speaks of another's body as his own body; therefore, we know that the various emanated Buddhas of the ten directions revealed in the "Treasure Stūpa" chapter are all my own.
Regarding the second category, benefit through physical form (*rūpa-anugraha*), there are two stages:
first, the two phrases beginning with "Or manifesting his own body" clarify the body of the phenomenal realm (*vastu-gata-rūpa*), which is the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*);
second, the two phrases beginning with "Or manifesting his own deeds" clarify the deeds pertaining to the body, which is the secondary environment (*niśraya-vastu*).

Now, regarding the first point, "sometimes manifesting one's own body": this refers to manifesting one's own body as the body of another. Thus, although the beings of this land—the eight classes of the great assembly—are all sentient beings transformed by Śākyamuni, and the Lord of Dharma ought to be Śākyamuni, the one upon the Dharma seat is in fact Amitāyus Buddha; this is precisely manifesting one's own body as the body of another.

Regarding the phrase "or manifesting another's body," this means manifesting the body of another as one's own. Thus, for example, in the Western Land, the people and the fourfold assembly are all manifested by Amitāyus Buddha; yet, while the one upon the Dharma seat ought to be Amitāyus Buddha, the one on the Dharma seat instead has the appearance of Śākyamuni. This is precisely manifesting another's body as one's own body, clarifying both the transformation of another into oneself and the transformation of oneself into another.
"Or he manifests his own affairs. These two lines below constitute the second part of the "benefit through form," clarifying matters pertaining to the Buddha's own person.

Regarding "or he manifests his own affairs": this means manifesting one's own affairs as the affairs of others. Thus, for example, while Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land naturally has the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings there listening to the Dharma, those who constitute that Buddha’s retinue are all disciples within the retinue of Śākyamuni.

Regarding the phrase "or manifesting another's affairs": Śākyamuni himself should have his own retinue, yet his retinue consists entirely of the retinue of Amitāyus Buddha; this is thus an instance of manifesting another's affairs as one's own.
"All that has been spoken is true and not false"—this is the third specific conclusion clarifying that the benefit of the teaching is not in vain; only this third [point] is not further analyzed.

"Why is this so? From here below begins the fourth section, which provides a comprehensive explanation of the two benefits of the physical form and the teaching. Within this explanation, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the benefit of the physical form; second, from "Not as those in the three realms see the three realms" onwards, the explanation of the benefit of the teaching.
Within the explanation of the benefit of manifesting forms, there are three stages:

first, clarifying that the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings who possess responsive capacities for manifestation; second, clarifying the intention behind perceiving such capacities; and third, formally explaining that the benefit of manifesting forms is not in vain.

The statement that “the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are” first clarifies that the Tathāgata perceives the responsive capacities and physical forms of sentient beings within the three realms.

From the phrase “there is no birth-and-death” onwards, there are two lines which constitute the second stage; these clarify the reason why the Tathāgata is able to perceive such capacities. Because of the absence of the faults associated with the [concepts of] person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*), this is divided into two parts: the first line clarifies that the phenomena of arising and ceasing belonging to persons cannot be apprehended, while the subsequent line clarifies that persons who possess those phenomena of arising and ceasing also cannot be apprehended.
Regarding the statement, "There is no birth-and-death, whether as departing or as emerging": This is because the Tathāgata has long since severed the causes of birth; how, then, could there be birth?
If there were necessarily birth, there would have to be death; since birth does not exist, how could there be death?
This is discussed from the perspective of a single lifetime.
Regarding the phrase "whether regressing or emerging," death is what constitutes regression and birth is what constitutes emergence; since there is no death, how could there be further birth?
These two phrases are spoken in reference to successive lifetimes.
The preceding "not having" (wu you) applies as a prefix to each of the four-character units.

The phrase "there is likewise neither one who exists in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa" clarifies that even the person who practices the dharma of birth and death cannot be apprehended; the term "one" (zhe) simply refers to the practitioner.
"Neither real nor unreal, neither thus nor otherwise"—these four phrases constitute the third stage, correctly explaining that the manifested benefit is not in vain.
As for "not real," since it would then necessarily entail arising and ceasing, how could it be real?
If that which is not false provides real benefit through the arising and ceasing of phenomena, how can it be false?
If it is not suchness, then since this reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) ought to have arising and ceasing, how can it be suchness?
Regarding "not different": how could there be a difference between arising and ceasing and the attainment of benefit?
The phrase "not as the three realms" and what follows constitutes the second explanation, clarifying that the benefits of the teaching are not in vain; this also has three stages.
The first stage consists of two phrases, clarifying that the Tathāgata is able to perceive those who possess the capacity for a responsive response to the teaching.
The second [point] clarifies that the capacities (*indriya*) and characteristics of sentient beings differ;
the third clarifies that the benefits of the teachings and their explanations likewise differ.

Regarding the first two phrases: the initial statement, "Not as the triple world perceives the triple world," indicates that the Tathāgata’s perception of capacities is without distinction, thereby showing that while those within the triple world do not perceive the capacities [of others], the Tathāgata perceives them as clearly as forms.
The subsequent statement, "Such matters as these the Tathāgata perceives clearly and without error," correctly clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to perceive the capacities (*indriya*) of beings.

The section beginning with "Because sentient beings possess various natures" constitutes the second part, which sets forth that the capacities of sentient beings consist of their natures (*gotra*), desires (*chanda*), practices (*carita*), and mental recollections (*saṃjñā*); all of these represent the differences in the capacities that respond to the teaching.

From the passage beginning with "Desiring to cause various roots of goodness to arise, he teaches the Dharma in various ways through numerous causes, conditions, parables, and expressions," the third section correctly clarifies that the benefits of the teaching are likewise diverse.

The passage, "In this way, since my attainment of Buddhahood it has been a very long time," clarifies the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers and his benefit to sentient beings in the present world; there are three aspects to this, and here, as the third, it clarifies how he manifests extinction while remaining non-extinct.
There are also four layers of meaning:

first, the statement from "In this way, since my attaining Buddhahood" up to "permanently abiding without extinction" clarifies that birth in the royal palace was not a literal birth; for if it has been a long time since I attained Buddhahood, how could it be considered a literal birth?
The second section, beginning from "O sons of good family, the lifespan I achieved when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted," clarifies non-extinction.

The third part, beginning with "However, now it is not a true parinirvāṇa, yet he proclaims... and ending with "...by these skillful means he teaches and transforms sentient beings," correctly clarifies the manifestation of his passing into extinction.
The fourth section, beginning with "For what reason?
If the Buddha were to remain long in the world," explains the meaning of why he does not pass into extinction while manifesting extinction; it is solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
Within this commentary, there are four stages:

first, the correct explanation of the purpose for manifesting parinirvāṇa. It is because sentient beings see the Tathāgata remaining in the world for a long time that they fail to plant roots of goodness; being greedily attached to the five sensory objects and the six desires, they are unable to conceive the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter or develop a heart of reverence. For this reason, he manifests parinirvāṇa.

The second section, from "Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful expedients" down to "the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter," expresses the meaning that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare and hard to meet.
The third section, "When these sentient beings hear such words," and below, clarifies the signs of obtaining benefits through the manifestation of extinction.
The fourth section, from "Therefore, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass into extinction," and below, summarizes the purpose of manifesting extinction.
Among these four sections, the first contains two layers, the second contains three layers, while the third and fourth stages do not have such divisions. Regarding the two layers in the first:
the first two lines beginning with "For what reason" clarify that if the Buddha were to remain for a long time, it would lead to the non-arising of good and the arising of evil;
the second section, beginning with "If one sees the Tathāgata as eternally abiding and imperishable," clarifies the arising of arrogance and the non-arising of reverence.

Regarding the second section, the praise that a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter, there are three parts: first, the single line beginning with “Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful means” correctly clarifies that a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter;
second, the one and a half lines beginning with “Why is this so? cite the case of evil people who do not encounter a Buddha to explain the meaning of its difficulty;
third, the section beginning with “For this reason” concludes the discussion on its difficulty.
The fact that the lower two stages are not opened can be understood.

It clarifies that sentient beings see the Tathāgata dwelling long in the world yet fail to plant roots of goodness; hereafter, there should have been a section on future supernatural powers benefiting beings, but the text is briefly omitted. For now, let us infer this implicitly as a third section on the future, serving as the basis for the following parable.

"Furthermore, good sons, the dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are all like this. From here below, within the section on the explanation of the Dharma, there are originally four parts; this is the fourth, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s manifestation or concealment throughout the three periods of time to benefit sentient beings is not in vain.
There are also three sections: first, "The Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is thus," which first establishes that the paths of all Buddhas are identical;

second, "For the sake of delivering sentient beings"—this single phrase clarifies the intent behind the Buddhas' dispensation of teachings, specifically showing that the verbal instructions of the Buddhas throughout the three periods of time are all for the purpose of liberating sentient beings;
third, "All is real and not false"—this single phrase precisely clarifies its non-falsity.
"Suppose, for example, there were a skilled physician"—the following is the second part, the illustrative parable (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Within this, there are two sections: first, the opening of the parable; second, the application of the parable (*dārṣṭāntika*).

Now, first, it should be understood that within this section on the illustration there are four parts, which serve as analogies for the four preceding sections of the Dharma-exposition; however, the wording is merely abbreviated.
The first two and a half lines provide an analogy for the past supernormal powers benefiting sentient beings;
the second part, from "The sons later... onwards, consists of twenty-one lines and provides an analogy for the second [section], the present supernormal powers benefiting sentient beings.
The third section, "When the father heard his son," and the following line, serves as an analogy for the third [point]: benefiting beings through future supernormal powers.

The fourth section, "Good son, what do you think? and the following one and a half lines, serves as an analogy for the fourth [point]: that benefiting beings across the three periods of time through supernormal powers is not false.

Regarding the aforementioned three types of past supernormal powers that benefited sentient beings, the present [passage] does not serve as a metaphor for the first two stages; it serves as a metaphor only for the third stage.
Within the third stage above, there are naturally three layers; now, we do not use metaphors for the first two layers, but only provide a metaphor for the third layer. Why is this?
First, it clarifies that although the actual attainment of Buddhahood has been long, those who are deluded perceive it as recent; for this reason, no analogy is provided here.
Second, it clarifies the characteristics of the long duration since the actual attainment of Buddhahood, which itself contains two parts:
first, an explanation in terms of the Dharma (dharmadeśanā), and second, an explanation by way of analogy (aupamya).
The explanation that it has been a long time since [the Buddha] attained Buddhahood naturally consists of three stages:

first, making a simile and questioning Maitreya; second, Maitreya’s response; and third, the Tathāgata’s concluding response. Furthermore, this is not done for the sake of creating a simile; thus, the first two stages do not constitute a simile, but rather, only the third stage provides a simile to clarify how his supernatural powers benefited sentient beings in past lives.

The preceding section consists of three parts; the first, "From that time until now," first clarifies the places where he benefited sentient beings in the past. Within this, there are two levels: the specific and the general. At present, we shall not employ an analogy for this either.

Regarding the second point, concerning the different names for benefiting beings in past times, which itself contains two stages: the first stage precisely clarifies the names for benefiting beings; the second stage explains the reason why these names differ, namely, because they benefit sentient beings. These two stages are not used as metaphors here; therefore, the previous repetitions were both not treated as metaphors.

The third section, from "If there are sentient beings who come to my presence" onwards, correctly elucidates the benefits; now, for about two lines, a formal analogy is provided specifically for this purpose.
Furthermore, in the preceding text, there were originally four points arranged as two pairs; now, they are presented as four sections by way of analogy.

The phrase "For example, a skilled physician who is wise and discerning" serves as the second analogy for illuminating the wisdom that accords with capacities, corresponding to what was stated above: "I observe with the Buddha-eye the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, such as faith."

Regarding the phrase "skilled in prescriptions and medicines, adept at curing all illnesses," this serves as an analogy for the fourth teaching on benefit; it refers back to what was stated above: "Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma, causing them to give rise to a heart of joy."

Now, regarding the phrase "well-versed in prescriptions and medicines": being clearly proficient in the texts of the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s teachings is what is meant by being "well-versed in the meaning of the prescriptions.
Furthermore, thoroughly understanding the underlying principles beneath these twelve divisions of the scriptures is what is meant by "refining the medicine."

The phrase "that man has many sons, numbering ten, twenty, or even up to a hundred" is a metaphor provided in response to the first instance of a responsive capacity, referring back to the previous statement: "If there are sentient beings who come to my presence."

Regarding the phrase "having business matters, he has traveled far to another country," this serves as an analogy for the benefit of the third form [the parinirvāṇa]. Above, there were two statements: first, it was said that "he manifests different names and varying ages in various places according to what is appropriate," which clarifies the benefit of manifesting birth;

this is not used as an analogy here. Second, it was said that "he also manifests the statement that he shall enter nirvana," which clarifies the benefit of manifesting extinction; the current statement, "having business matters, he has traveled far to another country," is precisely used as an analogy for this.

"The sons later drank other poisonous medicines. The following constitutes the second section of the first part, which provides an analogy for benefiting beings through present supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

The original [section] consisted of three parts: first, it clarified birth appearing while there is no birth; next, the middle part clarified benefiting beings through supernatural powers; and here, it clarifies death appearing while there is no death.

Now, an analogy is provided for the three stages: the first one and a half lines serve as the analogy for the first stage; the second section, beginning with "The sons drink poison," serves as the analogy for the second stage; and the third section, beginning with "The others who have lost their minds," serves as the analogy for the third stage.
Regarding the four meanings of "not being born" yet appearing to be born within the present life:

first, it clarifies that sentient beings possess the capacity for responsive awakening; second, it clarifies the manifestation of birth by the Tathāgata; third, it clarifies that, in reality, there is no birth; and fourth, it explains the intent behind not being born while manifesting birth.

Now, I shall provide analogies only for the first two stages. Regarding the passage below that says, "The sons later drank other poisonous medicines," this serves as an analogy for the awakening of the spiritual capacity (*gotra*) caused by the first [type of] view. The preceding statement, "The Tathāgata sees that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings, having meager virtue and heavy defilements," is now followed by: "The sons later drank other poisonous medicines, and when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and confused, rolling about on the ground. This clarifies that although sentient beings had previously undergone the direct transformation of the Tathāgata’s correct teaching, after abandoning it, they encountered evil associates (*pāpa-mitra*) and received the instructions of false views. Each "drank other poisonous medicines" and extensively gave rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, which is like the "medicine taking effect. Subsequently, they transmigrate through the three miserable realms, which is like "rolling about on the ground."

"At that time, his father returns home"—this constitutes the second stage of the present-life analogy mentioned above, which refers to the statement: "For this person's sake, I said that I left home at a young age and attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*."
It is not used as an analogy for the third or fourth [cases].

"The sons drink poison and some lose their original minds"—the following section serves as an analogy for the second point within the present age: the manifestation of supernatural powers to benefit sentient beings during the interval after birth and before death.

The first part consists of four sections: first, clarifying the benefit of the teaching; second, clarifying the benefit of the physical form; third, concluding by clarifying that the benefit of the teaching is not in vain; and fourth, explaining the dual benefits of both the physical form and the teaching.

Now, I provide analogies only for the first three sections and do not provide an explanation for the fourth section, which explains the dual benefits of the physical form and the teaching; thus, the current order is not sequential.

The first two and a half lines serve as an analogy for the second benefit, that of the physical form. From the passage "The father saw his sons suffering in such a manner" onwards, it serves as a retrospective analogy for the first benefit, that of the teaching.
From the passage "Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds" onwards, it serves as an analogy for the third point, concluding that the benefit of the teaching is not in vain.
Now, first, an analogy is provided for the benefit of the second form. However, the original text above consists of two stages:

first, the two phrases beginning with "Or he manifests his own body" clarify the body belonging to the category of phenomena; next, the two phrases beginning with "Or he manifests his own affairs" clarify the affairs belonging to the category of the body.
Within this passage there are three sections: first, from "The sons have drunk poison or lost their original minds" onwards, it clarifies the joy of mental action (*manas-karman*);
second, from "They prostrate, kneel, and inquire after his health" onwards, it clarifies the reverence of physical action (*kāya-karman*);
third, from "We are foolish and ignorant" onwards, it clarifies the request of verbal action (*vāk-karman*).
Now, this serves as an analogy for the two preceding stages.
The passage beginning with "The father saw his sons suffering thus" is inverted to serve as an analogy for the benefit of the second teaching.

However, the original text above consists of two parts. The first states, "All the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of delivering and liberating sentient beings"; this is a general application of the teaching's benefit. Now, first a parable is made for this purpose, concluding with the words, "all are fully complete."
However, the characteristics of dharmas possess names, such as "form" (rūpa);
they possess substantial characteristics, such as "fragrance";
and they possess underlying principles, such as "exquisite flavor."

Therefore, such things as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are called "names. The three types of suffering constitute "suffering" (duḥkha); the afflictions constitute the "origin" (samudaya); the place where the three minds cease is called "cessation" (nirodha); and precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth are called the "path" (mārga). Such categories are termed "essences": it is called "suffering" because it oppresses and afflicts; it is called "origin" because it gathers and invites [suffering]; it is called "cessation" because the dharmas that originally existed return to non-existence; and it is called "path" because it leads universally to all things.
Such as these are called "meanings.
Regarding the phrase "pounding, sifting, and blending" that follows, it serves as a metaphor for the second stage within the aforementioned instruction on benefits.
The previous statement, "either speaking of one's own body or speaking of another's body," wherein suffering, its origin, and so forth are discussed, is "pounding."
“Suffering should be known” and so forth is like the “silk-cotton tree.
“Suffering has been known by me” and so forth is like the “conjunction.
From the passage “Among those sons, those who did not lose their minds,” and below, is the third concluding analogy for the teaching, demonstrating that the benefit is not in vain.
The preceding statement, "All that is spoken is true and not false," has now been established.

From the phrase "others whose minds have become deranged" onwards, the following serves as an analogy for the third point within the aforementioned benefit for beings in the present: that which does not perish even when appearing to perish.
The main text above consists of four sections:

first, clarifying birth and non-birth within the royal palace; second, clarifying extinction and non-extinction; third, clarifying that while [the Buddha] abides, he manifests extinction; and fourth, explaining the meaning of why he does not truly extinguish yet manifests extinction.
Now, this does not serve as an analogy for the first three stages; it serves as an analogy only for the fourth stage. In the preceding explanation, there were originally four parts:

first, [the failure] to give rise to the thought that the Buddha is difficult to encounter or to a mind of reverence while the Buddha was still in the world; second, praising the rarity of encountering a Buddha in the world; third, clarifying that even though he has entered parinirvāṇa, there is still benefit, leading one to generate reverence and plant roots of goodness; and fourth, summarizing the intent behind his entry into parinirvāṇa.
Now, I shall provide analogies only for the first three stages, not for the fourth concluding summary.
Here, the first three lines of reduction serve as the analogy for the first stage;
the remaining five lines from "The father had this thought" onwards serve as the analogy for the second stage, which praises the difficulty of encountering a Buddha in the world.

The third section, consisting of the four lines beginning with "At that time, the sons heard of their father's death," serves as a further analogy for the arising of reverence and the cultivation of wholesome roots.
Now, the meaning of this *Ekottarika* is clarified: the first [section] has two [analogies], the second has three, and the third has four.
Regarding the first analogy having two:

the first half-line and a half, beginning with "The others who had lost their minds saw their father coming," serves as the primary analogy for not generating reverence or performing wholesome deeds when seeing the Buddha while he was in the world.
The second section, beginning with "For what reason? and comprising one line and more, explains why good thoughts do not arise.
Within this second analogy, there are three parts:
first, from "The father thought to himself: 'This son is pitiable'" and below, for two lines and more, it serves as a direct analogy for the difficulty of encountering a Buddha in the world.
The second section, from "Then he spoke these words" for two lines, serves as an analogy for manifesting extinction through skillful means;
the third section, from "Having given this instruction, he again went to another country" for one line, correctly clarifies the analogy for entering nirvana at the twin śāla trees.

As for those disciples who have not yet reached a definitive realization and thus give rise to the notion that they have attained nirvana, it is no different from the sons who, seeing their father arrive in another land, still maintain the thought that he has not died, only reaching the thought that he is dead upon hearing that an envoy has arrived; it is likewise no different from those disciples who, after seeing the cremation of the body and the distribution of the *śarīra* relics, reach the definitive thought that he has entered nirvana.

Regarding the phrase "sending a messenger back," the traditional interpretation explains that it refers specifically to using the eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra* relics remaining after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa as the messenger.
Within the third section, which provides analogies for the arising of reverence and wholesome roots, there are four parts:
first, the single line beginning with "At that time, the sons heard of their father's death" generally clarifies their suffering and distress.

The second section, “And he had this thought: ‘If my father were still alive... (one line), clarifies the benefit derived when his father was present; this internal correspondence can be understood by itself.
The third section, “Now he has abandoned me and died far away in another land... (one line), specifically clarifies the distress caused by the loss of his father.
The fourth section, “His mind then became clear and alert... (the remainder of one line), serves as a direct analogy for the arising of wholesome states.

"The father hears that his son has fully recovered"—the following constitutes the third meaning, serving as an analogy for benefiting sentient beings through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) in future ages; it was not present in the preceding [text] and emerges from the profound depths.
This section also consists of three parts:
first, it clarifies that the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings in future ages who possess the capacity to respond to the appearance of a Buddha;
second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata will accordingly manifest birth, as expressed by the words, "he immediately returns."
The third section, "causing all to see it," precisely clarifies the manner in which benefit is bestowed during future ages by providing an analogy.

The passage beginning with "What do you think, sons of good family? constitutes the fourth section; this serves as the aforementioned fourth analogy, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s manifestation and concealment throughout the three periods of time to benefit sentient beings is not in vain.
"The Buddha said, 'I am also like this. This section below constitutes the second application of the analogy; herein, the third analogy is omitted briefly, and only the remaining three are applied.

Now, first we shall correlate the initial analogy. Of the four original analogies presented above, the single phrase "I am also like this" correlates with the first: "For example, there was a skilled physician, wise and sagacious."

The passage from "Since attaining Buddhahood, for immeasurable and boundless [aeons]" onwards corresponds to the fourth analogy, "Having business matters, he has traveled far to another land," but it does not correspond to the second or third analogies.

The second point above states: "He is proficient in prescriptions and medicines and skillfully treats all manner of illnesses. The third point states: "That man has many children—ten, twenty, or even as many as a hundred."

The section beginning with "For the sake of sentient beings" corresponds to the second analogy, which illustrates the benefit of beings through present supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). While the original [text] contained three analogies, here the first and second are not combined; only the third analogy is combined, namely, that [the Buddha] manifests extinction without actually being extinguished.
Within this third analogy, there are three parts:

first, it clarifies that one does not give rise to reverence when seeing the Buddha; second, it clarifies the difficulty of encountering a Buddha in the world; and third, it clarifies that one still gives rise to reverence even when witnessing his parinirvāṇa.
Now, this section corresponds only to the second analogy—that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter. Within this, there are three stages:

first, from "The father had this thought" onwards, it clarifies that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter; second, from "He then spoke these words" onwards, it clarifies the proclamation of his passing into extinction; third, from "Having given these instructions" onwards, it properly clarifies his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
Now, this corresponds only to the second stage of entering nirvana; it does not correspond to the first or third stages.
From the phrase "There is also none who can" onwards, it corresponds to the fourth analogy above concerning the non-falsity of benefiting sentient beings.
"Then he spoke in verse. Below this are twenty-five and a half lines; the second section of verses is also divided into two parts:
the first twenty and a half lines versify the preceding Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā);
the subsequent five lines, beginning with "Like a physician with skillful means," versify the preceding parable (aupamya).

However, within the text of the aforementioned "Supreme Dharma" (Anuttara-dharma), there are two sections of meaning divided into four; now, these twenty and a half lines are likewise divided into four sections:
the first two lines verseify the benefit of sentient beings in past ages;
the next three lines verseify the benefit of sentient beings in the present age.
Next, there are fourteen and a half lines which, in terms of their meaning, praise the benefit of sentient beings in the future;
next, there is one line which praises how the benefit of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is universally pervasive and not false.
However, among the three original [verses] concerning the past, the first delusion is not versified here; this refers to what is proximate.

Now, the first line of verse specifically explains the aspect of having long since attained Buddhahood, while the subsequent line specifically explains the benefit of sentient beings through supernormal powers.

However, in the second preceding section on the characteristics of long duration, there were both explanations of the Dharma and parables; now, this first line of verse only summarizes the explanation of the Dharma.
The next line summarizes the third preceding section, which correctly clarifies how supernatural powers benefit sentient beings. Regarding that previous section, there were three parts:
the first clarified the locations where beings were transformed, which is not summarized here.
The first two names differ and are not recited;
only the third, which correctly clarifies the benefits, is recited.
The former original [text] has two parts:
First is the mutual resonance between stimulus and response, which I shall not versify here;
I shall only versify the second part, which correctly elucidates the benefits.
Within this correct elucidation of the benefits, there are originally two sections:
The first is the benefit of form (*rūpa-anuśaṃsa*), which I shall not extol here;
I shall extol only the benefit of teaching (*dharma-anuśaṃsa*). Within this benefit of teaching, there are originally two types:

First, the primary clarification of the benefits of the teaching: it is said that "he further expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma through various skillful means," which is what the first half-verse of this stanza praises;

second, the clarification that the teaching accords with sentient beings: it is said that "he is able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy," which is what the second half-verse of this stanza praises.
Regarding the phrase "For the sake of delivering sentient beings," the following three lines praise the aforementioned present benefit of beings. Above, there were three sections;

here, we do not praise the first section on "not being born yet manifesting birth" (four stages), nor do we praise the second section on "correctly clarifying the characteristics of the supernormal powers that benefit beings" (four stages). Now, we only praise the third section on "not ceasing yet manifesting cessation."
However, the original text above consists of four sections:

first, it clarifies that birth in the royal palace is not actual birth; second, it clarifies that extinction is not actual extinction; third, it clarifies that he manifests the proclamation of extinction; and fourth, it explains the underlying intention for manifesting extinction despite not actually being extinguished.
Now, the first and second stages are not versified; only the latter two stages are versified.
The two lines beginning with "In order to deliver sentient beings" versify the third stage, the manifest entry into parinirvāṇa;
the line beginning with "The multitude sees me enter parinirvāṇa" versifies the fourth stage, the explanation.
The original text above consisted of four sections, but now only the third remains, which covers from "sentient beings see their extinction" up to "the mind of reverence.
Following the words "Sentient beings have already believed and submitted," there are fourteen and a half lines; these constitute a thematic summary of the future.
Now, the judgment consists of four sections:
the first, comprising five and a half lines, first clarifies that the Tathāgata will appear in the future world three times;
the second, consisting of one line, indicates the places where he will benefit people in the future.
The third section, consisting of seven lines, resolves doubts;
the fourth section, consisting of one line, concludes by citing the long duration of the Tathāgata’s lifespan.

Regarding the first part, concerning the three times of appearing in the world: the first two lines and a half clarify one appearance in the world; the subsequent line and a half beginning with “In other lands there are sentient beings” further clarifies another appearance in the world; and from the line beginning with “I see all sentient beings,” the following line and a half again clarifies yet another appearance in the world.

The line "With such supernormal powers, he has always remained on Vulture Peak for incalculable eons" indicates that the second [section] immediately follows by showing the places where he will benefit beings in the future.
The seven lines beginning with “When sentient beings see the world at the end of the kalpa being consumed by a great fire” constitute the third section, which clarifies doubts.

Within this, there are four parts: first, the two lines directly clarify that while the kalpa ends, the Pure Land does not perish; second, the line beginning with “The devas beat their celestial drums” clarifies that the Three Jewels are eternally present; third, the two lines beginning with “My Pure Land is not destroyed” clarify that those who have committed offenses do not perceive it; fourth, the two lines beginning with “All those who cultivate merit” clarify that those with blessings and virtue constantly behold it.
The line beginning with "Such is my power of wisdom" (my intellectual capacity) is the fourth [verse], which concludes by citing the long duration of the Tathāgata’s lifespan.
The line beginning with "You who possess wisdom" is the fifth, which praises the aforementioned fourth point—that [the teaching] is not in vain.

"Like a physician with skillful means"—the following five lines of verse are an illustrative parable, which is itself divided into two parts: the first line of verse provides the analogy, while the subsequent four lines apply it to the subject at hand.
However, there were four analogies above; now, for brevity, the third is not versified.
Within this current single verse, the first line versifies the first analogy mentioned above.
The two lines following "For the sake of taming the mad sons" constitute a verse on the second analogy above.
The line "There is no one who can speak falsehoods" constitutes a verse on the non-falsity of the fourth analogy above.
"I am also the Father of the World"—the following four lines of verse combine the metaphors; likewise, the third metaphor is omitted from the combination.
The first half-line of verse combines with the first metaphor above.
The two and a half lines below "For the sake of the perversions of ordinary beings" correspond to the second [verse].
The line beginning with "Every time he thinks to himself" corresponds to the fourth, "Not in vain."
Chapter Sixteen: Distinguishing Merits (Part One) This chapter distinguishes the extent of the merits obtained from hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, it is titled accordingly.

The fourth section of the *Self-Clarification of the Fruit* extensively elucidates the long duration of his lifespan in order to sever doubts and engender faith; it consists of three parts: first, the formal elucidation of the long duration; second, the general bestowal of predictions; and third, from Maitreya’s verses onwards, the explicit demonstration that [the assembly] has likewise attained understanding.

Now, the following section constitutes the second prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Within it, there are three parts: first, the sūtra-narrator describes the manner in which the assembly attained understanding upon hearing the discourse on the lifespan; second, the actual prediction; and third, the sūtra-narrator’s description of the manner in which the devas made offerings.
"At that time, the World-Honored One... and below is the second section, the Bestowal of Prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
Within this Bestowal of Prophecy, there are three types of prophecy:

first, the prophecy regarding the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) by way of elevating the path of increase; second, the prophecy regarding the stage of the fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) by way of diminishing birth; and third, the prophecy for those on the level of external ordinary beings (*bāhya-prthagjana*) who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment.
In the bestowal of prophecies regarding the stage of practice (*bhūmi*), there are generally six kinds of prophecies, which constitute the bestowal of prophecies for the six stages.

The first is "attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This clarifies that a bodhisattva prior to abiding [in the formal stages], upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s description of the signs of the Buddha’s long lifespan, advances to ascend to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Having finally emerged from the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they darkly accord with non-arising; because this is attained for the first time, it receives the name "non-arising. Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* praises the bodhisattva of the first stage, saying: "Born into the family of the Buddhas, their lineage is beyond reproach," concluding with the words, "because of the dharma of immovability."

Second, regarding "attaining the dharani-door of hearing and retaining": this clarifies that a bodhisattva of the first stage, upon hearing the exposition of the lifespan, attains the second stage. *Dharani* is a term from foreign lands; in this region, it is called *zongchi* (total retention).
3. Regarding "attaining the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech," this clarifies that a bodhisattva of the second stage, upon hearing the teaching on the lifespan, attains the third stage.

4. Regarding the "Infinite Revolving Dhāraṇī," this clarifies that a bodhisattva of the third stage, upon hearing the teaching on the lifespan, attains the fourth stage; as for the revolving dhāraṇī, it is a universal retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*).
5. Regarding "being able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma," this clarifies that when Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage hear the teaching on the lifespan, they attain the fifth stage.
This fifth point clarifies non-retrogression.

Sixth, regarding "being able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma": this clarifies that when a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage hears the teaching on the lifespan, they attain the sixth stage. For a Bodhisattva of the sixth stage, the radiance of the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests before them. As for these various types of dharma-gates, they are established again based on estimations; each type of dharma-gate is cited here to correspond to the sixth stage.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, a small chiliocosm" constitutes the second section, which entrusts the stage of the fruit (*phala-bhūmi*) by means of the metaphor of destroying birth (*janma-vidhvamsana*).

Regarding what is called the "entrustment of the stage of the fruit," herein all instances cite the fruit to clarify the destruction of birth. While there are various interpretations among scholars regarding this destruction of birth, for now we shall follow the tradition of our own school: from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) up to the diamond-like mind (*vajra-citta*), there are nine grades that carry out the meaning of destroying birth. Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are the cause of birth, and because for those above the seventh stage the retributive fruits (*vipāka-phala*) have no fixed limit and are difficult to distinguish, we shall here explain the principle based on one specific type of the hundreds of thousands of millions of grades of severed afflictions.
From the seventh stage upward to the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed in nine grades: the superior-superior, superior-middle, and superior-inferior;
the middle-superior, middle-middle, and middle-inferior;
and the inferior-superior, inferior-middle, and inferior-inferior.
What are they? Those to be abandoned at the seventh stage are divided into two categories:
the superior grade and the superior-middle grade.
Those abandoned at the eighth stage are divided into two grades:
the lower-upper and the middle-upper;
those abandoned at the ninth stage are likewise divided into two grades:
The middle-middle grade and the middle-lower grade;
those abandoned at the ten stages are divided into two grades:
the lower-upper grade and the lower-middle grade.
That which is severed by the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) constitutes a single grade, the lowest-of-the-low (*adhamādhamā*).
Since all nine grades of afflictions can thus arise, it is said that there are "nine births.

If one explains *kṣānti* (patience/endurance) according to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, each stage (*bhūmi*) contains three types of patience. To interpret this scriptural passage, there are three patiences for each stage from the seventh upward. When a Bodhisattva of the sixth stage hears the teaching on the lifespan and attains the lower patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*) of the seventh stage, they immediately sever one grade of affliction. The remaining eight grades serve as the causes for eight births; therefore, it is said that "in eight births, one shall attain Bodhi."

When a Bodhisattva on the seventh ground who has attained the stage of "patience" (kṣānti) hears this teaching on the lifespan, they ascend to the stage of "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti) on the seventh ground; at that moment, they immediately sever one grade of affliction, eliminate two grades of rebirth, and shall attain enlightenment after seven more births.

When a Bodhisattva on the seventh stage hears the teaching on the lifespan and advances to the lower patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of the eighth stage, they immediately sever one grade of affliction (*kleśa*). Having already diminished three grades of birth, six grades of affliction remain; thus, through six more births, they shall attain *bodhi*.

When a Bodhisattva on the eighth stage who has attained the level of "patience" (kṣānti) hears this teaching on the lifespan, they advance to the level of "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti) on the eighth stage. At that moment, they immediately sever one grade; having already diminished four grades of birth, five grades remain, meaning they shall attain enlightenment after five more births.

When a Bodhisattva on the eighth stage, having heard the teaching on the lifespan, advances to the lower patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of the ninth stage, they immediately sever one grade of affliction (*kleśa*). Having already diminished five grades of birth, four grades remain; these constitute four more births before they shall attain enlightenment.

When a Bodhisattva of the lower stage of patience (*kṣānti*) in the ninth ground hears the teaching on the lifespan and advances to the upper stage of patience in the ninth ground, they immediately sever one grade [of affliction]. Having already diminished six grades of birth, with three grades of affliction remaining, they shall attain *bodhi* after three more births.

When a Bodhisattva on the ninth stage, having heard the teaching on the lifespan, advances to the lower patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of the tenth stage, they immediately sever one grade [of affliction]. Having already diminished seven grades of birth, with only two grades of affliction remaining, they shall attain enlightenment after two more births.

When a Bodhisattva on the tenth stage hears the teaching on the lifespan and advances to the "upper patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti) of the tenth stage, they immediately sever one grade of affliction (*kleśa*) and have already diminished eight grades of birth. With only one grade of affliction remaining to be severed by the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), they shall attain enlightenment in that very life.
However, because the phrasing is abbreviated, one proceeds from the eighth birth and directly transcends to the fourth birth.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, there are eight worlds" constitutes the third part of the formal bestowal of predictions; it records the prophecy for those who are ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*) and others who are subject to falling back.

"When the Buddha spoke thus regarding these bodhisattvas attaining the great benefit of the Dharma"—from here until the end of the prose section constitutes the third sub-section within the segment on the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). This clarifies how the sūtra compiler describes the manner in which the assembly of devas at that time presented various kinds of offerings.

"At that time, Maitreya spoke these verses. Below this are nineteen lines of verse; this is the third instance of Maitreya speaking verses in praise of the Buddha’s prose exposition, which carries the meaning of "comprehending and understanding" (*anuloma*).
Within this section on "Receiving Understanding," there are four distinct passages:
first, the two lines constitute the initial part, wherein the assembly rejoices because they have attained understanding of the Buddha’s lifespan;
second, the nine-line verse beginning with "Or dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression" corresponds to the prose of the Buddha, which precisely conveys the meaning of receiving understanding.
The third section, "Raining Mandārava Flowers," consists of seven lines. It clarifies Maitreya’s own account of the events at that time; it does not serve as a verse summary of the preceding prose.
Some say: "It summarizes the preceding prose.

Since the preceding portion was composed by the compiler of the sūtra to describe the circumstances of the offerings at that time—and since the Buddha at that moment was neither speaking nor teaching—it would be inappropriate for Maitreya’s verses to summarize the words of the sūtra’s author."
"The Buddha’s fame is heard throughout the ten directions"—this single line is the fourth praise of the Buddha that serves as a summary of the understanding.

"Or dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression"—the nine lines following this constitute the second part, which directly versifies the prose of the Buddha and precisely expresses the meaning of the understanding.
Within the Buddha’s formal bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) above, there are three parts:

first, the prediction concerning the stage of causes; second, the prediction concerning the stage of fruition; and third, the prediction concerning those at the level of ordinary worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
Now, these nine lines are divided into four sections:
first, the three lines beginning with "Or abiding on the stage of non-retrogression" correspond to the first verse above, which bestows the prediction of the causal stage;

second, the four lines beginning with "Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm" correspond to the second verse above, which bestows the prediction of the resultant stage.

The third section, "Furthermore, there are sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds," consists of one line which versifies the third [part] above: the bestowal of predictions upon those who have resolved their minds while still being external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
The fourth section, beginning with "The World-Honored One speaks of the immeasurable," consists of one line that summarizes the bestowal of predictions; this does not versify what precedes it.
"Raining down māndārava flowers"—the seven lines following this constitute the third section, in which Maitreya himself describes the events of that time.
"The Buddha’s name is heard throughout the ten directions"—this single line is the fourth section, praising the Buddha and concluding with an expression of understanding.

Section on the Circulation (16): Chapter on the Differentiation of Merits (Part Two). From the passage "At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" onwards, for eleven chapters and a half, constitutes the third major section: the discourse on the circulation [of the sutra].
The preface to the section on circulation consists of two parts:
from here down to the end of the tenth chapter and a half, the "Chapter on King Wondrous Adornment," constitutes the first part, the circulation for transforming others;
the second part consists of the remaining "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation," which is the circulation for one's own practice.
Previously, it was further explained that within each of the two modes of circulation there are three parts.

Now, regarding the three parts of the circulation for the sake of others (*parārtha-pravartana*), first, from here down through the three and a half chapters ending with the "Chapter on the Never-Slighting One" (*Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*), the text praises the profound merit and heavy reward of those who can circulate [the teaching], and thus commands those who shall transmit the sutra. This refers specifically to the bodhisattvas of the lower direction, as the people of the lower direction had not yet been addressed by the previous command.

The second consists of the first five lines of one passage from the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhivikrīḍita-parivarta*), which records the command given to the assembly from the lower regions who were capable of transmitting the sutra.

The third comprises six and a half chapters of scripture, beginning from the point in the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" where "the Buddha extended his broad and long tongue before the great assembly of Mañjuśrī," and extending through the entirety of the "Chapter on King Suśobhana"; this constitutes the formal entrustment.
Within these three sections, the first and the third are each divided into three parts, while the middle one is not.
To clarify, there are three aspects within the first section:

first, this half-chapter addresses the person who can master the sutra from the perspective of the cause; second, the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (Suixi pin) addresses the person who can master the sutra by citing both cause and effect; and third, the two chapters "The Merits of the Dharma Master" (Fashi gongde) and "Never Disparaging" (Changbuling) address the person who can master the sutra by citing only the result.

How is this known? This chapter clarifies the merit of hearing the sutra; this merit of hearing the sutra is the cause. The subsequent two chapters clarify the attainment of the purity of the six sense faculties, which is the fruit.

In the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit," the merit of hearing this sutra is weighed and compared, and it is also clarified that one attains the perfection of the marks of a Great Man; thus, we know that both cause and effect are elucidated therein.
Within this section on the three periods of time, there are two parts each.
To clarify the first period, there are two:

first, explaining the merit of four types of people hearing the sutra while the Buddha is in the world; second, explaining the merit of five types of people hearing the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Now, regarding the first point—clarifying the four classes of people while the Buddha was in the world—it is divided into four sections:
within the first class of people, there are both prose passages and verse hymns, whereas the remaining three classes all lack verse hymns.
"Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching," this refers to persons of the second grade.
"How much more so for those who hear this sutra extensively," this refers to the merit of hearing the sutra for persons of the third grade while the Buddha is in the world.

“Ajita, if any man or woman hears of the long duration of my lifespan and believes and understands it with a profound mind, they shall see the Buddha as always dwelling on Vulture Peak. This is the merit of the fourth grade of people hearing the sutra while the Buddha is in the world.

Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata" until the end of this chapter constitutes the second section, which clarifies the merit of five types of persons hearing the sutra after the Buddha’s extinction; it consists of two parts: the prose and the verses.

Among the five classes of persons described in the prose section, only the first class is clarified as being those who, upon hearing the sutra, immediately give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and do not produce slander; yet this person’s merit is the most inferior and is not yet subject to formal calculation. Since this class consists only of the prose and lacks the verses, this first class of persons is set aside to be brought into the "Chapter on the Merit of Sympathetic Joy" (*Anumodanā-puṇya-parivarta*) for subsequent evaluation.

Even if one were to practice the giving of kingdoms and cities, and even go so far as to teach and transform all sentient beings so that they all attain the four fruits of the path, if one does not oneself act in this manner as a person of the foremost class who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), this point shall be further clarified in the chapter on "The Merit of Sympathetic Joy."

The second section, "How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it—such persons shall carry the Tathāgata upon their heads," refers to the merit of the second class of people hearing this sutra. This does not mean that they actually carry the Tathāgata on their heads; it simply means that their reverence for the Tathāgata is no different from carrying him upon one's head.
The third section, "Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa one hears this sutra," refers to the merit of hearing the sutra for those of the third grade.
The fourth section, "How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while also practicing giving," refers to the merit of hearing the sutra for those of the fourth grade.
The fifth section, beginning with "If a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra," describes the merit of the person who hears the sutra in the fifth chapter.
The second verse serves as a summary of the prose; it does not summarize the person from the first chapter.
The following nineteen and a half verses are divided into four sections:
the first five and a half verses praise the persons mentioned in the second chapter;
"If one can uphold this sutra," the following three verses praise the persons mentioned in the third chapter.
"If there are those with faith and understanding"—the three lines below this surpass the persons of the fifth chapter mentioned above;
"how much more so for those who uphold this sutra while also observing the precepts"—the eight lines below this reiterate the persons of the fourth chapter mentioned above.

Chapter Seventeen: The Merit of Rejoicing. This chapter measures the extent of the merit obtained by one who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and gives rise to a mind of rejoicing; thus it serves as the title of this section.

Regarding the first section, "Identifying Those Who Transmit the Sutra," there are originally three parts. The first half of this fascicle concludes the identification of those who transmit the sutra by way of the cause (*hetu*). This present fascicle is the second part, which identifies those who transmit the sutra by way of both cause and effect (*hetu-phala*). The remaining two fascicles, "The Merits of the Dharma-preacher" and "Never-Despising," constitute the third part; these clarify the attainment of the retribution of the purity of the six sense organs by way of the result alone (*phala-mātra*), thereby identifying those who transmit the sutra.
Within the three sections of the fundamental discourse, this is further divided into two parts.
In this chapter, there are two:
first, the inquiry of Maitreya, and second, the response of the Tathāgata.

What Maitreya has now asked concerns the very person described in the preceding "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" as the lowest among the five grades of people who appear after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The preceding passage stated, "Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if there is someone who hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy. Since this person has not yet been evaluated, Maitreya now initiates his inquiry; therefore, that person is brought into this chapter to have their merit evaluated, and Maitreya is now specifically asking about this individual.
Furthermore, within each of these two sections there are two parts.
Regarding the two parts in the questions: it can be understood that the prose and the verse constitute the two.
Regarding the two parts in the Buddha’s answers: these likewise consist of the prose and the verse as the two.
However, in the prose response of the Buddha, the measurement of the merit of the five classes of people is established in five sections:

from the beginning down to the thirty-second and a half lines, it clarifies that the merit of the first person—through the successive instruction of fifty people, culminating in the fiftieth person hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—is immeasurable, let alone the merit of the very first person;
the second class of people, who intentionally come to the monastic quarters, possess immeasurable merit; [and so forth].
The third type of person is one who, at the place of discourse, encourages others to sit and listen, thereby attaining the signs of karmic fruition;
the fourth type of person further encourages others outside the assembly to go and listen;
the fifth type of person is able to listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and is also able to expound the Dharma for others.
Within the first category of persons, there are six stages:

first, the preliminary comparison followed by the selection of fifty people; second, the injunction to listen attentively; third, the posing of questions to Maitreya regarding the fifty people; fourth, Maitreya’s response; fifth, the Buddha’s confirmation and clarification; and sixth, the conclusion of the response.
Moreover, regarding the merit of this person, it is limited to the number of fifty people; there are three ways in which these fifty people teach one another:
first, they surpass each other; second, they are equal; and third, they fall short of one another.

Now, regarding these three types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), there are those that are difficult and those that are easy to attain: those that are superior are difficult to obtain, those that are equal are rare, while only those that are inferior are common.

Now, according to the majority of treatises, even the last person among the fifty who heard it was not inferior; this person’s merit is already immeasurable, boundless, unspeakable, and incalculable—how much more so for the first person to hear the sutra and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy?
This passage provides the direct answer to Maitreya’s question.

From the words "Ajita, as for that fiftieth person" onwards constitutes the second stage; intending to take the measure of the fiftieth person and thereby bring out the measure of the first person, it exhorts Maitreya to listen attentively.

From the passage beginning "If four hundred trillion... onwards is the third stage. Here, he asks Maitreya about the merit obtained from performing the two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—clarifying that a donor uses precious treasures to give to sentient beings of the four modes of birth, bestowing upon each and every being as much gold, silver, and rare jewels as would fill the entire Jambudvīpa.

Furthermore, even if one were to teach and transform various sentient beings, causing them all to attain the four fruits of the śrāvaka path, the merit of this donor would still not equal that of the fiftieth person who hears a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra and rejoices in it.
The objector says:
"How can beings born from the four modes of birth, such as snakes and vipers, possess the characteristics of white hair and wrinkled faces?
Furthermore, how is it that they are now riding in chariots and wearing necklaces?"
The ancient commentary states:

"Suppose these sentient beings were all simultaneously transformed into humans, and one were then to bestow precious jewels upon them as gifts; having made these offerings, one might subsequently teach and transform them so that they attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa. It is for this reason that it is said thus.
Yet, even this does not equal giving rise to a single thought of sympathetic joy upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
The commentary explains:

"Although this person suddenly renounced his kingdom and city and further attained the four fruits of the śramaṇa, these are merely worldly fruits of retribution and do not exempt one from birth and death."

Now, since this person has heard what is taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—that five hundred yojanas must be traversed and that the state of Buddhahood, which is supremely wondrous, must be sought—they then give rise to a single thought of resolve, with a single-minded intent to leave behind this cycle of birth and death and seek that fruit of Buddhahood; such merit is truly vast.

However, the Bodhisattva fundamentally takes self-cultivation as the foundation and the transformation of others as the primary goal; having resolved to cross five hundred *yojanas* to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he does so with a mind to transform others, causing the sentient beings of the six realms to leave behind the five hundred perilous difficulties and together attain the perfectly ultimate, wondrous fruit. Therefore, this mind is profound and vast, truly not comparable to the bestowal of kingdoms, cities, or the four fruits of the śrāvaka path.

Furthermore, it is heard that by planting blessings through this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there is no [fruit] like this; one possesses the supreme and wondrous retribution of the purity of the six sense faculties, which cannot be calculated by number.
The questioner said:

“In the past, among the three vehicles, bodhisattvas gave rise to the intention of seeking afar based on their own resolve for broad transformation. If this is so, what is the difference between now and then?”
The commentator says:

"In the past, the Bodhisattva spoke only of severing the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*) as leading to ultimate attainment. Today, through skillful means, he further clarifies that the path is perilous, difficult, and far-reaching, and that one must go forth and deliver others. Thus, whereas in the past the two practices of self-cultivation and transforming others were not yet perfected, today both self-cultivation and the transformation of others are fully accomplished. One must not use the limited and narrow scope of the past to categorize the vast and expansive scope of the present."
The section from "Maitreya addressed the Buddha" onwards is the fourth; herein the Tathāgata immediately ascertains this person’s merit.
The section from "The Buddha told Maitreya: 'I shall now distinguish and speak to you'" onwards is the fifth.
From the passage "Ajita, such is the fiftieth person" onwards, this is the sixth Buddha’s concluding response, illustrating by comparison the merit of this person.

From the passage "Furthermore, Ajita, if a person goes to a monastery for the sake of this sutra," onwards, this concerns the merit of the second person; the first person was the primary subject of the comparative evaluation.
The four individuals below are all extensively described.
"If there is another person who sits in a place where the Dharma is being preached"—this and what follows refers to the third person.

"Ānanda, if there is another person who speaks to yet another person"—the following section concerns the fourth type of person, clarifying that even those outside the assembly, upon hearing the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, are encouraged to go and listen.
"Ānanda, you should observe this. The following refers to the fifth person.
"And he spoke in verse"—the eighteen lines of verse below constitute the second part of the response, which summarizes the five persons mentioned in the preceding prose.

First, there are nine lines summarizing the first person; next, there are five lines summarizing the fourth person by skipping ahead; next, there are two lines summarizing the second person in retrospect; next, there is one line summarizing the third person; and finally, there is one line summarizing the fifth person mentioned above.

Originally, there were six stages among those foremost among men; now, within these nine practices, the fourth is not recited. Here, the first one and a half lines of verse praise the first stage, while the subsequent portion takes up the fiftieth person.
The half-line, "The last person shall obtain merit," praises the second exhortation to listen attentively.
The five lines beginning with "Such a great donor" praise the third section above, which raises the two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—to question Maitreya.

Since the fourth section, Maitreya’s response to the Buddha, is not versified here, this single line at the very end of the fiftieth [section] corresponds to the fifth section: the Tathāgata’s summary and reconciliation.
The single line, "Thus heard by successive transmission," is a verse summarizing the sixth point of the preceding response.
The following five lines, beginning with "If one encourages even a single person," likewise skip ahead to summarize the fourth person mentioned above.
"If one intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling"—these two lines below follow as a summary verse for the second type of person mentioned above.
"If at a place where the Dharma is being preached"—this single line summarizes the third type of person mentioned above.
"How much more so for one with a single mind"—this single line summarizes the fifth type of person mentioned above.

Chapter 18: The Merits of the Dharma Master (*Dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa-parivarta*). This chapter elucidates the five kinds of merits of a Dharma master—namely, upholding, reading, reciting, explaining, and copying—and for this reason, the compiler has designated it as a chapter title.

The following two chapters constitute the third section, which specifically addresses individuals who, based on the gateway of the fruit, attain mastery over both life and sustenance through the sūtras.
Within this section there are also two parts:

first, this chapter, which correctly elucidates the individuals who, based on the fruit, attain mastery over life and sustenance through the sūtras; second, the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," which serves as proof that this karmic retribution is not in vain.

Now, within this chapter itself, there are two sections: first, a general explanation of how hearing the sutra results in the karmic reward of the purification of the six sense faculties; second, a detailed and specific exposition of the characteristics of the purification of these six faculties.

From the passage "Good sons and good daughters, by virtue of their birth from their parents" onwards, the eyes obtain eight hundred [merits], the nose obtains eight hundred, and the body obtains eight hundred; three times eight is twenty-four, which together constitute two thousand four hundred merits.
Next, the ear attains twelve hundred, the tongue attains twelve hundred, and the mind attains twelve hundred; combined, these total three thousand six hundred.
When added to the previous total, they constitute six thousand merits. These six thousand merits all cite the causes to designate the results.
When sentient beings give rise to goodness, it does not transcend the three karmas and the ten wholesome paths of action.
These ten wholesome paths are twofold: first, the goodness of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*); second, the goodness of performance (*anabhisamskāra-kuśala*).
For now, we shall discuss them with reference to the goodness of restraint; in this practice of the ten wholesome paths, each element mutually illuminates and assists the others.

Why is this? It is because, for example, taking the precept against killing as the primary foundation, one subsequently cultivates the other nine wholesome factors to assist its fulfillment; continuing in this manner until taking right view as the head, with the other nine assisting its fulfillment—thus, by mutually supporting one another, they collectively constitute the hundred wholesome actions.
However, based on these one hundred good deeds, the intention of a bodhisattva is established as four hundred.
Why is this? Performing one hundred good deeds oneself constitutes the first hundred;
To teach others to perform one hundred good deeds is the second hundred;
to rejoice in others performing one hundred good deeds is the third hundred;
and to praise those who perform one hundred good deeds is the fourth hundred.

However, these four hundred [virtues] are calculated based on five types of Dharma-preachers; yet, even considering only the preacher who upholds [the Dharma], there are likewise four hundred virtues.

Why is this? Upholding it oneself, teaching others to uphold it, rejoicing in others' upholding of it, and praising others' upholding of it—each constitutes one hundred, which together make four hundred virtues.

When reading the sutras, there are likewise four hundred merits; when reciting the sutras, there are likewise four hundred merits; explaining them brings another four hundred, and transcribing them brings another four hundred. Thus, four times five makes twenty, which constitutes two thousand merits.

However, the mind of a Bodhisattva in this stage desires to advance all myriad practices; first, there are two thousand of the lower grade, followed by the cultivation of two thousand of the middle grade, and then the cultivation of two thousand of the upper grade, thereby accomplishing six thousand merits.

These six thousand merits together induce the attainment of a single faculty (indriya), just as the five precepts together result in a human body. This is intended merely to demonstrate the application of one's own practice and the transformation of others—distinguishing between their clarity and obscurity—across the six faculties. Three faculties involve a lesser application of self-practice and transforming others, while three faculties involve a superior application; therefore, three faculties each receive eight hundred merits, and three faculties each receive twelve hundred.
The treatise states:
"Gold and silver have no fragrance; the diamond has no taste.
How can it now be said that gold, silver, and all manner of precious gems can fully perceive fragrances upon smelling them?
The commentary explains:
Just as one knows that gold and silver are present merely by smelling their fragrance, so too the karmic fruit of upholding this sutra is inconceivable;
it is like a person of omniscience who employs all six sense faculties simultaneously to perceive all sensory objects.

Chapter Nineteen: Never Disparaging This chapter clarifies that when the Tathāgata was formerly a bodhisattva, he preached to the fourfold assembly on the principle of the ultimate convergence [of all beings]. He bestowed predictions upon the fourfold assembly that they would attain Buddhahood, constantly speaking the words, "I do not disparage you. Because the fourfold assembly continued to address this bodhisattva as "Never Disparaging," this serves as the title of the chapter.

Regarding the citation of those who attained the fruit and mastery of life as found in the sūtras, there are two sections; this chapter is the second, citing the case of Viśeṣacinti (Not-Light) to demonstrate that his present attainment of the fruit of retribution proves [the teaching] is not false.
Now, within this chapter, there is a general division into two sections:
first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (śloka).
Within the prose section, there are five sub-sections:

First, by contrasting right and wrong, he seeks out those who can explain the sutra; second, he first discusses the fundamental origin of the matter; third, he correctly elucidates the actual event; fourth, he praises the sutra; and fifth, based on this, he further exhorts people to receive and uphold it.
Now, regarding the mention of right and wrong: if there are those who slander this sutra, they will receive an evil retribution, as described at the end of the verses in the "Fire House" chapter.
If one is able to master this sutra, they will obtain the karmic rewards of the six sense faculties, as clarified in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master."
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in ages long past"—the following constitutes the second section of this chapter, which first clarifies the origin of the event.

"At that time, among twenty trillion Bhagavats named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvāsana-rāja), there was a bodhisattva"—the following constitutes the third section, which properly clarifies the fundamental narrative.
Now, within this context, there are two parts:
first, the prior clarification of the two causes—good and evil deeds; second, from "When that bhikṣu is approaching death" onwards, the clarification of the two results—good and evil fruits.
Now, within the context of causes consisting of both clarity and practice, there are naturally six stages in which good and evil alternate.
