First, I shall clarify the prostrations of Never-Disparaging, which records the cultivation of good causes for the sake of others' future fruits.
The second clarifies the causes for the conduct of evil persons, beginning from "among the fourfold assembly.
The third clarifies the causes for the virtuous conduct of this bodhisattva, beginning from "having thus passed many years" and below.
The fourth further clarifies the causes for the evil deeds of wicked people; this begins from the passage "When these words were spoken.
The fifth further clarifies the causes for the good deeds of this bodhisattva; this begins from the passage "He fled and dwelt far away."
The sixth section further clarifies the causes for the evil deeds of wicked people; this begins from the passage "Because he constantly spoke these words.
The section beginning with "When that bhikṣu was about to die" is the second part, clarifying the attainment of the two fruits of good and evil.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies that virtuous people obtain virtuous fruits, namely the case of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging;
second, it clarifies that evil people obtain evil fruits.
Within these two layers, there are two parts each.
Regarding the first, which clarifies the attainment of wholesome fruits, there are two:
first, it clarifies the attainment of the fruit; second, it reconciles ancient and modern views.
Furthermore, within the realization of the fruit, there are naturally six stages:

first, it is explained that because he previously heard the twenty quadrillion verses spoken by King Awesome Sound (Vaiśvānara-svara-rāja), he immediately attained the retribution of the six sense faculties.

The second section, from "Having attained this purification of the six sense faculties" onwards, clarifies the further increase in lifespan and the fruit of maturation in teaching and transforming sentient beings.
The third section, from "After his life has ended" onwards, clarifies that he again encountered the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
The fourth section, beginning with "For this reason," clarifies his encounter with the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja.

The fifth section, beginning with "Mahāsthāmaprāpta was the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging," clarifies that he further encountered thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas who preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The sixth section, from "Having accomplished merit, he shall become a Buddha," clarifies his attainment of Buddhahood.
"What do you think, Mahāsthāmaprāpta?"—the following section is the second reconciliation within the discussion of virtuous results.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time, the fourfold assembly"—this is the second [section], clarifying how evil persons obtain evil results; herein there are also two parts:
first, three layers of explanation to clarify the attainment of evil results, and second, the reconciliation thereof.
Regarding the threefold clarification of obtaining evil retribution:
first, it clarifies that one does not encounter the Triple Gem;
second, from the passage beginning with "for a thousand kalpas" onwards, it correctly clarifies the actual attainment of evil retribution.

Third, from the passage "Having completed these offenses" onwards, it shows that one still attains wondrous fruits; this demonstrates that the Bodhisattva does not act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings, precisely because the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging acted as an external condition for their transformation.
"What do you think, Mahāsthāmaprāpta?"—the following constitutes the second section, which correlates the ancient with the present.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this is the Lotus Sūtra"—the following constitutes the fourth praise of the sūtra within the prose section.
"Therefore, all bodhisattvas"—from here below is the fifth section, which continues to exhort others to accept and uphold [the teaching].
"And he spoke in verse"—from here below are nineteen and a half lines; this is the second part of this chapter, a reiteration in verse of the preceding prose.
In the preceding prose section there were five stages; here, the first stage—which raised the issue of right and wrong—is not versified.
Now, the first one and a half lines first versify the second matter, the fundamental basis;
from "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" onwards, these fourteen lines versify the third matter, the original narrative.
Next are two lines;
these verses praise the fourth section of the sutra above.
The following two lines praise the fifth section above, which consists of exhortations and encouragement.
In the third section above, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of the two causes—good and evil deeds; second, the clarification of the two results obtained from good and evil deeds.
Within the current fourteen stanzas, four stanzas clarify the causal practice, while ten stanzas clarify the attainment of the results.
Regarding what was explained above concerning the six stages within the causes for practice, here we obtain only three types in verse:
the first three lines first provide a verse on the cause of practicing good;
next, the half-line stating "When people have heard it" provides a verse on the cause of practicing evil.
The latter half of the verse on "the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" praises the good causes.
From the line "When his offenses have been exhausted," the following ten lines praise the attainment of results, which are also divided into two parts:
the first five lines praise the good results, and the subsequent five lines praise the evil results.
Within the section on the supreme fruits of goodness, there are originally two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the fruits of goodness; second, the reconciliation and integration.
Herein, four and a half verses explain the fruits, while the remaining half verse provides the reconciliation and integration.
In the preceding section, which clearly elucidated the fruits, there were originally six; now, only three are presented in verse:
the first, second, and third.
The passage beginning with "At that time, the fourfold assembly" clarifies how wicked people obtain the fruit.
In the preceding prose section, there were originally two parts:
first, the formal exposition on attaining the fruit; second, the reconciliation and clarification.
Now, one and a half verses concern the attainment of the fruit, while three and a half verses concern the reconciliation and clarification.

In the original text, there were three [sections] within the "Attaining the Fruit" (上得果); here, only the fourth is versified. The two lines beginning with "Billions upon billions of kalpas" (億億萬劫) versify the fourth section of the prose, which is the praise of the sutra.
The two lines beginning with "Therefore, the practitioner" praise and encourage the upholding [of the teaching], as found in the fifth section of the prose commentary.
Chapter 20, "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Ṛddhipāda): This chapter clarifies that the Tathāgata possesses eight kinds of supernatural powers; thus, this serves as the title of the chapter.

Regarding the dissemination for the sake of transforming others, there were originally three sections. In this chapter, the first five lines of single characters constitute the second section, which is capable of disseminating the sutra;
the third section, concerning receiving the mandate to disseminate, is not opened here.
"At that time, the World-Honored One"— the six and a half fascicles of scripture following this constitute the third section, which correctly clarifies how the Tathāgata formally entrusts the sūtra.
As previously explained, within these three sections, the first and the last each contain three sub-sections, while the middle one does not.
Now, regarding this intermediate section, there are three parts:
first, the preceding half-chapter clarifies the causal origin of the entrustment;
second, the chapter "Entrustment" (*Parīndanā*) itself clarifies the actual entrustment.
The third [section] consists of five chapters of sutra, which clearly elucidate the general principles and rules for the application of phenomena.
Now, within the *Pratītyasamutpāda* (Dependent Origination) itself, there are two sections:
first, the prose (*gadya*), and second, the verse (*śloka*).
Within this long discourse, there are naturally two sections:
first, the elucidation of supernatural powers; second, the praise of this sutra based on those powers and the exhortation to practice it.
For now, within the elucidation of supernatural powers, there are two parts:
First, the assembly for whom this was performed is listed; second, the supernatural powers are correctly explained, totaling eight kinds of supernatural power.
The text is divided into six sections:
the first section explains the long tongue and the emission of light together as one unit.
The section beginning with "At one time" is the second segment, which further clarifies two kinds of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*): namely, the two powers of coughing and snapping the fingers.

The section beginning with "The earth shook" is the third segment, which clarifies the fifth supernatural power; it intends to cause all sentient beings of the six realms to be inspired to apply themselves to the meaning of this sutra.

The section beginning with "Among those sentient beings" constitutes the fourth segment; this elucidates the sixth supernatural power, specifically clarifying how the Tathāgata’s power enables the great assembly to see clearly throughout the ten directions.

The section beginning with "At that moment, the various devas" constitutes the fifth segment, which clarifies the seventh supernatural power; it explains how the devas proclaim and call out so as to cause sentient beings to make offerings.

The section beginning with "the various objects scattered" constitutes the sixth segment, clarifying the eighth supernatural power; it signifies that the various virtues cultivated bring about the fruit of Buddhahood in the future.

"At that time, the Buddha addressed Superior Progress and the others. This section below constitutes the second part of the prose (*gadya*), wherein he continues to praise the sūtra and exhort practice.
"And he spoke in verse": the following seventeen lines of verse constitute the second part, which is a summary (*śloka*) of the preceding prose.
This is also divided into two parts:
the first four lines of verse praise the first section above, which first clarifies the eight kinds of supernormal powers;
the second part, consisting of thirteen lines beginning with "Because of entrusting this sutra," praises the second section above, which extols the sutra and exhorts its practice.
Chapter 21: Entrustment (Parindanā-parivarta). This chapter is the twenty-first; it is titled as such because it correctly elucidates the time when the Tathāgata entrusted the sutra to the assembly.
This chapter is divided into three major sections:

first, the formal entrustment of the sutra by the Tathāgata; second, the acceptance of this entrustment by the assembly; and third, the manifestation by the Tathāgata of the signs that the matter of entrustment is concluded.
Furthermore, within each of these three sections there are three parts.

Regarding the first part, which correctly explains the entrustment of the sutra, there are three sub-sections: the first correctly clarifies the entrustment of the sutra itself; [the second concerns the entrustment of the Dharma; and the third concerns the entrustment of the Sangha].
The second [section], explaining the meaning of the entrustment, begins with "Why is this so?";
the third, concluding the entrustment, begins from "You all should also... onwards.
"At that time, the various bodhisattvas... From here below is the second section on receiving the entrustment, which also has three parts:
first, clarifying the joy within the inner mind;
second, from "increasing their reverence" onwards, clarifying the expression of respect through outward form.
The third section, "Simultaneously Uttering Words," correctly clarifies the formal reception of the entrustment.
From the passage "At that time, Śākyamuni... onwards is the third segment, which demonstrates the signs that the matter of the entrustment is concluded; it also consists of three parts:
first, the initial proclamation that the various emanated Buddhas each return to their respective abodes.
The second part concerns the closing of the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, beginning from the word "Prabhūtaratna" below;
the third part clarifies the joy of the great assembly, beginning from the phrase "when these words were spoken" below.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja. This chapter elucidates how Bhaiṣajyarāja practiced austerities in the past to master this sutra; thus, it takes his name as its title.
Below this are five chapters; this constitutes the third section, which demonstrates the rules for the universal application of the sutra.

Although the rules were already clarified within the preceding explanation of the causes, the reason they are clarified again here is that while the previous section on "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber" and so forth clarified the Dharma as the rule for universal application, this section specifically takes figures such as Bhaiṣajyarāja as the rule in terms of persons.
These five chapters demonstrate the method for others to universally propagate the sutra; they are now divided into three sections:
First, the three chapters on "Bhaiṣajyarāja," "Gandhavyūha," and "Avalokiteśvara" correctly demonstrate the method for others to universally propagate the sutra.

Second, the "Dhāraṇī Chapter" encourages those in the assembly who might regress or fall away by expounding divine mantras to protect these propagators of the sutra; therefore, one must not fail to disseminate the sutra.

The third chapter, "The Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment," demonstrates that the transmission of this sutra brings benefit, specifically by transforming the father’s false views so that he returns to correct understanding.
Now, within the first section of this chapter, there are two sub-sections:
first, this "Chapter on the Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta) first clarifies how the practice of asceticism for the sake of transmitting the sutra serves as a model for sentient beings.

The second section, consisting of the two chapters on "Wonderful Sound" (Ghoṣadatta) and "Avalokiteśvara," clarifies how the Universal Manifestation of Physical Form (Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana) propagates the sutra and benefits sentient beings.
If one explains the ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja, the same applies to the [other] two individuals below;

and if one explains how the latter two individuals propagate the sutra and benefit beings through the Universal Manifestation of Physical Form, it should likewise apply to Bhaiṣajyarāja. Therefore, these cases are presented alternately to mutually illuminate one another like reflections and echoes.

However, this Medicine King is a bodhisattva from our own land, while Wonderful Sound, Avalokiteśvara, and others are great beings from other lands. Specifically, Wonderful Sound is a bodhisattva from the East, and Avalokiteśvara is a great being from the West. Although they differ in their respective directions, they gather together in one place; this is intended to manifest the principle of returning to the same source and to verify the teaching of non-duality.
Now, for the sake of this chapter, it shall be broadly divided into four sections:

first, the question posed by Śrīgarbha; second, the Tathāgata’s response; third, the narrator’s account of the benefits obtained within this chapter; and fourth, the clarification that among the assembly at the time of the Many Treasures Buddha’s praise, it was Śrīgarbha who was capable of posing the question.
This section has three parts:
first, the formal inquiry regarding the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s difficult and painful practices;
second, the single phrase “Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will briefly explain,” which is the request for instruction; and third, the actual teaching.
The third section, beginning with "the devas, nāgas, and spirits," identifies the assembly for whom [the teaching] is intended.
From "At that time, the Buddha addressed... onwards constitutes the second part of this chapter: the Tathāgata’s response.
Now, within this response, there are six sections:
first, the initial clarification of the fundamental matter;
second, from "At that time, that Buddha... onwards, the clarification of how the past Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for this bodhisattva.
Third, from "All Sentient Beings Who Delight to See" onwards, it correctly elucidates the original account of ascetic practices for the circulation of this sutra;
fourth, from "The Buddha told Śaradvatīputra" onwards, it correlates the past with the present;
fifth, from "Śaradvatīputra, if there are those who resolve their minds... onwards, it exhorts the transmission of the sutra.
The sixth section, beginning with "For example, like the King of Constellations," extensively praises the sutra and correctly clarifies its circulation.
From "At that time, the Buddha addressed Śuddhipuṣpa" for more than eleven lines, this is the first part clarifying the fundamental matter.
"At that time, that Buddha"—the following section is the second part of the Buddha’s response, clarifying how in the past that Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for this bodhisattva.
"All these sentient beings"—the following section constitutes the third part of the Buddha’s response, which correctly elucidates the original events.
Within this, there are four sub-sections:
the first, beginning with "the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana," clarifies hearing the sutra and practicing it.
The second section, from "After twelve thousand years had passed, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies" onwards, clarifies the attainment of the manifest fruit;
the third section, from "He then had this thought" onwards, clarifies the recognition of kindness and the intention to repay it;
and the fourth section, from "Immediately he entered this samādhi" onwards, correctly clarifies the repayment of kindness through offerings.
Regarding this fourth section, there are two parts:
first, making offerings with the present body; second, making offerings with future bodies.
Within the section on making offerings with the present body, there are further two subdivisions:
The first section, from "Immediately entering this samādhi" onwards, first clarifies the offering of material wealth;
the second section, from "Arising from samādhi and thinking to himself" onwards, correctly clarifies the offering of self-immolation.
Now, regarding the practice of offering by burning one's own body, there are five stages within it:
first, the explanation of the preliminary intention to burn the body;
second, from "Then he partakes of various incenses" onwards, the explanation of partaking of incense.
The third section, from "When one thousand two hundred years have passed" onwards, explicitly clarifies the self-immolation;
the fourth section, from "The Buddhas therein" onwards, records the praise of the Buddhas;
and the fifth section, from "His body ablaze with fire" onwards, clarifies the duration of time elapsed.
From the passage beginning with "Sarvasattvapriyadarśana" onwards is the second section, clarifying the offerings made in his final birth.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the preliminary clarification of the origin of the offerings;
The second section, from "At that time, Sarvasattvapriyadarśana... onwards, correctly explains the ascetic practices throughout the sutra.
For now, within the context of the causal origination (*nidāna*), there are nine stages;
first, it clarifies his birth into a royal family.
The second section, beginning with "He then addressed his father, the King," explains the original causes and conditions for the sake of the King.

The third section, beginning with "Great King, I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha," clarifies that he has already informed the King of his intention to make offerings to the Buddha Pure Bright Virtue (Viśuddhaprabhāsa).
The fourth section, beginning with "Having made the announcement," clarifies ascending into the air and departing.
The fifth section, beginning with "Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling," clarifies arriving at the Buddha’s location and paying homage.
The sixth section, beginning with "At that time, all," clarifies the Buddha-way.
How could the Buddha still be present?
This interpretation is not to be used here; it is merely an expression of self-congratulation, saying, "I am still able to reach the World-Honored One while he is in the world."
The seventh section clarifies the answer given by the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa, stating that "the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived.
The eighth section, beginning from "Furthermore, he commanded," clarifies how the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa entrusted the Dharma to this bodhisattva.
The ninth section, beginning with "In this way, the sun and moon were pure and bright," clarifies that the Buddha Pure and Bright Virtue entered *nirvāṇa*.
This concludes the explanation of dependent origination.
From "At that time, all... onwards is the second part, which correctly elucidates the ascetic practices of his final existence throughout the sutra.
Now, within this section there are four parts:
first, it clarifies how seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa gives rise to a heart of longing and attachment;
second, it uses the sandalwood from this side of the ocean to illustrate the offering of cremating one's own body.
The third [section] clarifies the offering of the *śarīra* after the fire has been extinguished;
the fourth, from "At that time, all... onwards, clarifies the continued offering by sacrificing his arm.
Within this fourth section, there are seven sub-sections:
The first section, from "From this" onwards, announces his intention to burn his arm before the great assembly.
The second section, from "Having spoken these words" onwards, clearly describes the actual burning of the arm.
The third section, beginning with "causing countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle," clarifies the benefits gained by the assembly at that time.
The fourth section, beginning with "at that time, the various bodhisattvas," describes the distress of the assembly at that time.
The fifth section, beginning with "At that time, Sarvasattvapriyadarśana," clarifies the making of the vow.
The sixth section, beginning with "Having made this vow," clarifies the restoration of his arm to its original state.
The seventh section, "At that time," clarifies the signs of being moved.
From the passage beginning "The Buddha said to Śubhavyūha, 'What do you think? onwards, there are six segments; this is the fourth segment, which reconciles the ancient and the modern.
"If, O Rājan, there should be those who resolve their minds... from here below is the fifth section, which continues to exhort people to practice asceticism and propagate the sutra.
"Rājanpuṣpa, it is like all the streams, rivers, and great rivers... from here below is the sixth section, which extensively praises the sutra and clearly elucidates its circulation.
Within this, there are two sections:
the first praises the sutra; the second, beginning with "Therefore, O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña," correctly elucidates the dissemination [of the teaching].
Each of these two sections contains two stages. Regarding the praise of the sutra, there are two parts:
first, a general praise for this entire scripture; second, a specific praise beginning from the passage, "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there be anyone who hears [this]."
Each of these two stages has three tiers.
Regarding the general praise of the intermediate stage, there are three parts:
first, the ten similes beginning with "For example, like all flowing rivers," which constitute a comparative praise.
The second section, beginning with "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this sutra can save all beings," is a praise based on its essential nature;
the third section, beginning with "If anyone should hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*," is a praise by way of citing its efficacy.
"O Rājāgraputra, if there be anyone who hears this [teaching on] Bhaiṣajyarāja... and so forth, constitutes the second specific praise.
Within this, there are also three parts:
first, from "From this point onward," the present world is cited for the purpose of praise;
The second section, beginning with "If, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction," praises by taking up the future world;
the third section, beginning with "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this bodhisattva has accomplished such [qualities]," is the concluding praise.
The second section, which clearly elucidates the entrustment for circulation (*pravartana*), contains two parts:
first, from "Therefore, O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña" onwards, this single chapter is entrusted for circulation;
second, from "Nakṣatrarāja, you should, by means of your supernormal powers... onwards, this entire work is entrusted to clearly elucidate its circulation.
Within this, there is both the main text and its commentary.
"When this 'Chapter on the Medicine King' was being preached"—from here below is the third section of the chapter, which records how the assembly attained benefits as described by the sūtra compiler.
"Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata": from here below is the fourth section, clarifying that Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata continues to praise Śubhavyūha for his inquiry.

Chapter 23: "The Chapter on the Wondrous Sound. This chapter describes the supernatural power of this bodhisattva’s universal manifestation of physical forms; thus, the chapter is named after this bodhisattva.

The following two chapters constitute the second part of the section demonstrating the scriptural rules for the universal manifestation of objects; they clarify how these two Great Beings universally manifest their physical bodies to propagate the sutra and benefit sentient beings, the significance of which has already been explained above.
Now, within this chapter, there are six major sections:
first, it clarifies how the Tathāgata emits light to summon Gadgadasvara to come;

second, from the passage beginning with "Then [he addressed] the Buddha Pure Flower Wisdom," it clarifies how that bodhisattva, having received the command, departs from the eastern direction to come to this land.

Third, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha" onwards, it correctly clarifies the method of the sutra for the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound’s universal manifestation of the form-body;
fourth, from "When this Chapter on Wondrous Sound was being preached" onwards, it clarifies the benefits for humans and devas in both the eastern and western regions;

fifth, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound made offerings to Śākyamuni" onwards, it clarifies how this Bodhisattva, having finished beholding the universal manifestation of the form-body, took leave of the Buddha here and returned to the eastern region.

Below the sixth section, "When this 'Chapter on the Arrival and Departure of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara' was being preached," it clarifies that the scribe of the sutra describes how the assembly at that time found benefit from the preaching of this chapter.
Now, within the first part, "The Tathāgata Emits Light to Summon [the Assembly]," there are three stages:
first, it first clarifies that this light shines sideways upon other lands.
The second section, beginning with "After this number has passed," clarifies that these rays of light illuminate the land of this Bodhisattva.
The third section, beginning with "At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment," clarifies that the Tathāgata’s light illuminates the body of this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.

The section beginning with "Then [the Bodhisattva] Pure White Flower" constitutes the second part of this chapter, clarifying how this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (Ghoṣadatta) has come at the command [of the Buddha].
This section itself contains five parts:
first, it clarifies how Wonderful Sound takes leave of the Buddha and departs.
Second, it clarifies that the Buddha further exhorted this Gadgadasvara;
third, it clarifies that Gadgadasvara received and accepted the intent of that exhortation;
fourth, it clarifies that this Gadgadasvara manifested the signs of having come from that place.
The fifth section correctly clarifies that the Sublime Sound (Ghoṣa) has come from that [Buddha-field].
Now, first, there are approximately four lines which constitute the first part, clarifying that the Sublime Sound has come from that Buddha with his words.
"At that time, the Buddha Pure Flower Wisdom"—the following constitutes the second section, clarifying the exhortation issued by that Buddha.
"The Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound addressed the Buddha, saying"—the following constitutes the third section, wherein he receives and honors the intent of the Tathāgata’s exhortation.
"Then, the Sublime Voice"—the following constitutes the fourth section, which demonstrates the manner of his arrival from that place.
Within this fourth section alone, there are further six stages:
first, it clarifies the manifestation of precious lotus flowers here in this world.
The second section, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī" onwards, consists of Mañjuśrī’s inquiry to the Buddha regarding the meaning of these auspicious signs.
The third section, from "At that time, Śākyamuni" onwards, clarifies the Tathāgata’s response to Mañjuśrī.
The fourth section, "Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha," and following, clarifies that Mañjuśrī still wishes to see this Sound of Wondrous Virtue (Ghoṣadeva).
The fifth section, "At that time, Śākyamuni," and following, clarifies that Śākyamuni replies that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna himself shall summon him for you.
The sixth section, beginning with "At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna," clarifies that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna immediately summoned this Gadgadasvara at the request of Mañjuśrī.
From "At that time, Gadgadasvara" onwards is the fifth section, which properly clarifies Gadgadasvara’s departure for and arrival here.
This fifth section consists of nine stages:
first, it clarifies how Gadgadasvara arrives with his retinue;
second, from "the various countries he traversed" onwards, it describes the manifestations of supernatural power displayed by Gadgadasvara along the way.
Third, from "The Bodhisattva’s eyes were like the broad petals of a great blue lotus" onwards, it clarifies the physical appearance of this person as described by the author of the sutra;
fourth, from "Entering the seven-jeweled terrace" onwards, it clarifies that Gadgadasvara arrives riding upon a jeweled seat;
fifth, from "Having arrived" onwards, it clarifies that once he has reached this place, he prepares offerings.
Sixth, from "Then he addressed the Buddha," below, it clarifies that Gadgadasvara transmits the greetings of that Buddha;
seventh, from "World-Honored One, I now wish to see," below, it clarifies that Gadgadasvara addresses the Buddha, expressing his vow and desire to see the Buddha Prabhūtaratna;
eighth, from "At that time, Śākyamuni," below, it clarifies that Śākyamuni immediately addresses the Buddha Prabhūtaratna on behalf of [Gadgadasvara].
The ninth section, beginning with "At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna," clarifies how the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, from within his jeweled stupa, summons Gadgadasvara from afar.

The passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī addressed the Buddha" constitutes the third segment of this chapter, which specifically elucidates how Gadgadasvara manifests his universal form-body (*sarvarūpakāya*) to propagate the sutra.
Within this, there are naturally two rounds of question and answer, forming two sections.
Here, we clarify that within the first round of question and answer, the question is singular.
Within the Buddha’s response, there are naturally four stages:
The first is the direct answer, explaining that the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara attained this fruit today because he cultivated excellent causes in the past;
the second, beginning with "What do you think, Flower Virtue," reconciles the ancient and the present;
the third, beginning with "Flower Virtue, you see only the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," extensively clarifies how this Gadgadasvara universally manifests in form-bodies to propagate the sutra.
Below the fourth section, "The Accomplishment of the Wondrous Sound of Flower Virtue," is the concluding response.
From the passage, "At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha," onwards is the second round of question and answer, which clarifies the name of the samādhi.

"When this 'Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara' was being spoken"—the following section is the fourth part of this chapter, clarifying how those from both the eastern and western lands obtained benefits, namely, the attainment of this samādhi.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara made offerings to Śākyamuni. The following constitutes the fifth section of this chapter, clarifying that after Gadgadasvara had finished explaining the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body, he took his leave and returned to his own land.
Within this, there are three stages:
first, the initial clarification of the words "the Tathāgata";

second, from the passage "the various countries he traversed" onwards, the clarification of the manifestation of supernatural powers on the road when Gadgadasvara departs; [and third, the arrival at the place].
The third section, from "Having arrived in his own land" onwards, clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] reached that place and paid homage to that Buddha.

From "When this 'Chapter on the Coming and Going of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara' was being preached" onwards is the sixth segment of the chapter, which clarifies how the members of the assembly received benefits as recorded by the author of the sūtra.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Avalokiteśvara Avalokiteśvara has four names. The first is Avalokiteśvara;
in its correct terminology, this means "observing the sounds of the world" in order to deliver and liberate them.
The second is Avalokita-kāya, which means "observing the bodily karma of sentient beings" in order to deliver and liberate them.
The third is called "Contemplating the World’s Intent," which means observing the mental karma of sentient beings to deliver them;
the fourth is named "Contemplating the World’s Karma," which encompasses the preceding three types.
Question: "If that is so, for what reason is he specifically designated as Avalokiteśvara? The commentator says:
"It is easy to practice only through verbal karma, whereas it is difficult to practice virtue through both bodily and mental karma.
Furthermore, in the Sahā world, the Buddha-work is mostly performed by means of sound; for this reason, he received his name from Avalokiteśvara."
Now, within this chapter there are also six sections:
first, a preliminary praise of this bodhisattva;
second, from the passage "How does he roam the Sahā world? onwards, the explicit exposition of the sūtra on the universal manifestation of supernatural powers.
The third section, beginning with "Therefore, you all should single-mindedly make offerings," continues to exhort people to make offerings to this Bodhisattva.
The fourth section, beginning with "Ajita, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such sovereign spiritual powers," concludes by extolling this Bodhisattva.

The fifth section, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat," clarifies the role of the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara as a representative; placed at the end of this chapter, it further extols the virtues of Avalokiteśvara.
The section following "When the Buddha spoke the 'Universal Gate Chapter'" at the end of the sixth chapter clarifies the benefits obtained when this chapter is preached.
Now, first, regarding the praise, there are two parts: namely, the question and the answer, which constitute the two.
Now, it should be understood that within the Buddha’s response there are two sections:

first, a praise based on names; second, from the passage beginning "Ajita, if there were someone who upholds [this dharma] for sixty-two billion years," onwards, which is called a praise by way of comparison.
There are four parts to the eulogy based on names:
first, the initial eulogy of Avalokiteśvara;
second, the eulogy of Avalokiteśvara’s intention, beginning with the passage "If there are sentient beings who have much lust."
The third section, beginning with "If there are women who wish to obtain a son," praises the body of Avalokiteśvara;
the fourth section, beginning with "Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold [this]," concludes by exhorting them to receive and uphold it.
Within the first section on Avalokiteśvara, there are three parts:

first, from "If there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions" onwards, it generally clarifies the sound of the world’s suffering as perceived by Avalokiteśvara;
second, from "If there are those who uphold the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara" onwards, it specifically clarifies how Avalokiteśvara rescues from the seven kinds of calamities.
The third section, "The Awesome Spiritual Power of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Inexhaustible Intent," serves as a concluding eulogy.
Regarding the second part, which concerns the rescue from seven kinds of calamities:
first, the one and a half lines beginning with "If there be those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara" describe the rescue from the calamity of fire.
The second section, beginning with "If one is being swept away by great waters," lacks one line and addresses the peril of water.

The third section, beginning with "If there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings," spans five and a half lines and clarifies the rescue from the peril of wind; although this passage generally refers to *rākṣasas*, it does not specifically clarify the *rākṣasas* themselves.
Since wind has no color inherently, it is said to be "black" because it specifically clarifies that this wind blows up black [clouds].
The fourth section, beginning with "If there should be another person who is about to be harmed," and extending for two lines less, rescues one from the danger of blades and staves.
The fifth section, beginning with "If [there were] a trichiliocosm," and extending for two and a half lines, rescues one from the danger of rākṣasas.
The sixth section, beginning with "Furthermore, if there should be a person who has committed a crime," consists of two lines and rescues one from the hardship of shackles and fetters.
The seventh section, beginning with "If in a trichiliocosm world-system," consists of six lines and more, and rescues one from the hardship of bandits and thieves.
“Thus, Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is ultimately as majestic as this” is the third summary praise of Avalokiteśvara.
“If there are sentient beings who have much lust,” from here below is the second praise of Avalokiteśvara’s intent; within this, there are two parts:
first, the actual praise.
The second section, from "Ajita" down to "therefore sentient beings should constantly keep this in mind," is the concluding exhortation.
The third section, beginning with "If there is a woman," praises the body of Avalokiteśvara; within this, there are also two parts:

first, the actual physical act of prostration to seek a son and obtain a son, or to seek a daughter and obtain a daughter; and second, from "Ajita" down to "merit shall not be in vain," which is the concluding exhortation.
"Therefore, sentient beings"—the following is the fourth summary praise within the first section, the praise based on names.
"Ajita, if there were someone who received and upheld sixty-two billion [verses]"—the following is the second section, the praise by way of comparison (*kalāpamāna*), which also contains four stages:
first, the Buddha first poses a question to Ajita regarding the merit of such comparison.
The second [section] is the answer to the Buddha: "Very much, World-Honored One.
The third [section], beginning with "The Buddha said: 'If there should be another person...'," clarifies the Tathāgata’s synthesis and conclusion.
The fourth [section], beginning with "Endless Meaning (Akṣayamati) received and upheld the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...," is the final summary and praise.

"Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha," from here below is the second section of this chapter, which correctly elucidates the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body’s propagation of the sutra; it consists of two parts:
first, the question, and second, the Buddha’s answer.
Now, to clarify the inquiry herein, there are two intentions and three textual passages:
first, the question asks, "How does one roam in the Sahā world? This question concerns form.
Second, the question asks, "How does one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? This question concerns teaching.

"What is the nature of the power of skillful means? This is the third summary of the preceding questions; both the formal (form) and the instructional (teaching) dharmas are the power of skillful means.
The Buddha’s response consists of two parts:
first, the direct answer; second, the concluding answer.

Within the direct answer, there are nineteen responses, each of which answers both of the preceding questions. "Manifesting forms" answers the former question regarding form, while "preaching the Dharma" answers the latter question regarding teaching.

Now, regarding the first phrase, "If there are sentient beings who should be liberated by means of the Buddha-body," this clarifies the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings; the subsequent phrases are all analogous in this way, though the sutra text omits the word "sentient beings" for brevity.
"O Akṣayamati, this is Avalokiteśvara"—the following is the second summary and response.
"Therefore, you all should with one mind make offerings"—from here on is the third section of the chapter, which exhorts people to make offerings to Avalokiteśvara; it consists of seven stages:
first, the Tathāgata’s formal exhortation to make offerings.
The second section clarifies how Akṣayamati, having received the Buddha’s instruction, offered his necklace as an act of worship;
the third section, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara," clarifies that Avalokiteśvara did not accept it;
the fourth section clarifies Akṣayamati’s request for him to accept it.
The fifth section, beginning with "At that time the Buddha said," clarifies that the Tathāgata himself commanded Avalokiteśvara to accept [the offering].
The sixth section, beginning with "Then Avalokiteśvara," clarifies that Avalokiteśvara immediately accepted it.
The seventh section, beginning with "Dividing it into two parts," clarifies that after this Bodhisattva had accepted it, he proceeded to practice the dedication of merit through giving.
"Akṣayamati," and so forth, constitutes the fourth section of this chapter, which summarizes and extols Avalokiteśvara.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara," and so forth, is the fifth section within this chapter, clarifying how Dharaṇīdhara generally extols the virtues of this Avalokiteśvara.
"When the Buddha preached this 'Universal Gate' Chapter" marks the sixth section of this chapter, clarifying how the narrator describes the benefits obtained from the chapter.
Chapter Twenty-five: The Dhāraṇī Chapter. This chapter elucidates the divine spells (*dhāraṇīs*), and thus it serves as the title of the chapter.
Within the "Exposition of the Rules for the Text," there are originally three parts.
The first three chapters correctly clarify the rules for using humans as the means to penetrate the sūtra.

This present chapter is the second intention, which clarifies how the Tathāgata preached the great divine mantra to encourage the propagation of the sūtra and to protect the Great Beings who penetrate the Dharma.
Now, within this chapter, a general division is made into three sections:
First, there is one sequence of questions and answers that first evaluates the merit of those who can master and propagate the sutra;

second, from "At that time, Bhaiṣajyarāja" onwards, there is another sequence of questions and answers which specifically clarifies how five persons shall preach divine mantras to protect those who propagate the sutra.
The third section, "The Chapter on Explaining This Dhāraṇī," in its first line, clarifies that the assembly at that time obtained benefits.
As for the five persons: first, Bhaiṣajyarāja; second, Śūradatta; third, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; fourth, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and fifth, the rākṣasī.
Chapter 26: The Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment. According to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta*, this should instead be called the "Chapter on Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra."

However, this is precisely the case with a king of antiquity whose false views were rampant and who did not believe in the Triple Gem; yet, the two sons, Sunetra and his brother, were great bodhisattvas who were destined to be born into this family to transform the king’s false views and lead him to the understanding of right view. Because they received their names from the categories of those they converted, these serve as the titles for the chapters.
Now, within this chapter, there is a general division into six sections:
first, the fundamental matter is clarified;
second, the two sons are praised for their profound virtue and excellent conduct.
The third section clarifies that the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-King preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for him;
the fourth section correctly elucidates the past events of the two sons converting their father, which constitutes the purpose of this chapter’s introduction;
the fifth section further reconciles the ancient and the modern.
The sixth section clarifies how the members of the assembly gained benefit when the sūtra master recited this chapter.
Here, we first clarify the fundamental facts: the names of the land and eon, and the title of the Tathāgata.
From "He had two sons" onwards is the second section, which first extols the profound virtue and beautiful conduct of the two sons.
From "At that time, that Buddha... onwards is the third section, in which that Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the two sons.

"At that time, the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra... This section below constitutes the fourth division, which specifically elucidates the past events of how the two sons transformed their father; within this, there are three sub-sections:
first, an explanation of the causal conditions for transforming the father;
second, from "Thereupon, the two sons... onwards, the actual account of transforming the father.

The third section, beginning with "At that time, the father saw his sons' supernatural powers were such as this," clarifies how the father king and his two sons informed their mother and went to the Buddha's dwelling.

The second section, beginning with "The mother said to her sons," clarifies how the mother instructed her sons to lead the father king away from his wrong views. The third section, beginning with "The two sons, Viśuddhigarbha and [his brother]," clarifies how the two sons gave rise to feelings of resentment and lamentation. The fourth section, beginning from "The mother said to her sons," clarifies the exhortation for the sons to transform their father.
From "Thereupon" onwards is the second section, which correctly explains how the two sons perform eighteen transformations for their father, the king.
From "At that time, the father saw his sons" onwards is the third section, explaining how the father-king receives the transformation; herein there are fourteen stages in total:
first, it clarifies the dialogue between the father-king and his sons.
The second section, beginning with "Then these two sons," records the dialogue between the two sons and their mother;
the third section, beginning with "Then these two sons," clarifies how the two sons exhorted their parents to go to the Buddha’s dwelling;
the fourth section, beginning with "At that time, King Wonderful Adornment," clarifies that the king and his retinue were capable of receiving the true transformation of the Dharma.
The fifth section, beginning with "The two sons were thus," praises the virtue of the two sons in transforming their father, the king;
the sixth section, beginning with "Thereupon, King Subhavyūha," clarifies that the king and his retinue proceeded to the Buddha’s abode;
the seventh section, beginning with "At that time, that Buddha preached the Dharma for the king," explains in these two sentences that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for the king.
The eighth section, beginning with "The King was greatly delighted," clarifies that the king, having heard the Dharma and obtained its benefits, continued to make offerings;
the ninth section, beginning with "At that time, Cloud-Thunder-Sound," clarifies that the Buddha bestowed a prophecy upon him;
and the tenth section, beginning with "The king immediately," clarifies that the king left the household life to practice the Way.
Eleventh, from "He immediately ascended into the void" onwards, it clarifies that after the King had attained liberation, he recounted his gratitude for his sons' kindness;
twelfth, from "At that time" onwards, it clarifies that the Tathāgata declared these two princes to be true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
thirteenth, "King Wondrous Adornment immediately descended from the void," clarifies that the King extolled the virtues of the Buddha.
The fourteenth section, "Having spoken these words, he prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew," these two phrases clarify his departure from the Buddha and return to his kingdom.
"The Buddha addressed the great assembly"—from here below is the fifth part of this chapter, which synthesizes the ancient and the modern.
The section below, beginning with "Spoken by the Buddha," is the sixth segment of this chapter; it clarifies the benefits obtained by the sūtra compiler when narrating this chapter.

Chapter Twenty-Seven: Samantabhadra’s Exhortation to Resolve. In this chapter, it is explained that Samantabhadra comes from the east and exhorts people to personally resolve to hear this sūtra; hence, the title of the chapter.
However, the sutra consists of three sections; within the third section, the section on circulation, there are originally two parts:
the first comprises ten and a half chapters concerning circulation through transforming others, while this present chapter is the second, concerning circulation through one's own practice.
If one does not uphold it, this sutra will not circulate for that person;
if one upholds it oneself, this sutra will have the meaning of circulating for that person.
Within each of the two preceding sections, there were three parts; now, in this section, there are three as well:
first, it clarifies that this bodhisattva comes from the east, which serves as the cause for his exhortation;
second, from the words "addresses the Buddha" onwards, it properly clarifies the exhortation to hear the sutra.
Third, at the end of this chapter, the sūtra’s narrator describes the benefits obtained from this chapter.
Now, within the first section itself, there are four stages:
first, the formal description of Samantabhadra coming from the east.
The second section, beginning with "the various lands traversed," clarifies the characteristics of his supernormal powers;
the third section, beginning with "furthermore, together with," clarifies the characteristics of Samantabhadra’s retinue;
and the fourth section, beginning with "arriving at Sahā," clarifies the act of paying homage upon reaching the Buddha.
"Addressing the Buddha, he said": The following constitutes the second section of this chapter, which correctly elucidates the meaning of exhortation and inspiration.
Within this, there are four stages of the interaction between the interlocutor and the host:
first, Samantabhadra first asks the Tathāgata about the practice of exhortation and inspiration.
The second section, beginning with "The Buddha told Samantabhadra," clarifies the Tathāgata’s immediate response regarding the practice of exhortation;
the third section, beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra addressed the Buddha," correctly clarifies the encouragement provided by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
and the fourth section, beginning with "At that time, Śākyamuni praised him," clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation and completion of that encouragement.
Furthermore, within each of these four sections, there are three distinct parts.
Regarding the first three:
the first concerns the initial arrival of the Path for the sake of this sutra.
The second section, from "I only wish... onwards, clarifies the request for an answer;
the third section, from "If a good son... onwards, constitutes the actual question.
The section beginning with "The Buddha told him" is the second part of the Buddha’s response, which clarifies the practice of exhortation and inspiration.
Within this, there are also three parts:
first, the general announcement of the number of four dharmas;
second, from "The first" onwards, the specific enumeration of the names of the four dharmas.
The third section, beginning with "Good son," provides the concluding response.
From "At that time, Samantabhadra" onwards constitutes the third segment, in which Samantabhadra formally exhorts people to practice these four modes of conduct. Within this, there are three parts:
first, the general exhortation; second, the specific exhortation; and third, the concluding exhortation.
The passage beginning with "Whether this person is walking or standing" constitutes the second section, the specific exhortation. Within this, there are four types of exhortations:
first, the exhortation clarifying the auspicious omens, which states explicitly, "If one can receive and uphold [this], I shall mount a white elephant to protect them";
second, from the words "Furthermore, I shall also grant... onwards, it clarifies protection through divine mantras.

The third section, beginning with "If there are those who receive and uphold," clarifies protection through the Buddha's spiritual power: if one can receive and uphold this sutra, all Buddhas will protect them with their spiritual power.
The fourth section, beginning with "If one merely transcribes it," exhorts by citing the karmic rewards: if one can master this sutra, they will obtain excellent rewards.

"World-Honored One, I now, by means of my supernatural powers... This section below is the third conclusion and exhortation; it clarifies Samantabhadra’s own vow to resolve upon the great purpose of propagating this sutra and his compassionate intent to lead sentient beings—this constitutes the conclusion.
"At that time, Śākyamuni... and below is the fourth section, wherein the Tathāgata recounts his exhortations. Within this, there are also three parts:
first, he recounts the auspicious omens and the two protections of divine mantras to provide encouragement;
second, from "You should, by means of your supernatural power... onwards, he recounts and confirms the Buddha's protection as an encouragement.
The third section, beginning from "If Samantabhadra were a Tathāgata," describes the exhortation by citing the aforementioned rewards; by taking this up in turn, one immediately attains them.

"When the Buddha spoke this 'Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra'"—this following portion constitutes the third segment of the chapter, clarifying the benefits obtained by the narrator when recounting this chapter.
The *Fahua yiji* (Record of the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), Scroll Eight, is completed.
